Nowhere in the glossy brochure did it say a single word about men and women being segregated into separate wings of the building, or about a rule forbidding opposite-gender room visits.

"Okay, let's think the dorm setup through," I said quietly, reaching across our armrests to take Katie's hand. "We know dorm beds at any college are Twin XL, so one bed is going to be way too narrow for the two of us to sleep in together—even if we pushed it against the wall."

"And we know why regular colleges normally separate guys and girls in the dorms," Katie replied with complete, matter-of-fact logic. "They don't want boyfriends and girlfriends sharing a dorm room and then having some messy breakup in the middle of the semester where somebody gets kicked out or refuses to move."

Katie squeezed my fingers, a warm, confident smile lighting up her face.

"Except none of that applies to us, Nate," Katie said. "We're twin brother and sister! We can't break up! We've been at each other's side since we were little kids in cribs, and we've lived together every single day of our lives except for the fourteen months we were torn apart by our abusers. Since we're brother and sister—actual family—they should let us share one of those two-bed dorm rooms!"

"That makes total sense," I agreed, nodding as I looked back down at the glossy photo of the dorm room's wide six-foot sliding closet doors. "On paper, we'll put up with being assigned two separate Twin XL beds in the room so their housing chart is happy. And as long as that dorm closet is at least three feet deep by six feet wide like our hallway closet right here—when it's actually bedtime and we close our dorm room door—"

Katie glanced down our short carpeted right-hand hallway toward the open white bi-fold doors of our three-by-six half-pantry, half-coat closet, where our shared navy-blue sleeping bag and two white pillows lay lengthwise across the carpeted closet floor beneath the four tiers of white wire pantry shelves and hanging winter coats so the doors could close completely around us.

"—we'll just unroll our sleeping bag lengthwise inside the dorm closet, pull the closet doors shut so we feel completely enclosed and secure, and sleep cuddled up together like we always do!" Katie finished, grinning from ear to ear as she leaned across our armrests and wrapped both arms tightly around my neck. "Go to our PHP and SQL class during the day, eat in the dining hall, hang out in our room in the evening, and curl up together behind closed doors in the closet at night. We can totally make a dorm room work for a few months, Nate!"

Holding my twin sister close in the warm living room of Apartment 3, I hugged her back with all my strength, resting my cheek against her blonde hair as we folded the glossy Fishersville brochure into our laptop bag and rolled down the hallway to get ready for bed in our closet sanctuary.

# Twelve Days at Roosevelt Rehabilitation Center & Walking Out for Good

## Barton Hall Check-In, Rushing Voc Eval in One Week, & 'Door Greeter!?'

### Part 1: Sunday Check-In at Barton Hall, The Opposite-Gender Dorm Rule, & Expelling the Creepy Roommate

**Date:** 2007-03-04 at 11:15 America/New_York

![Inside the 1960s red-brick and terrazzo lobby of Barton Hall at Roosevelt Rehabilitation Center on Sunday, March 4, 2007, twenty-one-year-old fraternal twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie sit in their collapsible manual wheelchairs outfitted with right-armrest joysticks, spoked push-rim wheels, and rear rubber push-handles as Katie locks her brakes and firmly stops a staffer from grabbing her push-handles while their father David stands beside a luggage cart.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/mar_2007_rrc_barton_hall_checkin_push_handles_katie_nate_david.jpg)

#### Sunday, March 4, 2007, 11:15 AM — Why Dormitories Were Never Built for Us

![Inside the 1960s red-brick and terrazzo lobby of Barton Hall at Roosevelt Rehabilitation Center on Sunday, March 4, 2007, twenty-one-year-old fraternal twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie sit in their collapsible manual wheelchairs outfitted with right-armrest joysticks, spoked push-rim wheels, and rear rubber push-handles as Katie locks her brakes and firmly stops a staffer from grabbing her push-handles while their father David stands beside a luggage cart.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/mar_2007_rrc_barton_hall_checkin_push_handles_katie_nate_david.jpg)

"It was a whole lot easier for me to bring the two of them up here on a Sunday since I start my new weekday schedule up in Tysons Corner tomorrow morning," Dad explained to the residential staffer who met the three of us outside the flat-roofed 1960s red-brick entrance of Barton Hall at Roosevelt Rehabilitation Center in Fishersville.

"Oh, clients arrive on Sundays all the time, Mr. Prairie, so it's no big deal at all," the staffer smiled, propping the heavy glass vestibule door open against the chilly March mountain breeze as Katie and I guided our wheelchairs side by side across the threshold. Our backpacks hung over our canvas seatbacks, and Dad rolled a brass luggage cart stacked with our suitcases and laptop bags right behind us over the scuffed green-and-white terrazzo floor. "Come on back to the dorm office so we can introduce ourselves and get their intake paperwork started."

Looking down the wide cinder-block corridor, with its buzzing fluorescent troffers and faded 1970s brass plaques reminding visitors that the facility had stood on these former World War II Army hospital grounds since November 1947, I reached across my armrest and brushed my knuckles against Katie's fingers. She gave my hand a quick, grounding squeeze before we rolled into the intake office behind a wooden counter.

"Here are their updated medical clearances and my emergency contact numbers," Dad said, setting a manila folder on the blotter in front of the Sunday residential coordinator, a middle-aged woman whose plastic badge read *Linda*. "You'll see two addresses listed for me. My Virginia driver's license has my new primary residence on Sunset Drive near King Street in Alexandria, right down the road from my new engineering job in Tysons Corner, and the second number is our brick ranch on Arvin Road off Indian River Road and Military Highway down in Virginia Beach. I bought that Virginia Beach house from my old landlord years ago and kept it when their West Ocean View apartment lease ended on Wednesday so the twins always have their familiar home and routine waiting for them in Hampton Roads."

"Got both numbers right here on the top sheet," Linda said, clipping the page into two green intake folders. She glanced over the counter at our wheelchairs—regular folding manual cross-brace frames with spoked push-rim wheels and rear rubber push-handles that Dr. Carter's seating clinic had fitted with right-armrest joystick power-drive kits—and raised her eyebrows slightly. "I see the vocational counselor's note here says you two left your full-size power chairs in Virginia Beach?"

"Dr. Carter had these folding frames rigged up with joystick drives for the trip," I explained, resting my palm on my right-hand controller. "Neither of us has the wrist or upper-arm strength to push manual hand-rims across a campus, so we still drive everywhere with the joysticks, and if we ever catch a ride off campus in a regular compact sedan, you just unclip the battery box underneath and the frame folds flat into a trunk."

"Very smart," Linda said, sliding our two green folders and two brass room keys on plastic tags across the counter. "Now, for your initial Vocational Evaluation period here in Barton Hall, Nathaniel, your room is down on the men's wing, and Katie, you are in Room 157 over on the women's wing. Please remember that under Roosevelt Rehabilitation Center residential policy, there is strictly no visiting dorm rooms of the opposite gender."

Katie and I looked at each other across our armrests as that announcement hit us like a bucket of ice water. Back in Norfolk, when we had looked at the glossy brochure from the DARS office showing a two-bed college-style dorm room in Barton Hall, we had figured that since regular colleges only separate men and women so boyfriends and girlfriends don't have messy breakups—and since we were twin brother and sister who had been at each other's side since we were little and had lived together our entire lives except when we were separated by our abusers—they would let us share a room, put up with two Twin XL beds on paper, and cram ourselves into our sleeping bag in the dorm closet at bedtime.

Keeping my voice completely polite, I leaned forward in my chair toward the counter.

"Excuse me, ma'am—I think there might be a misunderstanding," I said politely. "Katie and I aren't a boyfriend and girlfriend who might break up; we're fraternal twins—brother and sister. We thought since we're family, we'd be able to share one of the two-bed rooms. We've been at each other's side since we were little, we've lived together for the last three and a half years while earning our associate degrees at the Community College of Hampton Roads—except when we were separated by abusive partners—and whenever one of us gets overwhelmed at night, the other one is right there."

"I understand you're brother and sister, Nathaniel, and that you're used to sharing an apartment," Linda replied in a practiced, unyielding voice, tapping the highlighted paragraph on the housing sheet, "but this is a state residential facility, not an off-campus apartment. We keep men and women on separate wings because we can't have male and female clients in the same dorm rooms hooking up behind closed doors."

Katie and I blinked at her, both of our literal autistic brains stalling on the slang phrase.

"Hooking up?" Katie asked politely, tilting her head. "Like hooking up a computer monitor? What does 'hooking up' mean?"

Linda paused, her cheeks coloring slightly as she looked across the counter at the two of us and lowered her voice a notch. "It means having sex, Katie."

Katie and I looked at each other and then looked straight back at Linda in complete earnestness. Both of us knew as a memorized rule that brothers and sisters are not supposed to have sex with each other—even if neither of us had ever really understood why people made such a big deal about it.

"Oh!" Katie said matter-of-factly. "Well, we're brother and sister—we know brothers and sisters aren't supposed to have sex with each other, so of course we won't have sex!"

"Yeah, of course we won't," I agreed earnestly, nodding right alongside my twin sister.

Linda stared at the two of us for a second, momentarily flustered by how plainly we had just said that across the intake counter, before clearing her throat and falling right back on the rulebook.

"Be that as it may, nobody shares a room across the gender line here, and opposite-gender room visitation between six and eleven in the evening is an earned privilege reserved exclusively for Level 4 clients over in Cantor Hall," Linda said firmly. "All newly arriving clients here in Barton Hall start at Level 2. You two are more than welcome to spend time together in the dorm lobby, the outdoor courtyard, the recreation hall, or the dining hall—just not inside the dorm rooms proper. Since you just arrived today, I'm going to escort you down the halls right now so you can help each other unpack your bags, but once your suitcases are unpacked, you'll each have to leave the other's room."

Katie and I exchanged a deeply unhappy look across our armrests, biting our tongues and staying polite at the counter even as our hearts sank at being forced into separate rooms on opposite wings. As Linda stood up from her chair and stepped around the counter, however, the male residential staffer who had held the front door lingered by the office threshold, looked down at the standard rubber push-handles sticking out the back of Katie's folding frame, and reached both hands straight for her grips without asking as if he were about to wheel her down the corridor himself.

Katie clicked her joystick controller off, slammed both manual wheel-locks forward with a sharp metal *clack*, whipped her head around, and went straight after him with an aggressive edge in her voice that she almost never used back home.

"Get your hands off my wheelchair right now!" Katie barked across the lobby. "Do not touch my push-handles! Do I look like a piece of luggage to you?! Our chairs have joysticks on the armrests for a reason—my brother and I drive ourselves, and if you grab my chair without my permission again, you and I are going to have a serious problem!"

"Hey—watch your tone with residential staff, young lady," the staffer bristled, jerking his hands back from her rubber grips while his face turned red.

"Watch your hands around my sister's wheelchair!" I shot right back, guiding my own chair flush alongside Katie's so nobody could step between us.

Linda held up a hand between the counter and the doorway, frowning sharply at the two of us. "Katie, Nathaniel, I'm going to let that slide with a verbal warning since you two just walked through the door five minutes ago and I know check-in day is stressful, but aggressive outbursts toward staff are a write-up offense here at Roosevelt."

Neither Katie nor I apologized. Instead, both of us fixed the staffer by the doorway with identical, disgusted looks—staring him straight in the eye with an unblinking glare that amounted to a flat-out dare: *go ahead and write us up right now if you want to.*

The staffer swallowed, looked away from our twin glares, and shoved his hands into his pockets without touching his clipboard.

With Linda walking beside us down the men's corridor first, Katie and Dad helped me unload my clothes and laptop bag onto my side of the narrow cinder-block two-bed room—where my assigned roommate was already lounging on the opposite mattress watching us in silence—before we rolled across the building to Room 157 on the women's wing to help Katie unpack alongside her new roommate, who greeted all three of us warmly.

As soon as the last suitcase was stowed under Katie's bed and we rolled back out to the neutral territory of the Barton Hall lobby with our MagnaBook laptops resting on our lap trays, Katie steered her wheelchair flush against mine and leaned close to my ear.

"I noticed your roommate was staring at my tits the entire time I was helping you unpack," Katie said quietly, her jaw tight.

"I noticed it too, and I wasn't thrilled about it for a second," I answered, my blood simmering as I put my arm around my sister's shoulders while our laptops booted up. "Your roommate back in Room 157 seemed like a genuinely nice person, whereas I think I got stuck with a complete jerk of a roommate. What do you want to do?"

"No offense, Nate, but your roommate gave off a really bad first impression," Katie sighed, before turning in her seat and pulling me into a tight, reassuring hug so I knew she didn't blame me for who the housing office had put in my room.

A moment later, Dad walked out of Linda's office tucking our signed carbon copies into his coat pocket. "All right, you two, the paperwork is finished," Dad said warmly. "Come on—I'm taking both of you into Waynesboro to get a real lunch before I have to get on the highway toward Alexandria."

***

#### 3:00 PM — House Guard 2 in the Dorm Lobby, Cafeteria Rations, & The 11:00 PM Curfew Check

"I wish they had an actual lap pool here instead of just the small therapeutic pool, but oh well," Katie sighed, peering through the interior observation glass of the campus recreation hall at the quiet, steamy natatorium before glancing down at her wristwatch as her stomach gave an audible rumble. "I'm already hungry again and it's only three o'clock, even after that big lunch Dad bought us in Waynesboro."

"Look at the board games over on that table—half the boxes are missing their lids, and the TV in the lounge is turned up way too loud," I said, turning my chair beside hers. "Want to head back across the walkway to the Barton Hall lobby?"

"Please," Katie nodded, rolling out the automatic doors beside me into the cool afternoon air.

We parked wheel-to-wheel on the far side of the Barton Hall lounge chairs, well out of earshot of the front desk.

"If it weren't for that silly opposite-gender dorm rule, I'd say let's just head back to one of our rooms and close the door," I muttered, looking toward the two separate wing doors at opposite ends of the lobby.

Instead, I unzipped my backpack, pulled out a two-way stereo headphone splitter, and plugged both of our headsets into the audio jack of my laptop. Sliding a DVD into the drive, we queued up the brownstone booby-trap sequence of one of our favorite childhood Christmas comedies, *House Guard 2: Lost in Manhattan*—right where the kid stands on the rooftop throwing bricks down at the two bumbling burglars.

Within two minutes, both Katie and I were shaking with laughter across our armrests—laughing so hard that half a dozen other students sitting around the dorm lobby looked over and asked what on earth was so funny. Grinning, Katie hit the rewind button back to the scene where the two bandits were robbing the toy-store cash register, unplugged the headphone splitter so the sound played through my laptop speakers, and angled the screen toward the lounge so the other students could crowd around and laugh right along with us.

When the sequence wrapped up at quarter to five, we shut down the DVD player and zipped our laptops back into our bags.

"How about we roll inside the courtyard together for some fresh air," Katie suggested, lacing her fingers through mine, "and then we'll split up for two minutes just to drop our backpacks off in our rooms, wait for each other right outside the wing doors, and head to dinner together?"

"Deal," I said, giving her a quick hug before we parted at the hallway junction.

When I unlocked my door on the men's wing and rolled inside to set my backpack on my desk chair, my roommate looked up from his pillow with a sleazy smirk. "Hey, man—who was the hot blonde babe in here with you earlier?"

I didn't dignify him with a single word. Locking my desk drawer, I spun my wheelchair around in the narrow aisle, rolled straight back out to the courtyard walkway where Katie was waiting for me, and told her verbatim what he had just said.

"Gross," Katie said, curling her lip in disgust as we turned toward the covered breezeway at five-thirty with the stream of residential students heading to the main cafeteria. "If he walks past us tonight, hold my hand so he gets it through his thick skull not to talk to me."

Inside the noisy dining hall, we picked up two plastic trays, balanced them across our lap trays along the stainless-steel rail, and steered over to a small table for two near the wall.

"Looks like burgers and french fries," Katie said, picking up a limp, lukewarm fry from her plate. She took one bite and made a face. "That tastes nasty!"

At the next table over, a veteran student in a faded hoodie snorted around his plastic fork. "You two must be new here. Get used to your rations."

"Well," I sighed, poking dubiously at my gray hamburger patty, "the food definitely isn't the greatest, but what choice do we have?"

As soon as we dumped our trays at the dish window and rolled back out into the cool dusk air toward Barton Hall, Katie reached across our armrests and took my hand, giggling softly under her breath. "Just in case your creepy roommate is watching from the sidewalk—I want it to look like we're dating."

"Where to now?" I asked as the front doors of Barton Hall slid open. "Dorm lobby?"

"Yeah," Katie said softly, her smile fading a little as she looked toward the separate hallway doors. "Until it's time for bed. I miss living together back home."

We parked in our quiet corner of the lobby, where I wrapped my arm around her shoulders and Katie snuggled against my chest with a long yawn. "We'll have breakfast together first thing in the morning," I promised, resting my cheek against her hair, "and then we're staying right at each other's side through every minute of evaluation."

By nine o'clock, both of us were nodding off in our chairs. Tearfully, we hugged each other goodbye in the middle of the lobby before reluctantly turning down our separate wings for the night.

When I rolled into my room on the men's wing, the bed across from mine was empty. Relieved to have the room to myself, I changed into my pajamas, locked my wheelchair brakes beside the frame, and transferred under the stiff institutional blanket—lying awake in the dark waiting for the eleven-o'clock curfew check.

Five minutes past eleven, the hallway door clicked open and a night staffer shone his flashlight inside, pausing when the beam hit the empty mattress across from mine.

"Where's your roommate?" the staffer asked.

"I haven't seen him at all tonight," I said from my pillow. "And considering the sexually suggestive things he was saying about my sister earlier today, I really don't want to see him right now."

The staffer stepped inside and lowered his clipboard. "What did he say?"

"Right after I finished unpacking, he asked me, 'Who's the hot blonde babe?'" I replied. "And earlier, while my sister was helping me unpack, she noticed him staring at her breasts."

"What's your sister's name?" the staffer asked, uncapping his pen.

"Katie. Katie Prairie. Room 157," I replied.

When my wristwatch alarm beeped at quarter to seven on Monday morning, I looked across the narrow room and saw my roommate passed out face-down on top of his bedspread in his street clothes, reeking of stale beer and marijuana. Keeping silent so I wouldn't wake him, I got dressed, transferred into my wheelchair, and rolled straight out to the Barton Hall lobby, where Katie came through the women's wing doors less than a minute later and wrapped her arms around my neck.

Before we could head out the front doors toward the cafeteria, the weekday morning dorm supervisor—a tall, no-nonsense woman with steel-gray hair—stepped out of the residential office and beckoned to the two of us.

"Nathaniel, Katie, step into my office for thirty seconds," she said, closing the door behind our wheelchairs. "I wanted both of you to know before you head to breakfast that Nathaniel's roommate is being expelled and escorted off the property by Campus Police this morning. At eleven-fifteen last night, night staff caught him trying to sneak past the fire doors into the women's dormitory wing to pressure another female client into sleeping with him, and just like you, Katie, that young woman wanted nothing to do with him and turned him straight in because he wouldn't stop harassing her. Between that, his prior write-ups, and staggering back onto campus intoxicated after curfew, he is done here. You have that room to yourself, Nathaniel."

Katie let out a long breath beside me, her shoulders dropping two inches in pure relief as we thanked the supervisor and rolled back out into the morning hallway together.

### Part 2: Rushing Voc Eval in One Week, Auto Shop & 'Door Greeter!?', Refusing Separation, & Staying Stuck on Level 2

**Date:** 2007-03-05 at 07:15 America/New_York

![Inside the 1960s painted cinder-block Vocational Evaluation break room in the Bates-Harding Building at Roosevelt Rehabilitation Center in March 2007, twenty-one-year-old twins Nathaniel and Katie Prairie sit parked wheel-to-wheel in their collapsible manual wheelchairs outfitted with armrest joysticks, spoked push-rim wheels, and rear push-handles, locking hands across their armrests and loudly expressing their displeasure as evaluator Ms. Hollis and aide Mr. Miller try to separate them during social time.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/mar_2007_rrc_voc_eval_social_break_refusing_separation_katie_nate.jpg)

#### Monday, March 5, 2007, 7:15 AM — The Medication Line, Auto Shop & Woodworking, & "Door Greeter!?"

![Inside the 1960s painted cinder-block Vocational Evaluation break room in the Bates-Harding Building at Roosevelt Rehabilitation Center in March 2007, twenty-one-year-old twins Nathaniel and Katie Prairie sit parked wheel-to-wheel in their collapsible manual wheelchairs outfitted with armrest joysticks, spoked push-rim wheels, and rear push-handles, locking hands across their armrests and loudly expressing their displeasure as evaluator Ms. Hollis and aide Mr. Miller try to separate them during social time.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/mar_2007_rrc_voc_eval_social_break_refusing_separation_katie_nate.jpg)

"We need our breakfast," Katie said as we rolled side by side out of the Barton Hall lobby toward the dining hall breezeway.

"I'm guessing breakfast is going to be just as nasty as dinner was last night," I replied as the automatic doors slid open into the crisp March mountain air.

Twenty minutes later, after pushing watery scrambled eggs and limp toast around our plastic plates, we rolled down the corridor to join the long single-file line of Level 2 clients waiting outside the dispensary window for our morning maintenance medication.

"This is so stupid," Katie whispered in exasperation as we inched forward in our joystick-outfitted wheelchairs. "We're twenty-one years old, and we're both used to managing our own medication bottles back home in our apartment."

When we reached the counter, the dispensary nurse leaned toward the opening and spoke to us in a high-pitched, sing-song voice as if we were seven-year-olds learning how to swallow a chewable vitamin. "Good morning, friends! Ready to take our morning pills with a big sip of water?"

I looked straight across the counter at her. "Ma'am, we have associate degrees and we've managed our own prescriptions in our own apartment in Norfolk for three and a half years," I said flatly. "You don't need to talk down to us like children. Just hand us the paper cups and check our names off the clipboard."

The nurse's patronizing smile vanished immediately, and she handed over our pleated paper cups in silence.

"I don't think I'm going to like it here," I said quietly to Katie as we rolled away from the window, slipping my arm around her shoulders.

"I already miss the apartment," Katie whispered back, leaning against my arm.

Right then, angry screams echoed from the main entrance doors down the hall.

"You are not my boyfriend anymore, and I don't ever want to see you again!" a girl shouted, shoving through the doors.

"Get out of my life too, jerk!" a boy shouted right back at her.

Down the hallway from us, another student sighed and shook his head. "Those two. Always fighting. Always arguing."

Katie looked over at me with a wry, grateful smile. "I'm glad we're siblings, Nate."

I pulled her into a warm hug across our armrests and whispered, "Yeah. No boyfriend-girlfriend drama between us."

At eight-thirty sharp, we followed the directional signs into the Vocational Evaluation wing of the Bates-Harding Building and parked side by side at a scarred laminate table at the front of the intake room. At the dry-erase board stood the lead evaluation specialist, Ms. Hollis, holding a thick stack of yellow checklists while her evaluation aide, Mr. Miller, passed them down the rows.

"Welcome to Vocational Evaluation," Ms. Hollis announced briskly. "Before any client at Roosevelt Rehabilitation Center is permitted to enter a vocational training classroom, you will spend the next two full weeks right here in Voc Eval completing three mandatory requirements under Department for Aging and Rehabilitative Services guidelines. First, you will demonstrate independent-living skills to our staff—making your dorm bed with proper corners, doing a load of laundry, and preparing a basic meal in the test kitchen. Second, you will rotate with Mr. Miller through our campus trade shops—auto mechanics, woodworking, nursing assistant, food service, and retail—so we can determine which trade is the best fit for you. And third, our team will grade your daily socialization and appropriate social skills."

Katie raised her hand immediately. Neither of us had been prepared for any of this—not the rules, not the baby-talk at the dispensary window, and certainly not two weeks of mandatory Vocational Evaluation. We had zero interest in the rehabilitation side of RRC; we had come to Fishersville strictly for the Web Applications Developer class, fully expecting to treat the center like college—go to class, sleep in the dorm, and be done with it.

"Excuse me, Ms. Hollis?" Katie said. "Nathaniel and I already have our associate degrees from the Community College of Hampton Roads, we lived in our own off-campus apartments in Norfolk for three and a half years, and our vocational counselor in Hampton Roads specifically sent us here for the Web Applications Developer PHP and SQL track. We've been writing HTML since seventh grade and Quantum Basic since high school. Why do we need to spend two weeks touring auto mechanics, woodworking, and nursing?"

Ms. Hollis tapped her pen against her clipboard with a tight, practiced smile. "Everyone follows the same two-week evaluation protocol here, Katie. Nobody skips the trade rotations. Mr. Miller, take the group down to the auto mechanics bay first."

For the next three hours, Katie and I sat side by side in mounting disbelief as Mr. Miller led our cohort from one manual-labor shop to the next. In the auto mechanics bay, we sat parked beside a hydraulic lift smelling burnt motor oil while an instructor demonstrated a heavy pneumatic impact wrench that neither Katie nor I had the upper-body strength to lift off a workbench, let alone use standing under a car chassis. Forty-five minutes later, Mr. Miller marched the group into the woodworking shop, where fine oak sawdust drifted over our lap trays and screaming table saws vibrated through the concrete floor. Right before lunch, we were wheeled into the nursing assistant training lab to watch students practice two-person transfers lifting a hundred-and-fifty-pound plastic mannequin onto a hospital bed.

As soon as Mr. Miller led the group back into the Bates-Harding evaluation room at eleven-thirty, I steered straight up to Ms. Hollis's desk with Katie right beside me.

"Ms. Hollis, that tour makes zero sense for the two of us," I said bluntly. "We're both in wheelchairs with progressive neuromuscular weakness in our legs and arms. We can't stand under a hydraulic lift in an auto shop, we can't stand at a table saw in a woodworking shop, and we certainly can't lift hospital patients in nursing school. We came here to write server-side PHP and SQL code."

Ms. Hollis looked down at our wheelchairs—never once glancing at our CCHR transcripts in her folder—and put on a bright, syrupy smile.

"Now, Katie, Nathaniel, here at Roosevelt we have to evaluate realistic physical alternatives in case the stamina demands of software engineering prove too taxing," Ms. Hollis said, tapping her pen on the desk blotter. "If the computer track doesn't pan out, we have a wonderful partnership with ValueMart right down the road in Waynesboro! We could train Katie to be a ValueMart Door Greeter—it has very minimal physical requirements, and you just sit in the vestibule and smile at shoppers—and Nathaniel, with your polite voice, we could place you in our Food Service Prep or stockroom tagging track!"

Katie stared at her in utter, stunned disbelief.

"Door greeter!?" Katie repeated out loud, her voice ringing off the painted cinder-block walls so loudly that every student in the room turned around to look. "My brother and I have associate degrees with honors! We write HTML, CSS, and Quantum Basic by hand, we run a regional transit analysis website read by city councilors across six cities, and you look at two people in wheelchairs and think our career ceiling is sitting by the sliding doors at ValueMart saying hello to shoppers?!"

"I'm simply explaining all of the options DARS offers our clients," Ms. Hollis said stiffly, her cheeks reddening as Katie and I exchanged a look of pure disgust and rolled back to our table.

***

#### Tuesday, March 6, 2007, 9:15 AM — "Do Not Grab Our Wheelchairs!" & Refusing Separation at Social Break

"All right, group, let's head down the hall to the independent-living test kitchen so we can check off your meal-prep rubric!" Mr. Miller called out at nine-fifteen on Tuesday morning as Katie and I closed our testing binders and powered on our right-armrest joysticks to roll out into the Bates-Harding corridor.

Before we had even cleared the doorway, Mr. Miller walked briskly up behind the two of us without saying a word, reached out, and clamped his right hand onto Katie's rear rubber push-handle and his left hand onto my rear rubber push-handle to shove both of our wheelchairs down the hallway himself.

The sudden manual shove against our motorized wheel hubs jolted both of our cross-brace frames forward at once.

"Hey—take your hands off our wheelchairs right now!" I barked loudly, my voice echoing down the terrazzo corridor as both Katie and I clicked our drives off and slammed our manual wheel brakes locked, stopping Mr. Miller dead in his tracks.

"Excuse me!" Katie shouted, twisting around in her seat so every evaluator and student in the corridor heard her displeasure. "Do not grab my wheelchair! Our chairs have joysticks on the armrests—we drive ourselves! Grabbing somebody's wheelchair without asking is no different from grabbing our bodies in the middle of the hallway!"

Mr. Miller jerked both hands back as if the rubber grips had burned his palms, his face turning pink. "Oh—now wait a second, Katie, Nathaniel, I was just trying to be helpful and get everyone down to the test kitchen on time—"

"If you want us at the test kitchen, you tell us where the door is with your voice, just like you tell every walking student in this hallway!" I said loudly, refusing to lower my volume by a single decibel. "In our community, a wheelchair is an extension of the person sitting in it. You wouldn't walk up behind a standing twenty-one-year-old woman and shove her down the hall by her shoulders without asking, and you do not put your hands on our push-handles to push us around this center!"

Mr. Miller muttered a flustered apology and kept six feet behind us all the way to the test kitchen—where Katie and I briskly fried eggs, toasted bread, scrubbed the skillet clean, and checked off every single independent-living box on the clipboard in twenty minutes flat.

By two-fifteen on Wednesday afternoon, however, during the scheduled Vocational Evaluation social break in the painted cinder-block break room, Ms. Hollis marched across the linoleum toward the quiet corner where Katie and I sat parked wheel-to-wheel drinking two cans of ginger ale and sketching relational database tables—with Mr. Miller trailing right behind her.

"Nathaniel, Katie," Ms. Hollis said, rapping her pen against her clipboard with a disapproving frown, "for the past three days, the evaluation team has noted that the two of you have not separated once—not in the evaluation room, not during break times, not in the cafeteria, and not in the Barton Hall lounge."

Katie and I looked up from our notebook at the exact same second. "That's because we're twins, ma'am," Katie said firmly. "We do everything together."

"Well, while you are in Vocational Evaluation, that needs to change—especially during social times," Ms. Hollis said briskly, gesturing toward two opposite corners of the break room. "Part of your evaluation is proving that you have independent social skills. You two are twenty-one years old—you are supposed to be branching out, making your own individual friends, and going your separate sibling ways during the day. Starting right now for the rest of social break, Nathaniel, you are going over to Table One, and Katie, you are going over to Table Four. Mr. Miller, go ahead and wheel Katie over to Table Four."

Before Mr. Miller could bring his fingers within six inches of Katie's rear push-handles, Katie and I reached across our armrests, locked our hands together in an unbreakable grip, and let the entire room hear our displeasure at full volume.

"Keep your hands off my sister's wheelchair!" I barked across the break room, making every conversation at Tables One through Four stop dead. "We told you yesterday—nobody touches our chairs, and nobody pushes us around!"

"And we are NOT being handled or separated like five-year-olds during break time!" Katie said loudly, her blue eyes blazing straight at Ms. Hollis.

Ms. Hollis blinked, visibly rattled by two Level 2 clients telling her no in front of the entire cohort. "Excuse me, Katie? Nathaniel? Refusing a socialization directive during social time goes down as a deficiency on your Vocational Evaluation rubric."

"Then write it down in capital letters as a deficiency!" Katie shot back loudly enough for the whole wing to hear. "My brother and I are perfectly polite to everyone in this room! Just Sunday afternoon in the Barton Hall lobby, we shared our DVD with half the building and had everyone laughing together! We know how to talk to people, we already passed your bed-making, laundry, and kitchen checks yesterday, and we already have associate degrees! What we do not tolerate is Center staff grabbing our wheelchairs like they own our bodies or trying to pry twin brother and sister apart during social time just to check a box on your clipboard!"

"And we are not sitting in Vocational Evaluation for a second week," I added loudly and evenly, holding Katie's hand tightly across our armrests. "Put the entire two-day Web Applications Developer technical, mathematical, HTML, and logic exam battery on our table at eight-thirty tomorrow morning. Either we test out of Voc Eval in one week and start the Web Applications Developer class on Monday morning, or we will call our father in Alexandria right now, pack our suitcases in Barton Hall, and go home tonight!"

Every student at the four break tables was staring straight at Ms. Hollis and Mr. Miller. Pressing her lips into a thin line, Ms. Hollis motioned for Mr. Miller to step back. "Fine," she said clippedly. "Be at Testing Table Two at eight-thirty sharp tomorrow morning, and we'll see if you can pass the full Web Applications packet in one sitting."

***

#### Thursday, March 8, 2007, 8:30 AM — The Outdated 1990s Exam Battery & Proving We Don't Cheat

When Katie and I rolled into the Vocational Evaluation testing room at eight-twenty-five on Thursday morning and locked our manual wheel brakes side by side at Testing Table Two, Ms. Hollis and Mr. Miller were already waiting for us with matching looks of smug anticipation.

Having watched us refuse to sit at separate tables during Wednesday afternoon's social break, both of them were clearly convinced that the real reason Katie and I insisted on sitting wheel-to-wheel was so we could cheat off each other—either whispering answers back and forth or letting one twin carry the other through the math and coding sections so she could disqualify us both and ship us right back to the ValueMart Door Greeter and Food Service tracks.

Ms. Hollis stepped up to the laminate tabletop and slapped down two three-inch-thick, spiral-bound exam packets, two green optical bubble sheets, two lined legal pads for scratch work, and four sharpened No. 2 pencils.

"Since the two of you flatly refused to sit at separate testing tables," Ms. Hollis announced pointedly, resting her palms on the packets, "I have pulled two different versions of the five-part Web Applications Developer entrance battery. Nathaniel, you have Form A. Katie, you have Form B, where all of the problem sets and multiple-choice items are scrambled in a completely different order. You have until three-thirty tomorrow afternoon to complete all five booklets: Computer Hardware and Operating Environments, HTML and Web Page Design, Applied Algebra, Binary and Boolean Logic, and Relational Database Normalization."

She gestured to Mr. Miller, who pulled a metal folding chair right up to the opposite side of Testing Table Two—barely four feet from our front casters—and sat down holding a clipboard and a digital stopwatch while Ms. Hollis positioned herself directly behind our wheelchairs.

"Mr. Miller will be sitting right here facing your hands and eyes the entire time, and I will be monitoring from behind your chairs," Ms. Hollis said coldly. "If either of you whispers a single word, glances sideways at the other person's booklet or bubble sheet, taps a code on your wheelchair armrests, or shares a single line of scratch paper, both of your exams will be confiscated on the spot for academic dishonesty, you will receive an automatic failure on your DARS evaluation rubric, and you will be permanently disqualified from the Information Technology track. Do we understand each other?"

Katie looked straight up at Ms. Hollis without flinching. "Ma'am, my brother and I graduated with honors from the Community College of Hampton Roads three months ago," she said evenly. "We don't sit together to copy answers. We sit together because we're twins, and neither of us has ever cheated on a test in our lives. Start your clock."

Ms. Hollis pressed the button on her stopwatch. "Begin."

Without looking at each other once, Katie and I rested our inner forearms lightly along our adjacent wheelchair armrests—just enough familiar twin contact to keep our nervous systems calm—and flipped open the heavy cardstock covers of Booklet One at the exact same second.

Ten seconds into page one, I heard Katie let out the exact same quiet, disgusted sigh through her nose that had just escaped mine.

It was March of 2007. Katie and I had been hand-coding HTML since seventh grade at Morrison Middle School in 1997, writing Quantum Basic 6.0 since high school in 2001, and building modern standards-compliant web pages at CCHR—and the official Department for Aging and Rehabilitative Services "Web Applications Developer" Vocational Evaluation exam battery sitting on our table hadn't been updated since the mid-1990s.

In Booklet One—Computer Hardware and Operating Environments—there wasn't a single question about modern 2007 web servers, USB flash drives, or broadband ethernet networks. Instead, Question Three asked how many 1.44-megabyte three-and-a-half-inch floppy disks were required to back up an eleven-megabyte directory without compression. Question Nine asked how to set physical plastic jumpers on an ISA expansion card to resolve an IRQ interrupt conflict between a parallel printer port and a serial mouse. Question Fourteen asked how to edit startup configuration files in Q-Core so a desktop computer could free up enough conventional memory below the 640-kilobyte barrier to launch a database utility, and Question Twenty-Two asked us to calculate how many minutes it would take to download a three-megabyte uncompressed bitmap image over a 28.8-kilobit-per-second dial-up telephone modem.

Shaking my head in silent disbelief as I darkened the green bubbles on Form A, I flipped to Booklet Two—HTML and Web Page Design—and nearly groaned out loud.

Every single question treated 1996 browser wars and long-deprecated HTML 3.2 markup as if they were the pinnacle of modern software engineering. Instead of cascading style sheets or semantic markup, the test demanded to know the exact body-tag attribute to tile a repeating sixteen-color GIF image across a webpage background, how to format paragraph text using deprecated inline font-face tags, how to slice a 640-by-480-pixel VGA screen into three separate scrolling framesets, and which proprietary tag made a line of warning text blink on and off or scroll horizontally across the screen like a stock ticker. Beside me, I could hear the crisp, irritated scratch of Katie's No. 2 pencil writing a brisk margin note on her written-response sheet before she bubbled in the obsolete answer the grading key wanted.

And yet, for the next three hours, Mr. Miller sat four feet away leaning forward on his elbows, staring unblinkingly from my eyes to Katie's eyes, while Ms. Hollis paced back and forth behind our rear push-handles every four minutes waiting to pounce on a sideways glance that never came.

She caught nothing—because there was nothing to catch.

Neither Katie nor I spoke a syllable, tilted a page, or lifted our eyes from our own paperwork. When ten o'clock arrived and Mr. Miller cleared his throat to announce the fifteen-minute morning restroom and water-fountain break, both of us simply shook our heads without looking up and kept right on working. On my yellow legal pad on the left side of the table, I worked front-to-back through Form A's two's-complement binary arithmetic, hexadecimal memory conversions, Boolean truth tables, and quadratic word problems in neat, vertical block columns; on the right side of the table, Katie tore through Form B's scrambled logic gates, algebraic proofs, third-normal-form relational database diagrams, and hand-written SQL join queries using her own distinct step-by-step factoring notation—ending with a final section that absurdly asked us to diagram how an HTML form passed query strings to a 1990s Perl CGI-BIN script over a dial-up intranet.

At eleven-forty-five—fifteen minutes before the lunch bell, having completed the entire two-day, twelve-hour testing battery in three hours and fifteen minutes flat—Katie and I closed the back covers of Booklet Five within ten seconds of each other, set our No. 2 pencils down on the laminate, and rolled side by side up to Ms. Hollis's desk.

"We're finished," I said, sliding Form A, my bubble sheet, my written SQL and HTML packet, and my scratch pad across her blotter as Katie laid Form B right beside mine.

Ms. Hollis stared down at the two completed stacks, her eyebrows shooting up in open skepticism. Convinced that we had either Christmas-treed the bubble sheets at random just to get out before lunch or found some clever way to copy off each other right under Mr. Miller's nose, she pulled the laminated Form A and Form B plastic grading overlays out of her locked desk drawer and lined them up over our answer sheets right in front of us while Mr. Miller stepped over to check our written database normalization and scratch pads against the instructor key.

As Ms. Hollis's forefinger moved down the columns of green bubbles on Form A and then Form B, the smug expectation drained right out of her face.

"Ninety-nine percent on Form A," Ms. Hollis murmured under her breath, blinking twice before recounting the holes on Katie's overlay, "and ninety-eight percent on Form B."

Even more damning to her cheating theory, the single multiple-choice question I had missed on Booklet One wasn't even the same question Katie had missed on Booklet Three. Suspiciously, Ms. Hollis snatched up our two yellow scratch pads and held them side by side, hunting for identical handwriting, copied formulas, or matching erasures.

"Their scratch work is completely different from page one to the end, Ms. Hollis," Mr. Miller admitted quietly, pointing to our written SQL and HTML packets. "He solved all the hexadecimal conversions by factoring through base-two, and she solved hers by direct base-sixteen division. And on the written HTML and database section, they both got one hundred percent—in fact, on Question Forty-Two, Katie wrote a three-sentence citation in the margin explaining that the test key's 1996 HTML 3.2 syntax was officially deprecated by the World Wide Web Consortium in 1999, and she wrote out both the obsolete 1996 tag from our answer key and the modern CSS2 rule so we couldn't mark it wrong."

Katie folded her hands neatly on her lap tray and looked straight across the desk at Ms. Hollis.

"And while we're on the subject of Question Forty-Two, Ms. Hollis, that entire exam battery is an embarrassment," Katie said bluntly. "Whoever wrote those five booklets hasn't updated a single page since my brother and I were in seventh grade in 1997. Half the hardware questions were asking about 28.8k dial-up modems, 1.44-megabyte floppy disks, and ISA jumper pins, and the web design section tested HTML 3.2 font and blink tags that nobody in the real world has used in almost ten years."

"If we had handed in HTML 3.2 framesets and font tags like that at the Community College of Hampton Roads," I added dryly, "our professors would have failed us on the spot. At least once we're out of Vocational Evaluation and inside Mr. Alderman's Web Applications Developer lab on Monday morning, we'll be working in an actual 2007 computer classroom instead of filling out 1990s paper packets."

Pressing her lips into a thin, bloodless line, Ms. Hollis couldn't say a word in rebuttal. With two near-perfect answer sheets, forty pages of independent scratch work, and our Monday ultimatum hanging over her desk, she uncapped her pen, stiffly signed both of our one-week Vocational Evaluation completion forms, and cleared us to start the Web Applications Developer class on Monday morning.

***

#### Saturday, March 10, 2007, 1:00 PM — Still Stuck on Level 2 in Barton Hall & Hating the Yellow Hall Pass Rule

"Look at this yellow slip of paper, Nate," Katie whispered in disgust on Saturday afternoon as we sat parked wheel-to-wheel in the Barton Hall lobby holding two signed yellow paper Level 2 Hall Passes while we waited by the glass doors for the Center recreation van. "We rushed the entire two-week Voc Eval in one single week so we could start our Web Applications Developer class on Monday morning, and we're still stuck right here in Barton Hall on Level 2!"

"Because moving over to Cantor Hall is part of earning Level 3, and nobody who's only been on campus for six days has been here long enough to earn Level 3, let alone Level 4," I muttered, looking down at the counselor's signature on my yellow paper pass. "Back home in Norfolk or Virginia Beach, if we want to go buy snacks or browse computer books at Chapters & Co., we just roll out our front door to the nearest CVTA bus stop, pay our fare, and go wherever we please like normal adults. Up here in Barton Hall, a Level 2 client can't even roll past the front gates on Roosevelt Avenue to catch the local VATS shuttle bus between Staunton, Fishersville, and Waynesboro without begging the dorm office for a signed yellow Hall Pass stating where we're going and what minute we'll be back."

"And if you don't want to wait two hours on the shoulder of Route 250 for the VATS bus on a Saturday," Katie added, gesturing toward the recreation clipboard hanging outside the lobby office where students had to sign up for chaperoned van trips to The Spot recreation hangout or the Waynesboro ValueMart, "you have to sign up for a chaperoned Center van ride! We will be twenty-two years old in four weeks, Nate. We have associate degrees, we run our own regional transit website, and we had to get a signed Hall Pass from a dorm counselor just to ride four miles down the road to buy laundry detergent and ginger ale at ValueMart—the exact store Ms. Hollis thought I should stand at the door and greet shoppers for!"

"And tonight makes our seventh night in a row being forced down separate hallways for the eleven-o'clock bed check," I whispered back, lacing my fingers tightly through hers across our armrests as the white Center van pulled up to the curb outside. "Let's see what Mr. Alderman's PHP class looks like on Monday morning, Katie—because I am already sick to death of this place."

## Starting Web Apps While Stuck in Barton Hall, Sleeping in the Closet, & The Chickenshit Report

### Part 1: Starting Web Apps While Stuck on Level 2 in Barton Hall, Quantum OS 2000 Professional, & Meeting Tina, Jim, and Sheila

**Date:** 2007-03-12 at 08:00 America/New_York

![Inside the 1970s institutional computer lab of the Web Applications Developer classroom at Roosevelt Rehabilitation Center in March 2007, Nathaniel and Katie Prairie sit side by side in their collapsible manual wheelchairs outfitted with armrest joysticks, spoked push-rim wheels, and rear push-handles with their personal laptops open in front of unused beige CRT state monitors while short, petite, jet-black-haired Caucasian classmate Tina in glasses stands beside Katie telling it like it is to the new administrator as Sheila and Jim back them up.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/may_2007_rrc_web_apps_class_personal_laptops_tina_sheila_jim_katie_nate.jpg)

#### Monday, March 12, 2007, 8:00 AM — "Death Before Dishonor, NOTHING Before Coffee!", Adult Bathroom Rules, & Sitting Together in Class

"*Death before dishonor, NOTHING before coffee!*" Katie read aloud with a grin at eight o'clock on Monday morning as we rolled our joystick-outfitted wheelchairs down the 1970s concrete-block corridor of the Information Technology wing and paused outside the interior office window of the Computer Hardware lab right next door to our classroom, where a bold vinyl sticker was plastered across the glass above a gurgling twelve-cup commercial coffee brewer.

"That's Mr. Culpepper's office window," a middle-aged student with a salt-and-pepper beard chuckled, stepping out of the adjoining hardware doorway holding an empty ceramic mug while half a dozen hardware students hovered around the counter waiting for the amber pot to finish dripping. "He teaches the Computer Hardware and network cabling lab next door, and I'm telling you right now, that classroom never gets started for the day until the coffee is brewed and ready. Those guys swear by their morning coffee."

"More for you guys, then," I laughed as Katie and I pulled two cold cans of ginger ale out of our backpack side pockets. "Neither my sister nor I can stand the taste of coffee."

"You two must be Nathaniel and Katie Prairie," our Web Applications Developer instructor, Mr. Alderman, said with a welcoming smile, stepping out of the adjacent computer lab doorway as Mr. Culpepper gave us a friendly wave through his sticker-adorned office window next door. Mr. Alderman gestured toward the long double workstation table near the front of our lab where two wide wheelchair bays sat side by side. "I saw how the two of you tore through the entire Voc Eval coding packet in a single sitting on Thursday morning. Take those two stations right there together—you've got plenty of room to park your chairs wheel-to-wheel."

"Thank you, Mr. Alderman," Katie said, exhaling the first genuine breath of relief either of us had taken since arriving in Fishersville as we steered into the adjacent bays and locked our manual wheel brakes side by side. "After Ms. Hollis spent last week trying to split us up to opposite corners of the break room, we half-expected another lecture about sitting apart."

"Not in my classroom, and not in Mr. Culpepper's lab next door either," Mr. Alderman said firmly, leaning against the instructor podium while the aroma of Mr. Culpepper's fresh-brewed coffee drifted through the open connecting doorway and Katie and I popped the tabs on our cold ginger ales. "We treat our students like grown adults on a real job site. You sit where you work best, and one more thing so you know you're not in Voc Eval anymore: in this classroom, you never have to raise your hand or ask permission to go to the bathroom. Simply tell me you're heading to the restroom so I know where you are, and go. How's Barton Hall treating you two so far?"

"Honestly, we're already counting the hours on our fingers," I admitted as Katie and I unzipped our backpacks. "Even though we rushed Voc Eval in one week so we could start your class today, we're still stuck over in Barton Hall on Level 2 because moving to Cantor Hall is part of earning Level 3, and nobody stays long enough in seven days to earn Level 3 or Level 4. That makes eight straight nights of being forced down separate men's and women's wings at eleven o'clock with flashlights shining in our faces, plus begging for signed yellow paper Hall Passes just to step off campus."

"Ah, watch out for the overnight dorm log over there," Mr. Alderman said with a dry chuckle, shaking his head. "Half the night staff in the dorms love writing down every petty little thing they can find on what the teachers around here call the Chickenshit Report. Just keep your heads down in my lab and you'll be fine."

***

#### 9:00 AM — Quantum OS 2000 Professional, Meeting Tina, Jim, and Sheila, & Refusing to Be Pushed Around

"All right, everyone, now that Mr. Culpepper's coffee pot next door is finally done brewing and the building is officially awake, go ahead and hit the power switches on the desktop towers so you can see what the Commonwealth left us with," Mr. Alderman called out at nine o'clock once the rest of the class had settled into their seats.

Katie and I pressed the round plastic power buttons on the two beige Commonwealth of Virginia property-tagged desktop towers sitting on our table. As the bulky CRT monitors flickered to life with a high-pitched static hum, both of us stared in disbelief at the splash screen.

"Quantum OS 2000 Professional?" Katie whispered, blinking at the screen. "Nate, it's March of 2007! This operating system is seven years old!"

I clicked the Start menu to open a command prompt and check the local PHP configuration—and immediately hit a glaring red system dialog box: *ADMINISTRATOR ACCESS DENIED — CONTACT VITA SYSTEM ADMINISTRATOR*. Not only was the operating system seven years out of date, but VITA—the Virginia Information Technology Agency in Richmond—had locked the machines down with group-policy permissions so suffocating that a student login couldn't install up-to-date software or a modern web browser, couldn't edit a local PHP configuration file, couldn't start or stop a local web server service, and couldn't even open the control panel.

Across the aisle from our wheelchairs, the middle-aged man with the salt-and-pepper beard who had been waiting on Mr. Culpepper's coffee pot earlier tapped his keyboard twice, stared at the locked-down Quantum OS 2000 Professional desktop, and let out a dry laugh. "Well, if the Commonwealth wants us to build database-driven web applications on these dinosaurs, I hope they're planning to give us until the year 2030."

"Where are you from?" I asked, hearing the unmistakable Tidewater cadence in his voice.

"Virginia Beach," he grinned, setting his mug down and reaching across the aisle to shake my hand and then Katie's. "I'm Jim. Spent twenty years working on computer hardware and network cabling down at the Oceanfront and Lynnhaven before my back gave out and Voc Rehab sent me up the mountain to retrain."

"No way—we're from Virginia Beach too!" Katie beamed. "We grew up in Kempsville and went to Northwood High School and the Community College of Hampton Roads before we lived in West Ocean View!"

At the two workstations immediately to Katie's right, two middle-aged women turned their chairs around with warm smiles. The woman sitting closest to Katie was short and petite, Caucasian, with straight jet-black hair and sharp eyes behind her glasses; beside her sat a cheerful woman with a sketchpad full of interface wireframes.

"I'm Tina, from up Route 340 in Luray," the petite woman in glasses said, shaking Katie's hand and then mine, "and this is Sheila—she commutes down I-81 from Harrisonburg every morning and does all our digital graphics and UI layouts. While half the twenty-year-olds in the dorms spend all day screaming at each other in the cafeteria, the three of us actually came here to build software."

"And there is only one way any of us writes real PHP and SQL in this room," Sheila added, sliding the beige state keyboard all the way to the back of her desk against the CRT monitor.

Right beside Katie, Tina unzipped her shoulder bag, pulled out her own sleek personal laptop, and set it right on the desk in front of the useless state keyboard—alongside a well-thumbed, spiral-bound copy of the Roosevelt Rehabilitation Center Student Handbook bristling with sticky notes.

"Every single student in this class—Jim, Sheila, Sarah, Amanda, Bryan, Sean, and me—brings our own personal laptop and runs a local web server, PHP 5, and an SQL database on our own hard drive," Tina told us plainly, adjusting her glasses. "Technically the Center rules say no personal computers in class, but Mr. Alderman and the old vocational administrator let us do it because they know VITA locked these state towers down so tight you can't code a single script on them."

"Wait—why do you have sticky notes all through the student handbook?" Katie asked, glancing at Tina's spiral booklet.

Tina grinned behind her glasses. "Because I'm short, I stay in the dorms here four nights a week before I drive my compact sedan home to Luray every Friday afternoon at three-thirty sharp, and I don't let anyone at this center push me around. I tell it like it is straight to their faces, and the RRC staff hate it—but they can't write me up or touch me because I never break a single rule in this book. I heard down the hall how the two of you rushed Voc Eval in one week flat and told off Ms. Hollis when she tried to split you up at social break. Good for you. Half the staff here think a clipboard—or seeing rubber push-handles on the back of a wheelchair—gives them a license to boss you around. Follow the handbook to the letter and call them on their nonsense, and there's not a thing they can do to you."

At four o'clock that very afternoon, when class let out and Tina walked over to the Barton Hall lobby with us to drop off a PHP reference binder before heading to her car, we saw Tina's method in action firsthand.

Katie and I rolled side by side up to the Barton Hall front counter, laid our signed yellow paper Level 2 Hall Passes on the blotter to log our departure for the VATS shuttle bus into Waynesboro, and turned our wheelchairs toward the automatic glass doors—just as a prickly afternoon residential supervisor named Mr. Vance marched out of the inner office and stepped right in front of our front casters with his arms crossed.

"Hold on right there, you two," Mr. Vance barked, reaching his right hand out to grab the rear rubber push-handle of my manual frame as if he were about to wheel me backward away from the exit. "Where do you think you're rolling off to at four o'clock? You two are still Level 2 clients here in Barton Hall!"

"First, take your hand off my brother's wheelchair push-handle right now," Katie said sharply, locking her joystick brakes alongside mine without backing up a millimeter. "Second, we know we're still Level 2, Mr. Vance, which is why our counselor signed our yellow Hall Passes at three-thirty and they are sitting right there on the desk blotter in front of you."

"Under Section Three of the residential handbook," I said evenly, pointing down at the two signed yellow slips clipped to the desk ledger, "Level 2 clients who have completed their afternoon training block and hold a signed Hall Pass are permitted off campus until eight o'clock in the evening. Just because our wheelchairs have manual push-handles on the back so they can fold into a car trunk doesn't mean staff get to grab them or push us around when we've followed your rules to the letter."

Standing right beside Katie's chair with her car keys in her hand, Tina peered up at Mr. Vance through her glasses, her jet-black hair framing a look of cool, unapologetic amusement.

"They've got you dead to rights on page twelve of the handbook, Mr. Vance," Tina said bluntly in front of half the lobby. "Their yellow passes are signed in ink, they logged their departure time, and neither of them is breaking a single rule in this building. If you keep grabbing his chair and blocking the doorway when they've complied with Center policy, the only person violating the handbook here is you."

Mr. Vance's face flushed crimson from his collar to his hairline. He glared at Tina and then down at Katie and me, searching desperately for something to cite us for—and finding nothing at all, he let go of my push-handle and stepped stiffly out of the doorway.

***

#### Tuesday, March 13, 2007, 9:30 AM — Coding on Personal Laptops & Standing Up to the New VITA-Obsessed Administrator

"Mr. Alderman," a sharp voice rang out from the doorway of the Web Applications Developer classroom at nine-thirty on Tuesday morning, "why are all of these students using personal laptops instead of the Center-provided computers?"

Katie, Tina, Sheila, Jim, and I all paused with our fingers hovering over our personal laptop keyboards and looked toward the center aisle. Standing there in a pressed navy suit with a clipboard tucked against her arm was the brand-new vocational division administrator who had started on campus that week—frowning down the row of open personal laptops sitting in front of the dark, powered-off state CRT monitors.

"Because, ma'am," Katie spoke up politely from her wheelchair before Mr. Alderman even had to step around the podium, "the Center-provided computers on these desks are horribly outdated. They're still running Quantum OS 2000 Professional, and VITA has the permissions locked down so hard that we can't install up-to-date software, configure a PHP server, or run a local database."

The new administrator marched over to our front workstation table, looking down at Katie and me in our wheelchairs as if she expected the two of us to shrink back and shut our laptop lids. "VITA has assured my office that every workstation on the Commonwealth network is configured with standard agency software and mandatory security lockdowns," she said sharply. "You are clients here, not the IT department. Close those personal laptops right now and use the computers VITA provided."

Neither Katie nor I touched our laptop hinges.

"No, ma'am, we won't do that," I said calmly from my chair, meeting her stare without blinking. "Our state vocational rehabilitation plans specifically fund us to complete the Commonwealth's accredited Web Applications Developer syllabus in PHP 5 and relational database design. If you force us onto seven-year-old Quantum OS 2000 Professional machines where VITA has blocked local web servers and command prompts, you are preventing us from completing the state-mandated curriculum."

Right beside Katie's chair, Tina stood up to her full petite height, pushed her glasses up the bridge of her nose, opened her spiral-bound handbook, and looked the new administrator straight in the eye.

![Inside the 1970s concrete-block Web Applications Developer computer classroom at Roosevelt Rehabilitation Center in March 2007, twenty-one-year-old fraternal twins Katie and Nate Prairie sit facing each other in their collapsible black manual wheelchairs outfitted with right-armrest joysticks, spoked manual wheels with metal push-rims, and rear rubber push-handles while holding hands in front of their open personal laptops and the unused beige state CRT monitors; standing right beside Katie's wheelchair, Tina—a petite Caucasian middle-aged woman with glasses and straight jet-black hair—points to the rules in her spiral-bound student handbook as she calmly confronts the new clipboard-toting administrator while Jim and Sheila stand behind them]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/may_2007_rrc_web_apps_class_personal_laptops_tina_sheila_jim_katie_nate.jpg)

"Let me tell you how it is, since somebody needs to say it plainly," Tina said, her voice steady and fearless while Sheila and Jim stood behind us. "None of us is breaking a single VITA network rule—not one of these personal laptops is plugged into the Commonwealth's ethernet jacks. VITA configured those beige dinosaurs on the desks for someone typing memos in a seven-year-old word processor, not for web application developers. We need computers with up-to-date software, and we need permissions not to be locked down so hard that we can't even start a local web server or edit a configuration file. Unless VITA is going to walk in here today and install modern software with developer permissions on those towers, closing our laptops means shutting down the entire class."

"And if you shut down the class," Katie added evenly from her wheelchair, reaching across our armrests to hold my hand, "my brother and I—and everyone else at these desks—will be happy to call our regional Vocational Rehabilitation counselors before lunch and explain that the new administration in Fishersville won't let us write code."

The new administrator stared from Tina's unblinking glasses to Katie's and my twin wheelchairs. Because not a single personal laptop in the room was plugged into the state ethernet wall jacks, we weren't violating a single VITA network regulation, and she knew Mr. Alderman, Mr. Culpepper next door, and the regional counselors would back us up. Muttering under her breath about "consulting with VITA compliance," she turned on her heel and walked out the door, leaving the five of us to exchange satisfied grins and go right back to coding on our personal laptops: Katie, Tina, and I writing the PHP back-end logic, Sheila designing the interface graphics, and Jim keeping everyone's hardware humming.

### Part 2: Emergency in the Therapeutic Pool, Caught Sleeping Together in a Closet, Calling the Staffer's Bluff, & The Chickenshit Report

**Date:** 2007-03-13 at 16:15 America/New_York

![Inside a 1970s brick-and-wood-paneled office in the Bates-Harding Building at Roosevelt Rehabilitation Center on Wednesday morning, March 14, 2007, twenty-one-year-old Katie and Nate Prairie sit side by side in their collapsible black manual wheelchairs outfitted with right-armrest joysticks, spoked manual wheels with metal push-rims, and rear rubber push-handles; holding a small paper cup of water in one hand, Katie leans over the wooden desk to write 'I LET HIM COVER MY DIGNITY!' in bold block letters on a legal pad while Nate holds her shoulder and the duty supervisor sits across the desk deleting the overnight pool-deck entry from his computer]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/jul_2007_rrc_bates_harding_counselor_office_dignity_note_katie_nate.jpg)

#### Tuesday, March 13, 2007, 4:15 PM — Emergency at the Therapeutic Pool & The Towel Showdown

"I told you to leave her alone!" I shouted across the ninety-two-degree water of the indoor therapeutic pool at Roosevelt Rehabilitation Center, projecting my voice intentionally loud so the recreation staffer sitting behind the office glass would hear me.

Across the warm water from where our two joystick-outfitted wheelchairs sat parked at the top of the sloped therapeutic pool entry ramp, Chris—an aggressive student from the IT class cohort who had been pestering Katie since Monday morning and refused to accept that my twin sister had zero interest in dating him—smirked and wading-stepped closer.

"Come on, Nate, let's swim up to the shallow ramp," Katie said tightly, turning in the warm water to get away from him.

We pushed off through the buoyant water toward the shallow ramp together, and Chris plowed straight through the water right behind us. Before I could pivot between them, he lunged forward and slammed both hands down into the water right in front of Katie's face—striking her hard across the bridge of her nose and cheek while his flailing fingers caught and tore the front piece of her two-piece swimsuit top.

Katie gasped, clutched onto my left forearm with one hand while clapping her other hand over her face, and burst into sobs.

My heart dropped into my stomach. Katie never cried over splashes or arguments; if Katie was crying, she was hurt.

Wrapping my arm around her waist in the buoyant water, I guided her immediately up the submerged shallow ramp to our parked wheelchairs at the edge of the wet tile deck and helped her transfer into her seat while I pulled myself into mine right beside her. When I gently eased her hand back half an inch to check her face, I saw two things at the exact same second: Chris's hand had split the thin skin right across the bony bridge of her nose while rupturing the blood vessels inside her nostrils so bright red blood was pouring steadily from her nose, and the front piece of her swimsuit top had been ripped away in the water, leaving her chest bare while both of her hands had to stay pressed tightly over her bleeding nostrils.

"Get me Student Health and Campus Security!" I roared at the top of my lungs across the natatorium. "My sister's nose is bleeding!"

Since Katie was in no condition to speak with both of her hands occupied holding her bleeding nose, I angled my wheelchair right in front of hers and leaned forward to use my own hands to cover up my sister's bare breasts and shield her modesty on the open pool deck while we waited for someone to bring a towel.

Instead of grabbing a towel from the rack by the wall, the poolside staffer walked over with a clipboard in his hand and frowned at me.

"You know I'm going to have to report you for inappropriate contact," the staffer said, staring straight at my hands covering my sister's chest while blood dripped between her fingers onto the wet tile.

"Either report me or get a towel to cover my sister's dignity!" I retorted angrily, not giving a damn what he thought while my sister sat bleeding and exposed in front of the pool.

Staring at the blood running down Katie's wrists and her torn swimsuit top floating by the gutter, it finally dawned on the staffer why my hands were covering her chest. He hurried over to the rack and brought back a thick white bath towel just as the Recreational Therapy supervisor rushed out with a walkie-talkie crackling that both Student Health and RRC Campus Police were on the way.

Only when that dry towel was wrapped securely around Katie's chest and shoulders did I let go.

Seconds later, two Student Health nurses pushed through the double doors and immediately pressed a sterile gauze pack over Katie's bleeding nose and swollen cheek, while a Campus Police officer pulled out his notepad to take a formal written statement from me and three other students who had witnessed Chris lunge at her in the water.

Over the edge of the bloody gauze pack, Katie fixed the poolside staffer who had threatened to write me up with a furious glare.

"You're going to write up my brother for trying to cover my boobs while no one wanted to get a towel or something?" she stammered thickly past the bandage.

The staffer looked down at his shoes without a word as the Recreational Therapy supervisor ordered everyone out of the water, closing the natatorium so maintenance could scrub the tile coping with a one-to-ten bleach solution, shock-chlorinate the ninety-two-degree water to four parts per million, and run a full sixty-minute filtration turnover hold.

While Student Health escorted Katie across the walkway to the clinic in the Bates-Harding Building, one of Katie's female friends from our class hurried into the women's locker room and brought all of Katie's dry clothes and backpack out to me. Stacking her bag on the seat of her wheelchair, I rolled both chairs over to the Student Health waiting room and sat stubbornly outside the exam door until evening—refusing to be more than ten feet away from my sister while she was hurt.

***

#### 7:30 PM – 11:25 PM — Closing Time at the Rec Hall, Locking the Seasonal Closet From the Inside in Street Clothes, & Accused of Having Sex

"I don't want to leave your side," Katie whispered at seven-thirty that evening as the Student Health clinic door opened and she rolled out wearing her swimsuit bottom and a worn-out oversized loaner T-shirt. Once the clinic nurses had finally gotten the heavy bleeding inside her nostrils to clot and stop, they had had to pull the split skin across the bony bridge of her nose together with sterile MedStrip wound-closure strips and tape a protective white gauze-and-paper-tape dressing across the bridge of her nose and swollen right cheek, instructing her to keep the MedStrips and white tape bandage dry and in place across her nose for a full seven days so the split bridge wouldn't reopen. Reaching across our armrests for my hand as we rolled toward Barton Hall in the gathering dusk, she started sobbing again. "I don't give a damn about the Level 2 dorm rule... please don't leave me tonight, Nate."

"We used to live together!" she stammered as we paused outside the Barton Hall entrance so she could run into her room just long enough to change out of her damp swimwear into dry street clothes—blue jeans, sneakers, and a zip-up fleece hoodie. "We used to share a bed! Hell, we would sleep in closets together!"

Looking at the fresh white gauze taped across my trembling sister's swollen nose after eight straight nights of forced separation in Barton Hall, I made up my mind on the spot. We weren't going to try rolling down the dorm hallways in pajamas carrying pillows and blankets off our beds—that would be a dead giveaway to every staff member on duty. Instead, once Katie came back out in her dry jeans and hoodie, the two of us rolled over to the campus Rec Hall to spend the evening together in a corner booth where no one could separate us.

At ten-forty that night, the Rec Hall staffer flicked the overhead lights twice and called out across the game tables that it was five minutes until ten-forty-five—the mandatory departure time for all Level 2 clients to head back to Barton Hall ahead of the eleven-o'clock curfew check, while Level 3 and Level 4 clients from Cantor Hall were allowed to stay until the Rec Hall closed at eleven sharp.

Still dressed in our full daytime street clothes and shoes, Katie and I looked at each other and nodded without saying a word. First, both of us went to the bathroom one last time so neither of us would have to open a door in the middle of the night.

When we rolled back out of the restrooms at ten-forty-four, while the staffer at the Rec Hall front counter was busy collecting billiard balls and board games and the other Level 2 students were filing out the front glass doors toward Barton Hall, Katie and I checked over our shoulders to make sure no one was looking—and slipped quietly down a darkened hallway off the rear of the Rec Hall.

At the end of that darkened hallway stood the heavy solid-wood door to the seasonal storage closet—a walk-in closet big enough to fit both of our wheelchairs inside out of sight.

I reached out and tried the brass doorknob. To our relief, it turned smoothly—it was unlocked!

Immediately, Katie and I rolled both of our joystick-outfitted wheelchairs all the way inside the dark closet, pulled the door shut behind us, and twisted the interior thumb-turn lock until it clicked, locking the door from the inside.

In the quiet darkness, smelling of cedar and cardboard boxes, we clicked off our wheelchair power switches and felt around the shelves and floor for anything soft. Packed along the back wall were lumpy canvas storage bags stuffed with spare winter coats, folded fabric stage curtains, and foam cushions. Still wearing our full street clothes, jeans, hoodies, and sneakers, we pulled two lumpy bundles onto the linoleum floor to use as makeshift pillows, spread a thick folded stage curtain over our shoulders as a makeshift blanket, and transferred out of our wheelchairs onto the floor.

Wrapping both of our arms tightly around each other in the dark, Katie tucked her head beneath my chin with a long, shaky exhale. Confident that nobody would ever find us locked inside a back seasonal closet, we started to drift off to sleep in our street clothes.
