At eleven-twenty-five, just as I was sliding into sleep with my arms around my sister, the sound of footsteps echoed down the darkened Rec Hall hallway outside our closet.

Both of us went completely still in the dark.

The footsteps stopped right outside our door. Someone grabbed the outer brass doorknob and tried to turn it—*rattle, rattle*—finding it locked from the inside.

Katie and I held our breath and remained dead quiet, not moving a muscle in the dark.

Then, right outside the wood, we heard the metallic jingle of a master key ring. A key scraped into the outside lock cylinder, the bolt clicked back as someone unlocked the door, and the solid-wood door swung wide open as a blinding flashlight beam swept past our two parked wheelchairs and shone straight down onto the two of us huddled in our street clothes on the floor.

"Aha! I knew it!" the night supervisor barked, glaring down at us while the Rec Hall staffer stood behind him in the hallway. "What the hell do you two think you're doing locking yourselves inside a dark closet to have sex?! You know the Center rule—if two clients are caught having sex anywhere on this campus, at any time, both of you get kicked out of Roosevelt Rehabilitation Center!"

We had already heard plenty of stories from other students during our first week and a half about clients sneaking off to have sex being a rampant thing all over campus, and the second the supervisor barked *"I knew it!"* without even pausing to look at us, we figured this back closet in the Rec Hall was probably one of the places where clients got caught hooking up.

Neither Katie nor I shrank back an inch. Pushing the makeshift curtain off our shoulders as we transferred back up into our wheelchairs in our full street clothes and sneakers, both of us went straight back at the night supervisor at full volume.

"Have sex?!" I roared in disgust, staring at him like he had lost his mind. "Are you out of your sick mind?! First of all, she's my twin sister! Second, look at us—we're wearing our full street clothes, jeans, hoodies, and shoes! We locked ourselves in here to sleep using lumpy bags as pillows because my sister got her nose broken open in your pool this afternoon and your stupid Level 2 dorm rules wouldn't let us stay together!"

"Look at my face!" Katie snapped furiously, pointing straight at the swollen purple bruise on her cheek and the white medical tape across her broken nose. "My nose was broken open in your therapeutic pool five hours ago by a creep in our class, your poolside staffer tried to write my brother up for covering my dignity when nobody brought a towel, and when we just wanted a quiet closet where my brother could hold me so I wouldn't be alone all night, you unlock the door and accuse twin brother and sister of having sex?!"

"I don't care what story you give me—locking yourselves inside a dark seasonal closet together and skipping the eleven-o'clock curfew check is grounds for expulsion!" the night supervisor barked, shaking his clipboard in our faces. "Keep yelling at me like that, both of you, and I will have you kicked out of this Center and sent home right now!"

Katie and I called his bluff on the spot.

"Do it! Kick us out right now!" I fired right back at him without blinking, unlocking my wheelchair brakes and rolling straight out of the closet into the Rec Hall corridor. "It's eleven-twenty-five at night—don't wait until morning! Walk right down the hall to the Rec Hall's front-desk telephone and call our father in Alexandria right now! Tell him to get in his pickup truck and come pick us up tonight!"

"Go on, walk over to the Rec Hall desk phone and call our Dad in Alexandria right now!" Katie dared him at the top of her lungs, rolling right out beside me and pointing down the hallway toward the front counter. "Wake him up at eleven-twenty-five, tell him you're kicking us out, and then explain to him why my nose is bandaged! We're ready to leave this place right now—we'll go back across to Barton Hall and pack our suitcases this second!"

The night supervisor froze dead in his tracks with his pen in the air.

He stared from my face to Katie's bandaged nose, realizing in an instant that we weren't scared teenagers begging not to get expelled—we were dead serious and ready to roll across to our rooms and pack our bags that very minute. Within three seconds, every ounce of bluster drained out of his face, and he backed all the way down.

"Nobody is calling your father tonight, and nobody is getting kicked out," the night supervisor muttered stiffly, lowering his clipboard and refusing to take a single step toward the Rec Hall desk telephone. "Your vocational counselor is off work tomorrow on Wednesday. I am putting a residential write-up in the overnight log for missing eleven-o'clock bed check, and your counselor will speak to the two of you about this on Thursday morning when she returns. Now get across to Barton Hall and go to your assigned beds."

Only when we were back in our separate rooms in Barton Hall ten minutes later with our laptop webcams open on our nightstands so we could watch over each other through the screen did Katie speak quietly into her microphone.

"Wait a second, Nate," Katie whispered, frowning thoughtfully past the white tape across her nose. "Everybody on campus knows the rule: if two students are caught having sex anywhere at any time, both of them get kicked out of the Center automatically. He automatically assumed that's what we were doing and threatened to kick us out on the spot—so why did he back down the very second we told him to call Dad in Alexandria and said we were ready to leave tonight?"

"Because he realized kicking us out wasn't a punishment to us—we actually wanted to leave," I said quietly.

"I think it's more than that, Nate," Katie said slowly, her sharp eyes narrowing on the screen. "Think about how hard Voc Eval pushed to keep us here for two full weeks, and how fast that supervisor just panicked when he saw two full-time Web Applications students ready to pack their suitcases in Week Two. I bet the Center's funding from the state is tied to how many dorm beds and classroom seats they keep filled. They only kick people out when they think you'll beg to stay—the second he saw we'd gladly walk out the door tonight, he backed down so they wouldn't lose two seats."

"Whether it's their headcount funding or covering their own behinds over the pool, we now know their threats are hollow," I whispered back.

"I just need to be hugged," Katie murmured toward the webcam, her bandaged nose and swollen cheek catching the glow of her screen.

"I know," I said softly, keeping my hand resting beside the camera lens until her eyelids drooped, "and I'll be waiting right outside your suite door first thing in the morning. Goodnight, Katie."

***

#### Wednesday, March 14, 2007, 8:30 AM — The Bates-Harding Office & "I LET HIM COVER MY DIGNITY!"

"I'm still so upset," Katie whispered in my ear at quarter to eight on Wednesday morning as we met right outside her women's-wing suite door and I pulled her into a tight morning hug across our armrests.

"I understand," I whispered back, rubbing her shoulder. Hoping to coax even a tiny smile out of her, I asked, "You ready to go eat some more garbage?"

Katie giggled just a bit against my collar, though when I started to ease back from the hug, she held on tightly to my jacket sleeves and refused to let go—making it crystal clear without words: *please don't let go*.

As we finally rolled side by side past the Barton Hall front desk toward the dining hall breezeway, the morning desk clerk looked up from the overnight binder and tapped a pink slip of paper. "Nathaniel, Katie—just so you know, your regular vocational counselor has her scheduled day off today, so your disciplinary write-up meeting for getting caught in the hallway closet at eleven o'clock last night is on her calendar for Thursday morning. Also, check the lobby board after dinner tonight—housing is running the mid-month dormitory room reassignments this evening."

Neither of us cared about Thursday's closet write-up meeting—and as soon as we finished breakfast at eight-thirty, an administrative runner paged both of us over to the student-services duty supervisor's office in the Bates-Harding Building regarding Tuesday afternoon's incident at the pool.

Rolling through the wood-paneled office door beside Katie, I took one look at the printout sitting on the duty supervisor's desk—the morning Chickenshit Report—and saw the poolside staffer's entry from Tuesday afternoon literally accusing me of *"fondling Katie's bare breasts while she was in distress, after having been assaulted and her swimsuit top destroyed by the person who assaulted her."*

Katie rolled her eyes and growled across the desk, "Delete that from the record! I told him to cover my boobs while we waited for someone to get a damn towel! None of this shit would've happened if that boy didn't cause me a nosebleed in the first place!"

My sister was furious—Katie never cussed like that in front of staff—and she kept right on going: "And I don't care if you call our Dad! He would tell you himself that my brother acted protectively in covering them!"

Having riled herself all the way up on top of Tuesday's pool assault and getting dragged out of the closet at eleven o'clock the night before, Katie's nervous system overloaded all at once, her voice cutting out as she descended straight into a full autistic meltdown.

Instinctively, I steered my wheelchair flush against hers, locked my brakes, and held her tightly in my arms while she trembled against my shoulder.

The duty supervisor looked into Katie's blank, overloaded eyes, seeing immediately that the only reason she had gone completely silent was because her autistic brain was in a full sensory shutdown.

"Let me try something," the supervisor said quietly, pressing the intercom button on his desk phone. "Could we please get a cup of water brought in for Katie?"

Turning back to the two of us while I held my trembling sister, he spoke in a calm, steady voice. "You really care about her, don't you, Nathaniel? No, I don't think you were touching her inappropriately. I think you were acting on instinct and shielding her from further humiliation while you waited for a towel to cover her up, and while she was busy trying to stop her nose from bleeding until help could arrive. I have the medical report from the nurses in Student Health right here on my desk that says the exact same thing."

When the secretary brought in a small paper cup of cool water and Katie slowly took a few sips, her breathing steadied. Reaching across the wooden desk, Katie pulled a yellow legal pad toward her wheelchair, picked up a thick black marker, and wrote down in firm block letters:

*I LET HIM COVER MY DIGNITY!*

![Inside a 1970s brick-and-wood-paneled office in the Bates-Harding Building at Roosevelt Rehabilitation Center on Wednesday morning, March 14, 2007, twenty-one-year-old Katie and Nate Prairie sit side by side in their collapsible black manual wheelchairs outfitted with right-armrest joysticks, spoked manual wheels with metal push-rims, and rear rubber push-handles; holding a small paper cup of water in one hand, Katie leans over the wooden desk to write "I LET HIM COVER MY DIGNITY!" in bold block letters on a legal pad while Nate holds her shoulder and the duty supervisor sits across the desk deleting the overnight pool-deck entry from his computer]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/jul_2007_rrc_bates_harding_counselor_office_dignity_note_katie_nate.jpg)

"Katie, I'm agreeing with you," the supervisor said gently, tapping his keyboard and deleting the Tuesday afternoon poolside entry from my record on the spot. "That pool-deck entry is gone. Your regular counselor will still see the two of you tomorrow morning at ten o'clock regarding last night's eleven-o'clock seasonal closet write-up, since she's out of the office today, but as far as yesterday afternoon at the pool goes, you did the right thing looking out for your sister, Nathaniel."

"Back home in our apartment, we are at each other's side twenty-four hours a day," I told him bluntly before we unlocked our brakes to roll over to Mr. Alderman's classroom. "In case there's a meltdown or an emergency in the middle of the night, the other one is right there. We are not used to being apart—and we are not staying somewhere that treats keeping my sister safe like a rule violation."

Fifteen minutes later, when we rolled into the Web Applications Developer lab and told Tina, Sheila, and Jim that the poolside report had been deleted—while our ten-o'clock disciplinary meeting over getting locked in the seasonal closet was still on our counselor's calendar for Thursday morning—Tina immediately flipped open her sticky-noted Student Handbook to the residential discipline section and lowered her voice behind her glasses.

"Watch yourselves at ten o'clock tomorrow morning, you two," Tina warned us seriously. "Up until last night, the two of you were driving the staff crazy by bending the rules and lawyering the handbook without technically breaking a single written policy. Skipping the ten-forty-five Rec Hall departure and locking yourselves inside that seasonal closet after curfew, though, is the first time you actually broke a written rule. And since the night supervisor already saw last night that threatening to kick you out doesn't scare you, they're going to try to hit you tomorrow morning with a Level 1 restriction."

"What's a Level 1 restriction?" Katie asked, frowning past the white tape across her nose.

"Level 2 is where every new student starts in Barton Hall—you can go anywhere on campus freely without signing out, and if you leave campus you either need a signed yellow paper Pass or you sign up at the Rec Hall desk for a Center-sponsored trip to places like The Spot or ValueMart, while Level 3 over in Cantor Hall only has to sign out to leave campus and Level 4 can come and go off campus as they please without any pass or sign-out," Tina explained, tapping page eighteen of her handbook. "Level 1 is the disciplinary punishment tier. If they demote you to Level 1 tomorrow morning, they strip away all of your off-campus Pass and trip privileges for up to thirty days so you can't even ride the VATS bus or leave the campus gates, lock you into your separate dorm wings right after supper with flashlight bed checks every thirty minutes, and force you to sign a written Behavioral Contract ordering mandatory separation during meals, breaks, and recreation hours. And under Center rules, if you refuse to sign a Level 1 Behavioral Contract, they threaten to expel you for non-compliance and call your family to come pick you up."

Katie and I looked at each other across our wheelchair armrests, and the exact same fire lit up in both of our eyes.

"We will never sign a Level 1 restriction or a separation contract," I promised Tina flatly. "Not a single word of it."

"I dare anyone in that counseling office to try to make us sign a piece of paper ordering my brother and me to stay apart or locking us into separate wings after supper!" Katie said fiercely, her hand gripping mine across our armrests. "And if they tell us that refusing to sign their Level 1 contract means we're kicked out of the Center and they're calling our father in Alexandria to come pick us up, we'll look them straight in the eye and say, *'Go ahead!'* Dad will be in his pickup truck heading down Interstate 81 before they even hang up the phone."

## The Dormitory Room Mix-Up, Tina's Daybed in Luray, & Leaving RRC After Twelve Days

### Part 1: The Dormitory Room Mix-Up, Blind Red-Tape Room Reassignments, & A Sleepless Night for Natalie

**Date:** 2007-03-14 at 21:15 America/New_York

![Inside the 1970s red-brick dormitory lobby of Barton Hall at Roosevelt Rehabilitation Center on Wednesday night, March 14, 2007, twenty-one-year-old Nathaniel ('Nate') Prairie sits in his collapsible black manual wheelchair outfitted with a right-armrest joystick, spoked manual wheels with metal push-rims, and rear rubber push-handles with his silver laptop open on a small table in front of him; at the wooden front counter, Tina—a petite Caucasian middle-aged woman with glasses and straight jet-black hair—points firmly at the scrambled room-assignment ledger while evening residential staffer Herb scratches his head in confusion and classmate Jim inspects his reassigned plastic room keycard]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/jul_2007_rrc_cantor_hall_room_mixup_keycards_tina_herb_jim_nate.jpg)

#### Wednesday, March 14, 2007, 9:15 PM — When Red Tape Blindly Follows a Scrambled Room Roster

"What are you doing in here, Tina?" I asked in surprise at nine-fifteen on Wednesday night as the door to my men's dormitory room in Barton Hall clicked open and in walked our short, petite classmate with her glasses and straight jet-black hair, holding a newly issued plastic room keycard and an overnight bag.

Tina pushed her glasses up the bridge of her nose and held up the white plastic keycard with a look of sheer disbelief. "I thought something was fishy when the front desk handed me this keycard ten minutes ago and told me my room had been reassigned over here to Barton Hall."

Sitting in my wheelchair at my desk with my laptop webcam connected to Katie's room on the women's wing, I swiveled my laptop screen toward the doorway so the camera faced Tina. "Katie, look who just walked into my dorm room with a keycard."

Over the live video window, Katie's eyes went wide behind the white tape across her nose. Before Tina could say another word, the outer corridor door opened again and two more classmates from our Web Applications Developer cohort, Jim and Amanda, stepped into our hallway holding their own reassigned keycards and printed room slips.

"Wait a second—they moved Amanda and me out of Cantor Hall into the Barton Hall men's wing too?" Tina said, comparing the printed room numbers stapled to their keycards against Jim's slip. "Look at this roster sheet. The computer printout scrambled the men's and women's room numbers across the whole campus, and because of the ridiculous red tape around here, the front-desk staff just followed the printout blindly and handed out the keys anyway—putting women in men's rooms and men in women's wings without once using their brains to question the sheet!"

"Thank goodness I go home to Luray every Friday afternoon," Tina added, shaking her head in disgust, "because four nights a week of this bureaucracy is already pushing my limit."

"What's going on over there?" Katie asked nervously through my laptop speakers. "Do not close this chat window, Nate. I'd come over to your room right now, except I need to stay by my things in case someone comes to my room."

"Makes sense," Tina said, gesturing toward the doorway. "And nobody at that front desk is pushing us around tonight. Come on, Nate, Jim—let's roll out to the lobby counter and get this sorted out right now."

Rolling out to the Barton Hall lobby counter with my open laptop balanced on my lap tray, we found the only evening dorm staffer on duty: Herbert—whom every student on campus called Herb because he was the one genuinely decent staffer who organized weekend video-game tournaments in the lounge, even though he had zero administrative authority to override housing red tape.

![Inside the 1970s red-brick dormitory lobby of Barton Hall at Roosevelt Rehabilitation Center on Wednesday night, March 14, 2007, twenty-one-year-old Nathaniel ("Nate") Prairie sits in his collapsible black manual wheelchair outfitted with a right-armrest joystick, spoked manual wheels with metal push-rims, and rear rubber push-handles with his silver laptop open on a small table in front of him; at the wooden front counter, Tina—a petite Caucasian middle-aged woman with glasses and straight jet-black hair—points firmly at the scrambled room-assignment ledger while evening residential staffer Herb scratches his head in confusion and classmate Jim inspects his reassigned plastic room keycard]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/jul_2007_rrc_cantor_hall_room_mixup_keycards_tina_herb_jim_nate.jpg)

"I can't even get through to my boss on the phone because it's after hours, and the system locked me out of the housing database so I can't check the master roster either," Herb explained, holding up both hands helplessly behind the wooden counter as Tina tapped the scrambled room-assignment ledger. "Now, all of you in the IT class, I know you don't break the rules—"

"Thanks, Herb," Katie said through my laptop speaker.

At that exact second, on my laptop screen, the door to Katie's dorm room on the women's wing swung open.

"Katie, do you mind pointing the laptop toward the door?" Herb asked, leaning over the counter toward my screen. "I would like to see who it is."

Katie turned her laptop camera toward her doorway—and froze in terror as Chris, the exact guy who had broken her nose open and torn her swimsuit top in the therapeutic pool the afternoon before, stood in her doorway waving a reassigned plastic keycard and launching into an aggressive verbal altercation with her.

I didn't hesitate for half a second.

"Katie: pack your things and come to my room," I said into the microphone. Turning my wheelchair toward Tina and Jim, I said, "I'm going to go get my sister. Jim, please come with me just in case that boy tries something."

I looked straight back into the webcam lens where Chris stood in Katie's doorway and said coldly, "You touch my sister again and I will personally murder you." Then I flashed a single look across the counter at Herb that said plain as day: *Don't even think about arguing with me.*

Herb looked back at me with quiet respect. "You really care about your sister, don't you?"

I nodded once and pushed my joystick full forward down the corridor toward the women's wing, with Jim and two more classmates from our class, Bryan and Sean, striding right beside my wheelchair.

By the time we turned into Katie's hallway, Chris had bolted out the side exit and Katie was shoving her clothes into her open suitcase with trembling hands. Rolling straight inside, I helped her sweep the rest of her clothes and toiletries into her bags while Jim, Bryan, and Sean lifted her suitcases to carry them back to my room on the men's wing.

Tears were streaming down Katie's cheeks around her nasal bandage as she rolled her wheelchair into my room beside me. Taking one look at her face when he checked the doorway, Herb didn't say a word about Level 2 visitation rules; he could see Katie was one breath away from snapping.

Katie wrapped her arm tightly around my shoulders, and I looked straight at Herb. "I don't care what the rules state." Turning to Tina, who held the reassigned keycard to the second bed in my room, I asked, "Would you care if my sister and I shared my bed tonight?"

*"Campus Police to Barton Hall,"* crackled loudly over Herb's walkie-talkie.

Herb hurried out of the hallway toward the main lobby to answer the radio call, leaving Amanda, Bryan, Jim, Katie, Kim, Sarah, Sean, Tina, and me inside the room. Looking through her glasses at the frightened expression on Katie's face, Tina spoke with warm, unmistakable kindness.

"She needs you right now, Nate," Tina said. "I have no problems at all, as long as you two think you both can fit on that tiny bed."

Once the door closed and we sat together on the edge of my narrow mattress, I took my sister's shaking hands in mine. "Katie, what's wrong?"

Katie looked at me with wide, terrified blue eyes and squeaked, "Thank you for insisting I come down here."

Leaning close against my shoulder so her voice barely rose above a whisper, she trembled. "Nate... right before he opened my door, I heard crying down the hall. I think he hurt Natalie!"

Like a dam breaking, Katie buried her face against my neck and sobbed. Across the room, Tina, Sarah, and Jim exchanged grim, horrified looks: everyone on campus knew that while Natalie was chronologically an adult, cognitively she had the mind of a young child.

Tina sat down on the chair beside us, resting a steadying hand on Katie's arm while the rest of our classmates kept watch by the door.

"Would you like to change into your PJs?" I asked my sister gently.

"Please," she whispered, clutching my wrist and bringing me into the bathroom with her so she wouldn't have to be alone behind a closed door for even sixty seconds.

When we came back out in our pajamas, Tina looked at the two of us with quiet resolve. "You know I drive my compact sedan home to Luray every single Friday afternoon anyway," Tina said. "How about this weekend the two of you come with me and spend it at my house in Luray?"

"That might not be a bad idea," Katie whispered, wiping her eyes with her sleeve.

"Pack yourselves a duffel bag tomorrow, and we will leave on Friday at three-thirty sharp as soon as Mr. Alderman's class is over," Tina promised, reaching for the wall switch to turn off the overhead fluorescent light as Katie and I climbed onto my narrow twin mattress together.

"On one hand, I'm glad we are back together again," Katie whispered in the dark, pressing her forehead against my collarbone, "but yet on the other, I feel so weird and sick about what happened tonight."

I wrapped both arms securely around her and whispered back, "I can't wait to get out of here with Tina on Friday."

Neither of us slept a single wink all night, lying wide awake in each other's arms on that narrow institutional mattress until the sky outside the window turned gray.

***

#### Thursday, March 15, 2007, 6:15 AM — Canceled Write-Up Meetings & Sweeping Wednesday Night Under the Rug

At six-fifteen on Thursday morning, having not slept a minute, Katie, Tina, Sarah, and I dressed quietly and rolled out of my room into the main Barton Hall lobby, where Herb and the weekday morning supervisor, Kellie, were standing behind the counter surrounded by stacks of handwritten room rosters.

"Morning, you four," Kellie said in his deep voice, gesturing toward the dark computer terminal on his desk without a single word of reprimand about Katie sleeping in my room the night before. "Our housing database is still completely locked up from last night's scrambled bed reassignments, and the entire counseling wing is in an emergency staff meeting trying to sort out who is sleeping where—so Nathaniel, Katie, your counselor's ten-o'clock disciplinary meeting over Tuesday night's closet write-up is canceled."

"Thank you for letting us know," I said, keeping my left arm wrapped around my twin sister's shoulders as the four of us rolled back out of the lobby toward the dining hall breezeway.

Once the automatic glass doors slid shut behind us, Tina glanced over her glasses at Katie and me with a dry, knowing smirk. "Well, how about that. If their own room database hadn't blown up in their faces last night, your counselor would have been sliding a Level 1 restriction and a mandatory separation contract across her desk at ten o'clock this morning—and the two of you would already be on the phone calling your dad in Alexandria to come get you today."

"And instead, their own chaos just bought us today and tomorrow in Mr. Alderman's lab to copy the rest of the PHP and SQL curriculum onto our laptops before we head to Luray with you tomorrow afternoon," Katie whispered back, squeezing my hand.

Right outside the cafeteria doors, Katie gasped softly and pointed toward the concrete bench by the bushes. Sitting on the bench surrounded by three of her friends was Natalie, sobbing inconsolably and rocking back and forth.

"That thing... he pees from..." Natalie stammered through her tears, rubbing at her eyes like a hurting seven-year-old child who only understood that what had been done to her had caused sharp physical pain, with no adult comprehension of the violation itself or the lifelong weight of its consequences.

"I think... well... I don't even want to consider it," Katie whispered in horror beside me, her hand shaking in mine as Jim walked up behind us and saw the look on our faces. Every single one of us knew right then what Chris had done to Natalie before he had walked down the hall with that reassigned keycard to Katie's door.

"Katie, I'm so glad I insisted on you spending the night with me," I whispered, holding her hand tightly as the dining hall doors opened at six-thirty.

Carrying our trays to the far corner table away from the noise, Katie, Sarah, Tina, and I sat together in grim silence.

"What happened to Natalie last night—and Chris walking straight up to your door with a dorm keycard twenty-four hours after breaking your nose in the pool—is an absolute disgrace," Tina said quietly behind her glasses. "And watch: the center administration is going to drag its heels and bury the whole thing so they don't look bad in Richmond."

Trying to coax even a faint breath out of my pale sister, I tapped my plastic fork against the rock-hard gray square sitting on my plate that was supposed to be toast and asked rhetorically, "What is *this*?!"

Less than an hour later, as we rolled along the walkway from the dining hall toward Mr. Alderman's classroom at seven-fifty, we stopped by the curb and watched in stunned, furious silence as two RRC staffers escorted Chris out to a waiting passenger van by the front gate carrying his duffel bag—with not a single state trooper cruiser, sheriff's deputy, or pair of handcuffs in sight.

"Wait—they're just kicking him out and putting him in a van?" Tina said aloud on the sidewalk beside Katie's wheelchair, her voice shaking with anger. "He assaulted Katie in the pool on Tuesday, he attacked Natalie in the dorms last night during their own keycard mix-up, and instead of calling the State Police and having him arrested in handcuffs, the administration is just escorting him off the property and sweeping the whole thing under the rug so it doesn't show up on a state incident report?!"

"Look at the courtyard," I said bitterly as the eight-o'clock bell rang and classes resumed across campus as if nothing had happened at all, while Natalie's friends led her weeping toward the clinic. "They wouldn't even let Katie and me sleep in a hallway closet together without threatening to write us up, and they just let a predator walk out the front gate without calling the police."

### Part 2: Sharing the Daybed at Tina's House in Luray, Walking Out After Twelve Days, & Coming Home to Kempsville

**Date:** 2007-03-16 at 15:45 America/New_York

![In the student parking lot outside the 1960s and 1970s flat-roofed red-brick buildings of Roosevelt Rehabilitation Center in Fishersville, Virginia on Friday afternoon, March 16, 2007, twenty-one-year-old fraternal twins Katie (with a small white MedStrip and gauze bandage taped across the bridge of her nose from Tuesday's pool injury) and Nate Prairie sit side by side on the rear passenger bench seat of Tina's silver four-door compact sedan holding hands through the open rear door; at the open trunk of the car, Tina—a petite Caucasian middle-aged woman with glasses and straight jet-black hair—smiles back toward the twins as she easily lifts their collapsed black manual wheelchair frame (with spoked wheels, metal push-rims, rear rubber push-handles, and right-armrest joystick) into the trunk for the weekend drive up Route 340 to Luray]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/jul_2007_rrc_tina_compact_sedan_trunk_collapsing_wheelchairs_luray_trip.jpg)

#### Friday, March 16, 2007, 3:45 PM — Collapsing Our Wheelchairs into Tina's Compact Sedan & The Living-Room Daybed in Luray

"See how easy that is when you don't have two four-hundred-pound power bases to wrestle with?" Tina smiled back at Katie and me through her glasses at three-forty-five on Friday afternoon, standing at the open trunk of her silver four-door compact sedan in the Roosevelt Rehabilitation Center student parking lot.

Sitting side by side on the rear passenger bench seat holding hands through the open back door with our packed duffel bags and laptop cases tucked at our feet—and the white MedStrip and gauze bandage from Tuesday's pool assault still taped across the bridge of Katie's nose for the rest of the week—Katie and I watched as Tina unclipped the compact battery boxes from underneath our two folding wheelchairs, pulled straight up on the canvas seat straps to collapse both cross-brace frames flat, and lifted the folded frames—spoked push-rim wheels, rear rubber push-handles, and right-armrest joysticks and all—smoothly into her trunk side by side.

![In the student parking lot outside the 1960s and 1970s flat-roofed red-brick buildings of Roosevelt Rehabilitation Center in Fishersville, Virginia on Friday afternoon, March 16, 2007, twenty-one-year-old fraternal twins Katie (with a small white MedStrip and gauze bandage taped across the bridge of her nose from Tuesday's pool injury) and Nate Prairie sit side by side on the rear passenger bench seat of Tina's silver four-door compact sedan holding hands through the open rear door; at the open trunk of the car, Tina—a petite Caucasian middle-aged woman with glasses and straight jet-black hair—smiles back toward the twins as she easily lifts their collapsed black manual wheelchair frame (with spoked wheels, metal push-rims, rear rubber push-handles, and right-armrest joystick) into the trunk for the weekend drive up Route 340 to Luray]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/jul_2007_rrc_tina_compact_sedan_trunk_collapsing_wheelchairs_luray_trip.jpg)

"Dr. Carter knew what she was doing when she had us leave our full-size SwiftChairs back at the house in Virginia Beach," I said, letting out a long breath as Tina closed the trunk lid, climbed behind the steering wheel, and turned out of the campus gates onto Route 250 toward Route 340 North.

"Take a good look in the rearview mirror, you two," Tina said cheerfully as the flat-roofed 1960s and 1970s red-brick dormitories of Fishersville disappeared behind the tree line and the Blue Ridge Mountains rose to our right along the Shenandoah River. "Every Friday at three-thirty, I put that place in my mirror and don't think about a single clipboard until Monday morning."

An hour and fifteen minutes later, when Tina turned into her driveway in the quiet green valley of Luray and unfolded our wheelchairs by the front porch, rolling inside her sunlit house felt like stepping out of a monochrome prison into another world. In Tina's kitchen, a pot of homemade beef stew was simmering on the stove; in the living room, where afternoon sunlight slanted across a braided rug with not a single laminated institutional rule sign on the walls, Tina had already pulled out her wide living-room daybed and made it up with crisp cotton sheets, four fluffy pillows, and a thick patchwork quilt specifically for the two of us.

At ten-thirty that night, after eating two bowls apiece of real home-cooked stew and talking PHP arrays and SQL joins around Tina's kitchen table, Katie and I changed into our pajamas and climbed onto the wide living-room daybed together.

"Goodnight, you two—sleep as late as you want tomorrow morning, and nobody is knocking on any doors at eleven o'clock in my house," Tina said warmly, clicking off the hallway lamp on her way to her bedroom.

In the quiet dark of Tina's living room, Katie curled straight into my arms under the quilt, buried her face against my collarbone, and let out a long, shuddering sigh that released twelve solid days of tension all at once.

"Nate," Katie whispered, lacing her fingers tightly through mine, "I am never spending another night in Barton Hall. Twelve days of that place is more than enough for an entire lifetime."

I listened to the quiet mountain wind rustling the trees outside Tina's front window, holding my twin sister close.

"We don't have to go back, Katie," I whispered, rubbing her back under the quilt. "Before we shut down our laptops in Mr. Alderman's lab at three-thirty today, we copied the entire PHP 5 and SQL course syllabus and every textbook exercise onto both of our hard drives. We already have our associate degrees from the Community College of Hampton Roads. We don't need to stay locked up in Barton Hall as Level 2 clients begging for yellow Hall Passes—or stay at a center that sweeps what happened to Natalie under the rug just to protect whatever state funding they get for keeping their dorm beds and classroom seats filled—when we can master server-side PHP and SQL from home."

***

#### Sunday, March 18, 2007, 1:00 PM — Calling Dad to Pack Up Barton Hall & Returning to Our Routine in Virginia Beach

"I don't blame you two one bit," Tina said over hot pancakes and fresh apple juice at her dining table on Saturday morning, setting her coffee mug down and adjusting her glasses beneath her jet-black hair after Katie and I told her our decision and dialed Dad's number in Alexandria on speakerphone. "Between the aides grabbing your wheelchair push-handles during Voc Eval, that insulting ValueMart door-greeter pitch, keeping you stuck in Barton Hall on Level 2 with yellow Hall Passes, the Chickenshit Report after the pool, writing you up for sleeping in a closet, and the disgusting way the administration swept what Chris did to Natalie under the rug on Thursday, I wouldn't stay another night in those dorms either if I were in your shoes. You already copied Mr. Alderman's full PHP and SQL curriculum onto your laptops, and Sheila, Jim, and I are online every afternoon. We'll share every lecture note, review each other's database code over instant messenger, and build our projects together without a single dorm supervisor breathing down your necks."

"Listen to me, both of you," Dad's voice came through the speakerphone from his house on Sunset Drive in Alexandria, warm and fierce at the same time. "I couldn't be prouder of you for standing up for each other and walking away from a place that refused to respect your dignity or your bond. Stay right there at Tina's house today and rest up. Tomorrow morning I'm driving my pickup truck down Interstate 81, we'll stop by Fishersville just long enough to clear the rest of your clothes out of Barton Hall and drop your room keys on the front desk, and I'll bring you straight home to Virginia Beach."

At one o'clock on Sunday afternoon, March 18, 2007—exactly fourteen days after we had first rolled through the doors of Barton Hall—Dad backed his pickup truck up to the curb outside Barton Hall while Tina parked her compact sedan right beside him. The second Dad stepped out of his truck and saw the white MedStrip and gauze bandage still taped across the bridge of his daughter's nose from Tuesday's pool assault, his jaw set into solid granite as he wrapped both of us in a fierce hug. Within twenty minutes, Dad, Jim, and Tina had loaded the rest of our suitcases from our dorm rooms into the bed of the pickup truck, and Katie and I rolled side by side up to the Barton Hall front counter.

Without waiting for a single exit interview or the canceled Thursday counselor write-up meeting over the hallway closet, Katie and I dropped our Level 2 room keys onto the wooden blotter simultaneously.

"We're checking out permanently," Katie told the startled Sunday desk clerk, before both of us spun our wheelchairs around, rolled out the automatic glass doors into the sunshine, and hugged Tina, Sheila, and Jim tightly in the parking lot.

"Log onto instant messenger as soon as you get unpacked down at the coast," Tina told us, squeezing Katie's hand and then mine before we transferred into the cab of Dad's pickup truck. "Module Four on database normalization starts Monday morning at nine sharp, and Sheila, Jim, and I expect your code in the shared folder!"

"Count on it!" Katie grinned out the passenger window as Dad pulled out of the lot and headed east toward Afton Mountain and Interstate 64.

"Are you sure it's no trouble for us to move back into the Arvin Road house while you're working up in Tysons Corner during the week, Dad?" I asked as the pickup climbed toward the Blue Ridge tunnel.

"Trouble? Nate, that's the entire reason I kept the Virginia Beach house when I bought the place on Sunset Drive in Alexandria and updated my driver's license," Dad said, reaching across the console to pat my knee and Katie's shoulder. "I bought that brick ranch on Arvin Road off Indian River Road and Military Highway from our old landlord years ago so the two of you would always have your own ramp, your own walk-in closet sanctuary, and the Kempsville streets and bus routes you know by heart. That house is yours for as long as you want it."

When Dad pulled into the driveway on Arvin Road in Virginia Beach at dusk that Sunday evening and unlocked the front door at the top of the aluminum wheelchair ramp, Katie and I transferred out of the travel frames right back into our full-size SwiftChair power wheelchairs, rolled side by side to our familiar dining table, and opened our laptop lids together just as Tina, Sheila, and Jim's names lit up green on our screens.

# Unofficial Homeowners: Back Home in Virginia Beach (2007–2008)

## Arvin Road, Crossing Without a Crosswalk, Horizontal IDs on Route 12, & Yearly Passes at Fairlawn

### Part 1: Unofficial Homeowners, One Bedroom and One Office, & The Closet We Both Know We'll Use

**Date:** 2007-03-18 at 18:30 America/New_York

![Inside the shared bedroom that had been Katie's room since 2001 at the single-story brick ranch on Arvin Road off Indian River Road and Military Highway in Virginia Beach on Sunday evening, March 18, 2007, twenty-one-year-old fraternal twins Katie (with the white MedStrip and gauze bandage from Tuesday's pool injury across the bridge of her nose) and Nate Prairie sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs holding hands as their father David finishes smoothing the navy-and-slate-blue comforter on their newly installed queen-size bed beneath the framed blue butterfly print—while to their right, the wide bedroom closet doors stand open revealing a plush sleeping bag and four pillows laid out across the clean closet floor as all three share a warm, knowing smile]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/mar_2007_dyer_place_shared_bedroom_queen_bed_and_closet_sanctuary_katie_nate_david.jpg)

#### Sunday, March 18, 2007, 6:30 PM — Unofficial Homeowners & The Address on Our State ID Cards

"Oh, thank goodness," Katie breathed at six-thirty on Sunday evening the second she slid off the folding manual travel chair onto the padded contoured seat of her full-size black SwiftChair inside our front foyer, resting her right hand on the familiar fingertip joystick. "No rear push-handles for strangers to grab, no clunky clamp-on battery box underneath, and no yellow Level 2 Hall Pass required to roll down our own hallway."

"Amen to that," I said, transferring into my own full-size SwiftChair right beside hers and powering on my controller as Dad lifted our two collapsed manual travel frames—spoked push-rim wheels and all—and tucked them neatly into the back of the front hall utility closet in case Tina or another friend ever picked us up in a compact car.

Rolling side by side out of the foyer into the warm kitchen of our single-story brick ranch on Arvin Road at the corner of Indian River Road, Katie and I stopped by the dining table and simply took in the quiet. Outside the kitchen window, the familiar neighborhood streetlamps of Kempsville were flickering on in the March dusk.

Dad walked in from the garage carrying the last of our suitcases from the bed of his pickup truck, set two newly cut brass house keys and a blue leather household binder on the table between our wheelchairs, and pulled up a wooden dining chair across from us.

"Alright, you two," Dad said warmly, opening the front flap of the binder to show us the printed account sheet and sliding two reloadable Meridian debit cards across the laminate tabletop toward our hands. "Before we start moving furniture and before I have to head back up to Alexandria tonight for work in Tysons Corner tomorrow morning, let's go over how everything works here so neither of you has to worry about a single bill. The mortgage on this house, the City of Virginia Beach real-estate taxes, the homeowner's insurance, the electric bill, the water and sewer, and the high-speed cable internet are all set to automatic payment straight out of my main checking account up in Northern Virginia. You don't ever have to touch a utility bill."

He tapped the two debit cards sitting in front of Katie and me.

"Every Friday morning when my paycheck clears, your grocery and spending money goes straight into this joint checking account," Dad continued. "Until your own software and web-development work starts paying what you want it to pay, every dime of your groceries, bus passes, computer parts, and spending money is covered. As far as day-to-day life goes, the two of you are the unofficial homeowners of our house here on Arvin Road."

Katie reached into her crossbody bag, unzipped her wallet, and pulled out her laminated Virginia Department of Motor Vehicles identification card, setting it down on the table beside her debit card.

"Look at the address line, Nate," Katie smiled, tapping the plastic card with her fingernail.

I pulled my own wallet out of my jeans pocket and laid my Virginia State ID card right beside hers. Printed across the front of both cards in crisp black DMV block letters was the exact Arvin Road address in Virginia Beach where we were sitting right now.

"We never even have to go to the DMV to change our address," I said, grinning across the table at Dad. "That's the exact address we've had on our State ID cards ever since the three of us left Mom back in September 2001. Neither of us ever bothered updating our IDs when Katie was up in Williamsburg or when I was over in Norfolk, because this house was always home base."

"And because we turned eighteen right here at this table in April 2003 when we were seniors at Northwood High," Katie added, her blue eyes lighting up as she connected the dots, "our Virginia Beach voter registrations at the Kempsville precinct have been anchored to this exact address for four straight years too."

"Which means as far as the Commonwealth of Virginia and the City of Virginia Beach are concerned," Dad chuckled, patting both of our hands across the table, "you never left. Now—I've still got three hours before I need to get on Interstate 64 and head up to Alexandria, and we've got three bedrooms down that hallway to set up the way you two want them. Tell the moving crew what the floorplan is."

***

#### 7:15 PM — Reconfiguring the Three Bedrooms: Dad's Room, Our Dual-Desk Office, & The Queen Bed With the Closet Sanctuary

Katie and I exchanged a single glance across our wheelchair armrests—having already mapped out every square foot of the hallway during the drive down from Luray in the cab of Dad's pickup truck—and rolled side by side down the hardwood corridor with Dad walking right behind us.

"First," I said, pausing outside the open door of the master bedroom at the end of the hall, "the master bedroom stays a hundred percent yours, Dad. Whenever you drive down from Alexandria on the weekends or for holidays, or whenever you have work down in Hampton Roads and need a place to sleep, your room and your bed are right here waiting for you."

"Deal," Dad smiled. "What about the two bedrooms you two have had since 2001?"

Katie released her joystick brake and rolled three feet left to the doorway of the middle bedroom—the room that had been mine during high school—before turning to point across the hall to the room that had been hers since 2001, where the framed watercolor print of a blue butterfly still hung on the cream drywall.

"After twelve days of Barton Hall forcing us onto separate wings every night at eleven o'clock," Katie said firmly, her fingers lacing through mine between our chairs, "Nate and I made our decision together. We are living together in this house as brother and sister, and we don't want two separate sleeping bedrooms anymore. We're going to sleep in the room that was my bedroom, and put the queen-size bed in there."

"And the bedroom that was my room," I picked up seamlessly, gesturing into my old room across the hall, "becomes our office. If we take my old twin bed frame out to the garage storage bay, we have a whole twelve-by-twelve room along the front window where we can put two wide computer desks side by side, wire our ethernet switch and our local Linux testing server right into the cable modem, and roll both of our SwiftChairs up next to each other all day while we work through Mr. Alderman's PHP and SQL modules with Tina, Sheila, and Jim."

"And one more thing inside our bedroom," Katie added softly, looking up at Dad with earnest blue eyes as she pointed toward the wide double doors of her bedroom closet. "Inside the closet, we want to clear the floor completely clean and put our thick sleeping bag and four pillows down on the carpet—so whenever we want that quiet, confined space together to feel completely secure, it's already set up waiting for us."

Dad looked at the two of us holding hands between our wheelchairs, and his expression softened with unmistakable fatherly pride and understanding. He didn't ask a single skeptical question, didn't lecture us about "normal" adult bedrooms, and didn't bat an eye.

"Then let's get to work," Dad said, rolling up the sleeves of his flannel shirt.

For the next hour and a half, the three of us transformed the hallway. First, Dad unbolted the steel rails of my old twin bed, stacked the frame neatly against the dry wall of the garage, and helped us slide two sturdy six-foot laminate worktables flush against each other along the wall of my old bedroom. While Katie organized our spiral notebooks and reference manuals on the lower bookshelf that we could reach easily from our wheelchair seats, I plugged our surge protectors, gigabit switch, and laptop docking cables underneath the desks—testing the clearance so both of our SwiftChairs could roll straight under the tabletop side by side with less than an inch between our armrests.

Across the hall in Katie's room, Dad carried in the queen box spring and mattress, centered the headboard directly beneath the framed blue butterfly print, and helped us pull on the fitted cotton sheets and the soft navy-and-slate-blue queen comforter set we had bought together at Chesapeake Bay Mall back in November 2005.

Then Dad stepped over to the wide bedroom closet, moved the low shoe rack and spare boxes into the hall storage cupboard, vacuumed the closet carpet from corner to corner, and helped us spread our thick double sleeping bag and quilted pad across the floor of the closet, banking four plush pillows in a neat row against the interior wall.

![Inside the shared bedroom that had been Katie's room since 2001 at the single-story brick ranch on Arvin Road off Indian River Road and Military Highway in Virginia Beach on Sunday evening, March 18, 2007, twenty-one-year-old fraternal twins Katie (with the white MedStrip and gauze bandage from Tuesday's pool injury across the bridge of her nose) and Nate Prairie sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs holding hands as their father David finishes smoothing the navy-and-slate-blue comforter on their newly installed queen-size bed beneath the framed blue butterfly print—while to their right, the wide bedroom closet doors stand open revealing a plush sleeping bag and four pillows laid out across the clean closet floor as all three share a warm, knowing smile]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/mar_2007_dyer_place_shared_bedroom_queen_bed_and_closet_sanctuary_katie_nate_david.jpg)

Stepping back with his hands on his hips, Dad looked from the freshly made navy-and-slate-blue queen bed in the center of the bedroom over to the open closet doors, where the sleeping bag and four pillows sat tucked inside the quiet three-by-six-foot alcove.

A slow, knowing grin spread across Dad's face, and Katie and I started laughing right along with him.

"Now, that queen bed looks mighty sharp sitting there in the middle of the room," Dad chuckled, shaking his head affectionately as he looked down at the two of us, "even if all three of us in this room know perfectly well that you two are probably going to sleep in that closet every single night."

"Hey, the queen bed is great for reading code books in the afternoon and folding laundry," Katie giggled, her cheeks warming as she squeezed my hand, "and the closet doesn't have any windows or hallway noise."

"And nobody in this house is ever going to yank the closet door open at eleven o'clock with a flashlight," I said quietly, looking at the soft pillows tucked inside the alcove.

"Not in your house, Nate," Dad said firmly, resting a hand on my shoulder and then on Katie's. "In this house, you sleep wherever the two of you feel safest."

***

#### 9:45 PM — Dad Heads Back to Alexandria, Locking Our Front Door, & Our First Night Back in the Closet

After a quick eight-thirty run across Indian River Road in Dad's pickup truck to the Market Square supermarket to load the kitchen refrigerator and pantry with two gallons of cold milk, cartons of chocolate milk, two twelve-packs of ginger ale, cereal boxes, bread, sandwich turkey, and frozen dinners, Katie and I rolled out onto the front porch at the top of our aluminum wheelchair ramp at quarter to ten to see Dad off.

"I'll call you both tomorrow evening on my way home from Tysons Corner—and I've already cleared Tuesday afternoon on my calendar so I can drive back down and be right there in the exam room with you at Dr. Carter's office when she checks Katie's nose and takes that bandage off," Dad said, bending down in the cool March night air to wrap Katie and me in a tight three-way hug at the top of the ramp. "Have fun jumping into Module Four with Tina, Sheila, and Jim in the morning—and enjoy having your house back."

"Drive safe up I-95, Dad, and call us when you get to Alexandria," Katie told him, hugging his neck before waving from her wheelchair as he climbed into the cab of his pickup truck.

We sat side by side at the top of the aluminum ramp, holding hands as Dad backed down the driveway, tapped his horn twice in a soft goodbye, and turned off Arvin Road onto Indian River Road toward Military Highway and Interstate 64.

Once the red taillights disappeared behind the pine trees at the corner, we wheeled back across the threshold into the warm foyer, pushed the solid wooden front door shut, and turned the brass deadbolt until it clicked firmly into place.

For the first time in our adult lives, the entire house was ours.

Rolling side by side down the quiet hallway past our newly wired dual-desk office, we brushed our teeth together at the bathroom sink, turned into our bedroom, and clicked off the overhead ceiling fixture until only the warm amber glow of the small nightstand lamp illuminated the room.

Right in front of us sat the pristine navy-and-slate-blue queen bed. Three feet to our right stood the open doors of the bedroom closet, where our thick sleeping bag and four plush pillows waited in the quiet, enclosed shadows.

Even with our own front door deadbolted behind us, both of our nervous systems were still raw—still shaken, scared, upset, and angry over those twelve days at Roosevelt Rehabilitation Center, from the pool and Wednesday night's keycard terror to the staffer yanking the Barton Hall closet door open at eleven o'clock and writing us up for holding each other.

Katie looked at the queen bed, looked over at the open closet doorway, and reached for the hem of her shirt.

"Closet?" I whispered.

"Closet," Katie whispered back without half a second's hesitation. "And no pajamas tonight, Nate. Just us."

We rolled our two SwiftChairs right up to the edge of the open closet doorway, parked them side by side with our armrests touching, switched off both joystick controllers, and helped each other slip out of our clothes, folding them neatly across our wheelchair seats. Lowering ourselves smoothly inside our single shared sleeping bag on the carpeted closet floor, I reached out and pulled the closet door almost all the way shut until just a thin ribbon of warm light filtered across the carpet, zipped the sleeping bag up around our shoulders, and wrapped both of my arms tightly around my twin sister, skin to skin.

Pressing her warm cheek against my bare chest and tangling her legs with mine inside the dark, enclosed space—doing the exact thing that would have gotten us written up and thrown out of Barton Hall—Katie let out a long, trembling breath that finally melted the last knot of Fishersville tension from her shoulders. Holding each other close while the queen bed out in the bedroom sat completely untouched, we drifted straight off to sleep in our own closet, in our own home, where nobody in the world could ever separate us again.

### Part 2: Dr. Carter's Exam Room, Skin to Skin in the Closet, & No Crosswalks at Military and Indian River

**Date:** 2007-03-20 at 14:00 America/New_York

![Inside a warm ground-floor examination room at Dr. Evelyn Carter's family medicine practice in Virginia Beach on Tuesday afternoon, March 20, 2007, twenty-one-year-old fraternal twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs holding hands tightly across the gap between their chairs with their father David standing supportively right behind them while Dr. Evelyn Carter, seated on a rolling stool in a white lab coat and blue nitrile gloves, gently peels the seven-day white MedStrip and gauze bandage off the healed bridge of Katie's nose]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/mar_2007_dr_carter_office_medstrip_removal_annual_physical_katie_nate_david.jpg)

#### Tuesday, March 20, 2007, 2:00 PM — Dr. Evelyn Carter's Exam Room, Peeling Off the Seven-Day Bandage, & Our Annual Physicals With Dad

"You're safe right here with me and Dad, Katie," I whispered at two o'clock on Tuesday afternoon inside Exam Room Two at Dr. Evelyn Carter's family medicine office on Kempsville Road, keeping both of my arms wrapped tightly around my twin sister's shoulders across the gap between our parked SwiftChairs.

With our inner armrests flipped up and out of the way so our wheelchairs could sit flush against each other, Katie buried her cheek against my collarbone and hugged me back with both arms just as tightly. Right behind our chairs, having driven his pickup truck down from Northern Virginia that morning so he wouldn't miss a minute of the appointment, Dad stood with one steady hand resting on my shoulder and the other on Katie's back.

Even in Dr. Carter's familiar ground-floor office—where she had been taking care of the two of us ever since Dad moved us into the brick ranch on Arvin Road back in the autumn of 2001—just sitting under fluorescent clinical lights next to a paper-lined examination table only seven days after the Bates-Harding clinic nurses had taped Katie's split nasal bridge had both of our nervous systems on high alert. Holding onto each other in a full two-arm embrace was the only way to keep the memory of Fishersville out of the room.

A gentle two-beat knock sounded at the wooden door before Dr. Evelyn Carter stepped inside carrying both of our thick manila medical charts and a stainless-steel tray with sterile saline packets and gauze pads. Seeing Katie and me locked in a tight two-arm hug between our wheelchairs with the white gauze-and-paper-tape dressing across the bridge of Katie's nose, Dr. Carter didn't rush us or ask us to pull apart. Instead, she pushed the exam room door firmly shut, set her charts on the counter, and rolled her cushioned stool over in front of us with quiet, unmistakable concern.

"Take all the time you two need," Dr. Carter said softly, looking from Katie and me up to Dad. "David told me on the phone yesterday that he brought you both home from Fishersville for good on Sunday, and that a male client struck Katie in the face in the therapeutic pool last Tuesday. Tell me what happened up there."

Still holding onto each other, Katie and I told Dr. Carter everything while Dad stood right behind us—starting on our very first afternoon when an aide grabbed Katie's manual wheelchair push-handles without asking and tried to steer her down the women's wing like a shopping cart, and going right through the Vocational Evaluator who looked at our accredited computer-science associate degrees from the Community College of Hampton Roads and pitched us a partnership to work as door greeters at the Waynesboro ValueMart. We told her how they kept us stuck on Level 2 in Barton Hall begging for signed yellow paper Hall Passes because moving to Cantor Hall required earning Level 3; how Chris struck Katie in the face and ripped her swimsuit top in the ninety-two-degree pool while a poolside staffer wrote me up on the morning Chickenshit Report for covering my sister's bare chest while she held her bleeding nose with both hands; how a night supervisor unlocked a hallway seasonal storage closet with a master key after the eleven o'clock bed check and accused us of having sex when we were in full street clothes holding each other on bags of curtains; and how the administration scrambled on Thursday to sweep Chris's Wednesday night keycard assault on Natalie under the rug without calling the police just to keep their dorm beds and classroom seats filled.

"We never want to set foot inside Roosevelt Rehabilitation Center ever again, Dr. Carter," Katie said fiercely, lifting her chin from my shoulder as her blue eyes met the doctor's.

"Not for a single day," I added right beside her, my arm still around her waist. "We already have our associate degrees, and we copied the entire PHP and SQL web-development curriculum onto our laptops before we left on Friday. We just want to go home to our house on Arvin Road and live together where no one can ever tell us that we aren't allowed to share a bed or even a closet!"

Dr. Carter's jaw tightened with visible indignation as she uncapped her fountain pen, opened both of our medical charts on her lap, and wrote several firm lines in black ink across the top of each clinical summary sheet.

"Then neither of you will ever set foot in that place again," Dr. Carter said firmly, looking straight at Dad and then back at the two of us. "I am documenting right here in both of your permanent medical files that any institutional program that forcibly separates the two of you, threatens you with isolation contracts for seeking sensory grounding together, or allows staff to grab your wheelchairs without consent is medically contraindicated and actively harmful to your cerebral palsy spasticity and autistic regulation. Your home on Arvin Road is exactly where you belong."

"Thank you, Evelyn," Dad said quietly, his hand squeezing Katie's shoulder.

"Now, Katie," Dr. Carter smiled warmly, snapping on a pair of blue nitrile gloves and opening a warm sterile saline swab, "let's take a look at the bridge of that nose and get those seven-day wound-closure strips off your face so you don't have to look at them in the mirror anymore."

Taking a slow breath together, Katie and I eased out of our tight two-arm hug so Katie could sit upright facing the doctor—and immediately relaxed to holding hands, lacing my right fingers through her left fingers across the gap between our wheelchairs while Dad kept his hand on her shoulder.

![Inside a warm ground-floor examination room at Dr. Evelyn Carter's family medicine practice in Virginia Beach on Tuesday afternoon, March 20, 2007, twenty-one-year-old fraternal twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs holding hands tightly across the gap between their chairs with their father David standing supportively right behind them while Dr. Evelyn Carter, seated on a rolling stool in a white lab coat and blue nitrile gloves, gently peels the seven-day white MedStrip and gauze bandage off the healed bridge of Katie's nose]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/mar_2007_dr_carter_office_medstrip_removal_annual_physical_katie_nate_david.jpg)

Never letting go of my hand, Katie held completely still as Dr. Carter moistened the paper tape with warm saline, lifted the outer white gauze square away, and then carefully peeled off the three narrow, sterile MedStrip wound-closure strips that the Bates-Harding clinic nurses had taped across the split skin on the bony bridge of her nose the previous Tuesday.

Switching on her penlight, Dr. Carter examined the bridge of Katie's nose closely, gently palpated the nasal bone and cartilage, and checked inside both nostrils.

"That knitted together beautifully, Katie," Dr. Carter said, clicking off her penlight and handing Katie a small hand mirror from the counter. "Keeping those MedStrips dry for the full seven days did the trick. The split skin across the bridge has closed into a clean, flat seam that will fade completely over the next couple of weeks, your septum is straight, and the hairline contusion on the nasal bone is stable and healing right on schedule."

Katie tilted the small mirror toward her eyes, touched the smooth bridge of her nose lightly with her free right fingertips, and beamed at me across our joined hands. "Look, Nate—no more bandage! And right in time for us to go to the Buckner Boulevard DMV on Friday to get our horizontal twenty-one-and-over State ID pictures taken!"

"And speaking of turning twenty-two on April eighth," Dr. Carter said, glancing down at the preventive-care tabs on our two open charts with a warm smile, "you two are less than three weeks away from your annual physical date anyway. Since you're both already sitting right here in my exam room and David is here with you before he drives back up to Alexandria tonight, how would you feel about knocking out both of your annual physicals right now so you don't have to make a second trip next month?"

Katie and I looked at each other across our wheelchairs. As long as nobody asked us to let go of each other's hand, getting our annual checkups done in one sitting meant uninterrupted weeks at home in our new office on Arvin Road.

"Let's do it right now," Katie said, and I nodded right along with her.

For the next twenty-five minutes, with Dad sitting right beside us and our fingers stayed laced together across our wheelchair armrests, Dr. Carter completed both of our annual physicals side by side—checking our blood pressure cuffs on our outer arms, listening to our hearts and lungs with her warmed stethoscope, checking our ears and reflexes, and evaluating our lower-extremity cerebral palsy muscle tone and seated posture in our full-size SwiftChairs. By two-forty-five, she had signed off on a clean bill of health for both of us, and after Dad took us out for an early dinner and gave us one more fierce hug at the top of our aluminum porch ramp on Arvin Road before heading back up Interstate 64 to Alexandria for the rest of the workweek, our house was completely ours again.

***

#### Wednesday, March 21, 2007, 8:30 AM — Waking Up in Our Closet Sanctuary & Morning PHP With Tina, Sheila, and Jim

![Inside their shared bedroom on Arvin Road in Kempsville in March 2007, while the wooden queen bed beneath the framed blue butterfly print sits completely untouched behind their two parked black SwiftChair power wheelchairs, twenty-one-year-old twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie cuddle closely in a soothing two-arm embrace inside their shared sleeping bag on the floor of the open walk-in closet.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/mar_2007_arvin_road_bedroom_closet_full_cuddle_sanctuary_katie_nate.jpg)

"You're warm," Katie murmured sleepily at eight-thirty on Wednesday morning, her bare shoulder pressed tightly against my chest inside our single shared sleeping bag on the carpeted floor of our bedroom closet.

I kissed the top of her blonde hair in the quiet dark and kept my arms wrapped securely around her waist. Outside in the main bedroom, three feet past the nearly closed closet door, the navy-and-slate-blue comforter on our queen-size bed hadn't been unfolded once since Dad helped us make it on Sunday night.

Neither of us had the slightest interest in sleeping out on that open mattress. Even after telling Dr. Carter everything yesterday afternoon, our minds were still raw—still carrying the lingering fear of Chris standing in Katie's doorway with a reassigned dorm keycard after hurting Natalie, the fury of watching the administration escort him into a van without calling the police, and the humiliation of a night-shift staffer yanking the Barton Hall hallway closet door open at eleven o'clock to write us up for holding each other. Waking up undressed together inside our own dark, enclosed closet on Arvin Road—feeling each other's steady breathing skin to skin and knowing we were doing the exact thing that would have gotten us punished and separated at Roosevelt Rehabilitation Center—was the only medicine that kept the nightmares away.

"Nobody knocking on the door," I whispered against her temple. "Nobody checking Hall Passes."

"Just us," Katie whispered back, hugging my ribs tightly for another full minute—her face finally free of the seven-day nasal bandage Dr. Carter had peeled off the afternoon before—until we unzipped the sleeping bag, reached up to pull our folded shirts and jeans off the seats of our parked SwiftChairs just outside the closet doorway, and transferred up into our chairs.

After helping each other shower on the padded transfer bench in the hall bathroom and pouring two bowls of cereal with cold milk in the kitchen, we rolled across the hardwood hallway into my old bedroom—now officially our dual-desk software office.

At nine o'clock sharp, right as we slid our two SwiftChairs side by side underneath the twelve-foot span of laminate worktables with our armrests touching, our instant-messenger client chimed. On our screens, Tina, Sheila, and Jim popped online from the Web Applications Developer classroom back in Fishersville.

"Look at the two of you sitting in a real office without a single yellow Level 2 badge in sight!" Tina typed into the group chat window, waving quietly at her webcam before her instructor walked past the front whiteboard. "Mr. Alderman just handed out the Module Four exercise sheet on relational foreign keys and PHP session arrays. Check your shared folder—I just uploaded the prompt!"

For the next few days, while morning sunlight slanted through the front blinds onto our keyboards, Katie and I worked on a couple of the copied PHP and SQL exercises unofficially from home while chatting with Tina, Sheila, and Jim. We didn't care one bit that rolling out of Roosevelt Rehabilitation Center after twelve days meant we were technically RRC dropouts who had never officially completed the program; both of us already held an Advanced Studies Diploma from Virginia Beach City Public Schools at Northwood High School and an accredited Associate of Applied Science degree from the Community College of Hampton Roads, and we had realized during our first week in Fishersville that an RRC piece of paper meant nothing in the real world compared to our associate degrees and actual working code.

Even better, it didn't take long working on those copied RRC modules unofficially from home before Katie and I looked at each other across our desks and decided to stop following RRC's rigid classroom exercises altogether and start doing our own thing—staying friends with Tina, Sheila, and Jim on instant messenger while we focused one hundred percent on rebuilding our transit blog, Ideas for Coastal Virginia Transit, from the ground up into a custom database-driven PHP web application where every route timetable, transfer window, and municipal service comparison across all six Hampton Roads cities could be queried dynamically.

***

#### 2:15 PM — Crossing Without a Crosswalk to Market Square

When we rolled into the kitchen at two-fifteen that afternoon to make turkey sandwiches for lunch, I opened the refrigerator door and held up the plastic milk jug. Less than half an inch of milk sloshed across the bottom, and the bread bag on the counter was down to the two heel slices.

"First solo grocery run without Dad's pickup truck," Katie said, glancing out the kitchen window toward the corner of Arvin Road and Indian River Road. "Good thing there's a Market Square supermarket right across the street."

"Let's see how much our two chairs can haul in one trip," I grinned, rolling back to the hall closet to grab two heavy-duty canvas backpack panniers and two insulated reusable grocery totes.

We slipped the padded straps of the backpack panniers securely over the contoured high backs of both of our SwiftChairs, tucked the folded insulated totes beside our thighs, checked that our battery gauges showed all green bars, and rolled out the front door and down our aluminum porch ramp into the crisp March afternoon.

Exiting the house, we made a right onto quiet Arvin Road and another right onto the sidewalk along Indian River Road, rolling west toward the major signalized intersection where Indian River Road met eight-lane Military Highway.

Across the street sat the brick storefront of the Market Square grocery plaza.

Getting across the asphalt to reach it, however, made both of us stop our wheelchairs dead at the concrete curb cut and stare.

![At the busy multi-lane intersection of Indian River Road and Military Highway in Virginia Beach on Wednesday afternoon, March 21, 2007, twenty-one-year-old fraternal twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs at the concrete curb cut beside the traffic signal pole where heavy traffic roars across bare asphalt with zero painted crosswalks between the CVTA Route 12 and Route 15 bus stops and the Market Square grocery plaza across the street]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/mar_2007_indian_river_military_hwy_no_crosswalk_grocery_run_katie_nate.jpg)

"Wait a second, Nate," Katie said, raising her voice over the deafening roar of eighteen-wheelers, dump trucks, and commuter sedans barreling through the intersection. "Look at the pavement between our curb cut and the curb cut on the other side of the street."

I looked down at the wide, oil-stained expanse of multi-lane asphalt.

The intersection had overhead traffic lights. It had sloped concrete curb cuts poured into the corners. Right behind us stood bus stops for CVTA Routes 12 and 15 where transit riders got off the bus every half hour to walk home or buy groceries.

Yet across the entire intersection of Military Highway and Indian River Road, there was not a single painted white crosswalk stripe—and no pedestrian countdown head—anywhere on the pavement.

"How do you pour wheelchair curb cuts at a major intersection with two bus routes and a supermarket across the street," I asked in disbelief as a pickup truck whipped a fast right turn on red two feet in front of our footplates without even glancing at the sidewalk, "and not paint a single crosswalk line to tell drivers that people cross here?!"

"Stay right beside my left wheel, and don't move an inch until the through-lane turns red and I check every right-turning bumper," Katie said, her hand steady on her joystick.

We waited through an entire two-minute signal cycle until the cross-traffic halted, made direct eye contact with the driver at the front of the turning lane so he wouldn't gun his engine into us, and pushed our joysticks full forward side by side across the bare, unmarked lanes of asphalt. The second our front casters climbed the opposite concrete curb cut into the Market Square parking lot, both of us let out a breath at the exact same time.

Inside the bright, fluorescent aisles of Market Square, our two-wheelchair shopping system worked like clockwork. Instead of struggling with a clumsy metal shopping cart that couldn't be steered alongside a joystick controller, Katie held the open insulated tote bags on her lap while I pulled a gallon of milk, two cartons of chocolate milk, loaves of whole-wheat bread, sliced turkey, cheddar cheese, apples, and boxes of pasta off the low and middle shelves.

At the checkout register, after swiping the joint checking debit card Dad had given us on Sunday night, we balanced the load evenly between our two chairs like a pair of cargo engineers: the gallon of milk and canned goods went into the heavy canvas backpack slung over the back of my SwiftChair, the chocolate milk, soda six-pack, and frozen boxes went into Katie's rear pack, and the lighter bags of bread and fruit rode flat across our laps inside the insulated totes.

After waiting through two more heavy traffic cycles to cross the unmarked, crosswalk-free lanes of Indian River Road back to the Arvin Road corner and unpacking our haul into the kitchen fridge, Katie didn't even take her jacket off before rolling straight into our office bedroom and tapping my monitor.

"Pull up the new PHP admin panel for Ideas for Coastal Virginia Transit, Nate," Katie said, her blue eyes bright with purpose. "We just took our first solo grocery trip from Arvin Road, and our readers—and the traffic engineers at Virginia Beach City Hall—are going to read all about what happens when you put CVTA Route 12 and Route 15 bus stops and a grocery store at Military Highway and Indian River Road with curb cuts, heavy traffic, and zero crosswalks."

### Part 3: Crossing Both Roads for Route 12, Buckner Boulevard DMV, & Horizontal State IDs on the Spot

**Date:** 2007-03-23 at 09:40 America/New_York

![Inside the Virginia DMV Customer Service Center on Buckner Boulevard in Virginia Beach on Friday morning, March 23, 2007, twenty-one-year-old fraternal twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs at the photo counter in front of the blue DMV backdrop as a friendly clerk hands them their warm, freshly printed horizontal 21-and-over Virginia State ID cards on the spot alongside their old 2001 vertical Under-21 cards]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/mar_2007_buckner_blvd_dmv_vertical_to_horizontal_state_ids_katie_nate.jpg)

#### Friday, March 23, 2007, 9:40 AM — Crossing Both Roads to Catch the Southbound Route 12

"Look at how baby-faced we were in these pictures," Katie laughed on Friday morning as we sat side by side in the hallway by the front door, holding up our two vertical Virginia State identification cards before slipping them into our lanyard pouches.

Both of us had gotten those original vertical Under-21 State ID cards back in October 2001, right after we turned sixteen and moved with Dad into this house on Arvin Road when he was first renting it from the landlord—years before he eventually bought the place outright. Across the top of each vertical card ran the bright red banner announcing the date we would turn twenty-one, and printed underneath our names was our exact street address here on Arvin Road.
