Crucially, neither of us had ever bothered telling the Virginia Department of Motor Vehicles about a single one of our temporary moves over the past three and a half years—not when Katie went up to Williamsburg for her freshman year of college and then down to Fishersville, and not when I moved into our Norfolk apartments on Greenway Court and West Ocean View Avenue before heading to Fishersville with her. As far as the DMV's computer database in Richmond was concerned, Katie and I had lived continuously at this exact house on Arvin Road since we were sixteen years old.

Now that we were twenty-one—and only sixteen days away from turning twenty-two—we wanted to trade in those worn vertical Under-21 cards for proper adult horizontal State ID cards before heading over to Fairlawn Recreation Center on Monday to sign up for resident memberships. And since the nearest DMV Customer Service Center was over on Buckner Boulevard in Virginia Beach, getting there meant taking CVTA Route 12.

At nine-forty that morning, we rolled out our front door and down the aluminum porch ramp into the sunny March air.

Getting from our driveway to the Route 12 stop heading toward the Community College of Hampton Roads required a specific two-stage crossing. Exiting the house, we made a right onto Arvin Road and another right onto the north sidewalk of Indian River Road, rolling west down the block to the roaring multi-lane intersection of Indian River Road and Military Highway.

Because the bus stop for southbound routes sat on the far southwest corner of the intersection, crossing one street wasn't enough—we had to cross both Indian River Road and Military Highway without a single painted crosswalk stripe on either roadway.

"Indian River first while the through-lanes on Military have the green," Katie called out over the rumble of a passing dump truck as we lined our SwiftChairs up side by side at the concrete curb cut.

The moment the turning traffic cleared, we pushed our joysticks forward in tandem across the unmarked asphalt of Indian River Road to the median island and the opposite corner, pivoted ninety degrees at the curb cut, waited through the next signal cycle while eight lanes of Military Highway traffic thundered past our footplates, and then rolled straight across Military Highway to the southbound CVTA bus stop sign.

That southbound stop on Military Highway was a workhorse corner for our end of Kempsville: it served CVTA Route 12 heading east toward the Community College of Hampton Roads Virginia Beach Campus, as well as CVTA Route 15 heading south toward either Emerald Creek Mall or Robert Hall Boulevard in Chesapeake on an alternating basis.

Seven minutes later, a low-floor CVTA Route 12 coach with *12 CCHR* glowing across its amber front destination sign pulled up to the curb, kneeled its front suspension, and unfolded its metal ramp onto the sidewalk so Katie and I could roll aboard and lock down our chairs for the ride over to Buckner Boulevard.

***

#### 10:35 AM — Two Tickets (`B042` and `B043`), The DMV Waiting Rite of Passage, & Horizontal Cards Printed on the Spot

Rolling through the double glass doors of the Buckner Boulevard DMV Customer Service Center at ten-thirty-five, Katie and I wheeled side by side up to the check-in podium near the entrance.

"Good morning," Katie told the information clerk. "My twin brother and I live together at the same address, and we both need to trade our vertical Under-21 State ID cards for horizontal cards now that we're over twenty-one. Can we just use one ticket number together?"

"Sorry, honey—DMV policy is one ticket number per person, one transaction per ticket," the check-in clerk replied without missing a beat, tapping the touchscreen on the electronic queue ticket dispenser twice and handing Katie a paper slip printed with **B042** and me a second slip printed with **B043**—the **B** prefix routing us into the queue for driver's license and identification card renewals and reissues.

"Two separate ticket numbers for twins living in the same house," I grumbled under my breath as we rolled over to the open space beside the waiting room chairs.

"At least they're right next to each other," Katie whispered back, glancing up at the red LED matrix board where **B039** was flashing. "How long could three numbers possibly take?"

Famous last words.

Over the next ten minutes, the robotic female voice on the overhead ceiling speakers chimed through **B040** and then called out:

*"Ding-dong... Now serving... Customer Number... B-zero-four-one... at Window... four."*

Katie and I both sat up straight in our SwiftChairs and rested our right hands on our joysticks, ready to roll the second **B042** was called.

Instead, the DMV's automated queue computer decided that **B041** was the end of the **B** batch—and immediately launched into a twenty-five-minute marathon of every other letter in the alphabet.

*"Ding-dong... Now serving... Customer Number... T-one-one-eight... at Window... nine,"* the robotic voice droned, routing vehicle title and registration paperwork down the hall.

*"Ding-dong... Now serving... Customer Number... C-zero-two-seven... at Window... two,"* it chimed two minutes later for the compliance and suspension desk, followed by a string of **A** tickets for original learner's permits, **D** tickets for combined multi-step transactions, and **E** tickets for the express window.

Every time the two-tone chime echoed across the acoustic ceiling tiles, Katie and I looked up expectantly at the red LED board—only to groan in unison as another **T** or **C** flashed on the display while **B042** and **B043** sat frozen in limbo.

Finally—just when I was starting to wonder if the computer had forgotten the letter **B** existed—the speaker chimed again:

*"Ding-dong... Now serving... Customer Number... B-zero-four-two... at Window... six."*

"Finally!" Katie exhaled, and both of us pushed our joysticks forward to roll side by side up to the lowered accessible counter at Window 6.

"Good morning to you both," the DMV representative behind Window 6 smiled as we pulled up.

"Good morning, ma'am," Katie said, sliding her **B042** ticket and her 2001 vertical card across the laminate counter while I tried to slide **B043** and my vertical card right beside hers. "My brother and I both need new horizontal State ID cards now that we're over the age of twenty-one."

The representative glanced down at my **B043** slip and shook her head with an apologetic smile. "I can't open **B043** in the computer until I close out **B042**, young man—you'll have to wait your turn until **B043** is called."

I let out a quiet sigh and backed my SwiftChair half a foot to the right to wait my turn while the representative processed Katie's renewal first.

Typing Katie's identification number into her terminal, the representative glanced at her screen. "Are you still at the same address on Arvin Road here in Virginia Beach that we've had on file since October 2001?"

"Yes, ma'am—still the exact same house on Arvin Road," Katie smiled, confirming that her Virginia Beach voter registration in the Kempsville precinct was still current as well before rolling two feet over to the adjustable camera post in front of the pull-down sky-blue backdrop to have her new photo snapped.

The second Katie's photo registered in the system and the representative closed out **B042** to send Katie's card to the thermal printer behind the counter, the representative pressed the queue button on her keyboard.

Right above our heads, the ceiling speaker chimed:

*"Ding-dong... Now serving... Customer Number... B-zero-four-three... at Window... six."*

"Now it's officially your turn," the representative chuckled as I rolled my SwiftChair six inches forward to the exact spot Katie had just vacated and slid **B043** and my 2001 vertical card across the counter.

After confirming that I also still lived at the exact same Arvin Road address on file since October 2001, verifying my voter registration, paying our two card fees with our joint debit card, and having my own picture snapped in front of the blue screen, I rolled right back beside Katie's chair at Window 6 while the thermal card printer behind the counter whirred through its second pass.

![Inside the Virginia DMV Customer Service Center on Buckner Boulevard in Virginia Beach on Friday morning, March 23, 2007, twenty-one-year-old fraternal twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs at the photo counter in front of the blue DMV backdrop as a friendly clerk hands them their warm, freshly printed horizontal 21-and-over Virginia State ID cards on the spot alongside their old 2001 vertical Under-21 cards]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/mar_2007_buckner_blvd_dmv_vertical_to_horizontal_state_ids_katie_nate.jpg)

A moment later, with both transactions completed, the representative smiled warmly and handed Katie and me our two brand-new, still-warm plastic Virginia identification cards—printed horizontally on the spot, with no red Under-21 banner anywhere in sight and our Arvin Road address gleaming crisply across the front.

***

#### 11:45 AM — Dropped Off by the Bank on Northbound Military Highway

By eleven-forty-five, after riding the westbound CVTA Route 12 bus back from Buckner Boulevard, I reached up and pulled the yellow chime cord as the bus approached Indian River Road.

On the return trip home, Route 12 dropped us off on the northbound side of South Military Highway right in front of the brick Piedmont Bank branch at the southeast corner of the intersection.

Once the bus ramp folded back inside and the coach pulled away through the traffic light, Katie and I rolled up to the corner curb cut in front of the bank, waited for a clean break in the turning cars, and crossed the unmarked lanes of Indian River Road to the northeast sidewalk.

From there, we made a right onto the sidewalk of Indian River Road—rolling east against the flow of westbound traffic with our new horizontal Virginia State ID cards tucked safely inside our lanyards—and then made a left onto quiet Arvin Road, where our brick ranch house sat waiting for us on our left.

### Part 4: The :07 Bus From Glenrock Mall, Yearly Memberships at Fairlawn Rec Center, & The 1977 Building's Quirks

**Date:** 2007-03-26 at 10:31 America/New_York

![Inside the 1977 brick lobby of the original Fairlawn Recreation Center in Virginia Beach on Monday morning, March 26, 2007—just inside the dark-bronze-framed glass entrance vestibule looking out toward the concrete walkway and flagpole—twenty-one-year-old fraternal twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs at the wood-laminate front desk receiving their newly laminated yearly resident membership cards beside the key-locked elevator door in the brick wall]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/mar_2007_fairlawn_rec_center_1977_lobby_concrete_ramp_memberships_katie_nate.jpg)

#### Monday, March 26, 2007, 10:31 AM — Catching the :07 Route 25 Past the Newtown Road Border

"Make sure we're on the ten-thirty-one northbound Route 15 and not a minute later," Katie reminded me on Monday morning as we waited side by side in our SwiftChairs at the bus stop on Military Highway and Indian River Road. "If we miss the eleven-oh-seven Route 25 departure out of Glenrock Mall, the eleven-thirty-seven bus turns around at Newtown Road and stays in Norfolk, and we'll be stuck waiting a whole hour until twelve-oh-seven just to cross into Virginia Beach."

"Don't I know it," I said, shaking my head at the folded paper timetable in my hand as the northbound CVTA Route 15 bus pulled up to the curb.

Fourteen minutes later, at ten-forty-five sharp, Route 15 dropped us off at the transit transfer bay outside Glenrock Mall in Norfolk, giving us twenty-two minutes to roll over to the Route 25 stop before the eleven-oh-seven bus pulled out.

On paper, CVTA Route 25 ran every thirty minutes out of Glenrock Mall. In reality—thanks to the infamous city-line service cliff—every second bus only ran as far as Greenwich Road and Newtown Road at the Norfolk border before turning right back around. Only the buses departing Glenrock Mall at seven minutes past the hour, from six-oh-seven in the morning until six-oh-seven in the evening on Monday through Friday, actually crossed the city line and continued all the way down Princess Anne Road to the Community College of Hampton Roads Virginia Beach Campus.

Boarding the eleven-oh-seven Route 25 side by side, Katie and I rode east across the Newtown Road border and down Princess Anne Road until I pulled the yellow stop cord just before Edwin Drive.

Once the operator lowered the ramp at the corner of Princess Anne Road and Edwin Drive, we rolled our two SwiftChairs side by side down the sidewalk along Edwin Drive, turned onto Marlborough Drive, and steered right into the entrance of Fairlawn Recreation Center—carefully weaving our front casters around the deep, familiar potholes cratering the asphalt parking lot outside the low 1977 brick building with its sloped metal roof.

***

#### 11:40 AM — Yearly Memberships, The Concrete Spiral Ramp, & Two Locker Room Doors

Rolling through the front entrance doors into the first-floor lobby felt like traveling straight back into our Kempsville childhood.

Right ahead of us on the left stood the wood-laminate front counter, and across the speckled terrazzo floor on the right—wrapping straight around behind the brick elevator enclosure with its key-locked call button—rose the rec center's unmistakable 1977 architectural centerpiece: a massive, unpainted gray concrete ramp with metal pipe railings that climbed from the first floor up to the second and third floors. Because the building had opened in 1977—thirteen years before the Americans with Disabilities Act was ever signed into law—that concrete ramp was nowhere near ADA compliant.

![Inside the 1977 brick lobby of the original Fairlawn Recreation Center in Virginia Beach on Monday morning, March 26, 2007—just inside the dark-bronze-framed glass entrance vestibule looking out toward the concrete walkway and flagpole—twenty-one-year-old fraternal twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs at the wood-laminate front desk receiving their newly laminated yearly resident membership cards beside the key-locked elevator door in the brick wall]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/mar_2007_fairlawn_rec_center_1977_lobby_concrete_ramp_memberships_katie_nate.jpg)

"Two adult resident yearly memberships, please," Katie smiled up at the recreation clerk behind the front counter, sliding the brand-new horizontal Virginia DMV State ID cards we had just picked up on Buckner Boulevard on Friday alongside our joint debit card across the laminate ledge.

The clerk glanced down at the Virginia Beach street address on Arvin Road printed across both of our IDs, typed our names into the desktop terminal, and had us pause in front of the webcam lens on the counter before handing back two freshly laminated plastic Fairlawn Recreation Center annual passes.

"Welcome back to Fairlawn," the clerk said, holding up a brass key on a coiled wristband. "Did you two want me to come around and unlock the elevator for you to get up to the second floor, or are your power chairs okay on the concrete ramp?"

"With electric motors and full batteries, we can take the spiral ramp just fine," I smiled, clipping my new membership card onto my lanyard beside Katie's. "Wait until you see someone try to push a manual chair up that grade, though."

Before climbing to the second floor, we took a nostalgic loop down the first-floor wing. Everything about the 1977 building still had the exact endearing, slightly worn neighborhood quirks we remembered from middle and high school. Past the meeting rooms sat the snack lounge, where a hand-lettered paper sign taped across the glass of the vending machines warned patrons in bold marker that the front desk could not issue refunds when the coils ate your dollar bills and that you had to call the vending company's phone number yourself. Across the hall, we peeked into the Adult Lounge—which had pool tables and board-game tables just like the Youth Lounge down the corridor, minus the arcade cabinets—and rolled past the little two-lane bowling alley, where, right on cue, a laminated yellow sign hung between the ball returns reading *LANES CLOSED FOR PINSETTER MAINTENANCE*.

"Some things in Kempsville never change," Katie giggled, squeezing my hand before we steered our SwiftChairs onto the bottom apron of the massive dark-gray concrete spiral ramp.

With our dual electric motors humming steadily against the steep 1970s incline, we spiraled side by side up the concrete helix around the lobby walls to the second-floor check-in desk. Down one corridor sat the open-gym basketball court and the enclosed racquetball court; down the other, through a sudden blast of warm, chlorine-scented air, lay the twenty-five-meter indoor pool, where the air and water stayed at a constant, humid eighty-four degrees while the non-humidified hallway outside sat at a brisk seventy-two.

Standing in the seventy-two-degree corridor between the hallway and the pool deck, however, Katie and I stopped our chairs in front of the two heavy doors leading into the changing area.

The door on the left was marked *MEN*. The door on the right was marked *WOMEN*. There was no other changing room anywhere on the floor.

Katie looked at the two separate doors, then looked down at her legs and over at me, the smile fading slightly from her lips.

"Well, that's going to make swimming here tricky," Katie said quietly.

At home on Arvin Road, neither of us ever thought twice about getting dressed or undressed because we always had each other right there to steady an elbow, help pull a wet swimsuit strap over a fatigued shoulder, or assist with the transfer bench. Here in the 1977 recreation center, once Katie rolled through the women's locker room door and I rolled through the men's door, there was no legal way for a brother and sister to help each other change into swim gear—and out on the pool deck beyond the tile showers, the five-foot-to-eight-foot pool didn't even have a mechanical transfer chair to lower a wheelchair user into the water.

"For today, we've got the Adult Lounge pool tables, the open gym, and our yearly cards in our pockets," I said, reaching across our armrests to take my sister's hand as we turned our wheelchairs back toward the top of the concrete spiral ramp to head down and catch the northbound Route 25 back to Glenrock Mall. "And if the two-lane bowling alley downstairs ever actually has both pinsetters working on the same afternoon, we'll treat it like a holiday."

## A Near-Miss at Dying Glenrock Mall, Locking Down WHOIS, & Forming Our Virginia LLC

### Part 1: A Dying Single-Story Mall, Spotting Brenda in the Concourse, & The WHOIS Wake-Up Call

**Date:** 2007-03-29 at 15:25 America/New_York

![Inside the bright, welcoming single-story concourse of Glenrock Mall in Norfolk on Thursday afternoon, March 29, 2007, twenty-one-year-old fraternal twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs tucked out of sight behind a wide structural column—while along the bright concourse sit closed retail storefronts with For Lease signs and faded label scars on the sign bulkheads where store names used to be, as their estranged mother Brenda stands fifty feet away holding a printed webpage and questioning a kiosk vendor]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/mar_2007_glenrock_mall_dying_single_story_concourse_brenda_near_miss_katie_nate.jpg)

#### Thursday, March 29, 2007, 3:25 PM — Behind the Pillar in a Dying Single-Story Mall

"Nate—stop your chair right now and pull behind this pillar," Katie whispered sharply at three-twenty-five on Thursday afternoon, her left hand shooting across our armrests to cover my wrist just as we rolled inside the north corridor doors of Glenrock Mall to get out of the chilly March wind while waiting for our three-forty-five southbound Route 15 bus home.

I didn't ask a single question. Hearing the sudden ice in my twin sister's voice, I feathered my joystick backward and pivoted my SwiftChair in complete silence beside hers until both of our wheelchairs were tucked squarely behind a wide, beige-tiled structural column next to a lush indoor planter.

Unlike the two-story concourses of Emerald Creek Mall or Chesapeake Bay Mall, Glenrock Mall in 2007 was a sprawling, single-story 1970s shopping center that was visibly dying in slow motion even though its main concourse remained bright, clean, and welcoming under warm overhead skylights. All along the brightly lit single-level corridor stretching toward the center court, more than half of the inline retail storefronts sat closed and empty behind pulled-down security grilles with *FOR LEASE* signs taped inside the glass—their upper fascism bulkheads marked by faded, ghostly "label scars" in the paint and stucco where the illuminated letters of familiar national chain stores had been unbolted and hauled away. Aside from a discount shoe outlet, a watch-battery kiosk, and a cellphone-case cart in the middle of the polished terrazzo floor, the bright concourse was remarkably quiet.

And standing fifty feet down that single-story concourse in front of the cellphone-case cart—holding two stapled sheets of computer printer paper in her hand—was our estranged mother, Brenda.

![Inside the bright, welcoming single-story concourse of Glenrock Mall in Norfolk on Thursday afternoon, March 29, 2007, twenty-one-year-old fraternal twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs tucked out of sight behind a wide structural column—while along the bright concourse sit closed retail storefronts with For Lease signs and faded label scars on the sign bulkheads where store names used to be, as their estranged mother Brenda stands fifty feet away holding a printed webpage and questioning a kiosk vendor]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/mar_2007_glenrock_mall_dying_single_story_concourse_brenda_near_miss_katie_nate.jpg)

My heart slammed against my ribs so hard I could hear my pulse in my ears. Beside me behind the wide column, Katie's hand gripped mine like a vise.

Neither of us had seen our mother's face since late August 2001, when the Virginia Beach court had granted Dad sole custody and exclusive possession after the cruise ship security tape—and the only time we had heard her voice since then was that terrifying Saturday night in August 2003 when she had lurked in the back alley behind the iron fire-escape stairs at Greenway Court in Norfolk while we hid inside our dark square closet.

"They're twenty-one years old—a boy and a girl, twins, blonde hair, both of them in black motorized wheelchairs," Brenda was saying loudly to the bored teenager working the cellphone-case cart, tapping the printed sheets in her hand. "I went by their old building on Greenway Court and up to that dump in Ocean View, and the managers said they moved out! Look at this printout from their little bus website—they wrote right here on Monday that they transfer between Route 15 and Route 25 at Glenrock Mall! You work right by the bus doors, don't you? Have you seen them roll through here today?!"

The teenager behind the cart shrugged his shoulders and shook his head without looking up from his magazine. "Lady, a hundred people walk through those bus doors every hour to catch the 15 and the 20. I don't keep track of who rides the bus."

Behind the beige-tiled pillar, Katie and I didn't breathe a sound.

As Brenda spun around in frustration and marched toward the opposite wing of the single-story concourse to badger the cashier inside the discount shoe store—her back turned completely away from the north entrance—Katie squeezed my fingers twice.

Moving in dead-silent synchronization with our speed dials turned down to a whisper-quiet crawl, we backed our two SwiftChairs ten feet from the column, glided out the automatic glass doors onto the exterior sidewalk apron, and rolled straight down the curb to the Route 15 bus bay just as the three-forty-five southbound bus pulled in from Little Creek Road and kneeled its front suspension.

Not until the hydraulic ramp folded back up, our four-point floor straps clicked tight, and the bus pulled out of the Glenrock Mall ring road onto southbound Military Highway toward Indian River Road did either of us let out the breath we had been holding.

***

#### 4:15 PM — Checking Our Domain WHOIS Behind a Deadbolted Door

The second we rolled up our aluminum ramp on Arvin Road at four-fifteen, pushed our front door shut, and turned the brass deadbolt, Katie's hands were still trembling.

Before we even touched our computers, the two of us rolled straight down the hallway into our bedroom, helped each other out of our jackets and clothes, climbed inside our shared sleeping bag on the closet floor with the door pulled shut, and held each other skin to skin in the quiet dark for twenty straight minutes until Katie's breathing slowed and the cold knot in my stomach uncoiled.

When we finally dressed and rolled side by side into our dual-desk office at quarter to five, I opened a terminal window on my Linux machine and ran a public WHOIS query on the domain name for Ideas for Coastal Virginia Transit.

"Look at the registrant output on my monitor, Katie," I said grimly, pointing at the plain-text lines returned by the public domain registry.

Back in November 2005, when we had registered the domain from our apartment in West Ocean View, the domain registrar had required a registrant mailing address and phone number—and by default, ICANN published that exact record for anyone on the internet to query for free.

"That's how she knew to go to West Ocean View after checking Greenway Court," Katie said, her jaw tightening as she read the screen over my shoulder. "She typed our website name into a public domain lookup, saw the old West Ocean View apartment address on the registration record, went up there after our lease ended on February twenty-eighth, and when the landlord told her we were gone, she started reading our blog posts to see which bus hubs we ride through!"

"Thank goodness we never updated the domain registration to Arvin Road when we got back from Fishersville," I breathed, my skin prickling at how close we had come to handing her a map to Dad's Virginia Beach house. "Because she has no idea this house on Arvin Road even exists. When Dad moved the three of us here in October 2001 after the custody order, she never got this address."

"And she is never going to get it," Katie said fiercely, picking up the desk phone on the table between our chairs and pressing the speed-dial button for Dad's cell phone up in Northern Virginia. "We need to lock down our domain registration today, Nate—and we need a real legal shield so our names and our home street never show up on a public database ever again."

### Part 2: Dad's Legal Consultation, Our Virginia LLC, & A Virtual Mailbox at The Parcel Center

**Date:** 2007-04-03 at 14:00 America/New_York

![Inside a ground-floor Virginia Beach law office off Independence Boulevard on Tuesday afternoon, April 3, 2007, twenty-one-year-old fraternal twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs across the mahogany conference table from family and business attorney Kenneth Vance, signing the Articles of Organization for their fifty-fifty Virginia limited liability company while David Prairie listens over the desk speakerphone]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/apr_2007_virginia_llc_consultation_registered_agent_shield_katie_nate.jpg)

#### Tuesday, April 3, 2007, 2:00 PM — The Registered Agent Shield & Prairie Twin Interactive, LLC

"Your father already took care of my consultation fee and the hundred-dollar State Corporation Commission filing fee by credit card this morning," attorney Kenneth Vance said warmly on Tuesday afternoon, sliding a blue legal folder across his ground-floor conference table off Independence Boulevard as Dad listened in over the walnut speakerphone from his lunch break up in Tysons Corner. "And when David told me that Brenda was spotted wandering around Glenrock Mall with a printout from your website trying to figure out where you two live, I pulled the corporate forms immediately."

Sitting side by side in our SwiftChairs across the mahogany table, Katie and I leaned forward together. Six years earlier, in late August 2001, Mr. Vance was the exact Virginia Beach attorney who had taken Dad's shipboard security tape into circuit court, won Dad sole custody of the two of us, and secured the divorce stipulation restoring Brenda's maiden name, Walsh.

![Inside a ground-floor Virginia Beach law office off Independence Boulevard on Tuesday afternoon, April 3, 2007, twenty-one-year-old fraternal twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs across the mahogany conference table from family and business attorney Kenneth Vance, signing the Articles of Organization for their fifty-fifty Virginia limited liability company while David Prairie listens over the desk speakerphone]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/apr_2007_virginia_llc_consultation_registered_agent_shield_katie_nate.jpg)

"We want to make sure our home street on Arvin Road never appears on a public website lookup, a domain database, or a business license," Katie told Mr. Vance clearly. "And once we finish our PHP and SQL coursework, we want to be able to build websites and software under a real business name without renting an expensive corporate office suite."

"Which is the smartest move you can make," Mr. Vance nodded, opening the folder to the Virginia State Corporation Commission Form LLC-1011, Articles of Organization, alongside a twenty-page Operating Agreement. "Right now, if you register a domain name or accept a check in your personal names from home, anyone who knows how to run a public database search can try to trace your residential address. By forming a Virginia limited liability company—owned strictly fifty-fifty by the two of you as Managing Members—the LLC becomes the legal owner of Ideas for Coastal Virginia Transit and every line of software you write."

He tapped the second paragraph on the state filing sheet with his fountain pen.

"Now look at Box Three and Box Four on the Articles of Organization," Mr. Vance explained. "Every Virginia LLC is required by statute to list a Registered Agent and a Registered Office address on the public State Corporation Commission database. If you list yourselves as your own Registered Agent, you have to put your home street address on the public state website. Instead, as a member of the Virginia State Bar, I am listing myself as your official Registered Agent and putting this law office right here off Independence Boulevard as your Registered Office."

"Wait—so if Brenda or anyone else searches our LLC on the state website in Richmond, the only address that comes up is your law office?" I asked, a huge wave of relief washing across my chest.

"My law office, my receptionist, and my security cameras," Mr. Vance smiled firmly. "And for Box Five—the LLC's Principal Office mailing address, which you'll also use for your domain WHOIS records, your bank checks, and your website footer—you don't need to lease a commercial office building. All you need to do on your way home today is stop at a commercial mail center like The Parcel Center, fill out United States Postal Service Form 1583 with your two Virginia State ID cards, and rent a commercial mailbox for fifteen dollars a month. That gives you a real commercial street address with a suite number. Every piece of business mail and every public WHOIS lookup goes to that suite number, while the two of you do one hundred percent of your work from your dual desks at home."

"What do you two think of that?" Dad's voice asked warmly through the speakerphone.

Katie looked at the corporate header printed across the top of the Operating Agreement—*PRAIRIE TWIN INTERACTIVE, LLC*—and laced her left fingers through my right hand before picking up the blue pen with her right hand.

"We love it, Dad," Katie said, signing her name cleanly on the first Managing Member line and passing the pen across our armrests to me so I could sign the second fifty-fifty Managing Member line right beside hers.

***

#### 3:45 PM — Signing Form 1583 at The Parcel Center & Scrubbing Our WHOIS Clean

Forty-five minutes later, on our bus ride back down toward Indian River Road, Katie and I rolled into the storefront of The Parcel Center in the commercial strip plaza near the highway.

Behind the counter, the clerk checked our two laminated Virginia DMV State ID cards, notarized our signatures on United States Postal Service Form 1583, and handed us two small brass mailbox keys along with a printed card showing our new commercial mailing address: a real commercial boulevard street number followed by *Suite 214*.

The moment we rolled back up our aluminum porch ramp on Arvin Road at four-thirty and deadbolted the door behind us, we wheeled straight into our office bedroom and logged into our domain registrar control panel.

Typing side by side, I replaced our personal names and the old West Ocean View apartment address on every domain record with *Prairie Twin Interactive, LLC* and our new *Suite 214* commercial mailbox address, enabled the registrar's full WHOIS privacy proxy shield on top of it, and triggered an immediate registry refresh.

When I opened the Linux terminal window sixty seconds later and ran a fresh public WHOIS query on Ideas for Coastal Virginia Transit, every trace of our personal names, our phone number, and our residential history had vanished completely from the public internet.

"Go ahead and refresh the page at the library now, Brenda," Katie whispered, leaning her head against my shoulder as she watched the clean terminal output on my screen. "You'll never find this house in a million years."

## Twenty-Two in Alexandria: Riding DMV Transit, Touring the White House & the U.S. Capitol, Meeting Senator James West, The Spark to Run for City Council, & Two Blue Passports

### Part 1: Accessible Taxi to Newport News, The ARTS Train to Alexandria, & Riding Northern Virginia Transit on Our Twenty-Second Birthday

**Date:** 2007-04-08 at 09:15 America/New_York

![On the red-brick platform of Alexandria Union Station beside the stainless-steel ARTS passenger train and the George Washington Masonic Memorial tower in the background on Saturday, April 7, 2007, twenty-two-year-old fraternal twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie roll their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs off the blue station wheelchair lift as their father David Prairie beams and welcomes them to Northern Virginia for their birthday week]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/apr_2007_alexandria_alx_platform_22nd_birthday_arrival_katie_nate_david.jpg)

#### Saturday, April 7 – Sunday, April 8, 2007 — Across the Water to Newport News & Rolling Into Alexandria

"Happy early twenty-second birthday, you two!" Dad beamed on Saturday afternoon, standing right beside the blue mobile wheelchair lift on the red-brick platform of Alexandria Union Station as the ARTS conductor lowered Katie and me down from the stainless-steel vestibule of the Northeast Regional.

"Dad!" Katie grinned, releasing her joystick brake the second the lift apron touched the brick and rolling straight into his outstretched arms while I wheeled right up beside her for a three-way platform hug.

![On the red-brick platform of Alexandria Union Station beside the stainless-steel ARTS passenger train and the George Washington Masonic Memorial tower in the background on Saturday, April 7, 2007, twenty-two-year-old fraternal twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie roll their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs off the blue station wheelchair lift as their father David Prairie beams and welcomes them to Northern Virginia for their birthday week]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/apr_2007_alexandria_alx_platform_22nd_birthday_arrival_katie_nate_david.jpg)

"How was the ride up from Newport News?" Dad asked, slinging both of our overnight duffel bags—including our rolled-up double sleeping bag—over his shoulders.

"Smooth as glass once we got across the harbor," I told him as we rolled side by side along the station platform toward the short pedestrian sidewalk running beneath the King Street railroad bridge.

Because Norfolk still had zero passenger rail service in 2007—forcing anyone on the Southside who wanted to catch an ARTS train to cross the water to the Peninsula—Dad had pre-paid a wheelchair-accessible lift taxi van to pick Katie and me up at our driveway on Arvin Road at six-thirty that morning and drive us through the Hampton Roads Bridge-Tunnel straight to the Newport News ARTS station on Warwick Boulevard. Since Newport News was the origin terminal for the morning train, the crew had plenty of time to wheel the station lift up to the accessible coach door, lock our SwiftChairs into the wide wheelchair bays across from the café car, and let us watch the Chickahominy swamps, the state capitol domes of Richmond, and the Rappahannock River bridges roll past our window all the way up to Northern Virginia.

Even better, when we rolled with Dad through the short underpass beneath the railroad tracks and emerged onto the west side of the tunnel, Dad's two-story brick house on Sunset Drive sat right there at the foot of the hill—less than three minutes from both the ARTS train platforms and the elevated Capital Transit Yellow and Blue Line station at King Street.

Inside the house, Dad had already set up the ground-floor front room for us with a portable aluminum threshold ramp over the front step, a roll-in shower bench in the downstairs bathroom, and a cleared, freshly vacuumed first-floor coat and linen closet where we immediately spread out our sleeping bag and four pillows. Before we even unpacked our clothes, Katie and I proudly pulled out our lanyards at the dining table to show Dad the brand-new horizontal Virginia State ID cards we had gotten on Buckner Boulevard—both still showing our uninterrupted 2001 Arvin Road address, with the red Under-21 banners officially gone for good. That night—our last night of being twenty-one—after eating Dad's homemade lasagna at the dining table, Katie and I slipped into that quiet downstairs closet, zipped our sleeping bag up around our shoulders, and slept skin to skin in each other's arms without a single worry in the world.

***

#### Sunday, April 8, 2007, 10:30 AM — High-Platform Level Boarding & A Transit Grid That Doesn't Quit at Dinner

When we woke up on Sunday morning, April 8—officially twenty-two years old—Dad was standing in the kitchen holding two mugs of hot chocolate and two crisp plastic Capital Transit CapitalPass farecards loaded with a full week of unlimited rail and bus passes.

"For your twenty-second birthday week," Dad announced, handing one plastic card to Katie and one to me, "before we head into Washington on Tuesday for your big birthday surprise, we're going to spend today riding the buses and trains up here in Northern Virginia so the authors of Ideas for Coastal Virginia Transit can see how a connected regional network operates."

Twenty minutes later, the three of us rolled across the bus loop to the King Street Capital Transit station, tapped our plastic farecards against the accessible wide-aisle faregate pads, rode the glass elevator up to the center island platform, and waited as a six-car Yellow Line train glided to a halt alongside the concrete edge.

When the bi-parting metal doors slid open, Katie and I both stared at the threshold between the station platform and the railcar floor.

The concrete platform sat at the exact vertical height of the train floor. There were no steps, no steep ramps, and no waiting ten minutes for an operator to unfold a mechanical lift.

Katie pushed her joystick forward, and her front casters glided straight across the two-inch rubber gap-filler strip into the railcar alongside mine in less than two seconds.

"Did you just see that, Nate?!" Katie gasped, her eyes shining as the chime sounded and the doors closed behind us. "We just rolled straight onto a train by ourselves in two seconds flat! And look at our farecards—when you transfer from the train to a local Alexandria or Arlington bus at the station loop, the electronic reader automatically discounts the transfer instead of handing you a soggy paper slip that expires while you wait for an hourly bus!"

All Sunday afternoon and evening, Dad took us everywhere across Alexandria and Arlington: riding the Blue and Yellow Lines up past National Airport and Pentagon City, transferring seamlessly onto low-floor local buses with working automated stop announcements and paved curb-cut boarding pads at every single corner, and eating our twenty-second birthday dinner together at a bright restaurant near Old Town at eight o'clock at night.

When we finished our birthday cake at quarter past nine on a Sunday night and rolled back out to the street, buses were still pulling up to the illuminated shelters every fifteen minutes, and trains were still running overhead in both directions until midnight.

"Look at the clock on my phone, Nate," Katie said softly as we rolled off the nine-thirty bus at King Street and headed through the underpass back to Dad's house on Sunset Drive. "It's nine-thirty on a Sunday night, and families, restaurant workers, and people in wheelchairs are still riding buses and trains home without a single worry about getting stranded. Why can't Hampton Roads have this?"

### Part 2: Unclipping Our Backpacks, Where Is President George W. Walker Today?, & The White House Tour That Sparked a Political Calling

**Date:** 2007-04-10 at 08:15 America/New_York

![Inside the historic State Dining Room on the State Floor of the White House on Tuesday morning, April 10, 2007, twenty-two-year-old fraternal twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs with no backpacks attached, holding hands across their armrests beside their father David Prairie and a Uniformed Secret Service Tour Officer as Katie looks up in quiet civic inspiration at the portrait of President Abraham Lincoln above the carved white marble fireplace mantel]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/apr_2007_white_house_state_floor_tour_fdr_and_lincoln_mantel_katie_nate_david.jpg)

#### Tuesday, April 10, 2007, 8:15 AM — Unclipping Our Wheelchair Backpacks on Sunset Drive

"Hold it right there before you two roll out the front door," Dad said with a grin at eight-fifteen on Tuesday morning in the hallway of his brick house on Sunset Drive, holding up the printed instruction sheet from Senator James West's office. "Rule number one on the Secret Service boarding sheet: zero backpacks, zero bags, zero cameras, and zero cell phones allowed inside the White House—and there are no storage lockers at the gate."

Katie glanced back over her shoulder at the black nylon backpack clipped to the backrest of her SwiftChair—where we normally carried our spare chargers, rain ponchos, and notebooks—and then looked over at mine.

"Not even a wheelchair bag?" I asked, reaching behind Katie's backrest so we could unbuckle each other's straps.

"Not in 2007," Dad said, helping me lift Katie's backpack off her frame while she unclipped mine and set both bags neatly beside the hall coat rack. "If you show up at the East Wing gate on Fifteenth Street with a bag or a camera, the Secret Service turns you right around, and the nearest place to rent a storage locker is all the way over at Union Station. All the three of us need in our pockets today are our CapitalPass transit cards, our White House tour confirmation letter, and those brand-new horizontal Virginia State ID cards of yours."

"Good thing we spent three hours at the Buckner Boulevard DMV waiting on tickets B042 and B043," Katie laughed, patting her wallet pocket as our chairs felt noticeably lighter without our everyday packs hanging behind our shoulders.

As we rolled side by side through the King Street railroad underpass toward the Blue Line platform on a crisp April morning, Katie looked up at Dad with genuine curiosity.

"How on earth did you manage to score three confirmed passes to tour the White House on three weeks' notice anyway, Dad?" she asked.

"By writing to our brand-new Senator from Virginia," Dad smiled as the elevator doors opened onto the King Street platform. "When you two decided in March to move back to Arvin Road and we planned this birthday week up here, I sent constituent tour requests to Capitol Hill. Everyone in Virginia knows our senior Senator, Senator John Warren, is an institution in the Senate, of course, and his office was booked solid with spring school trips—but our newly sworn-in junior Senator, Senator James West, just took office in January and wanted to prove right out of the gate that his office answers every constituent letter. His constituent-services director called me back personally within forty-eight hours, submitted our security clearance numbers to the Secret Service for a nine-thirty White House tour, and invited us up to his Senate office this afternoon to watch the Senate in session."

Katie looked down at the embossed tour pass in her hand, her blue eyes widening with quiet respect. "A brand-new United States Senator actually had his office call a regular family back in two days just to help two twins in wheelchairs see the White House and the Capitol?"

"Sure did," Dad said warmly as the northbound Blue Line train glided up to the platform edge. "And his staff told me he wants to step out of his office and say hello to you two himself when we pick up our gallery passes this afternoon."

***

#### 9:25 AM — Flashing Our Horizontal State IDs at the East Wing & Where President George W. Walker Is Today

At nine-twenty-five, after riding the Blue Line elevator up to the sidewalk at McPherson Square and rolling two blocks down Fifteenth Street alongside the black wrought-iron perimeter fence of the White House grounds, the three of us approached the uniformed Secret Service checkpoint at the East Wing visitor entrance.

Side by side, Katie and I reached into our wallets and handed our brand-new horizontal twenty-one-and-over Virginia State ID cards up to the uniformed Secret Service officer at the podium.

The officer held Katie's horizontal card and then mine alongside the cleared manifest clipboards, checked our photographs and our April 8, 1985 birthdates, and smiled down at both of us without a single blink.

"Katie Prairie and Nathaniel Prairie from Virginia Beach," the officer said, handing our horizontal IDs back to us. "Happy twenty-second birthday to both of you, and welcome to the White House. Because you're in power wheelchairs, Officer Henderson right inside the East Wing doors will take your family up the accessible ramp and the visitor elevator so you don't miss a single room on the route."

"Thank you, sir," Katie and I said together, tucking our horizontal State ID cards proudly back into our pockets as we rolled smoothly through the security pavilion and into the wood-paneled East Wing lobby.

Inside, a tall Uniformed Secret Service Tour Officer with a polished gold badge on his navy lapel—Officer Henderson—greeted the three of us warmly and guided our two SwiftChairs up the interior accessible ramp into the vaulted Ground Floor Corridor beneath the Executive Residence.

As our small tour group paused outside the Vermeil Room—lined with gilded silver services and portraits of First Ladies—and then looked into the red-and-cream China Room and the book-lined White House Library, a father standing next to us in a lightweight jacket raised his hand.

"Excuse me, Officer," the man asked hopefully. "Is there any chance our tour group might catch a glimpse of President Walker walking down the hallway today?"

Officer Henderson chuckled good-naturedly—the practiced, polite laugh of an officer who heard that exact question twenty times a morning.

"I always hate to disappoint folks on their first trip, sir, but White House public tours almost never cross paths with the President," Officer Henderson explained warmly, gesturing toward the west end of the vaulted corridor. "Even when the President is here at the complex, his working offices are over in the West Wing, and the First Family's private living quarters are upstairs on the Second and Third Floors—completely separate from the historic Ground Floor and State Floor reception rooms we tour here."

"Wait—doesn't the flag on the roof tell you whether the President is home, like Buckingham Palace?" the man's teenage son asked.

"A lot of people think that, actually, because of the movies," Officer Henderson smiled, shaking his head. "By federal law, the American flag over the White House flies twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week, whether the President is in Washington or halfway around the world. If you want to know the real insider secret for whether the President is working in the Oval Office, you look over at the exterior portico door of the West Wing. Whenever the President is physically inside the West Wing, a United States Marine sentry in full dress blues stands at rigid attention right outside that door. The minute the President leaves the West Wing—either to travel or to walk back to the Residence for the night—the Marine sentry steps down."

"And how do the reporters know when he's done with public appearances for the whole day?" Katie asked curiously from her wheelchair.

"That's called 'calling a lid,'" Officer Henderson answered with an appreciative nod toward Katie. "Whenever the President is finished with all public appearances, speeches, and travel for the day, the Press Secretary's office gets on the loudspeaker in the press briefing room and announces a 'travel and photo lid.' Once a lid is called, everyone knows the President is in for the evening and won't be seen in public again until morning. Today, though, there's no Marine sentry at the West Wing door for the opposite reason—President George W. Walker isn't even in the District of Columbia right now."

"Where is he today?" I asked.

"President Walker flew back late last night from Yuma, Arizona, where he spent Monday touring the southwestern border," Officer Henderson replied, leading our three-person family over to the wood-paneled Visitor Elevator so we could ride up to the State Floor while the walking group climbed the marble stairs. "And about twenty minutes ago, he headed across the Potomac River into Northern Virginia—right over to American Legion Post 177 in Fairfax, Virginia—to deliver a ten-fifteen address to military families and veterans on the emergency supplemental appropriations bill."

Inside the elevator cab, I leaned across our inner armrests, wrapped my arm around Katie's shoulders in a quick, warm squeeze, and whispered against her cheek with a grin.

"Hold on, Katie," I murmured as she leaned into my hug. "We rode the CCT bus right through the middle of Fairfax two days ago on our birthday, and today President Walker is in Fairfax while we're inside his house!"

Katie had to press her lips together to keep from laughing out loud as the brass elevator doors slid open onto the State Floor.

***

#### 10:05 AM — FDR's Wheelchair in the East Room, John Adams's Prayer in the State Dining Room, & The Spark Inside Katie

When we rolled out of the elevator into the vast, sunlit expanse of the East Room—with its gleaming oak parquet floors, gold silk damask draperies, and three towering Bohemian cut-glass chandeliers overhead—the lighthearted humor in Katie's eyes gave way to sudden, breathtaking awe.

Officer Henderson walked beside our chairs across the polished floor, pausing beneath the full-length 1797 Gilbert Stuart portrait of George Washington—the famous canvas Dolley Madison had ordered unscrewed from the wall and carried to safety before British troops burned the White House in August 1814.

Then Officer Henderson looked down at Katie's and my two black SwiftChairs and pointed toward the wide, flush oak thresholds connecting the rooms along the State Floor.

"A lot of visitors don't realize it when they walk through these rooms," Officer Henderson told the three of us quietly, "but for twelve consecutive years—from March 1933 until April 1945, through the depths of the Great Depression and the entirety of the Second World War—the President of the United States governed this country from a wheelchair right across these exact parquet floors. President Franklin Delano Roosevelt had wooden ramps built over the thresholds of the East Wing and the State Floor long before accessibility laws existed, and he held his regular press conferences and wartime briefings right in these halls. And decades later, the coalition work that led to President George H.W. Walker signing the Americans with Disabilities Act out on the South Lawn on July 26, 1990 came right through these doors."

Beside me, Katie's left hand found my right hand between our armrests and held on tight. Looking down at the oak parquet under her front casters—realizing that a President in a wheelchair had steered the United States through its darkest twentieth-century hours across the very floorboards beneath our tires—made the room feel less like a glass museum case and more like a living workshop of history.

From the East Room, we rolled side by side through the silk-walled Green Room—Thomas Jefferson's old dining room—and into the oval Blue Room at the center of the South Portico, looking out the tall floor-to-ceiling windows across the South Lawn toward the Jefferson Memorial gleaming beyond the Tidal Basin. Passing through the parlor walls of the Empire-furnished Red Room, we rolled into the final major room on the State Floor: the State Dining Room.

![Inside the historic State Dining Room on the State Floor of the White House on Tuesday morning, April 10, 2007, twenty-two-year-old fraternal twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs with no backpacks attached, holding hands across their armrests beside their father David Prairie and a Uniformed Secret Service Tour Officer as Katie looks up in quiet civic inspiration at the portrait of President Abraham Lincoln above the carved white marble fireplace mantel]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/apr_2007_white_house_state_floor_tour_fdr_and_lincoln_mantel_katie_nate_david.jpg)

Even with the velvet tour rope guiding visitors toward the Cross Hall, Officer Henderson let the three of us pause for a full minute in front of the carved white marble fireplace mantel on the west wall.

Above the mantel hung George Peter Alexander Healy's portrait of Abraham Lincoln seated in quiet, heavy contemplation, his chin resting on his hand as he carried the weight of a divided nation. Directly beneath the portrait, carved into the stone frieze of the fireplace mantel at President Franklin Roosevelt's direction, were the words President John Adams had written to his wife Abigail on his second night in the unfinished White House in November 1800:

*I Pray Heaven to Bestow the Best of Blessings on THIS HOUSE and on All that shall hereafter Inhabit it. May none but Honest and Wise Men ever Rule under This Roof.*

I turned my head to look at my twin sister.

Katie wasn't just admiring the painting or the gilded molding like a tourist anymore. Her posture in her SwiftChair was bolt upright, her blue eyes fixed on Lincoln's portrait and the carved words beneath it with a fierce, luminous intensity I had never seen on her face before.

As we rolled out through the red-carpeted Cross Hall between the marble columns and emerged through the Entrance Hall onto the accessible ramp of the North Portico overlooking Pennsylvania Avenue, Dad noticed the quiet fire in Katie's eyes too.

"You grew awfully quiet back there in the State Dining Room, Katie," Dad said gently as we paused on the North Portico driveway in the April sunshine. "What were you thinking about?"

Katie looked back up at the white sandstone columns of the North Portico and then down at our two wheelchairs resting side by side on the pavement.

"All my life, Dad," Katie said, her voice steady and almost startled by its own clarity, "whenever people on television talked about the White House or the government, it always felt like some distant planet run by people who didn't live in the real world we live in. Being inside those rooms—seeing the floors where President Roosevelt rolled his wheelchair, reading John Adams's prayer carved into that stone mantel, and realizing how many laws that affect every single day of our lives were signed or vetoed behind those walls—just made something click in my head."

She looked straight at me, her fingers still linked with mine.

"The people who govern in rooms like that aren't magical beings, Nate," Katie said softly. "They're just citizens who showed up and ran for office. And when people who ride public buses and use wheelchairs aren't in the room when the decisions get made, nobody speaks for us."

### Part 3: Beneath the Capitol Dome: Touring the Crypt, the Rotunda, National Statuary Hall, & the Historic Old Senate Chamber

**Date:** 2007-04-10 at 11:30 America/New_York

![Inside the soaring neoclassical United States Capitol Rotunda at midday on Tuesday, April 10, 2007, twenty-two-year-old fraternal twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs holding hands across their armrests beside their father David Prairie and a U.S. Capitol Guide in a crimson-red blazer, gazing up in wonder at the historic Revolutionary War paintings and the coffered dome overhead]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/apr_2007_us_capitol_rotunda_and_statuary_hall_tour_katie_nate_david.jpg)

#### Tuesday, April 10, 2007, 11:30 AM — The Capitol Police Checkpoint & The Compass Stone in the Crypt

From McPherson Square, the three of us rode the Capital Transit Blue Line beneath the National Mall to Capitol South Station, took the street elevator up to First Street SE in the late-morning sunshine, and rolled up the wide, curved walkways of Capitol Hill.

Because the new underground Capitol Visitor Center on the East Front was still a massive fenced construction site in the spring of 2007, constituent tours entered through the accessible South Wing pavilion near Garfield Circle. Waiting right inside the accessible entrance with three yellow visitor badges was a cheerful twenty-three-year-old staff assistant from Senator James West's office named Marcus, standing alongside a gray-haired historian wearing the unmistakable crimson-red blazer of the United States Capitol Guide Service.

"Welcome to the United States Capitol, Mr. Prairie, Katie, and Nathaniel," the U.S. Capitol Police officer at the screening table smiled as Katie and I proudly handed over our new horizontal twenty-one-and-over Virginia State ID cards for the second time that morning. "Still no bags or backpacks, I see—you two are making my job easy today! Right through the wide gate and enjoy your tour."

Once we clipped our visitor passes to our collars, our red-blazered Capitol Guide—Mr. Galloway—led the three of us and Marcus onto the elevator up to the first floor and out into the circular sandstone colonnade of the Capitol Crypt.

Forty massive Doric columns of Virginia Aquia Creek sandstone rose around us, supporting the vaulted groin arches that held up the weight of the Rotunda floor directly overhead.

"Roll right over here to the center of the ring," Mr. Galloway invited us, gesturing toward a sunken white marble star set inside a brass ring in the center of the stone floor. "Right beneath your wheels is the Compass Stone—the exact geographic zero-point dividing Washington, D.C. into its four quadrants: Northwest, Northeast, Southwest, and Southeast. Every street address in the federal capital is measured outward from this single stone."

Katie positioned her SwiftChair beside the brass ring so her front right caster rested on the Northeast line while mine rested on the Southeast line, reaching across her armrest to lace her fingers with mine.

"Think about the sandstone in these forty columns, too," Dad remarked, running his hand admiringly along the warm, fossil-flecked grain of one of the pillars. "Quarried down on Aquia Creek in Stafford County, Virginia, and barged up the Potomac River more than two hundred years ago."

***

#### 12:00 PM — Looking Up Into the Capitol Rotunda

A two-minute elevator ride brought the five of us up to the second floor, and when the bronze doors slid open and Katie and I rolled side by side through the sandstone archway into the United States Capitol Rotunda, both of us tilted our heads all the way back against our headrests in stunned silence.

![Inside the soaring neoclassical United States Capitol Rotunda at midday on Tuesday, April 10, 2007, twenty-two-year-old fraternal twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs holding hands across their armrests beside their father David Prairie and a U.S. Capitol Guide in a crimson-red blazer, gazing up in wonder at the historic Revolutionary War paintings and the coffered dome overhead]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/apr_2007_us_capitol_rotunda_and_statuary_hall_tour_katie_nate_david.jpg)

Rising one hundred and eighty feet straight above our wheelchairs was the soaring white cast-iron canopy of the Capitol Dome, flooded with midday sunlight streaming through the ring of tall peristyle windows. At the very crown of the oculus, Constantino Brumidi's fresco—*The Apotheosis of Washington*—seemed to float in midair above the continuous three-hundred-foot painted stone belt of the Frieze of American History.

Around the curved sandstone walls at floor level hung eight monumental historical oil paintings in heavy gilded frames, four of them painted from life by John Trumbull, who had served as George Washington's own aide-de-camp during the Revolutionary War.

While other tourists snapped photos of *Declaration of Independence*, Katie rolled her SwiftChair slowly across the flagstones to stop directly in front of two paintings side by side: *Surrender of Lord Cornwallis*, painted on the fields of Yorktown just thirty-five miles up the road from our home in Virginia Beach, and *General George Washington Resigning His Commission* at Annapolis in December 1783.

"Most visitors walk right past that fourth Trumbull painting on their way to Statuary Hall," Mr. Galloway observed approvingly, stepping up beside Katie's wheelchair and Dad. "Do you know why historians consider *General George Washington Resigning His Commission* the most important painting in the entire Rotunda?"

"Because he gave the power back," Katie answered immediately, her eyes fixed on the painted parchment scroll in Washington's outstretched hand. "He had the Continental Army behind him, and he could have stayed in power for life like a king—Wait, that's what King George III said when they told him Washington was going to resign and go home to Mount Vernon, isn't it? That if he did that, he would be the greatest man in the world?"

Mr. Galloway beamed from ear to ear. "Spot-on! In a republic, the highest office in the land doesn't belong to the person holding the commission—it's held in trust for the people and returned to civilian hands under the Constitution."

***

#### 12:35 PM — John Quincy Adams's Whisper Spot in National Statuary Hall & The Historic Old Senate Chamber

Rolling south through the tall bronze doors out of the Rotunda, we entered the semicircular Greek Revival amphitheater of National Statuary Hall—the original chamber of the House of Representatives from 1807 until 1857, ringed with marble and bronze statues contributed by the states.

Mr. Galloway guided Katie's and my wheelchairs over to a small brass plaque embedded in the black-and-white marble tiles on the east side of the floor, stamped with the name *JOHN QUINCY ADAMS*.

"Wait right here on this brass marker, Katie and Nathaniel," Mr. Galloway said with a twinkle in his eye, walking thirty-five feet away across the crowded floor toward the opposite side of the hall and turning his back to us.

Even with dozens of visitors talking across the room, Mr. Galloway's softest whisper traveled up the curved parabolic ceiling, bounced across the plaster arch overhead, and dropped straight down into Katie's and my ears as clearly as if he were leaning over our armrests:

*"When John Quincy Adams served in the House of Representatives after leaving the Presidency, he sat at this exact desk—and he could hear every word the opposing party whispered on the other side of the chamber!"*

Katie and I both grinned across the hall at him as Dad laughed out loud.

Before we headed through the underground tunnel to grab lunch in the Senate cafeteria prior to our one-forty-five appointment with Senator West, Marcus and Mr. Galloway took us on one final elevator ride up to the semicircular gallery entrance of the historic Old Senate Chamber—the intimate, crimson-and-gold room where the United States Senate had debated the fate of the Union from 1810 until 1859, and where the Supreme Court of the United States had subsequently sat for seventy-five years until 1935.

Looking across the two curved tiers of polished mahogany desks toward the crimson silk canopy and the gilded wooden eagle perched above the Vice President's dais, Katie asked Marcus and Mr. Galloway a question that made both men pause.

"When a bill comes to the Senate today," Katie asked, pointing toward the front row of desks, "how much of the actual text gets written during the speeches on the floor versus inside the committee rooms before the cameras ever turn on?"

"Ninety-five percent of it happens in committee and subcommittee markups, Katie," Marcus answered honestly, impressed by the question. "Floor speeches get the headlines on the six-o'clock news, but the Senators who sit down in committee, read every line of the statutory formulas, and write the amendments are the ones who actually decide whether a transit agency gets funded or a ramp gets built."

Katie nodded slowly, filing every word of that answer away inside her memory as we turned our chairs toward the elevator.

### Part 4: Meeting Senator James West, Watching the U.S. Senate From the Gallery, & Why Can't We Ride the Bus to City Hall?

**Date:** 2007-04-10 at 13:45 America/New_York

![Inside the third-floor wheelchair-accessible visitor gallery overlooking the United States Senate Chamber at the U.S. Capitol on Tuesday afternoon, April 10, 2007, twenty-two-year-old fraternal twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs holding their official Senate Gallery passes beside their father David Prairie, looking down in rapt awe at the semicircular rows of mahogany Senate desks below]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/apr_2007_us_senate_gallery_and_senator_james_west_visit_katie_nate_david.jpg)

#### Tuesday, April 10, 2007, 1:45 PM — Meeting Senator James West & Riding the Capitol Subway

At one-forty-five, after eating lunch with Dad in the Senate cafeteria, the three of us rolled down the marble corridor of the Senate Office Building and turned through the tall wooden double doors of United States Senator James West's suite, where the Great Seal of the Commonwealth of Virginia hung beside the entrance.

Before the receptionist had even finished handing us our three blue cardboard United States Senate Gallery passes, the inner door of the Senator's private office opened—and out walked Senator James West himself in his dark navy suit and striped tie.

He didn't stand stiffly behind a rope line or talk exclusively to Dad over our heads the way so many adults did when they saw two twenty-two-year-old twins in motorized wheelchairs. Instead, Senator West walked straight across the reception carpet to our chairs, leaned down to look Katie and me directly in the eyes, and shook Katie's hand and then mine with a firm, warm grip.

"Katie and Nathaniel, happy twenty-second birthday, and welcome to Washington," Senator West said in his steady Virginia cadence. "My staff told me the two of you just finished your computer science degrees down at the Community College of Hampton Roads in Norfolk, started your own vocational software course, and run your own regional transit blog down at the coast. How did the White House and the Capitol Rotunda treat you this morning?"

"They were unforgettable, Senator West," Katie said, her voice clear and earnest as she shook his hand. "Thank you so much for having your office arrange our passes. We couldn't believe how quickly your staff called our dad back."

"Don't ever let anyone tell you that these buildings belong to the lobbyists or the politicians, Katie," Senator West told her, looking from Katie's eyes to mine and then up at Dad. "The United States Capitol belongs to the people of the United States—and my number-one job as your Senator from Virginia is making sure when constituents from Virginia Beach knock on this door, somebody answers. I have to head over to the floor in ten minutes to speak on the transportation and veterans' appropriations bill, so I'm going to have Marcus take the three of you down to the Capitol subway right now so you can watch the live session from the front row of the gallery."

Watching a sitting United States Senator take the time in the middle of a busy legislative afternoon to look us directly in the eyes and remind us that the Capitol belonged to the constituents who knocked on its door left an impression on my sister that neither of us would ever forget.

Five minutes later, Marcus escorted the three of us down the elevator to the bright underground tunnel of the Capitol Subway system, guided our two SwiftChairs onto the level accessible car of the electric subway tram, and rode with us beneath Constitution Avenue straight into the basement of the Senate Wing.

***

#### 2:10 PM — Looking Down From the Third-Floor U.S. Senate Gallery

Riding the Senate wing elevator up to the third floor, we followed the gallery doorkeeper's quiet hand signals through the heavy padded double doors of the Visitors' Gallery and rolled our two SwiftChairs side by side into the level wheelchair alcove overlooking the United States Senate Chamber.

The moment we looked over the brass-and-mahogany balcony railing, Katie's breath caught audibly in her throat.

![Inside the third-floor wheelchair-accessible visitor gallery overlooking the United States Senate Chamber at the U.S. Capitol on Tuesday afternoon, April 10, 2007, twenty-two-year-old fraternal twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs holding their official Senate Gallery passes beside their father David Prairie, looking down in rapt awe at the semicircular rows of mahogany Senate desks below]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/apr_2007_us_senate_gallery_and_senator_james_west_visit_katie_nate_david.jpg)

Directly below us stretched the four semicircular tiers of a hundred historic mahogany desks arranged across the blue patterned carpet of the Senate floor. Down at the tiered marble rostrum, the presiding officer's gavel tapped once, the reading clerk called out the number of a pending amendment, and Senators rose behind their desks—including Senator James West and senior Senator John Warren on the Virginia aisle—to debate federal transit formula grants and veterans' medical care in live session.

When Senator James West rose behind his desk to speak, he glanced up briefly toward the third-floor gallery alcove where the three of us were sitting and gave a subtle, respectful nod before addressing the Chair.

For forty-five straight minutes, Katie didn't look away from the Senate floor once. She leaned slightly forward in her SwiftChair, her left hand resting warmly over mine on my armrest, watching how a single elected voice standing behind a mahogany desk could force an entire chamber—and an entire federal agency—to put its numbers on the public record and vote in the daylight.

***

#### 8:30 PM — Back at Dad's Dining Table in Alexandria: The 5:30 PM Last Bus Home & How to Run for City Council

That evening, after eating dinner near Capitol Hill and riding the Yellow Line train across the Potomac River bridge to King Street at eight-fifteen—transferring effortlessly onto a local evening bus just to see the neighborhood loop before rolling through the railroad underpass and retrieving our wheelchair backpacks inside Dad's brick house on Sunset Drive—Katie didn't head straight for the downstairs closet to rest.

Instead, she rolled her SwiftChair right up to Dad's dining table, opened her silver laptop beside mine, and pulled up two browser tabs side by side: the official meeting calendar of the Virginia Beach City Council, and the printed PDF timetables for Coastal Virginia Transit Authority Routes 12 and 33.

Dad walked in from the kitchen carrying three tall glasses of cold ginger ale, set them on coasters, and looked at the fierce, concentrated expression on my sister's face. "What are you looking at on there, Katie?"

Katie turned her laptop screen slightly so Dad and I could both see it, and her voice was shaking with genuine, righteous anger.

"Look at what the three of us just did tonight here in Alexandria and Washington, Dad," Katie said, tapping the corner of her keyboard. "Today we toured the White House, toured the Capitol Rotunda and Statuary Hall, watched the United States Senate in session from the gallery, ate dinner at seven-thirty, and rode public trains and buses all the way back to Sunset Drive at eight-thirty at night without a single problem. Now look at the schedule back home in Virginia Beach—the largest city in the entire Commonwealth of Virginia!"

She pointed her finger at the Virginia Beach City Council schedule on the left half of her screen, and then at the CVTA bus timetable on the right half.

"Virginia Beach City Council formal evening sessions and public-comment hearings down at the Municipal Center start at six o'clock in the evening," Katie said, her blue eyes flashing. "If Nate and I want to ride the bus from Arvin Road down to City Hall to speak to our own City Council during a six-o'clock meeting, we have to take Route 12 to the CCHR Virginia Beach Campus hub and transfer to Route 33 down to the Municipal Center. Now look at the return schedule from the Municipal Center!"

I leaned in over my armrest and read the black-and-white timetable columns aloud with her.

"To get back to the CCHR hub in time to connect to Route 12, Route 25, or Route 29," I said, "you have to leave the Municipal Center on the five-thirty PM Route 33 bus—because the very last Route 12 bus back to Indian River Road and Military Highway leaves CCHR at five-forty-eight PM!"

"Five-thirty PM!" Katie repeated, slapping her palm lightly against the tabletop. "City Council meetings start at six o'clock, and the last bus home for a citizen who needs to connect at CCHR leaves City Hall at five-thirty—thirty minutes before the meeting even starts! And even if you live right on Route 33 and don't have to transfer at CCHR, the last northbound bus going all the way to Sixty-Eighth Street leaves the Municipal Center at six-oh-one PM—one minute after the Mayor bangs the gavel! If you rely on a bus in Virginia Beach, you are literally locked out of attending your own City Council meetings unless you want to get stranded fifteen miles from home in the dark!"

Dad sat down in the wooden chair across from us, resting his forearms on the table as he looked at Katie. "And because none of the people sitting on the Virginia Beach City Council ever ride a bus, none of them even notices—or cares—that the schedule locks bus riders out of City Hall."

Katie stared at the screen for a long, quiet moment—remembering President Roosevelt's wheelchair path across the State Floor of the White House, the portrait of Abraham Lincoln above John Adams's carved prayer, the hundred mahogany desks she had looked down upon from the United States Senate Gallery that afternoon, and the words Senator James West had spoken to us in his reception room: *Don't ever let anyone tell you that these buildings belong to the lobbyists or the politicians.*

Then Katie opened a third browser tab and typed a search query into the address bar: *Commonwealth of Virginia State Board of Elections Candidate Qualification Guide — City Council*.

"What are you pulling up now, Katie?" I asked softly, rolling my chair flush against hers.

"How old you have to be, how many registered voter signatures you need on a petition, and what forms you have to file to run for the Virginia Beach City Council," Katie answered, her voice steady as steel as the PDF loaded on her screen. "Look right here under Code of Virginia Section 24.2-501: eighteen years old, a qualified voter registered at your residential address in the Kempsville District—which we've had on our Virginia State ID cards and voter registration on Arvin Road since 2001—and one hundred twenty-five certified voter signatures. If the politicians on the Virginia Beach City Council won't ride the bus or let bus riders attend their six-o'clock meetings, Nate, then we're going to learn every rule in this book, and I'm going to run for City Council so we can make the changes from the inside."

Flipping up the inner armrest between our two SwiftChairs, I leaned across and wrapped both arms tightly around my twin sister's shoulders. Katie exhaled a long, slow breath and buried her face against my neck, wrapping her arms around my chest as the familiar, steady deep pressure of our embrace settled our racing nerves—and twenty minutes later, inside the quiet, dark sanctuary of Dad's downstairs bedroom closet, we fell asleep cuddled up together inside our shared sleeping bag with the future of Virginia Beach already taking shape in our minds.

### Part 5: \

**Date:** 2007-04-19 at 13:15 America/New_York

![Inside a bright U.S. Post Office passport acceptance window in Virginia Beach on Thursday afternoon, April 19, 2007, twenty-two-year-old fraternal twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs raising their right hands to take the passport application oath in front of a uniformed postal clerk behind the counter—with their completed DS-11 forms, two-by-two passport photos, certified birth certificates, and horizontal Virginia State ID cards resting on the counter]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/apr_2007_post_office_passport_application_ds11_and_photos_katie_nate.jpg)

#### Thursday, April 19, 2007, 1:15 PM — "What's This?" and Why We Wanted Passports
