"Wait a second—what's this?" the young teller behind the counter at the neighborhood bank branch asked on Thursday afternoon, squinting down at the brand-new horizontal plastic card I had just slid under the acrylic window alongside our business checking signature card. "Do you have a driver's license?"

Sitting right beside my left wheel, Katie let out a slow, measured breath through her nose.

"It's a Virginia State ID card," I told the teller patiently, tapping my finger against the words *COMMONWEALTH OF VIRGINIA — IDENTIFICATION CARD* printed in bold letters across the top of the laminate. "It's issued by the Virginia Department of Motor Vehicles, and it's an official state identification card."

"Oh!" the teller blinked, glancing down through the glass partition at the two black motorized wheelchairs Katie and I were sitting in before her cheeks turned pink. "Right—sorry about that! I'm just so used to looking at driver's licenses all day that the top banner threw me off."

Every single adult who doesn't drive knows that exact moment. On paper, under every state and federal statute in America, a valid DMV-issued State ID card is 100 percent equal to a driver's license for proving who you are. In the real world, however, an astonishing number of clerks, tellers, and receptionists stare at a State ID card as if you just handed them a laminated grocery-store coupon and ask, *"What's this?"* until you explain to them that it is, in fact, an ID card.

As we rolled out of the bank lobby onto the sidewalk ten minutes later, Katie looked over at me with her mind already made up.

"You know what we're doing this afternoon while we're already out on the bus, don't you, Nate?" Katie asked.

"Getting United States Passports?" I grinned.

"Getting United States Passports," Katie declared firmly. "First of all, after riding the ARTS train up to Alexandria and Washington last week, I want the two of us to have real passports so if we ever decide to take the train all the way up to Montreal or Toronto—or fly across the Atlantic one day—we don't have to wait three months for paperwork. And second of all, I would love to see anybody in the Commonwealth of Virginia look at an official United States Passport with the gold eagle on the cover and ask us, *'What's this?'*"

***

#### 2:30 PM — Form DS-11, Two-by-Two Photos, & Raising Our Right Hands at the Post Office

That afternoon, back at our dual-desk office on Arvin Road, Katie and I downloaded two copies of U.S. Department of State Form DS-11—the official Application for a U.S. Passport for first-time adult applicants—and filled out every box in black ink, carefully leaving the signature line at the bottom blank just as the instructions required until we were right in front of an authorized Acceptance Agent.

From the fireproof steel document box Dad kept in the hall linen closet, we pulled out our original certified Commonwealth of Virginia birth certificates with the raised embossed seals from the Division of Vital Records in Richmond, tucked them into a rigid manila folder alongside our horizontal Virginia State ID cards and our checkbook, and rode the bus over to the U.S. Post Office passport window.

"Two first-time adult passport applications and two sets of passport photos, please," Katie told the uniformed postal acceptance clerk at two-thirty as we rolled our SwiftChairs side by side up to the passport counter.

"You two came prepared," the postal clerk smiled, checking our unsigned DS-11 forms and our raised-seal birth certificates before sliding a white pull-down screen down behind the end of the counter. "Roll right over here in front of the white screen one at a time so I can take your two-by-two photos. Chin level, shoulders square to the lens, and give me a natural look looking straight into the camera."

Because the backs of our SwiftChairs came up behind our shoulders in dark black upholstery, the clerk angled the camera slightly downward at seated eye level so the two-inch-by-two-inch frame captured our heads and shoulders cleanly against the plain white backdrop.

While the photo printer behind the counter spat out two glossy sheets of twin two-by-two portraits and the clerk trimmed them with a heavy metal die-cutter, a newer postal clerk at the adjacent register leaned over to glance at the two horizontal Virginia cards Katie and I had laid on the counter.

"Wait—what kind of cards are those?" the trainee clerk asked, squinting at the lack of a driver-class code.

Katie and I looked at each other and burst out laughing at the exact same second.

"They're Virginia State ID cards," Katie told him cheerfully. "And in about ten weeks, we're going to have two blue books to go right alongside them."

"Don't mind him—state IDs are 100 percent valid primary photo identification for a DS-11," our passport acceptance clerk chuckled, copying our Virginia ID numbers onto the verification block of our applications and stapling one two-by-two photo to Katie's form and one to mine.

She turned both clipboards around on the lowered counter and handed us each a black ballpoint pen.

"All right, Katie and Nathaniel—please raise your right hands," the clerk said officially. "Do you solemnly swear or affirm that the statements made on this application are true and that the photograph attached is a true likeness of yourself?"

![Inside a bright U.S. Post Office passport acceptance window in Virginia Beach on Thursday afternoon, April 19, 2007, twenty-two-year-old fraternal twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs raising their right hands to take the passport application oath in front of a uniformed postal clerk behind the counter—with their completed DS-11 forms, two-by-two passport photos, certified birth certificates, and horizontal Virginia State ID cards resting on the counter]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/apr_2007_post_office_passport_application_ds11_and_photos_katie_nate.jpg)

"I do," Katie and I said together, our right hands raised side by side from our wheelchairs.

Under the clerk's watchful eyes, we signed our full legal names inside the signature boxes on our DS-11 forms, wrote out the checks for the Department of State application fee and the Postal Service execution and photo fees, and watched her seal our applications and our certified birth certificates inside two tamper-evident transmittal pouches bound for the National Passport Center.

***

#### Ten Weeks Later (Saturday, June 30, 2007) — Two Crisp Blue Books in the Mailbox

Because the spring and summer of 2007 saw the largest nationwide passport backlog in modern history—triggered by new federal rules requiring passports for air travel across the Western Hemisphere—the routine six-week wait stretched into ten full weeks.

Every afternoon when the mail carrier walked up Arvin Road, I rolled out onto the front porch ramp to check the mailbox beside our front door.

Then, on Saturday afternoon, June 30, 2007, I opened the metal mailbox lid and pulled out four stiff envelopes from the United States Department of State: two flat manila envelopes returning our original raised-seal Virginia birth certificates, and two Priority Mail envelopes with stiff cardboard inserts inside.

"Katie!" I called out, wheeling straight down the hallway into our dual-desk office and holding up the four envelopes. "They're here!"

Katie spun her SwiftChair away from her keyboard so fast her front casters chirped against the floor mat. Side by side, we tore open the tear-strips on the two Priority Mail envelopes and slid out two brand-new, dark navy-blue United States Passports, the gold Great Seal of the United States and the new biometric electronic-chip symbol gleaming across the textured front covers.

Opening the inside covers, we stared down at our digitized two-by-two post-office portraits printed beneath the holographic eagles, valid for ten full years until June 2017.

"Look at that, Nate," Katie smiled, setting our two open passports on the desk blotter before flipping up her inner armrest and leaning right into my arms for a long, tight, deep-pressure hug. Pressing my cheek against her hair as we held each other close—feeling that unmistakable calm and security that always washed over both of us whenever we cuddled together—I listened to her whisper against my shoulder: "Our own house on Arvin Road, our own software LLC, our horizontal Virginia State IDs, and now two United States Passports. Wherever the rails go next, we have our tickets."

## Associate Degrees in Hand, 'Not the Right Skill Match,' & Launching Prairie Twin Interactive From Arvin Road

### Associate Degrees in Hand, 'Not the Right Skill Match,' & Putting Our Virginia LLC to Work

**Date:** 2007-06-14 at 14:15 America/New_York

![Inside a glass-walled corporate conference room off Virginia Beach Boulevard on Thursday afternoon, June 14, 2007, twenty-two-year-old fraternal twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs with their leather CCHR Associate Degree portfolios and printed PHP and SQL code samples open on the table, exchanging a quiet, knowing look as two corporate hiring managers offer practiced, legally sanitized smiles across the table]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/jun_2007_polite_hr_job_interview_rejection_wheelchairs_katie_nate.jpg)

#### Thursday, June 14, 2007, 2:15 PM — "Not Quite the Right Skill Match" & The Careful Language of Corporate HR

"Your PHP database queries and your Associate of Applied Science transcripts from the Community College of Hampton Roads are certainly impressive on paper," the human-resources director said in a smooth, carefully measured voice at two-fifteen on Thursday afternoon inside a second-floor office park off Virginia Beach Boulevard, folding her hands neatly atop our printed resumes without quite meeting our eyes. "However, after reviewing our current project pipeline this afternoon, we feel that your background isn't quite the right skill match for what our team is looking for right now, and we are looking for candidates with a bit more traditional in-house agency experience."

Sitting side by side in our black SwiftChairs across the glass conference table, Katie and I exchanged a single, quiet glance.

We didn't need a translator to know what had actually changed between eleven o'clock that morning—when the company's lead developer had practically begged us over the phone to come in as soon as possible after testing our live PHP and SQL transit-schedule database—and two-fifteen that afternoon.

At eleven o'clock on the telephone, we were two twenty-two-year-old software developers with accredited associate degrees from CCHR and clean, normalized SQL code. At two o'clock, when the elevator doors opened and Katie and I rolled into the reception lobby side by side in two motorized power wheelchairs after riding CVTA Route 15 and Route 20 to the office park, we watched the lead developer's smile freeze on his face before he hurriedly called the human-resources director into the room.

![Inside a glass-walled corporate conference room off Virginia Beach Boulevard on Thursday afternoon, June 14, 2007, twenty-two-year-old fraternal twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs with their leather CCHR Associate Degree portfolios and printed PHP and SQL code samples open on the table, exchanging a quiet, knowing look as two corporate hiring managers offer practiced, legally sanitized smiles across the table]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/jun_2007_polite_hr_job_interview_rejection_wheelchairs_katie_nate.jpg)

It was our sixth traditional job interview across Virginia Beach and Norfolk since returning from our birthday week in Alexandria and finishing the final PHP and SQL modules with Tina, Sheila, and Jim in May.

We had done everything the traditional employment playbook told young adults to do. We had filled out the multi-page paper and online applications. We had brought our framed Associate of Applied Science degrees from the Community College of Hampton Roads—never once regretting that we had rolled out of Roosevelt Rehabilitation Center after twelve days without an RRC certificate, because we knew an RRC piece of paper meant nothing in the real world next to an accredited college degree and live production code.

And in all six interviews, the exact same script had played out almost word for word.

No employer in 2007 was foolish enough to say out loud that they didn't want to hire two twenty-two-year-old twins in power wheelchairs who commuted by public bus. Every human-resources manager in Hampton Roads had been trained by corporate counsel on how to avoid running afoul of the Americans with Disabilities Act and Virginia's disability rights statutes. Their language was always impeccably polite, rehearsed, and legally bulletproof: *not quite the right skill match*, *looking for a different blend of experience*, *decided to go in another direction*.

Yet when a company posts an entry-level job asking for HTML, CSS, PHP, and SQL, raves about your live PHP database over the phone, and suddenly discovers ten minutes after seeing your wheelchairs that you "aren't the right skill match" while leaving the exact same job posting up on their website three weeks later, you don't have to be a lawyer to read between the lines.

"Thank you for your time this afternoon," Katie said politely, closing her leather portfolio binder and resting it across her lap as we turned our wheelchairs around, rolled out to the elevator, and headed back down to the bus stop on Virginia Beach Boulevard.

***

#### 4:00 PM — Putting Prairie Twin Interactive, LLC to Work From Our Dual Desks on Arvin Road

When we rolled back up our aluminum porch ramp on Arvin Road at four o'clock, poured two tall glasses of cold ginger ale in the kitchen, and wheeled side by side into our twelve-by-twelve office bedroom, neither of us was defeated. If anything, watching six corporate HR departments hide behind polite boilerplate had burned away the last shred of doubt about what we needed to do.

"You know what the funniest part of that interview was, Nate?" Katie asked, parking her SwiftChair flush beside mine under our twelve-foot span of worktables and tapping the framed Virginia State Corporation Commission certificate hanging on the wall above our monitors—*PRAIRIE TWIN INTERACTIVE, LLC*. "That agency's own corporate website is still running broken table layouts from 1999 that don't even validate in a modern browser, and their contact form throws an unescaped SQL error if you type an apostrophe into your last name."

I burst out laughing, the tension of the afternoon evaporating in an instant. "And they told us we didn't have the right skill match!"

"We don't need a corporate HR department to give us permission to write code and earn our own spending money," Katie said firmly, her fingers lacing through mine across our wheelchair armrests. "We already have our associate degrees from CCHR. We already have two six-foot desks, high-speed internet, and our own Linux server right here in this room. And thanks to Dad and Mr. Vance, we already have Prairie Twin Interactive, LLC registered with the state and our Suite 214 commercial mailbox at The Parcel Center so we can sign client contracts and cash business checks without ever putting Arvin Road on an invoice."

"And when a small business owner in Virginia Beach, Norfolk, or Chesapeake hires Prairie Twin Interactive over email and phone to build their PHP website or normalize their inventory database," I grinned, opening a fresh directory on our server to build our commercial portfolio site, "the code doesn't care that the two developers writing it are sitting side by side in power wheelchairs—or that we take our lunch breaks together in our own kitchen and sleep every night in our bedroom closet."

By the end of July, we had landed our first three paid web-development contracts—building a custom PHP parts-catalog database for an independent marine-supply shop in Norfolk, redesigning the schedule and registration portal for a Tidewater community music school, and coding an automated invoice tracker for a regional printing company.

The Friday afternoon in August when we rolled into The Parcel Center, unlocked Box 214 with our brass key, and pulled out our very first three client checks made payable to *Prairie Twin Interactive, LLC*, Katie held the envelopes up in the sunlight with tears of pride shining in her blue eyes.

Dad was still faithfully covering every household bill on Arvin Road from Alexandria, just as he had promised. Now, however, as we deposited our own self-earned software revenue into our business and joint accounts, bought our own thirty-day CVTA bus passes, upgraded our video camera gear, and spent every evening analyzing regional transit budgets side by side at our dual desks, we weren't just surviving anymore.

We were twenty-two-year-old business partners, unofficial homeowners, and best friends—and as 2007 turned toward the 2008 municipal election year across Hampton Roads, we were ready to take on City Hall.

# Do Better: Ideas for CVTA & The Kempsville City Council

## Do Better: Ideas for CVTA & The Four-Bus Mayoral Loop

### Part 1: Does the Bus Run? Calling Out CVTA's Complacency & The 2008 Regional Mayoral Challenge

**Date:** 2008-04-14 at 13:30 America/New_York

![Inside the Coastal Virginia Transit Authority boardroom on 18th Street in Norfolk on April 14, 2008, 22-year-old twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs at the public-comment microphone table presenting their route and schedule audit to the CVTA commissioners.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/apr_2008_cvta_18th_street_boardroom_public_comment_katie_nate.jpg)

#### Thursday, April 14, 2008, 1:30 PM — The Binders at Eighteenth Street & The "Good Enough" Mentality

![Inside the Coastal Virginia Transit Authority boardroom on 18th Street in Norfolk on April 14, 2008, 22-year-old twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs at the public-comment microphone table presenting their route and schedule audit to the CVTA commissioners.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/apr_2008_cvta_18th_street_boardroom_public_comment_katie_nate.jpg)

"Look at the open three-ring binder on the corner of the staff table, Nate," Katie whispered, leaning slightly across her SwiftChair armrest toward mine as we parked our wheelchairs at the end of the front visitor row inside the Coastal Virginia Transit Authority boardroom on Eighteenth Street in Norfolk. "That's our Tuesday post. They printed the whole thing out and highlighted the timetable chart in yellow."

I followed my sister's gaze across the polished laminate table where CVTA's senior operations staff and the appointed city council commissioners from around Hampton Roads were shuffling their agenda packets before the monthly Transportation District Commission meeting gaveled in.

Sure enough, clipped inside the deputy planning director's black binder—and photocopied into three separate packets along the commissioners' dais—were six pages printed directly from Ideas for Coastal Virginia Transit, complete with the coastal-navy header and the custom PHP route-comparison tables I had coded the week before at our dual desks in the brick ranch on Arvin Road off Indian River Road and Military Highway in Virginia Beach.

"Every weekday morning between eight and ten o'clock, our server logs show static IP blocks from this building and all six City Halls reading our PHP tables," I whispered back to Katie, glancing down the row of commissioners. "They read every word we write, Katie. They just don't know what to do with two twenty-two-year-old twins in power wheelchairs who won't pat them on the back for the status quo."

When the commission chair called the brief public-comment period at the start of the one-thirty afternoon meeting—scheduled, as always, in the middle of a Thursday workday when almost no working commuter could attend—Katie released her joystick brake and rolled smoothly up to the low microphone table at the front of the room, with me rolling right up beside her holding our printed schedule audit.

"Mr. Chairman, commissioners, and CVTA staff," Katie said clearly, her voice steady and polite as every head along the horseshoe dais turned toward our two wheelchairs. "My brother Nathaniel and I are the authors of Ideas for Coastal Virginia Transit. We ride CVTA buses in our power wheelchairs every week across Virginia Beach, Norfolk, Chesapeake, and the Peninsula, and we pay our regular thirty-day pass fares just like thousands of other citizens who depend on this network."

Down at the staff table, the senior service planner and the communications director exchanged an immediate, tight-lipped glance, recognizing our names at once.

"Over the past two years," Katie continued, resting her hand on the timetable charts across my lap, "we have documented why riders across Hampton Roads are being left behind—not because our region lacks the roads or the riders, but because this agency and our six member cities have settled for schedules that lock working people out. Look at your own printed Route 1 schedule between Downtown Norfolk and Pembroke East: on the Norfolk side of the line, from Downtown Norfolk through Wards Corner and Ocean View to the Amphibious Base, Route 1 runs every fifteen to thirty minutes and runs late into the night until 2:15 AM, seven days a week. The exact moment Route 1 crosses the city line into Virginia Beach toward Pleasure House Road, Haygood, and Pembroke East, most of the buses turn around at the border, service drops to once an hour, only runs during the day with the last bus leaving Pembroke East at 6:22 PM, and has no Sunday service at all. On Route 25 from Glenrock Mall to the CCHR Virginia Beach Campus, buses run every thirty minutes to Newtown Road at the city line, where half of them turn right back around into Norfolk, leaving the Virginia Beach side down Princess Anne Road to CCHR with hourly daytime-only service that ends at 5:53 PM. At the CCHR Virginia Beach Campus hub, the last Route 12 bus back toward Military Highway and Indian River Road leaves at 5:48 PM. If a citizen rides Route 33 to the Virginia Beach Municipal Center to attend a 6:00 PM City Council meeting and needs to catch Route 12, Route 25, or Route 29 at CCHR to get home, they have to leave City Hall at 5:33 PM—twenty-seven minutes before the council meeting even starts. Across the water, the last southbound Route 61 across the Hampton Roads Bridge-Tunnel still leaves Newport News Transit Center at 6:45 PM, and riders transferring on multi-bus routes are still getting penalized with a second fare because the two-hour paper transfer expires while they wait for sixty-minute local buses."

"We aren't here to bash public transit," I added from my chair beside Katie. "We love public transit. We need public transit to live our lives. We're here because CVTA can be so much better than this—with timed evening transfer pulses at CCHR, Glenrock Mall, and Hilltop, service running until at least ten or eleven o'clock at night, clean transit center restrooms, and a modern smart-card fare system that doesn't punish two-bus commuters—if the leaders on this commission have the political willpower to fund and demand it."

The commission chair offered a polite, practiced nod as the three-minute timer beeped. "Thank you both for your comments. Staff will take your blog submissions under advisement."

Twenty minutes later, when the board recessed into the hallway outside the Eighteenth Street conference room, CVTA's senior service planner and one of the veteran municipal council commissioners walked past our wheelchairs near the water fountain. Stopping beside us with a folder tucked under his arm, the planner offered the tired, defensive half-smile of a bureaucrat who had spent fifteen years guarding an unchallenged routine.

"Look, Katie, Nate," the planner said, lowering his voice as the commissioner nodded beside him, "we read your blog every week. You two obviously put a lot of math into those PHP charts of yours. But you have to be realistic about how transit works in a region like Hampton Roads."

"Realistic about what?" Katie asked, looking straight up at him from her SwiftChair.

The commissioner shrugged his shoulders, palms turned upward in the exact gesture that summed up thirty years of regional transit policy.

"Does the bus run?" the commissioner asked rhetorically. "Yes, the bus runs. Every morning the garages roll the fleet out across all six cities. Do people get to CCHR and the malls and the shipyards during the day? Yes. Is it good enough for what our city councils budget every spring? I guess so. Nobody at City Hall is clamoring to spend millions more running buses late into the night or overhauling transfer rules when the buses are already out there running their routes."

Katie and I looked at each other as the planner and the commissioner patted the folder and walked back into the boardroom.

There it was, spoken right out loud in the hallway of Eighteenth Street: the entire institutional philosophy of the Coastal Virginia Transit Authority.

*Does the bus run? Yes. Is it good enough? I guess so.*

For decades, CVTA and the politicians who funded it had hidden behind that exact complacency. As long as a diesel bus rolled past a stop sign once an hour during banker's hours and the annual federal grant paperwork got signed, the agency and the six city councils treated the box as checked. Until Ideas for Coastal Virginia Transit came along, nobody with the technical skills to dissect their Transportation Service Plans—and the daily lived reality of riding those buses in power wheelchairs—had ever stood up in public and told them to *do better*.

As we rolled our wheelchairs out the automatic glass doors of the Eighteenth Street headquarters toward the Granby Street bus stop to catch our ride home, Katie's jaw was set with quiet fire.

"Did you hear what that commissioner said, Nate?" Katie asked as we waited on the concrete sidewalk pad. "'Nobody at City Hall is clamoring to spend money or overhaul the routes because it's good enough.' He just admitted the truth. The problem isn't that CVTA can't be improved. Every single improvement we've written about on the blog is completely doable. The only thing missing is the political willpower from the mayors and city councils who control CVTA's purse strings and sit on that board."

"And half of those city halls are up for election this year," I said, the realization clicking into place as the low-floor CVTA bus pulled up to the curb and kneeled its front suspension.

"Every single one of them has elections in 2008," Katie said as the hydraulic ramp folded down onto the concrete and we rolled up into the front wheelchair securement bays. "And as soon as we get home to Kempsville, we are going to put their political willpower to the test in front of every voter in Hampton Roads."

***

#### Mapping the 2008 Regional Mayoral Elections & Issuing the Open Challenge

Back at our dual computer desks in the spare bedroom office of our new Kempsville house that evening, Katie and I pulled up the official 2008 Virginia State Board of Elections candidate filings across all six member cities of the Coastal Virginia Transit Authority: Virginia Beach, Chesapeake, Portsmouth, Norfolk, Hampton, and Newport News.

Sipping cold ginger ale from our glasses while my PHP editor and our browser tabs glowed side by side across our monitors, we mapped out the exact 2008 municipal calendar across the six cities.

"Look at how the 2008 mayoral calendar breaks down across the six CVTA cities," I said, pointing to the state election schedule on my screen. "Out of the six cities—Virginia Beach, Chesapeake, Portsmouth, Norfolk, Hampton, and Newport News—four of them are holding direct elections for Mayor here in 2008, while the other two are mid-term on their mayoral cycle."

Katie rolled her chair closer and read down the certified candidate lists with me.

"Norfolk and Newport News both elected their mayors to four-year terms back in May 2006, so neither Norfolk nor Newport News has a Mayor's race until May 2010—though both cities have City Council seats on the ballot next month on Tuesday, May 6, 2008," Katie noted. "Then, on that same Tuesday, May 6, 2008 spring municipal ballot, three CVTA cities are electing their Mayors: Chesapeake has an open-seat Mayor's race, Portsmouth has a contested Mayor's race, and Hampton has an open-seat Mayor's race across the water."

"And then our own city—Virginia Beach—moved its municipal elections to the fall general election ballot on Tuesday, November 4, 2008," I said, scrolling down to the Virginia Beach filings. "And look at the Virginia Beach Mayor's race: Mayor Myra Overton is running for another term after twenty years as Mayor, and she's facing three challengers in a four-way race for Mayor of Virginia Beach, right alongside the at-large and district City Council races."

Katie looked at Mayor Myra E. Overton's name on the screen and shook her head thoughtfully.

Every lifelong resident of Virginia Beach knew the paradox of Mayor Myra Overton. On a personal level, she was a genuinely sweet, gracious, grandmotherly lady who had gotten her start in civic and political life serving on the city's public library board and had championed the Central Library on Virginia Beach Boulevard for decades. If you met her at a ribbon-cutting or a neighborhood library reading, she couldn't have been nicer.

As a municipal politician overseeing transportation for the largest city in Virginia, however, her twenty-year tenure had been a disaster for anyone who rode a bus. Among daily CVTA riders, bus operators, and local political watchers, there was a famous story that had circulated for years to explain why Virginia Beach's bus service hours were so abysmal compared to Norfolk's. There was no way to confirm she had ever actually said the words out loud, of course, but as the local legend went, if Mayor Overton had her way, the Route 20 bus on Virginia Beach Boulevard would depart Downtown Norfolk, roll east down the Boulevard to Newtown Road at the city line, and turn right back around and stay in Norfolk—to keep the riff-raff out, of course.

Whether that story was literal truth or courthouse folklore, one glance at the printed Route 1 and Route 25 timetables—where frequent, late-night Norfolk buses hit the Virginia Beach border and suddenly shriveled into once-an-hour daytime-only runs that vanished after dinnertime—made it painfully obvious why everyone in Hampton Roads believed it.

Katie leaned forward, resting her forearms on the desk.

"Four mayoral elections across Hampton Roads in 2008—Chesapeake, Portsmouth, and Hampton in May, and Virginia Beach in November—plus City Council races in all six CVTA cities," Katie said. "Every single one of those candidates puts glossy photos on their campaign flyers claiming they care about regional transportation, traffic relief, working families, and citizens with disabilities. Let's see how many of them are actually willing to step out from behind a podium and ride the bus with the two of us."

Opening the PHP administrative dashboard for Ideas for Coastal Virginia Transit, Katie and I drafted our landmark open letter together, carefully checking every word before publishing it to the top of the front page and sending personalized copies directly to the official campaign email addresses of every certified candidate for Mayor in Virginia Beach, Chesapeake, Portsmouth, and Hampton—as well as the City Council candidates across all six CVTA cities:

> Thursday, April 14, 2008 — An Open Invitation to the 2008 Mayoral & City Council Candidates of Hampton Roads: Come Ride the Bus With Us<br><br>
> Whenever we speak with staff and commissioners at the Coastal Virginia Transit Authority about late-evening bus curfews, ninety-minute routes, expired two-hour paper transfers, and missing sidewalk curb cuts, we hear the same unspoken excuse: Does the bus run? Yes. Is it good enough? I guess so.<br><br>
> For the thousands of citizens across Virginia Beach, Chesapeake, Portsmouth, Norfolk, Hampton, and Newport News who rely on CVTA buses every single day to get to college, to work, to medical appointments, and to civic meetings—including wheelchair riders like the two of us—"good enough" is not good enough. CVTA can be improved into a first-class regional transit network, and the only ingredient missing is the political willpower of the elected mayors and city councils who fund and govern it.<br><br>
> This year, voters in four of our six CVTA cities—Chesapeake, Portsmouth, and Hampton on May 6, and Virginia Beach on November 4—will elect their next Mayor, while voters across all six cities will elect members of their City Councils. Therefore, Ideas for Coastal Virginia Transit is issuing a simple, non-partisan public invitation to every candidate for Mayor in Virginia Beach, Chesapeake, Portsmouth, and Hampton, and every candidate for City Council across the region:<br><br>
> Meet the two of us at a CVTA transit hub, leave your campaign car in the parking lot, pay the regular bus fare alongside us, and ride a real multi-bus loop on CVTA with two daily wheelchair riders. No staged press vans, no special charter buses, and no shortcuts—just the real schedules, the real transfers, and an honest conversation on camera about how we can give Hampton Roads the transit system our citizens deserve.

When I clicked Publish and dispatched the invitation emails across all four mayoral races and six cities, the comment section on Ideas for Coastal Virginia Transit lit up within twenty minutes. Daily bus commuters from Ocean View to Kempsville, CCHR students, shipyard workers in Newport News and Portsmouth, and even readers who had followed us over from the Seattle Transit Blog cheered the challenge on and began forwarding the link to local newspaper reporters and campaign managers.

Then we waited to see which politicians actually had the courage to show up.

***

#### Silence Across the Region — And the One Candidate Who Said Yes

Days turned into weeks as the May 6, 2008 municipal elections in Chesapeake, Portsmouth, Hampton, Norfolk, and Newport News approached and passed.

Every morning, Katie and I sat side by side at our desks in Kempsville with our hot chocolate or cold ginger ale, checking our campaign inbox and phone messages.

From the mayoral campaigns in Chesapeake: silence.
From the mayoral campaigns in Portsmouth: silence.
From the mayoral campaigns in Hampton: a single three-sentence form email from a campaign aide thanking us for our "interest in regional infrastructure" and stating that the candidate's schedule did not permit a multi-hour bus ride, followed by silence.
From the incumbent City Council members and establishment candidates across Norfolk, Newport News, Chesapeake, Portsmouth, Hampton, and Virginia Beach: not a single acceptance.

Even here in Virginia Beach, as the four-way November 2008 Mayor's race heated up through the summer, the twenty-year incumbent mayor's campaign ignored our invitation completely. The wealthy banking-executive frontrunner backed by the courthouse establishment didn't reply. The veteran budget-hawk former councilman didn't accept either. And every single incumbent and establishment candidate running for the Virginia Beach City Council pretended our email didn't exist.

"They really don't care, do they, Nate?" Katie said quietly one warm afternoon at our desks, staring at the spreadsheet on my monitor where almost every single row across Chesapeake, Portsmouth, Hampton, Norfolk, Newport News, and Virginia Beach still read *No Response*. "They want the title of Mayor or City Council member, and they want to sit on regional boards and cut ribbons on highway interchanges, but not one of them is willing to spend two and a half hours riding the bus system they fund."

Just as I reached for the mouse to update our public tracker post on the blog, my email client chimed with a new incoming message.

I blinked at the sender line on the screen, then clicked it open.

"Katie," I said, sitting forward in my SwiftChair. "Look at the inbox. Someone just replied."

Katie rolled her chair right up against mine and leaned in toward the monitor.

The email wasn't from a campaign press secretary or an automated mailing list. It came directly from the fourth candidate on the ballot for Mayor of the City of Virginia Beach—Scott Tanner, a young, thirty-something political-outsider Navy veteran who wasn't part of the entrenched City Hall establishment and didn't have the backing of the big beachfront real-estate donors.

His message was four sentences long:

> From: Scott Tanner for Mayor Campaign<br>
> To: Katie & Nate — Ideas for Coastal Virginia Transit<br>
> Subject: Re: Open Invitation to 2008 Mayoral Candidates — Come Ride the Bus With Us<br><br>
> Katie and Nate,<br>
> I read your blog post and your route analyses, and you're right—nobody asking to lead the largest city in Virginia should be afraid to ride the bus system our citizens depend on every day. I accept your challenge. Tell me which transit hub in Virginia Beach to meet you at, what time to be there, and which buses we're riding, and I'll leave my car in the lot and ride the whole loop with the two of you.<br>
> — Scott

Katie stared at the screen for three seconds, and then a slow, fierce grin broke across her face as she reached over and gripped my hand.

"Out of every mayoral candidate in Chesapeake, Portsmouth, Hampton, and Virginia Beach—and every City Council candidate across all six cities—only one person had the guts to say yes," Katie said, her blue eyes shining with determination as she pulled the folded CVTA Virginia Beach route map across our desk. "And he's running for Mayor right here in Virginia Beach. Come on, Nate—get your video camera batteries on the charger. We're going to meet him at the CCHR Virginia Beach Campus bus loop, and we're going to take him on the exact four-bus circuit across Virginia Beach and Norfolk: Route 29 to Hilltop, Route 20 to Glenrock Mall, Route 15 down Military Highway, and Route 12 right back to CCHR."

### Part 2: The Four-Bus Mayoral Loop, Silenced at Eighteenth Street, & Choosing to Run for the Kempsville Seat

**Date:** 2008-09-16 at 14:00 America/New_York

![Inside the Coastal Virginia Transit Authority boardroom at 509 East 18th Street in Norfolk on November 19, 2009, 24-year-old twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs at the public-comment table as CVTA Chief Operating Officer Richard Halstead leans over the dais to cut off their microphone.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/nov_2009_cvta_18th_street_mic_cutoff_and_jan_2011_commissioner_reckoning.jpg)

#### Tuesday, September 16, 2008, 2:00 PM — Four Buses Across Two Cities & The Expired Two-Hour Transfer

![Inside a moving CVTA Route 15 bus crossing the Elizabeth River bridge into Virginia Beach on September 16, 2008, 23-year-old Katie Prairie sits in her black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchair holding up printed CVTA bus timetables for stunned mayoral candidate Scott Tanner as he inspects his expired two-hour paper transfer slip, while twin brother Nate films the interview with a digital camcorder mounted on his SwiftChair lap tray.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/sep_2008_cvta_route_15_bus_mayoral_loop_interview_scott_tanner.jpg)

"Right on time," twenty-three-year-old Katie said, nodding toward the concrete island at the Community College of Hampton Roads Virginia Beach Campus transit hub as mayoral candidate Scott Tanner locked his sedan in the student visitor lot and walked over to our two compact SwiftChairs with a notebook tucked under his arm.

"Katie, Nate—good to meet you both in person," Scott said, shaking Katie's hand and then mine while I checked the microphone levels on the compact digital camcorder mounted to my wheelchair lap tray. "I brought crisp single-dollar bills and quarters just like your email said. Where does our loop start?"

"Right here on Route 29 northbound to Hilltop," Katie said, pointing up at the approaching forty-foot low-floor bus pulling into the CCHR bus loop. "We're going to ride a single continuous four-bus circuit across Virginia Beach and Norfolk and bring you right back to your car at this exact bus stop: Route 29 from CCHR up to Hilltop, Route 20 westbound down Virginia Beach Boulevard into Norfolk to Glenrock Mall, Route 15 southbound down Military Highway back across the city line into Virginia Beach, and Route 12 back here to CCHR."

When the front ramp of the Route 29 bus folded down onto the concrete pad, Katie and I rolled aboard into the dual front wheelchair securement bays and swiped our thirty-day CVTA magnetic passes through the farebox. Right behind us, Scott stepped up into the vestibule, fed his base fare plus the paper transfer fee into the bill validator, and took the timestamped paper transfer slip the driver tore off the cutter bar.

"Keep an eye on the punched time at the top of that paper transfer," I told Scott as I framed the timestamped slip in my camcorder viewfinder while the bus pulled out of CCHR onto Princess Anne Road. "It's good for exactly two hours."

Because Virginia Beach's local routes ran on forty-five- to sixty-minute headways without synchronized transfer pulses, the math of the two-hour paper transfer trap unfolded right in front of my camera lens in real time.

Our first leg on Route 29 carried us northeast up First Colonial Road to the Hilltop transfer stop, where we waited twenty-five minutes on an unsheltered concrete sidewalk pad in the September sun before boarding a westbound Route 20 bus down Virginia Beach Boulevard.

Halfway down the Boulevard past Little Neck and Newtown Road, an older Hispanic gentleman carrying a canvas tool bag boarded the bus and asked the operator a confused question in Spanish about which stop connected to the Military Highway corridor. Before the operator could shake his head, Scott leaned across the aisle and answered the rider fluently in Spanish—explaining the exact stop at Glenrock Mall where they could both transfer to Route 15.

"You speak Spanish?" Katie asked with genuine respect when the rider thanked Scott warmly and sat down two rows behind our wheelchairs.

"Picked it up during my Navy deployments to South America," Scott said simply. "Half the folks riding Route 20 work in the hospitality kitchens at the Oceanfront or the construction yards along the Boulevard. A mayor ought to be able to talk to the people who keep the city running."

When Route 20 dropped us off at the Glenrock Mall transit hub in Norfolk, we waited another twenty-eight minutes for our third bus—a southbound Route 15 heading down Military Highway toward Virginia Beach.

By the time the Route 15 bus rolled south along Military Highway and climbed the bridge over the Eastern Branch of the Elizabeth River to cross from Norfolk back into Virginia Beach, it was four-fifteen in the afternoon. Holding my camcorder steady on my lap tray with the river glinting through the bus window behind Katie and Scott, I recorded the conversation that became the centerpiece of our video.

"We're crossing back into Virginia Beach right now, Scott," Katie said on camera, holding up the official printed CVTA timetables for Route 33 and Route 12. "Let's talk about what happens if a taxpaying citizen of Virginia Beach who relies on the bus—like Nate and me, or a working parent, or a senior citizen—wants to attend a formal evening meeting of the Virginia Beach City Council down at the Municipal Center in Courthouse."

"Formal City Council meetings gavel in at six o'clock in the evening," Scott said, looking down at the printed schedule columns in Katie's hand.

"Six o'clock in the evening," Katie repeated clearly. "Now look at the Route 33 schedule serving the Virginia Beach Municipal Center. You can ride Route 33 down to City Hall in the afternoon just fine. If you live at the north end of the Oceanfront, the last northbound Route 33 all the way to Sixty-Eighth Street leaves the Municipal Center at 6:01 PM—one minute after the council meeting starts—and the 7:01 PM trip terminates early at Nineteenth Street. And if you live anywhere else in Virginia Beach and need to ride Route 33 from the Municipal Center back to the CCHR hub to catch your connecting bus home—like Route 12, Route 25, or Route 29—look at the departure times."

Katie tapped her finger against the bottom row of the Route 33 and Route 12 timetables so my camera lens could capture the exact numbers.

"The very last Route 33 out of the Municipal Center to CCHR leaves at 6:33 PM, and by the time it reaches CCHR, every single connecting route except Route 36 has already shut down for the night," Katie said. "Because Nate and I live in Kempsville and ride Route 12 home from CCHR toward Military Highway and Indian River Road, look at when the last Route 12 bus of the entire day departs CCHR: 5:48 PM. To catch that 5:48 PM Route 12 home from CCHR, we have to leave City Hall on the 5:33 PM Route 33 bus—twenty-seven minutes before the six o'clock City Council meeting even starts! Our last bus home literally pulls out of CCHR twelve minutes before the Mayor bangs the gavel."

Scott stared at the two printed timetables in disbelief, looking up into my camera lens. "So if you ride the bus to a six o'clock Virginia Beach City Council meeting to speak during public comment, you're stranded at City Hall with no way home."

"Every single Tuesday night," I said from behind the camera. "You cannot tell citizens that local government is open to the public when City Hall's own bus schedule locks bus riders and wheelchair users out thirty minutes before the meeting begins."

Twenty minutes later, when we rolled down the front ramp off Route 15 at Indian River Road and boarded our fourth and final bus—eastbound Route 12 back to CCHR to complete our circle—the final piece of CVTA's broken math played out right on cue.

Katie and I rolled up the ramp and swiped our thirty-day passes. Behind us, Scott handed his paper transfer slip to the Route 12 operator.

The operator glanced at the punched holes along the top edge of the paper slip and shook his head.

"Sorry, sir—this transfer expired nineteen minutes ago," the driver said, tapping the two-hour rule printed on the farebox. "That'll be another full dollar-fifty fare to ride back to the college."

Right on camera, Scott had to reach into his pocket and feed a second full fare into the box just to finish a single afternoon round-trip back to his parked car at CCHR—solely because waiting for hourly buses had eaten up more than two hours.

***

#### Thursday, November 19, 2009, 1:35 PM — Cut Off at the Eighteenth Street Microphone & Blackballed From TRAC

![Inside the Coastal Virginia Transit Authority boardroom at 509 East 18th Street in Norfolk on November 19, 2009, 24-year-old twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs at the public-comment table as CVTA Chief Operating Officer Richard Halstead leans over the dais to cut off their microphone.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/nov_2009_cvta_18th_street_mic_cutoff_and_jan_2011_commissioner_reckoning.jpg)

That night in September 2008, I edited our four-bus ride down into a crisp twelve-minute documentary video with full burned-in open captions and published it at the top of Ideas for Coastal Virginia Transit.

Within a week, the video had been watched more than forty thousand times across Hampton Roads and picked up by *The Tidewater Pilot* and every television station in Norfolk and Virginia Beach. In the November 2008 election, twenty-year incumbent Mayor Myra Overton was defeated, and although the wealthy banking-executive frontrunner edged out Scott Tanner in the four-way race, the public uproar over our video forced CVTA and City Hall to promise a "comprehensive review" of bus transfers and Virginia Beach evening service hours.

Fourteen months later, however, on a gray Thursday afternoon in November 2009 inside the CVTA boardroom at 509 East Eighteenth Street in Norfolk, we learned exactly what CVTA's executive suite thought of that promise.

Katie and I had ridden three buses into Norfolk carrying a twenty-four-page PHP audit we had compiled over the autumn, documenting more than nine hundred missed transfer connections at Glenrock Mall and CCHR alongside a formal request for CVTA's raw General Transit Feed Specification schedule tables so riders could build real-time trip-planning tools. Just two weeks earlier, I had also submitted my formal application to fill one of Virginia Beach's vacant citizen seats on CVTA's Transit Riders Advisory Committee—known around the agency as TRAC.

Parked side by side in our SwiftChairs at the low public-comment table in the center of the boardroom, I was two minutes and forty seconds into reading our findings into the record while CVTA President and Chief Executive Officer Leonard Sterling and Chief Operating Officer Richard Halstead sat slouched in their high-backed leather chairs along the raised executive tier.

"—and because the outbound Route 20 and southbound Route 15 schedules at Glenrock Mall are offset by four minutes in the master dispatch table without a hold-for-transfer rule," I said clearly into the gooseneck microphone, holding up our printed PHP chart, "evening commuters transferring back into Virginia Beach are missing the final southbound bus seven nights a week—"

*BZZZZT.*

Before I could finish the sentence, Chief Operating Officer Richard Halstead reached forward and jabbed the master cutoff switch on the clerk's console. The red ring at the neck of my microphone went dead in the middle of my word.

"Your three minutes are expired, Mr. Prairie," CEO Leonard Sterling said flatly without looking up from his leather portfolio. "Next speaker."

"Mr. President, if staff would simply release the raw GTFS schedule files we requested under the Freedom of Information Act—" Katie spoke up from her SwiftChair beside me, her voice carrying across the quiet room even without the microphone.

"Public comment is not a question-and-answer session, Ms. Prairie," Sterling interrupted, waving a hand toward the rear doors. "The commission has a full agenda."

Fifteen minutes later, when the board recessed briefly before its closed executive session, Katie and I rolled our wheelchairs out into the tiled corridor near the drinking fountain to speak with Chief Operating Officer Richard Halstead and the agency's government-affairs director as they walked toward the coffee credenza.

"Mr. Halstead," I said politely, holding out the bound copy of our twenty-four-page schedule audit and a thumb drive containing our PHP transfer-timing script, "we brought a clean copy of the Glenrock Mall and CCHR connection data for your scheduling department, and I wanted to check on the status of my application for the Virginia Beach citizen seat on the Transit Riders Advisory Committee."

Halstead stopped, looked down his nose at the thumb drive in my hand, and didn't even reach out to take it. A thin, patronizing smirk curled the corner of his mouth.

"Look, Nate, Katie," Halstead said, lowering his voice just enough that the reporters inside the boardroom couldn't hear him, "let's save everybody some time. My scheduling engineers don't take operational direction from statistically insignificant hobbyist bloggers, and we aren't handing over internal GTFS database files so the two of you can play armchair transit director from your living room."

Katie's blue eyes narrowed. "We ride your buses every single day of the week in power wheelchairs, Mr. Halstead. There is nothing 'hobbyist' about needing a bus that actually connects before dark."

"And as for the Transit Riders Advisory Committee," Halstead added smoothly, adjusting his silk tie as he turned back toward the executive suite door, "staff already forwarded our recommendations for the Virginia Beach TRAC vacancies this morning. Your name wasn't on the list, Nate. TRAC is reserved for constructive community stakeholders—not blog agitators with a laptop."

The heavy oak door of the executive suite clicked shut behind him.

For ten seconds, Katie and I sat side by side in the quiet hallway of 509 East Eighteenth Street, staring at that closed oak door. They had cut off my microphone at a hundred and eighty seconds, laughed at our engineering work, locked up public schedule data paid for by the taxpayers, and secretly blackballed me from a volunteer citizen advisory committee because we had dared to prove on camera that their schedules were broken.

And the final insult came four months later, in the spring of 2010, when the eleven-member Virginia Beach City Council met down at the Municipal Center to vote on the city's annual transit contribution. Rather than holding CVTA accountable or funding the evening connecting pulse we had proposed, ten-year Kempsville District incumbent Councilman Harold Dietz led the budget motion to strip out every dime of proposed late-evening bus funding—muttering into his dais microphone at the Tuesday afternoon work session that *"almost nobody rides the bus out of Courthouse after dark anyway."*

Sitting side by side at our dual coding desks in our house off Military Highway and Indian River Road in Kempsville that evening watching the archived City Hall webcast over cold glasses of ginger ale, Katie reached forward and clicked Pause on the video player.

"Of course nobody rides the bus out of Courthouse after dark, Councilman Dietz," Katie said to the monitor, her voice calm and razor-sharp. "There isn't a bus out of Courthouse after 6:33 PM! That's like taking the ramp off a building and claiming nobody in a wheelchair ever comes inside."

Katie turned her SwiftChair toward me, her blue eyes steady and bright.

"Leonard Sterling and Richard Halstead think they can cut off your microphone at Eighteenth Street and blackball you from TRAC because we're just two twenty-five-year-old bloggers in wheelchairs with no vote on their budget," Katie said. "And Harold Dietz thinks he owns the Kempsville seat on the Virginia Beach City Council for life. Well, Harold Dietz's seat is on the ballot this November, Nate. City Council elections in Virginia are non-partisan, and we live right here in our house in Kempsville. What do you say we stop asking Richard Halstead and Councilman Dietz for permission—and go take his seat on the City Council?"

"Let's do it," I said immediately, already opening a fresh PHP project directory on my MagnaBook Pro. "If they won't let us sit at the public-comment table for three minutes, we'll put you up on the dais where they have to answer to you."

## The Empty Podium on WHRC TV-15, The 94.1% Landslide, & Councilwoman Prairie

### Part 1: The Empty Podium on WHRC TV-15, The 8:24 PM Three-Bus Sprint Home, & The Front-Page Metro Headline

**Date:** 2010-10-14 at 19:28 America/New_York

![Under the studio lights of WHRC TV-15 on Hampton Boulevard in Norfolk on October 14, 2010, 25-year-old Kempsville City Council challenger Katie Prairie sits in her black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchair at an accessible mahogany desk beside the brightly lit, completely empty standing podium reserved for ten-year incumbent Councilman Harold Dietz, while twin brother Nate monitors the debate from his SwiftChair on the left.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/oct_2010_whrc_tv15_empty_podium_debate_katie_prairie.jpg)

#### Thursday, October 14, 2010, 7:28 PM — The Empty Mahogany Podium Under the WHRC Studio Lights

![Under the studio lights of WHRC TV-15 on Hampton Boulevard in Norfolk on October 14, 2010, 25-year-old Kempsville City Council challenger Katie Prairie sits in her black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchair at an accessible mahogany desk beside the brightly lit, completely empty standing podium reserved for ten-year incumbent Councilman Harold Dietz, while twin brother Nate monitors the debate from his SwiftChair on the left.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/oct_2010_whrc_tv15_empty_podium_debate_katie_prairie.jpg)

"Two minutes to air, Ms. Prairie," the WHRC TV-15 floor director called out quietly, holding up two fingers beside the center studio camera inside the public-television broadcast center at 5200 Hampton Boulevard in Norfolk. "Still no sign of Councilman Dietz or his campaign manager at the front desk, so per station rules, his podium stays lit and his microphone stays open."

Parked in my compact SwiftChair just outside the edge of the key lights next to the producer's monitor cart, I glanced across the blue-curtained television set toward my twenty-five-year-old twin sister.

Katie sat upright and composed in her black SwiftChair behind a low, wheelchair-accessible mahogany desk that the WHRC studio crew had set up on the left side of the stage, wearing a crisp royal-blue blazer over a cream blouse with a small brass lapel microphone clipped to her collar. Six feet to her right stood the second debate position: a tall, traditional standing mahogany podium bearing a white placard that read *COUNCILMAN HAROLD DIETZ — KEMPSVILLE DISTRICT*, bathed in a bright, unforgiving pool of overhead tungsten light and completely empty.

For five months, Katie and I had poured every ounce of our energy into the non-partisan Kempsville District race. We hadn't hired a political consultant, we hadn't taken a single check from Oceanfront hotel developers, and we hadn't hosted cocktail receptions. Instead, I had built a custom PHP precinct-mapping and sidewalk-canvassing engine on our home server off Military Highway and Indian River Road in Kempsville, and we had spent the spring, summer, and early autumn campaigning directly from the front wheelchair securement bays of CVTA Routes 12, 15, 20, 25, and 29 and rolling down the neighborhood sidewalks of Kempsville, Bellamy Manor, Brandon, and Larkspur with Dad driving down from Alexandria every weekend to knock on front doors that had brick steps.

Through it all, ten-year incumbent Councilman Harold Dietz had treated our campaign as if we were invisible. When Coastal Virginia Public Media had sent out the formal certified invitations in September for tonight's live forty-five-minute Kempsville City Council debate on WHRC TV-15—broadcast right from the edge of the Virginia Dominion University campus across all of Hampton Roads—Katie had returned her signed confirmation within twenty minutes. Councilman Dietz hadn't even bothered to reply. Because he had neither accepted nor formally declined the invitation, WHRC's strict non-partisan broadcast rules required the studio to leave his standing podium on the stage and give the viewing public an unfiltered look at who had bothered to show up for the job.

"Ten seconds," the floor director whispered, lowering his arm toward the center camera lens. "Five, four, three..."

The red tally light atop Camera One glowed bright in the darkened studio.

"Good evening, and welcome to Coastal Virginia Public Media's live 2010 Decision coverage from our WHRC TV-15 studios on Hampton Boulevard in Norfolk," the veteran public-television moderator began in his resonant baritone. "Tonight we examine the race for the Kempsville District seat on the Virginia Beach City Council. Seated to my left is challenger Katie Prairie, a twenty-five-year-old Kempsville homeowner, software developer, and co-founder of the regional transit watchdog website Ideas for Coastal Virginia Transit. To her right, as viewers at home can see, is the podium reserved for ten-year incumbent Councilman Harold Dietz. Although WHRC extended multiple invitations to Councilman Dietz's office over the past six weeks, our producers received neither an acceptance nor a decline, and his podium remains open should he arrive during tonight's broadcast. Because our non-profit public media rules require us to pose every scheduled municipal policy question to the stage, we will proceed with our full forty-five-minute forum. Ms. Prairie, the first question is yours."

Watching from beside the monitor cart with my MagnaBook Pro resting on my wheelchair lap tray, I felt a quiet surge of pride as the director punched up the wide two-shot on the studio monitors.

Every time the moderator asked a question about Kempsville stormwater drainage along Indian River Road, aging neighborhood sidewalks around Morrison Middle School and Northwood High School, small-business permitting, municipal transparency, or the city's annual transportation budget, the studio camera framed the stark visual contrast across every living room in Virginia Beach and Norfolk: on the left, a poised, razor-sharp twenty-five-year-old woman in a power wheelchair citing exact line items from the City of Virginia Beach's eight-hundred-page operating budget from memory without a single paper note on her desk; on the right, six feet of empty blue carpet and a vacant mahogany lectern where the ten-year incumbent hadn't cared enough to stand.

"Ms. Prairie, let's turn to regional transportation and your proposal for an Evening Civic Access Transit Pulse," the moderator said at the eight-minute mark before the end of the broadcast. "Critics on the current City Council have argued that extending CVTA bus service out of the Virginia Beach Municipal Center and the CCHR Virginia Beach Campus past six-thirty in the evening is an unnecessary taxpayer expense because ridership after dark is low. How do you respond?"

Katie looked straight into the glowing red camera lens.

"Saying nobody rides the bus out of the Virginia Beach Municipal Center after six-thirty at night when the last bus leaves at 6:33 PM is like taking the wheelchair ramp off City Hall and claiming nobody in a wheelchair ever comes inside," Katie said, her voice warm, clear, and unhurried. "Formal evening meetings of the Virginia Beach City Council gavel in at six o'clock. Yet if a working parent, a senior citizen, a college student, or a wheelchair user in Kempsville rides Route 33 down to City Hall and needs to connect to Route 12, Route 25, or Route 29 at the CCHR hub to get home, the very last Route 12 bus of the day leaves CCHR at 5:48 PM—meaning a citizen has to leave City Hall at 5:33 PM, twenty-seven minutes before the Council meeting even begins. For the cost of less than one-tenth of one percent of our city budget, we can run an evening bus pulse until ten-thirty at night so working people and citizens with disabilities are never locked out of their own local government again."

At 8:14 PM on the dot, the moderator thanked Katie, signed off to the viewers across Hampton Roads, and the red tally lights on the studio cameras clicked off.

And that was when the real moment of the campaign began.

***

#### Thursday, October 14, 2010, 8:14 PM — Crossing Six Lanes of Hampton Boulevard With Reporter Greg Mercer to Catch the 8:24 PM Route 2

![Under the amber streetlights of Hampton Boulevard in Norfolk at 8:24 PM on October 14, 2010, 25-year-old Kempsville City Council candidate Katie Prairie and her twin brother Nate roll their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs onto the deployed front ramp of a kneeling CVTA Route 2 bus while astonished Tidewater Pilot reporter Greg Mercer scribbles notes on the sidewalk.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/oct_2010_hampton_blvd_824pm_route_2_bus_ramp_reporter_greg_mercer.jpg)

The instant the studio floor director called *"We're clear!"* at 8:14 PM, Katie didn't linger on the stage to bask in the applause of the camera crew.

While the audio technician unclipped the brass lapel mic from her blazer, Katie glanced down at her wristwatch, released her joystick brake, and rolled swiftly down the studio ramp toward my wheelchair as I closed my MagnaBook Pro and slipped it into my padded canvas backpack.

"Eight-fourteen, Nate," Katie said quietly as our two SwiftChairs fell into formation heading for the heavy soundproof doors of Studio A. "We have ten minutes to make the crosswalk."

Out in the bright fluorescent lobby of the WHRC broadcast center, *Tidewater Pilot* Metro politics reporter Greg Mercer—a veteran city-hall journalist in a rumpled trench coat with a spiral reporter's notebook in one hand and a digital voice recorder in the other—stepped away from the reception counter and hurried straight toward us.

"Ms. Prairie! Katie!" Greg Mercer called out, clicking the record button on his handheld recorder. "Greg Mercer with *The Tidewater Pilot*. That empty podium on live television was something else. Do you have ten minutes to sit down here in the lobby and give me a quick post-debate interview for tomorrow morning's Metro section?"

Katie glanced at the round wall clock above the WHRC glass entrance doors—8:15 PM—and looked back up at Greg with a friendly, earnest smile.

"I'd be happy to answer every question you have, Mr. Mercer," Katie said as I hit the big silver ADA push-plate to swing the front lobby doors open into the crisp October night air, "as long as you don't mind walking fast across Hampton Boulevard with us right now."

Greg blinked in surprise, tucking his pen behind his ear as he stepped out onto the concrete sidewalk beside our two powerchairs. "Across Hampton Boulevard? Sure—did your campaign staff have to park your wheelchair van over in the university lot across the street?"

Katie and I exchanged a quick twin look as we set our SwiftChair speed dials to four miles per hour and rolled briskly down the WHRC front walk toward the signalized intersection at Forty-Ninth Street and Hampton Boulevard.

"We don't have campaign staff, Mr. Mercer," I said as Katie pressed the pedestrian crosswalk button at the curb, "and we don't own a wheelchair van."

Greg Mercer looked down at our two compact powerchairs, genuinely puzzled as six lanes of heavy port and university traffic rumbled past under the amber streetlights of Hampton Boulevard.

Wait—if the two of us didn't have a fifty-thousand-dollar wheelchair-lift van waiting in the lot, and our dad David wasn't down from Alexandria on a Thursday night, how on earth were two twenty-five-year-old twins in power wheelchairs getting all the way from the West Side of Norfolk back to Kempsville in Virginia Beach at eight-fifteen at night?

The white *WALK* silhouette flashed on across the six-lane boulevard.

"Come on, Mr. Mercer—this light only gives twenty-two seconds," Katie said cheerfully.

Jogging two steps to keep pace with our electric motors as we rolled straight across all six lanes of Hampton Boulevard to the opposite sidewalk, Greg held his digital recorder out toward Katie. "Wait a second—where are we going if your car isn't over here?"

Reaching the far curb cut on the southbound side of Hampton Boulevard, Katie and I braked our SwiftChairs side by side right beneath a blue-and-white metal sign bolted to a utility pole:

*CVTA BUS STOP — ROUTE 2 (HAMPTON BLVD / DOWNTOWN NORFOLK).*

Greg Mercer stopped dead in his tracks on the concrete sidewalk, his mouth slightly open as he looked up at the metal bus stop sign, then down at our two power wheelchairs, and then back up Hampton Boulevard where the twin headlights of an approaching forty-foot low-floor CVTA gill-window transit bus were cresting the rise three blocks north.

"You're taking the city bus?" Greg asked, staring at us in disbelief. "From a live television debate on Hampton Boulevard back to Virginia Beach—at eight-twenty at night?"

"Not just one city bus, Mr. Mercer—three of them," I said, checking the glowing digital readout on my watch: 8:22 PM. "And that's why we couldn't stay in the WHRC lobby for ten minutes."

"Walk me through this before that bus gets here," Greg said rapidly, holding his voice recorder right between Katie's chair and mine while his other hand scribbled furiously across his spiral pad under the streetlight. "What happens if you miss that bus coming down the street right now?"

"Look at the timetable math," Katie said calmly, pointing up Hampton Boulevard as the southbound CVTA Route 2 bus signaled toward the curb with its amber destination sign glowing *2 DOWNTOWN NORFOLK*. "The WHRC debate ended at 8:14 PM. This bus pulling up right now is the 8:24 PM Route 2 southbound. We have to catch this exact 8:24 PM bus down Hampton Boulevard to the Downtown Norfolk Transit Center, which gets us into Downtown Norfolk just before nine o'clock."

With a loud hiss of compressed air, the forty-foot Route 2 bus braked at the curb beside us and kneeled its front suspension. The folding glass doors swung open, and the warning chime beeped as the steel hydraulic wheelchair ramp unfolded onto the sidewalk concrete.

"Once we get to Downtown Norfolk Transit Center just before nine," I continued as I rolled backward up the steel ramp first to pull into the rear-facing curbside securement bay, "we have fifteen minutes to transfer onto the 9:15 PM Route 20 bus heading eastbound out Virginia Beach Boulevard."

"And that 9:15 PM Route 20 bus gets us out to the Glenrock Mall transit hub at 9:45 PM," Katie added, pausing at the bottom of the wheelchair ramp and looking back over her shoulder at Greg Mercer standing under the streetlight with his notebook and recorder. "At 9:45 PM at Glenrock Mall, Nate and I have to transfer onto the very last Route 15 bus of the night going south down Military Highway across the city line into Virginia Beach. If we had stayed in the WHRC lobby talking for ten minutes and missed this 8:24 PM bus right here on Hampton Boulevard, we would miss the 9:15 PM Route 20 in Downtown Norfolk, we would miss the last Route 15 of the night at Glenrock Mall, and the two of us would be stranded in Norfolk overnight in our wheelchairs with no way home."

Greg Mercer stared at Katie, stunned silent for two full beats as the bus driver waited patiently at the controls.

"My God," Greg breathed, his pen hovering over his pad. "You just debated for forty-five minutes on live television next to an empty podium because the incumbent didn't bother to show up, and now you're sprinting to catch a three-bus transfer chain across two cities before the system shuts down for the night."

"Mr. Mercer," Katie said simply, her blue eyes steady under the streetlight before she guided her SwiftChair smoothly up the metal ramp into the bus vestibule beside me, "improving the CVTA bus system—specifically Virginia Beach's locally funded share of the regional system—is the entire reason I'm running for City Council. Have a good night, and thank you for walking us to the stop!"

As we swiped our thirty-day CVTA passes through the farebox and locked our wheelchair brakes in the dual front bays, the hydraulic ramp folded back inside, the glass doors hissed shut, and the 8:24 PM Route 2 bus pulled away down Hampton Boulevard—leaving the veteran *Tidewater Pilot* reporter standing on the curb under the bus stop sign, staring after our taillights and scribbling in his notebook as fast as his hand could move.

***

#### Friday, October 15, 2010, 9:30 AM — Section B1 Above the Fold & All Ten Lines Lit on WHRC 89.5 FM

We made our 9:15 PM Route 20 transfer in Downtown Norfolk with eleven minutes to spare, caught the final 9:45 PM southbound Route 15 at Glenrock Mall, and rolled through the front door of our house off Military Highway and Indian River Road in Kempsville at ten-forty that night—tired, happy, and ready for a late cup of hot chocolate before bed.

At nine-thirty the next morning, while Katie and I were sitting side by side at our dual coding desks drinking cold orange juice and checking our overnight campaign emails, we heard the familiar sound of Dad's key turning in the front deadbolt.

"Morning, kids!" Dad called out, walking into our home office carrying a steaming travel mug of black coffee in one hand and a thick bundle of five freshly printed Friday morning editions of *The Tidewater Pilot* under his other arm. "I took a personal day in Tysons and drove down early so we could canvass Bellamy Manor this afternoon—and I bought out the newsstand box at the corner convenience store on my way in. Have you two seen Section B yet?"

"Not the print edition," I said as Katie and I rolled our chairs back from our desks. "Did Greg Mercer's blurb run inside the Metro pages?"

Dad let out a laugh that crinkled the corners of his eyes behind his glasses, pulled the Metro & Virginia section from the top of the bundle, and laid Section B1 flat across our desk.

It wasn't a two-paragraph blurb buried on page four.

Stretching all the way across the top of the Friday Metro front page above the fold in bold seventy-two-point black type was a banner headline written by Greg Mercer:

*AN EMPTY PODIUM—AND AN 8:24 P.M. BUS TO CATCH*
*Incumbent Dietz Skips Televised WHRC Debate; Challenger Katie Prairie Commands the Hour—Then Races Across Hampton Boulevard in Her Wheelchair to Make Last Bus Connection Home to Virginia Beach*

Directly beneath the headline sat two side-by-side color photographs spanning all six columns of the page. On the left was a crisp frame captured from the WHRC TV-15 broadcast showing twenty-five-year-old Katie seated at her accessible studio desk next to Councilman Harold Dietz's brightly lit, completely empty mahogany podium. On the right was a photograph taken by a *Tidewater Pilot* photographer Greg Mercer had reached by cell phone on Hampton Boulevard—showing Katie and me rolling our black SwiftChairs up the steel hydraulic ramp of the kneeling 8:24 PM CVTA Route 2 bus under the streetlights while regular night-shift commuters looked on from the windows.

Katie and I read down the twenty-eight-inch column together in amazed silence. Greg Mercer hadn't missed a single detail: he had printed the exact 8:14 PM debate sign-off, the twenty-two-second sprint across all six lanes of Hampton Boulevard, the minute-by-minute transfer math of the 8:24 PM Route 2 to the 9:15 PM Route 20 to the final 9:45 PM Route 15 at Glenrock Mall, and Katie's parting words from the bottom of the bus ramp right in the closing box quote.

"Look at the traffic counter on our campaign server, Katie," I said, glancing up at my real-time PHP analytics monitor. "Our website hits just passed twelve thousand for the morning, and small online donations of ten and twenty-five dollars are coming in every thirty seconds from Kempsville, Bayside, and Norfolk."

At twelve-oh-six that afternoon, while the three of us were eating turkey sandwiches at the kitchen table before heading out to canvass, I clicked open the live audio stream of Coastal Virginia Public Media's non-profit public radio station, WHRC 89.5 FM, during its flagship Friday noon regional call-in program.

"Welcome back to *Tidewater Forum* on WHRC 89.5 FM, I'm Catherine Lindsey," the host said over our desktop speakers. "Before we open the phone lines for our weekly Friday civic roundtable, I need to remind our listeners of the ground rules: as a non-profit 501(c)(3) public broadcasting organization, WHRC radio and television are strictly prohibited by federal law from endorsing or opposing any candidate for public office. However, judging by our studio switchboard over the last ten minutes, it appears half of Hampton Roads has read Greg Mercer's front-page Metro column in this morning's *Tidewater Pilot* about last night's Kempsville City Council debate here in our building. All ten of our studio call-in lines are flashing right now. Let's go first to Line One—Arthur in Kempsville, you're on WHRC."

*"Thank you, Catherine,"* an older gentleman's voice came over the radio clearly. *"I've lived off Kempsville Road for thirty-four years and I voted for Harold Dietz twice in the past. Last night I tuned in to Channel 15 to watch the debate, and I sat there for forty-five minutes looking at an empty wooden podium while that young lady in the wheelchair answered every single budget and drainage question like she'd been running the city for ten years. And then I open my paper over breakfast this morning and find out she and her twin brother had to hustle across six lanes of Hampton Boulevard in the dark just to catch three buses home before CVTA locked up for the night! You don't have to endorse anybody on the radio—the voters in Kempsville can see for ourselves who's actually working for a living."*

"Thank you, Arthur—let's go to Line Two, Brenda calling from a cell phone near Glenrock Mall," Catherine Lindsey said.

*"Hi, I'm a respiratory therapist and I ride that exact Route 20 and Route 15 transfer at Glenrock Mall three nights a week,"* the second caller said, her voice thick with emotion. *"I've seen Katie and her brother Nate in their wheelchairs on the front of the bus for years taking notes and talking to riders, and I never realized she was running for City Council until I saw the photo of them rolling up the Route 2 ramp in the paper today. For ten years City Hall has acted like those of us who ride the bus after eight o'clock at night don't exist. Everybody on my shift at the hospital is voting for Katie Prairie on November second!"*

Line after line, for forty consecutive minutes without a single negative call, listeners from Kempsville, Bellamy Manor, Larkspur, College Park, and across Hampton Roads lit up all ten phone lines on WHRC 89.5 FM—until the host finally had to laugh on air and remind callers that the program had other regional news topics on its rundown.

Sitting at our Kempsville kitchen table with Dad grinning over his coffee mug and Katie holding my hand across our wheelchair armrests, we finished our sandwiches, loaded four hundred fresh palm cards into our canvas side-bags, and rolled out into the crisp October sunshine for the final eighteen days of sidewalk canvassing before Election Day.

### Part 2: The WTGA 790 AM Disability Attack, The 94.1% Landslide, & The Eighteenth Street Reckoning

**Date:** 2010-10-28 at 08:15 America/New_York

![At the top of the newly constructed red-carpeted mahogany wheelchair ramp on the Virginia Beach City Council dais in Building 1 on January 4, 2011, 25-year-old Councilwoman-Elect Katie Prairie sits in her black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchair taking the secular constitutional affirmation of office on the Constitution of Virginia held by her twin brother Nate, with their father David standing proudly behind them.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/jan_2011_vb_city_council_dais_ramp_secular_affirmation_katie_nate_david.jpg)

#### Thursday, October 28, 2010, 8:15 AM — Five Days Before the Election: The Incumbent Attacks Katie's Wheelchair on WTGA 790 AM

"Turn the desktop speakers up a notch, Nate," twenty-five-year-old Katie said from her SwiftChair beside mine on the Thursday morning before the election, pausing her typing on our morning canvassing walk-sheets as the live web stream of conservative talk radio WTGA 790 AM—Tidewater Talk 790—crackled across our home office off Military Highway in Kempsville. "The host just said Harold Dietz called in unscheduled."

I reached over and turned up the volume knob beside my monitor while taking a sip of cold chocolate milk.
