For the past thirteen days since Greg Mercer's front-page Metro story in *The Tidewater Pilot* and the forty-minute switchboard takeover on WHRC 89.5 FM, Councilman Harold Dietz had vanished from public view—canceling two neighborhood civic-league appearances while our volunteer canvassing teams knocked on thousands of doors across Kempsville, Bellamy Manor, Brandon, and Larkspur. Now, with five days left before Tuesday's election, the ten-year incumbent had evidently decided to go live on Hampton Roads' loudest morning talk-radio microphone to try to stop the bleeding.

*"We're joined on the studio line right now by Virginia Beach City Councilman Harold Dietz, representing the Kempsville District,"* the WTGA morning host announced. *"Councilman, folks all over the city have been talking about that empty podium over at WHRC and the front-page story in the Tidewater Pilot about your twenty-five-year-old opponent catching three buses home at eight-twenty at night. Looks like you've got a real horse race on your hands out in Kempsville."*

When Harold Dietz's voice came through the broadcast compressor, he didn't sound like a calm ten-year incumbent. He sounded tight, defensive, and rattled.

*"Well, Mike, let's call that newspaper story what it was—a staged piece of political theater,"* Dietz snapped over the airwaves. *"The Tidewater Pilot loves a melodramatic human-interest angle, so they print a picture of my opponent rolling onto a bus at night as if riding a bus qualifies somebody to manage a one-point-seven-billion-dollar municipal corporation. Let's talk about the real world at City Hall that nobody at the newspaper wants to mention."*

Katie and I looked at each other across our wheelchair armrests, our fingers stilling on our keyboards.

*"First of all,"* Dietz ploughed ahead, his voice rising with irritation as he went completely off script, *"if my opponent were actually elected on Tuesday, do the taxpayers of Virginia Beach have any idea what City Hall facilities would have to do to the historic mahogany City Council chamber in Building One? They would have to tear out the woodwork on the side of the raised Council dais and spend tens of thousands of taxpayer dollars building a custom structural wheelchair ramp just to get one person up to a desk! And second, let's be honest with the voters about the demands of this job. Serving on the Virginia Beach City Council isn't a hobby you do from a laptop. We sit in six-hour afternoon budget workshops followed by six-hour evening sessions that run past midnight, plus regional commission meetings all over Tidewater. Are we really supposed to pretend that a twenty-five-year-old girl in a wheelchair—who has to have her twin brother rolling right beside her everywhere she goes just to get through the day—has the physical stamina to handle twelve-hour days on the City Council?"*

Inside our quiet home office in Kempsville, the silence lasted three full seconds.

Even over the radio broadcast, you could hear the WTGA morning host draw in a sharp, audible breath inside the Norfolk studio as he realized the incumbent councilman had just committed political suicide on live air in the largest military and veteran community on the East Coast.

*"Uh—Councilman Dietz,"* the WTGA host cut in quickly, his tone dropping an octave as the red warning lights on his studio call screener's board began flashing like a Christmas tree, *"hang on a second there, Harold. We have eighty thousand disabled veterans and wounded warriors living right here in Virginia Beach and Norfolk who use wheelchairs every day, and federal law under the Americans with Disabilities Act requires public buildings to be accessible anyway—"*

*"I'm just saying the voters deserve to know the practical reality and the cost, Mike!"* Dietz insisted defensively before the host hastily took the program to a commercial break—and when the show came back from the break three minutes later, Councilman Dietz was no longer on the line.

What followed over the next forty-five minutes on WTGA 790 AM was unlike anything we had ever heard on conservative talk radio.

The host didn't take a single call defending Harold Dietz—because there weren't any. Instead, caller after caller was a furious Navy chief, a retired Marine colonel, a wounded Iraq or Afghanistan veteran from Little Creek or Naval Air Station Oceana, or a lifelong conservative Kempsville homeowner calling in to blister the incumbent for attacking a candidate's wheelchair and mocking the bond between twin siblings who had lived with a spinal-cord condition since high school.

*"Mike, this is Senior Chief Petty Officer Miller calling from Bellamy Manor,"* a booming voice growled on Line One. *"I served twenty-four years in the Navy and I've voted Republican in every election for the last thirty years. My nephew lost the use of his legs in Anbar Province in 2007 and uses a power wheelchair just like Katie and Nate Prairie. For a sitting Virginia Beach City Councilman to go on the radio and complain about the cost of putting a wheelchair ramp on the City Council dais—and to insult a young woman's stamina because she uses a wheelchair and works alongside her twin brother—is the most disgraceful thing I've ever heard in this city. I walked out to my front yard five minutes ago, pulled Harold Dietz's sign out of my grass, and threw it in the trash can!"*

By noon on Friday, the fallout had turned into an avalanche. Three of Virginia Beach's largest business associations issued public statements revoking their endorsements of Councilman Dietz and clarifying that they stood for equal access for all citizens. When *The Tidewater Pilot* called our campaign phone asking for Katie's response to Dietz's radio remarks, Katie gave Greg Mercer a single, quiet two-sentence statement:

*"My brother Nate and I have used power wheelchairs since our legs gave out during our junior year at Northwood High School, and we have never once asked anyone in Virginia Beach for pity. All we have ever asked for is a ramp to the table and a bus that runs late enough for working people to get home."*

On Saturday morning, October 30—seventy-two hours before the polls opened—*The Tidewater Pilot* devoted the entire top half of its Editorial & Opinion page to a special full-width spread of reader letters under the banner headline:

*LETTERS TO THE EDITOR: DIETZ'S ATTACKS ON BUSES, WHEELCHAIR RAMPS CROSS THE LINE*

Sitting at our kitchen table with Dad over Saturday morning pancakes and orange juice, I read three of the printed letters aloud while Katie listened beside me:

> A Ramp to the People's Dais Is Not a "Special Favor"<br>
> As a retired Navy Master Chief who lost both legs above the knee to an IED outside Fallujah in 2006, I nearly drove my hand-control truck off Kempsville Road on Thursday morning listening to Councilman Harold Dietz complain on WTGA 790 AM about the cost of building a wheelchair ramp up to the City Council dais for Katie Prairie. When I came home from Bethesda Naval Hospital in a wheelchair, nobody told me I lacked the "stamina" to contribute to my community. If the mahogany dais in Building 1 doesn't have a wheelchair ramp after twenty years of the Americans with Disabilities Act, that isn't an indictment of Katie Prairie—it is an indictment of Harold Dietz and every politician who never thought a citizen in a wheelchair belonged up there.<br>
> — Master Chief Robert H. Callahan, USN (Ret.), Kempsville, Virginia Beach

> The 8:24 PM Bus Is Real Life, Not "Political Theater"<br>
> Councilman Dietz claims Katie and Nate Prairie catching the 8:24 PM Route 2 bus home from the WHRC debate was a "publicity stunt." Tell that to those of us who close the retail stores at Pembroke Mall and Glenrock Mall every night and pray our connecting Route 20 or Route 15 bus isn't five minutes late so we aren't stranded in the dark. Katie and Nate Prairie have ridden the bus with us in the rain and cold for five years. On Tuesday, the bus riders of Virginia Beach are going to send one of our own to City Hall.<br>
> — Denise T. Holloway, College Park, Virginia Beach

> We Remember the Day Their Legs Gave Out at Northwood High<br>
> Hearing Councilman Dietz mock Katie Prairie for having her twin brother Nate rolling beside her broke my heart and made my blood boil. I taught English at Northwood High School in September 2001 on the Friday afternoon when sixteen-year-old Katie and Nate's legs gave out within three hours of each other. Every teacher in that building watched those two teenagers refuse to give up, finish high school from hospital beds and wheelchairs, earn their degrees at CCHR, build their own software business, and make their home right here in Kempsville. Their bond isn't a weakness—it is the finest example of family courage in Virginia Beach.<br>
> — Margaret L. Sterling, Retired Teacher, Bayside, Virginia Beach

When I finished reading Mrs. Sterling's letter, Dad had to take off his glasses and wipe his eyes with his napkin, while Katie held my hand tightly across our armrests.

***

#### Tuesday, November 2, 2010, 7:19 PM — The 94.1% to 5.9% Landslide & The Four-Station Election Night Post-Mortem

![Inside their Kempsville home on Election Night, November 2, 2010, 25-year-old twins Katie and Nathaniel Prairie sit in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs pressing their foreheads together and clasping hands in joyful tears beneath the television displaying Katie's 94.1% victory projection, embraced from behind by their proud father David.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/nov_2010_kempsville_election_night_94_percent_landslide_katie_nate_david.jpg)

At seven o'clock on the evening of Tuesday, November 2, 2010, the polls closed across the City of Virginia Beach.

We hadn't rented a hotel ballroom at the Oceanfront. Instead, Katie, Dad, and I were gathered inside our living room off Military Highway and Indian River Road in Kempsville along with sixteen of our volunteer sidewalk canvassers, CCHR students, and fellow CVTA bus riders, with platters of warm pizza and two-liter bottles of ginger ale, orange soda, and flavored water set out on the dining table and a fresh pot of black coffee brewing in the kitchen for Dad. Across the living room wall, I had connected four television monitors and my dual laptop screens to our custom PHP precinct-return engine, which scraped the live precinct-by-precinct XML data feed straight from the Virginia State Board of Elections and the Virginia Beach Voter Registrar every fifteen seconds.

At 7:08 PM, the first four Kempsville precincts reported their optical-scan tabulator tapes.

Dad leaned over my shoulder, staring at my PHP dashboard screen through his glasses. "Nate... check your parser code on Kempsville Precinct Three and Bellamy Precinct One. Is a decimal point shifted?"

"The parser checksums match the state XML feed to the single vote, Dad," I breathed, my heart hammering against my ribs as five more precincts popped onto the screen in bright green. "Look at the raw totals."

At 7:19 PM—just nineteen minutes after the polls closed—all four local television network affiliates in Hampton Roads (WCVB-TV 10 Coastal News 10, WTID-TV 3 NewsChannel 3, WVHR-TV 13 13News, and WHRC TV-15) flashed simultaneous breaking-news graphics across the bottom of their screens with a loud electronic chime:

*PROJECTION — VIRGINIA BEACH CITY COUNCIL (KEMPSVILLE DISTRICT):*
*KATIE PRAIRIE (WINNER) — 94.1%*
*HAROLD DIETZ (INCUMBENT) — 5.9%*

Inside our living room in Kempsville, a roar went up that shook the framed blue butterfly print on the hallway wall. Dad wrapped both of his arms around Katie's shoulders and mine at the same time, his voice choked with pride, while Katie pressed her forehead against mine across our armrests with tears of pure joy shining in her blue eyes.

As the final precincts locked in over the next twenty minutes confirming the staggering 94.1% to 5.9% margin—the largest landslide defeat of a sitting incumbent in the modern history of Hampton Roads municipal politics—we unmuted the four television feeds and the radio stream to hear the stunned political analysts dissect what had just happened.

On WCVB-TV 10, Coastal News 10 anchor Don Roberts turned to Virginia Dominion University political science professor Dr. Quentin Marsh standing in front of the electronic precinct map.

*"Ninety-four point one percent to five point nine percent, Dr. Marsh,"* the anchor said, shaking his head at the big board. *"We have never seen numbers like this in a contested Virginia Beach City Council race. How does a ten-year incumbent get wiped out by eighty-eight points?"*

*"Don, what we just witnessed tonight in Kempsville is the textbook anatomy of a catastrophic one-two political knockout,"* Dr. Marsh explained, tapping the touchscreen map of Virginia Beach. *"Three weeks ago, before the WHRC debate, Harold Dietz was sitting on a comfortable eight-point incumbent lead mostly because voters didn't know who Katie Prairie was. Then came Punch Number One on October fourteenth: Dietz didn't even bother to RSVP to WHRC TV-15, leaving his podium empty on live television for forty-five minutes while Katie Prairie demonstrated complete command of the municipal budget—followed ten minutes later by Greg Mercer's front-page story in the Tidewater Pilot showing Katie and her twin brother Nate sprinting across six lanes of Hampton Boulevard in their wheelchairs to catch the 8:24 PM Route 2 bus so they wouldn't miss the last three-bus transfer chain home to Virginia Beach. We now know from campaign insiders that by the Monday after that story ran, Dietz's internal tracking poll had crashed from an eight-point lead down to a dead heat—48.2 percent to 47.8 percent, a razor-thin four-tenths of one percent margin right inside Virginia's automatic recount threshold—and his major Oceanfront donors threatened to freeze his final forty-thousand-dollar TV buy."*

Across the room on WVHR-TV 13, a live 13News remote camera panned across a cavernous, completely deserted ballroom at an Oceanfront resort hotel where untouched trays of shrimp cocktail sat under heat lamps beside a silent podium banner reading *RE-ELECT COUNCILMAN DIETZ*.

*"And that panic inside the Dietz camp led directly to Punch Number Two last Thursday morning on WTGA 790 AM,"* the WVHR-TV 13 political reporter told the studio anchors from the empty ballroom. *"Trying to look tough for his panicked donors, Councilman Dietz went on live talk radio, mocked the Prairies' three-bus ride home, complained about the taxpayer cost of building a wheelchair ramp up to the City Council dais in Building 1, and questioned whether a woman in a wheelchair rolling alongside her twin brother had the stamina to serve on Council. In a city filled with military families, disabled veterans, and working bus commuters, that radio call turned a 0.4 percent race into a 94 percent wipeout. The Councilman called Ms. Prairie three minutes ago to concede and left the hotel through a side kitchen door."*

Meanwhile, on WTID-TV 3 NewsChannel 3, the tech-desk correspondent pulled up a live graphic highlighting our grassroots ground game:

*"Don't overlook the engineering behind this victory, either,"* the WTID-TV 3 analyst noted. *"Katie and Nathaniel Prairie didn't spend a dime on outside political consultants. Nathaniel Prairie wrote their custom PHP voter-turnout and precinct-mapping software himself, and look at the precinct turnout bars along the CVTA Route 12, Route 15, Route 20, and Route 36 corridors—precincts that normally see 18 percent turnout in an off-year municipal election surged by 42 percent tonight because bus riders and working families came out in droves to vote for one of their own."*

Even over on conservative talk radio WTGA 790 AM, the evening election host sighed into his microphone as the 94.1% total scrolled across his screen: *"Folks, Harold Dietz dug his own grave right here on our morning airwaves last Thursday. When a twenty-five-year-old woman and her twin brother out-work you, out-debate you, ride three city buses home in the dark, and build their own software from scratch, attacking their wheelchairs in a Navy town is a guaranteed way to get sent into retirement."*

***

#### January to May 2011 — The Building 1 Dais Ramp, Locking $810,000 of CVTA Perks in Escrow, & Taking Seat on the CVTA Commission

![At the top of the newly constructed red-carpeted mahogany wheelchair ramp on the Virginia Beach City Council dais in Building 1 on January 4, 2011, 25-year-old Councilwoman-Elect Katie Prairie sits in her black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchair taking the secular constitutional affirmation of office on the Constitution of Virginia held by her twin brother Nate, with their father David standing proudly behind them.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/jan_2011_vb_city_council_dais_ramp_secular_affirmation_katie_nate_david.jpg)

During the eight weeks between Election Night in November 2010 and Reorganization Night in January 2011, municipal carpenters and accessibility contractors went to work inside the City Council Chamber of Building 1 at the Virginia Beach Municipal Center.

Removing the steep wooden steps on the right wing of the curved mahogany City Council dais, the city constructed a permanent, gently sloped, red-carpeted wheelchair ramp bordered by polished mahogany handrails leading straight up to the Kempsville District desk, where the heavy leather swivel chair was rolled away so twenty-five-year-old Councilwoman-Elect Katie Prairie could pull her compact black SwiftChair directly up to the voting console.

On Tuesday evening, January 4, 2011, with the chamber gallery packed wall-to-wall with Kempsville neighbors, CCHR students, bus operators, and retired Master Chief Robert Callahan sitting in the front row in his own wheelchair, Katie rolled up the new mahogany dais ramp to her Kempsville District seat, inviting Dad and me onto the dais beside her solely for the ceremonial swearing-in while I held open our bound leather copy of the Constitution of the Commonwealth of Virginia.

Neither Katie nor I believed in any religion or any god—and before the ceremony, Katie had politely notified the Clerk of the Circuit Court that under Article VI, Clause 3 of the United States Constitution, Article II, Section 7 of the Constitution of Virginia, and Section 49-9 of the Code of Virginia, she would be taking the secular constitutional affirmation on the Virginia Constitution rather than a religious oath on a Bible, omitting the optional parenthetical reference to a deity at the end.

Placing her left hand flat on the Virginia Constitution and raising her right hand, Katie repeated the constitutional affirmation of office as the newly elected Kempsville District Councilwoman in a clear, ringing voice that echoed to the back of the chamber:

*"I do solemnly affirm that I will support the Constitution of the United States, and the Constitution of the Commonwealth of Virginia, and that I will faithfully and impartially discharge all the duties incumbent upon me as a member of the Council of the City of Virginia Beach, according to the best of my ability."*

As soon as the applause thundered across the chamber, Dad and I descended the ramp back to the front row of the public gallery so Councilwoman Katie Prairie could take her official seat alone at the Kempsville console on the dais.

She didn't wait six months to keep the promise she had made to Greg Mercer at the 8:24 PM bus stop on Hampton Boulevard.

Just two weeks later, on Tuesday evening, January 18, 2011, Item 9B came up on the formal Virginia Beach City Council agenda: a request from the Coastal Virginia Transit Authority for a $1.42 million mid-year supplemental municipal appropriation to cover administrative cost overruns at CVTA's Norfolk headquarters.

Stepping up to the low citizen and staff microphone podium on the chamber floor below the raised mahogany dais were two men in tailored charcoal suits whom Katie and I knew very well: CVTA President and Chief Executive Officer Leonard Sterling, and Chief Operating Officer Richard Halstead—the exact two executives who, fourteen months earlier at 509 East Eighteenth Street, had cut off my public-comment microphone at the hundred-and-eighty-second buzzer, sneered in the hallway that we were *"statistically insignificant hobbyist bloggers,"* refused to release raw GTFS schedule files, and secretly blackballed me from the Transit Riders Advisory Committee.

Now, the roles were reversed. Sterling and Halstead were standing down at the floor microphone looking up at the raised mahogany dais—where twenty-five-year-old Councilwoman Katie Prairie sat in the elected seat of power looking down at them with her finger resting beside her microphone button, while I sat as a private citizen down in the front accessible bay of the chamber floor right beside the dais ramp with the PHP line-item audit I had prepared for her open on my MagnaBook Pro.

When CEO Sterling finished his five-minute presentation asking the City Council to approve the $1.42 million check with no strings attached, the Mayor turned toward the right wing of the dais.

"Councilwoman Prairie," the Mayor said, "you have the floor."

Katie pressed her white microphone button. The green indicator ring lit up—and this time, Richard Halstead didn't have a cutoff switch.

"Thank you, Mr. Mayor," Katie said, her voice calm, polite, and surgical as every camera in Building 1 zoomed in on her desk. "Mr. Sterling, Mr. Halstead, before the voters of Kempsville elected me to this Council by a margin of ninety-four point one percent, the two of you cut off my brother Nate's microphone at Eighteenth Street and told us in the hallway that CVTA doesn't take operational direction from 'hobbyist bloggers.' Now that you are asking the taxpayers of Virginia Beach for an extra one point four two million dollars, my brother and I have gone through every single line of your general ledger."

Down at the podium, Richard Halstead swallowed hard, a bead of sweat glistening at his temple under the television lights.

"Out of the one point four two million dollars you are requesting tonight," Katie continued, reading directly from the PHP audit sheet on her desk, "six hundred and ten thousand dollars goes toward fuel and frontline bus operator wages, which I fully support. The remaining eight hundred and ten thousand dollars, however, is earmarked for executive retention bonuses, out-of-state conference travel, fleet take-home sedans for senior staff, and proprietary scheduling consultant contracts. Meanwhile, here in Virginia Beach, the last Route 12 bus out of the CCHR hub still leaves at 5:48 PM, locking citizens out of our 6:00 PM Council meetings, and your agency still refuses to publish its raw General Transit Feed Specification database tables for the public."

Katie held up a two-page printed budget amendment she had drafted with the City Attorney that morning from our audit notes.

"Therefore, Mr. Mayor," Katie announced, "I move an amendment to Item 9B: the City of Virginia Beach will release the six hundred and ten thousand dollars for bus operators and fuel tonight, and we will lock the remaining eight hundred and ten thousand dollars of executive overhead in a restricted municipal escrow account. Not one penny of that eight hundred and ten thousand dollars will be released by the City Treasurer until CVTA meets two mandatory conditions: first, publishing its complete, unredacted GTFS schedule database online under an open public license within thirty days; and second, implementing the Evening Civic Access Transit Pulse—extending Route 33 out of the Virginia Beach Municipal Center until 10:30 PM on Council nights and operating a synchronized 9:00 PM and 10:00 PM evening connecting pulse for Routes 12, 25, 29, and 36 at the CCHR Virginia Beach Campus hub."

"Second!" called out At-Large Councilman Ronald Villa from the other side of the dais with a broad grin.

When the electronic voting board on the chamber wall chimed ten seconds later, all eleven lights glowed green: 11–0.

And the reckoning wasn't quite finished. Immediately after the budget vote, the Mayor called up Item 9C—the resolution appointing Virginia Beach's new municipal representatives to the governing board of the Coastal Virginia Transit Authority, the Transportation District Commission, to fill the seat vacated by former Councilman Harold Dietz.

By a second unanimous 11–0 vote, the Virginia Beach City Council appointed Councilwoman Katie Prairie as a voting Commissioner of the Coastal Virginia Transit Authority.

Nine days later, on the fourth Thursday of January 2011, while every other city council commissioner from across Hampton Roads drove into Norfolk and parked in the reserved VIP lot behind 509 East Eighteenth Street, CVTA's newest governing Commissioner arrived the exact same way she and I had always traveled: by riding a three-bus chain on CVTA—boarding Route 15 northbound on Military Highway, transferring to Route 20 westbound at Glenrock Mall into Downtown Norfolk, and riding Route 1 up Granby Street to Eighteenth Street while paying our regular fare.

When Katie and I rolled our SwiftChairs through the double doors of the Eighteenth Street boardroom, I parked at the front accessible citizen-advisor table while Commissioner Katie Prairie rolled straight up onto the raised Commissioners' horseshoe dais—right past Chief Operating Officer Richard Halstead's chair. Under New Business, the very first official action Commissioner Katie Prairie took from the dais was exercising her unilateral prerogative as a Virginia Beach Commissioner to make a citizen appointment to the Transit Riders Advisory Committee.

"Pursuant to Section 4.2 of the Commission bylaws," Katie said clearly into her Commissioner's microphone while looking straight across the table at Richard Halstead, "as a voting Commissioner for the City of Virginia Beach, I hereby appoint Nathaniel Prairie to the Virginia Beach citizen seat on the Transit Riders Advisory Committee, effective immediately."

By May 2011, CVTA had published its complete open GTFS schedule feed and launched the permanent Evening Civic Access Transit Pulse across Virginia Beach. For the first time in the history of our city, any citizen who rode a public bus or used a wheelchair could attend a six o'clock City Council meeting, speak at the public microphone, and ride a CVTA bus safely home afterward.

Inside Building 1 at the Municipal Center, Katie also established a daily office habit that baffled the veteran city hall staffers down the corridor: whenever she was sitting at her desk and the main constituent telephone line rang, she didn't wait for a city clerk or a shared administrative receptionist to screen the call and take a paper message. In Katie's literal autistic mind, her name was on the door, the voters of Kempsville had hired her to do the job, and sitting three feet away from a ringing telephone without picking it up would be rude and dishonest. So whenever she could reach the receiver, she pressed the button herself and answered, "Councilwoman Katie Prairie's office, this is Katie speaking," so the caller knew she was actually at her desk working for them—regularly leaving Kempsville homeowners and retired shipyard workers speechless for two full seconds when they realized their own City Councilwoman had picked up the phone on the first ring.

And on every single Tuesday night when the Virginia Beach City Council adjourned at nine-thirty, Councilwoman Katie Prairie rolled down the mahogany dais ramp in Building 1 to meet me at the front of the gallery, and the two of us rolled out to the Municipal Center bus shelter alongside the citizens who had come to watch the meeting, swiped our thirty-day CVTA passes, and rode the 9:45 PM Route 33 and Route 12 pulse right back home to Kempsville.

# The Gentlewoman from Virginia Beach: The House of Delegates

## Stopped at the Third-Floor Gallery, Seated by Delegate Ronald Villa, & Winning the 85th District

### Part 1: Stopped at the Third-Floor Gallery by Capitol Police, Seated on the House Floor Near Delegate Ronald Villa, & The Spark to Run

**Date:** 2012-02-09 at 11:35 America/New_York

![Seated side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs on the green carpet of the Floor of the Virginia House of Delegates on February 9, 2012, 26-year-old Virginia Beach City Councilwoman Katie Prairie and her twin brother Nate talk with Delegate Ronald Villa at his mahogany desk while Katie looks out across the chamber with the spark to run for the General Assembly.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/feb_2012_virginia_house_floor_seated_by_delegate_ronald_villa.jpg)

#### Thursday, February 9, 2012, 11:35 AM — Stopped Outside the Third-Floor Public Viewing Gallery by Capitol Police

"The public viewing gallery for the House of Delegates should be right around this corner on the left, Nate," twenty-six-year-old Katie said as the brass doors of the small historic passenger elevator slid open on the third floor of the Virginia State Capitol.

Side by side, we guided our compact SwiftChairs out of the narrow elevator cab onto the polished heart-pine floorboards of the third-floor balcony corridor.

It was a cold Thursday morning in February 2012, midway through the winter session of the Virginia General Assembly and thirteen months into Katie's term representing the Kempsville District on the Virginia Beach City Council. Earlier that morning at nine o'clock, after riding up from Hampton Roads to testify both as a Virginia Beach City Councilwoman and as co-founder of Ideas for Coastal Virginia Transit, Katie and I had presented our evening ridership numbers and bus-stop accessibility data to a House Transportation subcommittee down in the General Assembly Building—urging the state legislature not to slash the state transit operating funds that matched our new evening bus service in Virginia Beach. Since our afternoon train back home didn't leave until four o'clock, we had rolled through the underground Capitol tunnel hoping to sit in the public viewing gallery and watch the full House of Delegates convene at noon.

Ahead of us, a line of schoolteachers, college students, and day-trippers was filing past the velvet rope into the steeply tiered wooden benches of the third-floor House Public Gallery.

Before our front casters reached the doorway, however, a uniformed Virginia Division of Capitol Police lieutenant standing beside the gallery entrance stepped gently into the center of the corridor and held up a gloved hand.

"Good morning, folks—hold up just a second for me," the Capitol Police lieutenant said, his tone polite but firm as he looked down at our two power wheelchairs.

Katie and I braked our SwiftChairs together. "Good morning, Lieutenant," Katie said calmly. "We already cleared the security screening downstairs at the visitor entrance. We're just heading into the public viewing gallery to watch the noon House session."

"Yes, ma'am, I see your visitor stickers," the lieutenant replied, glancing toward the narrow gallery threshold and then back at our heavy powerchairs with genuine concern on his face. "I'm very sorry, folks, but we can't bring wheelchairs into the third-floor public viewing gallery."

My eyebrows drew together. "Is there not a level space at the top of the gallery aisle?"

"It's not the floor space inside the doorway, sir—it's emergency evacuation safety," the Capitol Police lieutenant explained earnestly, gesturing back toward the small retrofit elevator we had just ridden up and the steep, winding eighteenth-century stairwell at the end of the hall. "Thomas Jefferson designed this building in 1788. If a fire alarm goes off or we have to order an emergency evacuation of the Capitol while the House is in session, that passenger elevator automatically locks out and recalls to the ground floor. From this third-floor gallery, the only way out of the building is down three flights of steep, narrow historic stairs. My officers have no safe way to carry power wheelchairs down three stories of stairs in an emergency, and I can't put the two of you in a position where we couldn't get you out of the building safely."

Katie and I looked at each other across our armrests. Having spent more than ten years navigating every flavor of architectural barrier in Virginia, both of us could tell immediately that the Capitol Police officer wasn't trying to brush us off—he was looking at a genuine life-safety trap in a two-hundred-year-old building and taking his duty seriously.

"So there's nowhere in the State Capitol where a citizen in a wheelchair is allowed to watch their own House of Delegates vote?" Katie asked quietly, not angry at the officer, but with that familiar, steady look in her blue eyes whenever she ran into a systemic wall.

"I didn't say that, ma'am," the Capitol Police lieutenant said with a reassuring half-smile, reaching up to unclip the microphone of his shoulder radio. "Give me two minutes right here by the elevator. I'm going to walk downstairs and speak directly to the Sergeant-at-Arms and House Leadership to explain that we have a member of the public in a wheelchair and her companion upstairs who came to watch the House session, and that Capitol Police have emergency-egress safety concerns with the third-floor gallery. Let me see what Leadership can do."

We parked our SwiftChairs beside the marble bust in the third-floor elevator vestibule and waited while the ten-minute warning bell for the noon floor session chimed overhead.

Four minutes later, the brass indicator needle above the third-floor elevator swung upward. The doors slid open, and the Capitol Police lieutenant stepped out alongside a tall gentleman in a dark three-piece suit wearing the silver badge of the Sergeant-at-Arms of the Virginia House of Delegates.

"Councilwoman Prairie and Mr. Prairie?" the Sergeant-at-Arms asked warmly.

"Yes, sir," I said.

"The Lieutenant just spoke with me and the Speaker's office about the safety concern up here on the third floor," the Sergeant-at-Arms said, holding out two heavy cream-colored cards stamped in gold leaf with the seal of the Commonwealth. "House Leadership does not want any Virginian turned away from watching the people's House in session because of a wheelchair. By order of the Speaker, you and one ADA companion—or in your case, both of you together—have been granted a rare honor today. If you'll ride the elevator down to the first floor with me, we're going to seat you right on the Floor of the Virginia House of Delegates."

Katie's blue eyes widened slightly as she looked across at me, and we rolled our wheelchairs straight back into the elevator cab beside the Sergeant-at-Arms.

***

#### Thursday, February 9, 2012, 11:52 AM — Seated on the House Floor Near Virginia Beach Delegate Ronald Villa & The Spark

![Seated side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs on the green carpet of the Floor of the Virginia House of Delegates on February 9, 2012, 26-year-old Virginia Beach City Councilwoman Katie Prairie and her twin brother Nate talk with Delegate Ronald Villa at his mahogany desk while Katie looks out across the chamber with the spark to run for the General Assembly.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/feb_2012_virginia_house_floor_seated_by_delegate_ronald_villa.jpg)

When the elevator doors opened on the first floor, the marble rotunda corridor outside the House Chamber was packed three-deep with corporate lobbyists, reporters, and political staffers pressed against the brass velvet rope.

Under the rules of the House of Delegates, members of the general public and registered lobbyists were strictly barred from crossing that threshold onto the Chamber floor during session. Yet as the Sergeant-at-Arms stepped out of the elevator ahead of our two wheelchairs, the doorkeepers immediately unhooked the velvet rope and swung open the tall mahogany double doors.

"Make way, please—honored guests of the House coming through to the Floor," the Sergeant-at-Arms announced.

Thirty-five lobbyists in thousand-dollar suits parted in stunned silence as two twenty-six-year-old twins from Virginia Beach rolled their compact black SwiftChairs straight across the threshold onto the lush green carpet of the Virginia House of Delegates Chamber.

Rolling inside at floor level felt completely different from looking at photographs of the chamber. High above us rose the cream-and-gold coffered ceiling and the glittering crystal chandeliers; directly ahead stood the Speaker's elevated marble rostrum and the twin electronic voting boards listing all one hundred Delegates in alphabetical order. And instead of staring down at the tops of lawmakers' heads from a distant third-floor balcony, we were rolling right past the curved rows of polished mahogany desks where the elected representatives of the Commonwealth sat.

"Right over here on the outer right aisle, folks," the Sergeant-at-Arms whispered kindly, guiding our two wheelchairs to a wide, level carpeted bay near the rear row of desks on the first floor—twenty feet from an emergency ground-level exit door. "I figured two folks from Virginia Beach would feel right at home sitting next to one of your hometown Delegates."

At the mahogany desk immediately beside our wheelchair bay, a dark-haired Delegate in a crisp navy suit—with a brass nameplate on his desk reading *MR. VILLA — VIRGINIA BEACH (21ST DISTRICT)*—turned around in his leather swivel chair to see who was being seated beside him.

The instant his eyes landed on our two wheelchairs, Delegate Ronald Villa broke into a huge, genuine grin and stood right up to shake our hands.

"Katie! Nate!" Delegate Villa said warmly, clasping Katie's right hand and then reaching across to shake mine. "What a surprise! How did the two of you manage to score floor seats in the House of Delegates?"

"We tried to go upstairs to the third-floor public viewing gallery, Delegate Villa," I explained with a grin, "and Capitol Police stopped us because they were worried about how they'd evacuate our wheelchairs down three flights of stairs in an emergency. They talked to House Leadership, and the Sergeant-at-Arms brought us down here to sit next to you."

"Well, I couldn't ask for better company on my aisle!" Delegate Villa laughed, gesturing toward the two neighboring delegates seated to his left. "Hey, guys, let me introduce you to Virginia Beach City Councilwoman Katie Prairie from Kempsville and her twin brother Nathaniel. Long before Katie won her Kempsville Council seat, the two of them started the Ideas for Coastal Virginia Transit blog. Back when I was serving At-Large on the Virginia Beach City Council before I was elected to the House, I was actively fighting to get more covered bus shelters built for our bus riders so working folks and seniors wouldn't be standing out in the pouring rain along Kempsville Road, Princess Anne Road, and Holland Road. Every time city staff claimed we didn't know which bus stops needed shelters the most, Katie and Nate had already ridden every route in their wheelchairs and published the exact stop-by-stop boarding numbers and sidewalk photos on their website!"

The two neighboring delegates smiled and shook our hands across our lap trays as the noon bell rang and the Speaker rapped his wooden gavel to call the House of Delegates to order.

For the next hour and fifteen minutes, Katie and I sat side by side in our SwiftChairs right on the green carpet of the House Floor beside Delegate Ronald Villa's desk.

Whenever a bill came up on the electronic calendar board, Delegate Villa leaned over his desk armrest between votes to whisper a quick, friendly explanation of the parliamentary procedure—pointing out how the white request-to-speak buttons worked on the desk consoles, how committee chairmen signaled floor amendments, and how the red and green lights on the big wall boards tallied the yeas and nays in real time. Even though he sat on the Republican side of the aisle and knew our transit blog frequently called out state and local leaders in both parties when public transit got shortchanged, Delegate Villa treated us with the warm, unpretentious respect of a former At-Large City Councilman who genuinely cared about the bus riders in his city.

Then, at twelve-forty-five, the budget amendment Katie and I had testified for at nine o'clock that morning came up on the floor—a measure to restore four million dollars in state operating assistance for local public bus systems across Hampton Roads, Richmond, and Northern Virginia.

Sitting right on the House Floor, Katie and I watched the big electronic voting board on the front wall as the bell chimed and the red and green lights blinked on beside each lawmaker's name.

Right next to us, Delegate Ronald Villa reached forward and pressed his green *YEA* button to support the transit funds for Hampton Roads.

Across the chamber, however, the incumbent Delegate representing our own Eighty-Fifth House District back home in Kempsville—Delegate Richard Tatum, who had ignored three straight emails Katie had sent him asking for a ten-minute meeting to coordinate state matching funds for Virginia Beach's new evening bus routes—didn't even look up from his cell phone as he reached over and slapped his red *NAY* button, helping defeat the transit amendment by six votes.

I turned my head slightly to look at my twin sister.

Katie wasn't looking at the floor carpet anymore. Sitting upright in her compact SwiftChair on the floor of the Virginia House of Delegates, her blue eyes were locked onto the mahogany desks and the big electronic voting board at the front of the room. For the first time in her life, the Virginia General Assembly wasn't a distant, abstract institution behind a television glass screen or three stories below a balcony rail. She was sitting right on the Floor. She could see the buttons on the desks. She could hear how the bills were debated. And she could see firsthand that while she had fought for a full year on the Virginia Beach City Council to get evening buses running out of the Municipal Center, the Eighty-Fifth District's own State Delegate up here in Richmond was voting to starve those very same buses of state matching funds.

When the House recessed at one-fifteen and Delegate Villa shook our hands again before heading off to his afternoon committee meeting—promising to keep working with us on bus shelters and regional transit back home in Virginia Beach—Katie and I rolled out the tall mahogany double doors of the House Chamber into the first-floor marble corridor.

As we rode the elevator down toward the underground Capitol tunnel, Katie reached across our wheelchair armrests and took my right hand in a grip so steady and electric that I felt it all the way to my shoulders.

"Nate," Katie whispered as the elevator doors closed around just the two of us.

"Yeah, Katie?" I asked, looking straight into her eyes.

"Being stopped at the third-floor viewing gallery by Capitol Police and brought down to sit on the House Floor beside Delegate Villa today was the best thing that ever could have happened to us," Katie said, her voice quiet and ringing with unmistakable purpose. "Did you see how ordinary those mahogany desks are when you're sitting right next to them on the green carpet? Just like on City Council back home, all it takes to make room for a power wheelchair at one of those desks is pulling out a single wooden swivel chair."

My breath caught in my chest as I realized what my twin sister was saying.

"Richard Tatum didn't even look up from his phone when he voted against our buses today," Katie continued, squeezing my fingers tightly. "We proved on the Virginia Beach City Council that when you put a bus rider in a wheelchair at the table, you can change the schedules for the entire city. But as long as politicians in Richmond keep cutting state transit funds and blocking disability Medicaid waivers, local City Councils are fighting with one hand tied behind their backs. The next House of Delegates election is in November 2013. Let's go home, talk it over with Dad, and map out how we win the Eighty-Fifth District seat."

### Part 2: Telling Dad at Our Kempsville Kitchen Table, The 125-Signature Ballot Petition at CCHR, & Winning the Eighty-Fifth House District

**Date:** 2012-11-23 at 18:30 America/New_York

![At the Community College of Hampton Roads Virginia Beach Campus bus transfer loop in January 2013 with a CVTA Route 12 bus idling at the curb, 27-year-old Katie Prairie and her twin brother Nate sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs with their father David beside them, collecting 412 verified voter signatures on her House of Delegates ballot petitions.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/jan_2013_cchr_bus_loop_412_petition_signatures_katie_nate_david.jpg)

#### Friday, November 23, 2012, 6:30 PM — Brainstorming with Dad Around the Kempsville Kitchen Table

"Dad," twenty-seven-year-old Katie said after the three of us had finished our Friday evening Thanksgiving leftovers and I had set three fresh glasses of ice-cold ginger ale down on the oak kitchen table of our house off Military Highway and Indian River Road in Kempsville, "Nate and I have a big decision we want to talk through with you before the end of the year."

Sitting across the table from our two compact SwiftChairs in his flannel shirt, our fifty-four-year-old dad set his glass down, adjusted his eyeglasses, and looked from Katie's face to mine with a knowing fatherly smile.

"Wait—let me guess," Dad said warmly. "The last time the two of you gave me that exact synchronized twin look across this table was back in 2010 right before Katie told me she was going to run against Harold Dietz for the Kempsville seat on the Virginia Beach City Council. Who rattled your cage this time?"

"Delegate Richard Tatum," Katie answered without missing a beat, sliding my MagnaBook Pro laptop across the table so Dad could see the newly redistricted map of the Eighty-Fifth House District glowing on the screen. "Back in February, when Nate and I rode up to Richmond to testify for state public-transit matching funds, Capitol Police stopped us at the third-floor viewing gallery over emergency-evacuation concerns and House Leadership brought us down to sit right on the Floor of the House of Delegates next to Ron Villa's desk. We sat twenty feet away from Richard Tatum and watched him slap his red Nay button against Hampton Roads bus funding without even looking up from his cell phone."

"And after serving two years on the Virginia Beach City Council," I added, tapping the boundary lines on the laptop screen, "we've seen firsthand that almost everything we're trying to fix locally—dedicated regional funding for CVTA, clearing the state developmental-disability Medicaid waiver waitlist for Virginia families raising adults like our cousin Chelsea up in Newport, Rhode Island, and enforcing real accessibility rules—is controlled up in Richmond by the General Assembly. Look at the new decennial map for the Eighty-Fifth House District, Dad: it covers Kempsville, Bellamy Manor, Brandon, and Larkspur, right around Fairlawn Recreation Center on Marlborough Drive. Eighty-five percent of the precincts in the Eighty-Fifth House District are the exact same Kempsville neighborhoods that elected Katie to City Council in 2010."

Dad leaned over the table, studying the precinct map carefully before looking back up at Katie.

"I know my daughter, and I know that once the two of you set your minds to something, nobody in Virginia is going to stop you," Dad said proudly, though his voice turned serious and practical as he switched into systems-engineer problem-solving mode. "So let's brainstorm this right now from start to finish before the calendar flips to 2013. Walk me through every step between tonight and swearing-in day in January 2014. First question: Virginia Beach City Council is non-partisan under state law. If you run for the Virginia House of Delegates against Richard Tatum next November, you have to declare a party ballot line. How are you filing?"

"I'm running as a Democrat—Katie Prairie, D-Virginia Beach," Katie said without a second's hesitation. "City Council elections are non-partisan by law, so party labels weren't on the ballot in 2010, but you, Nate, and I have been Democrats our entire lives. Nate and I grew up in a Democratic household watching you vote for the Democratic ticket in every election, Dad. Back when we were teenagers in high school, we would have gladly voted for the Democratic candidates right alongside you if we'd been old enough to cast a ballot, and the three of us have voted Democrat in every single local, state, and federal election since the day Nate and I turned eighteen. Ron Villa has always been fair to us on bus shelters from the Republican side because he came up through City Council, but the House majority caucus in Richmond just spent the whole 2012 session cutting public transit, blocking healthcare expansion, and starving disability services. If I'm going up to Richmond to fight for working families, bus riders, and disabled Virginians, I'm running proudly under the party banner the three of us have always believed in."

"Damn right," Dad nodded with a proud grin, pulling a yellow legal pad and a ballpoint pen toward his elbow. "The three of us have never hidden what we stand for. Second question: what happens to your Kempsville seat on the Virginia Beach City Council during the campaign—and what happens to your software business here at home if you win?"

"Under Virginia law, a sitting City Council member does not have to resign her municipal seat just to run for the General Assembly," I explained, opening the Code of Virginia tab I had bookmarked in our browser. "Katie's four-year City Council term runs through 2014, and the House of Delegates election is in November 2013. That means Katie keeps representing Kempsville on the Virginia Beach City Council through the entire 2013 campaign so our neighbors never lose their vote at City Hall. Once she wins the House seat in November 2013, she'll serve through the final December 2013 Council meeting and then formally resign her City Council seat effective December 31, 2013—right before taking her oath in the House of Delegates on the second Wednesday in January 2014."

"And because the Virginia General Assembly is a part-time citizen legislature," Katie added, "session only runs for sixty days in even-numbered years and forty-five days in odd-numbered years during January and February. Ten months out of every year, Nate and I stay right here in our house off Military Highway in Kempsville running our software business and riding CVTA buses around the district. For January and February, we'll rent a one-bedroom accessible apartment right on a JRTC bus route in Richmond."

Dad wrote *Jan–Feb: 60/45-day Winter Session (Richmond Bus Route Apt)* at the top of his legal pad, then tapped his pen below it.

"Alright—now walk me through the official election-law timeline under Title 24.2 of the Code of Virginia," Dad said. "What paperwork has to be filed between January 1, 2013 and the ballot deadline so Tatum's lawyers can't try to knock you off the ballot on a technicality?"

I rotated the second browser tab toward Dad, where Katie and I had already built a step-by-step statutory checklist.

"Step one happens on January 2, 2013," I said. "We file Katie's Statement of Organization with the Virginia State Board of Elections in the COMET campaign finance system, register *Katie Prairie for Delegate*, and open a dedicated campaign checking account at our credit union within ten days. Under state law, every candidate committee has to designate an official Campaign Treasurer who lives in Virginia. Katie and I want me to serve as Campaign Manager and Chief Technology Officer—and we want to know if you'll serve as our official Campaign Treasurer, Dad."

Dad's chest swelled visibly behind his glasses. "Try and stop me. I balanced our household books down to the penny when I was putting myself through CCHR after the divorce—I'll make sure every campaign finance report we file with Richmond reconciles to the cent. What's step two?"

"Step two is ballot qualification between January 2 and the late-March primary filing deadline," Katie said, pointing to the four official State Board of Elections forms we had downloaded:

"To qualify for the June Democratic Primary ballot in a House of Delegates district," Katie explained, "a candidate has to file four things before five o'clock on the March filing deadline: first, the Certificate of Candidate Qualification under Section 24.2-501 certifying that I'm a qualified voter and resident of the Eighty-Fifth House District; second, the Declaration of Candidacy under Section 24.2-520 along with the party primary filing fee paid to the Virginia Beach Treasurer; third, the General Assembly Statement of Economic Interests under Section 30-111 disclosing our fifty-fifty software company and our house here in Kempsville; and fourth—the most important part—the Petition of Qualified Voters under Section 24.2-506."

"How many valid voter signatures does the Code of Virginia require for a House of Delegates candidate?" Dad asked, poised with his pen.

"The statute requires a minimum of one hundred and twenty-five signatures from qualified, registered voters residing inside the Eighty-Fifth House District, witnessed by a circulator who signs the affidavit on the back of each legal-sized petition sheet before a notary public," I said. "Professional campaigns sometimes get sloppy and turn in two hundred signatures, and then get disqualified when fifty of the signers turn out to live across the street in the Eighty-First or Twenty-First District. So we aren't turning in one hundred and twenty-five signatures. We're going to collect four hundred verified Eighty-Fifth District signatures—and before a single voter signs our clipboard, I'm going to look up their street address live on my laptop against the official Eighty-Fifth District registered-voter file so we have a one-hundred-percent validity rate."

"And where are we collecting those four hundred signatures?" Dad asked with a grin, already guessing the answer.

"Right at the CCHR Virginia Beach Campus bus transfer loop, along the Kempsville Road and Princess Anne Road bus stops, and out on the neighborhood sidewalks every Saturday morning in January and February," Katie smiled, reaching across our armrests to take my hand while extending her other hand across the table to Dad. "No paid petition mercenaries from out of town. Just the three of us."

Dad placed his large, warm hand over both of ours in the center of the kitchen table.

"Then on Saturday, January fifth, I'm driving down from Alexandria with three legal-sized clipboards and a box of black pens," Dad said. "Let's put a bus rider in the House of Delegates."

***

#### January to December 2013 — 412 Signatures at CCHR, Canvassing the 85th District, & Passing the Baton on City Council

![At the Community College of Hampton Roads Virginia Beach Campus bus transfer loop in January 2013 with a CVTA Route 12 bus idling at the curb, 27-year-old Katie Prairie and her twin brother Nate sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs with their father David beside them, collecting 412 verified voter signatures on her House of Delegates ballot petitions.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/jan_2013_cchr_bus_loop_412_petition_signatures_katie_nate_david.jpg)

On the first Saturday morning of January 2013, right after Katie and I filed her Statement of Organization with Dad listed as Treasurer, the three of us set up at the edge of the concrete passenger island at the CCHR Virginia Beach Campus bus loop.

Every time a CVTA Route 12, Route 25, Route 29, or Route 33 bus pulled into the college transfer hub, dozens of Kempsville residents stepped off the doors and recognized Katie immediately as the twenty-seven-year-old City Councilwoman in the black SwiftChair who had fought to keep their evening buses running until ten-thirty at night.

"Councilwoman Prairie! Are those petitions to run for State Delegate against Richard Tatum?" a CCHR nursing instructor asked excitedly on our very first morning, spotting the legal-sized State Board of Elections sheets clipped to Katie's lap tray. "Give me a pen right now—and wait two seconds while I call my husband and my daughter over from the Route 12 shelter so they can sign too!"

With Dad standing beside our wheelchairs holding the extra clipboards and signing the circulator affidavits in front of a mobile notary at the end of each afternoon, and with me verifying every signer's address and precinct number on my laptop on the spot, we didn't just hit the statutory minimum of one hundred and twenty-five signatures—by the end of February, we had collected four hundred and twelve verified signatures from registered Eighty-Fifth District voters.

When the five-o'clock primary filing deadline closed on the last Thursday of March 2013, not a single Democratic challenger had filed against a popular sitting Kempsville City Councilwoman who had turned in four hundred and twelve bulletproof grassroots signatures. The Virginia State Board of Elections officially certified Katie as the Democratic Nominee for the Eighty-Fifth House District without the expense of a June primary.

Two days later, a pair of sleek political consultants from Richmond rode down I-64 and asked to meet us at a restaurant near Pembroke Commons. Spreading glossy brochures across the table, they informed Katie that to run a "serious" House of Delegates campaign in Virginia Beach, she needed to pay their firm a forty-thousand-dollar retainer to lease the state party's voter-targeting software, hire an out-of-state direct-mail agency, and host high-dollar donor receptions at Oceanfront hotels.

Katie and I listened politely, took a sip of our ginger ales, and turned their entire forty-thousand-dollar sales pitch down flat.

"My brother and I are professional software engineers," Katie told the stunned consultants before we rolled out to catch our bus home. "Nate already wrote our custom PHP precinct-mapping and voter-turnout engine for my 2010 City Council victory, and it runs faster, cleaner, and with better precinct math than anything on K Street. Every dollar small donors give our campaign is going straight into printing accessible literature and reaching voters in Kempsville—not paying commissions to Richmond consultants."

From April through November 2013, the three of us ran the most disciplined grassroots campaign the Eighty-Fifth District had ever seen.

Every weekday after our software client work and Katie's City Council duties, Katie and I rode CVTA buses across the district and rolled down the residential sidewalks of Kempsville, Bellamy Manor, Brandon, and Larkspur. Whenever a house had two or three brick steps up to the front porch, Dad—who drove down from Alexandria every Friday night through Sunday evening, joined during the weekdays by a dozen volunteer CCHR students and fellow bus riders—walked up the steps to knock on the door while Katie and I parked our SwiftChairs right at the bottom of the front walk so the homeowner could step out onto the porch and talk directly with Katie eye-to-eye.

By mid-October, internal polling showed that Katie had erased Delegate Richard Tatum's twelve-point incumbent cushion.

Panicking during the final ten days of the race, Tatum's Richmond campaign consultants dropped a glossy, full-color attack mailer into every mailbox in Kempsville showing a photograph of the steps of the State Capitol with the headline: *THE GENERAL ASSEMBLY MOVES FAST—CAN KATIE PRAIRIE KEEP UP?* Inside, the mailer sneered that Katie "doesn't even hold a driver's license" and claimed that two twenty-eight-year-old twins who rode the city bus would be "out of their depth in Richmond."

The backlash across Virginia Beach was instantaneous.

Disabled veterans from Naval Air Station Oceana and Little Creek, parents of special-needs children at Morrison Middle School and Northwood High School, senior citizens along Kempsville Road, and hundreds of commuters who rode the evening buses Katie had championed on City Council flooded the local newspaper letters page and local television broadcasts with outrage. Even former At-Large City Councilman and sitting Republican Delegate Ronald Villa over in the neighboring Twenty-First District told a Norfolk newspaper reporter on the record, *"Anyone who thinks Katie and Nate Prairie can't keep up at the State Capitol has never watched those two work a transportation budget."*

On Election Night—Tuesday, November 5, 2013—sitting side by side with Dad at our kitchen table in Kempsville tracking the eighteen precincts of the Eighty-Fifth House District on my PHP dashboard, we watched the final returns lock in at 8:15 PM:

*Katie Prairie (D): 54.4% — Richard Tatum (R, Incumbent): 45.6%.*

At twenty-eight years old, my twin sister was officially Delegate-Elect Katie Prairie of the Eighty-Fifth House District.

Over the next eight weeks of November and December 2013, we completed every statutory transition step between Election Night and Opening Day:

First, on the Wednesday and Thursday after the election, the three-member Virginia Beach Electoral Board met at the Municipal Center to conduct the official canvass of precinct returns, transmitting the certified abstract up to the Virginia State Board of Elections in Richmond under Code of Virginia Section 24.2-675 so the Secretary of the Board could mail Katie her official, gold-sealed Certificate of Election.

Second, during the first week of December, we traveled up to Richmond for the one-day House Clerk's administrative intake—receiving Katie's office assignment in Room 518 on the fifth floor of the General Assembly Building—and met via video conference with attorneys at the Division of Legislative Services to draft and pre-file her first three legislative bills on regional transit funding, developmental-disability Medicaid waiver slots, and statewide ADA building enforcement ahead of the December pre-filing deadline.

Third, on the third Tuesday evening of December 2013, Katie rolled up the permanent ramp to the Virginia Beach City Council dais at the Municipal Center one last time. After casting her final municipal votes and thanking the people of Kempsville for three unforgettable years of service on City Council, Katie formally submitted her resignation from the non-partisan Kempsville Council seat effective at 11:59 PM on December 31, 2013—welcoming her newly elected Kempsville Council successor, Councilwoman Amelia Thornton, so she would never hold dual municipal and state legislative office when her House term began.

When Katie and I rolled out of the Municipal Center at nine-thirty that December night and boarded the 9:45 PM CVTA Route 33 bus that she had fought to create, the driver saluted her from behind the wheel.

"Next stop for you two is the State Capitol up in Richmond, Delegate-Elect Prairie!" the driver beamed.

"Only for forty-five and sixty days every winter," Katie smiled, holding my hand across the center aisle between our two wheelchair bays as the bus rolled toward CCHR. "And on Friday, January third, Nate and I are moving into an apartment right on West Broad Street so we can ride the Richmond city bus to the Capitol too."

## Freshman Session on West Broad Street & Riding JRTC Route 6 to the Capitol

### Part 1: The West Broad Street Loft, Unpacking Our Shared Queen Bed, & Weekend Reconnaissance on JRTC Route 6

**Date:** 2014-01-03 at 14:15 America/New_York

![Inside Apartment 104 of the Broad & Boulevard Lofts in Richmond on January 3, 2014, 28-year-old Freshman Delegate-Elect Katie Prairie and her twin brother Nate sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs holding hands by the tall warehouse windows with their father David beside them as a blue-and-white JRTC Route 6 bus glides down West Broad Street.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/jan_2014_west_broad_street_loft_window_jrtc_route_6_katie_nate_david.jpg)

#### Friday, January 3, 2014, 2:15 PM — Five Days Ahead of Opening Day at the Broad & Boulevard Lofts

![Inside Apartment 104 of the Broad & Boulevard Lofts in Richmond on January 3, 2014, 28-year-old Freshman Delegate-Elect Katie Prairie and her twin brother Nate sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs holding hands by the tall warehouse windows with their father David beside them as a blue-and-white JRTC Route 6 bus glides down West Broad Street.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/jan_2014_west_broad_street_loft_window_jrtc_route_6_katie_nate_david.jpg)

"I still apologize that we only had a one-bedroom accessible apartment left on the ground floor for the legislative session, Delegate Prairie," the property manager of the Broad & Boulevard Lofts said nervously as he held open the wide oak door of Apartment 104 and handed twenty-eight-year-old Katie two brass keys and a pair of electronic lobby fobs. "When the General Assembly convenes every January, the two-bedroom corporate units book up months in advance. If you and your brother need us to roll a folding cot into the living room—"

"No cot needed at all, Mr. Davenport, thank you," Katie said with a warm, reassuring smile from her compact black SwiftChair as she rolled smoothly across the threshold ahead of me and our fifty-five-year-old dad. "A one-bedroom apartment with one queen bed is actually the exact layout my brother and I asked for."

Behind us, pushing a wheeled bellhop cart loaded with our two dark-blue comforter bags from home, our dual laptop stands, and two plastic crates of kitchen staples that he had driven down I-95 from Alexandria in the bed of his pickup truck to meet our morning ARTS train from Norfolk, Dad chuckled softly at the property manager's polite blink of surprise.

Once Mr. Davenport wished us a good winter in Richmond and stepped back out into the wide brick-and-timber hallway, I clicked the deadbolt shut and looked around our new sixty-day winter sanctuary.

It was Friday, January 3, 2014—five full days before the Virginia General Assembly would gavel in at noon on Wednesday, January 8 for Katie's very first session representing the Eighty-Fifth House District back home in Kempsville and Virginia Beach.

When Katie had flipped the Eighty-Fifth District seat two months earlier in November 2013—running on the exact public-transit, disability-access, and working-family platform we had spent the previous eight years championing on Ideas for Coastal Virginia Transit—party staffers in Richmond had automatically sent us brochures for upscale high-rise apartments down in Shockoe Slip and luxury suites near the downtown hotels where veteran lawmakers stayed during the winter session.

Katie and I had taken one look at the transit map of Richmond and turned every single one of those downtown hotel brochures down.

Instead, we had chosen Apartment 104 inside the Broad & Boulevard Lofts—a renovated brick warehouse building on West Broad Street right near Boulevard at the edge of Scott's Addition and the Museum District. The building had a flush concrete entrance off the wide West Broad Street sidewalk with zero steps, blue ADA push-button automatic doors, forty-two-inch interior doorways, low-pile commercial carpet, and a roll-in bathroom with steel grab bars. Even better, thirty feet outside the front lobby glass stood a blue-and-white bus stop sign for the James River Transit Company—Richmond's public bus network, universally known across the capital region as the JRTC Transit System.

"Come look at this view out the living room windows, Nate," Katie called out, rolling her SwiftChair across the open floor plan toward the two tall industrial sash windows facing south over West Broad Street.

I rolled up beside her left armrest while Dad carried our bedding bags into the bedroom. Right below our first-floor windowsill, a blue-and-white forty-foot JRTC Stalwart low-floor transit bus with an amber LED destination sign reading *6 BROAD STREET — DOWNTOWN / CAPITOL* glided past the curb.

"Four separate JRTC trunk routes converge right along this stretch of West Broad Street," I said, resting my hand over Katie's fingers on her armrest as we watched a westbound bus pass in the opposite lane thirty seconds later. "Route 6 runs straight down Broad Street past the Science Museum and Central Virginia University to Ninth and Broad at Capitol Square in eleven minutes, and straight west to the shops and grocery store at Oak Lawn in ten minutes."

"And arriving five days early gives us all of Saturday and Sunday to learn the bus routes, test every transfer stop, and get our routine locked down before Monday morning's New Member Orientation even starts," Katie said, letting out a quiet, contented breath as her shoulders relaxed.

Because both of us were autistic, rolling cold into an unfamiliar city and a brand-new legislative building on the same morning would have been a recipe for sensory overload. Coming up to Richmond five days ahead of Wednesday's Opening Day gavel wasn't a vacation; it was how Katie and I mapped our perimeter so that by the time the session bell rang, every doorway, curb cut, bus stop, and timetable between our bed and the House Floor felt completely predictable.

We rolled into the bedroom to help Dad finish unpacking.

Although the apartment came furnished with a solid oak queen bedframe, a firm mattress, and two nightstands, Katie and I never slept well under stiff, bleach-scented corporate rental linens. Dad had already stripped off the rental bedspread and folded it onto the top closet shelf, and together the three of us spread out our own familiar cotton sheets, our heavy navy-blue winter comforter, and our four pillows from our shared bedroom back home in Kempsville.

"There," Katie said happily, smoothing the corner of our comforter from her wheelchair while I plugged our dual powerchair chargers into the wall outlet at the foot of the bed. "Now it smells like home."

Out in the front room, Dad helped us push the rectangular oak dining table right up in front of the tall windows overlooking West Broad Street. Within forty minutes, we had our two MagnaBook Pro laptops, our dual twenty-four-inch external monitors, our hardware firewall router, and our portable video-capture encoder cabled neatly across the tabletop.

Before Dad headed back out to his pickup truck at five-thirty to beat the Friday evening traffic north up I-95 to his house on Sunset Drive in Alexandria, he stood by the front door and pulled both of us into a long, tight hug across our wheelchair armrests.

"If anybody at that Capitol gives my daughter or my son a hard time next week, you call me," Dad said fiercely, kissing the top of Katie's blonde head and clapping my shoulder.

"We'll be fine, Dad," Katie smiled, hugging him back as I squeezed his forearm. "We've got each other, we've got our laptops, and we've got a bus stop thirty feet from the front door."

That Friday night, after eating a quiet supper of toasted cheese sandwiches and tomato soup at our window table while watching the headlights and blue-and-white JRTC buses roll down West Broad Street, Katie and I parked our two SwiftChairs beside the untouched queen bed in our exposed-brick bedroom and transferred down into our quilted navy-blue sleeping bag on the carpeted floor of the walk-in closet. Wrapping both arms closely around each other with Katie's cheek resting against my chest—feeling the calming deep pressure that always grounded us best in a brand-new city—we drifted off to sleep safe inside our new Richmond perimeter.

![Inside Apartment 104 of the Broad & Boulevard Lofts in Richmond on the night of January 3, 2014, while the queen bed against the exposed red-brick wall sits untouched behind their two parked black SwiftChair power wheelchairs, 28-year-old Delegate-Elect Katie Prairie and her twin brother Nate cuddle closely in a soothing two-arm embrace inside their navy-blue sleeping bag on the floor of the walk-in closet.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/jan_2014_west_broad_street_loft_closet_full_cuddle_sanctuary_katie_nate.jpg)

***

#### Saturday & Sunday, January 4–5, 2014 — Buying Regular 30-Day JRTC Passes & Mapping the Broad Street Spine

At nine o'clock on Saturday morning, bundled up in our matching winter parkas, knit gloves, and wool scarves with our canvas backpacks hooked behind our wheelchair headrests, Katie and I rolled out the automatic glass doors of the Broad & Boulevard Lofts to the West Broad Street bus stop.

The January air was crisp and clear at thirty-six degrees. Three minutes after we braked our SwiftChairs on the concrete waiting pad alongside a Central Virginia University nursing student and two restaurant cooks heading downtown for the Saturday lunch shift, an eastbound JRTC Route 6 Stalwart low-floor bus pulled smoothly to the curb.

The air brakes hissed, and as the front doors folded open and the front air suspension dropped four inches toward the sidewalk, the bus's external automated voice annunciator spoke through the doorway speaker in its crisp, unmistakable cadence—announcing the route once as the doors opened before switching to the safety warnings as the stainless-steel front flip-ramp folded out onto the concrete:

*"Route 6. Downtown. Welcome aboard JRTC!"*

*"Caution: bus is kneeling! Caution: lift is deploying!"*

"Morning, folks! Watch your roll coming aboard," the JRTC operator called out cheerfully, reaching down to flip up the two bench seats over the front left and right wheelchair securement bays.

"Good morning!" Katie said brightly as she rolled up the gentle slope of the low-floor ramp first and backed her SwiftChair deftly into the curbside wheelchair bay, while I rolled right up behind her into the street-side bay across the narrow aisle.

*"Caution: lift is stowing!"* the automated voice announced as the stainless-steel ramp folded back into the front threshold step with a solid clank.

After the operator clicked the four-point retractable floor straps onto our wheelchair frames and returned to his seat, Katie and I each reached forward to the farebox beside the steering column and fed crisp dollar bills into the bill validator to pay our standard one-dollar-and-fifty-cent base fares like any other rider in Richmond.

"Where are you two headed this cold Saturday morning?" the operator asked as he pulled the forty-foot bus back into the eastbound lane of West Broad Street.

"Ninth and Broad first so we can roll over to the JRTC customer service window and buy our thirty-day unlimited magnetic swipe passes for the winter," Katie replied, holding my hand across the center aisle between our two wheelchair bays. "We're staying right back there at Broad and Boulevard through the middle of March."

"Well, you picked the best bus line in the city of Richmond to live on," the driver said with a proud grin in his wide rearview mirror. "Between the 6, the 1, the 2, and the 3, you won't ever wait more than ten minutes on Broad Street from six in the morning till midnight."

As the bus rolled straight east down the wide six-lane boulevard—passing the domed neoclassical rotunda of the Science Museum of Virginia in the old Broad Street Union Station, the brick dormitories and classrooms of Central Virginia University around Monroe Park, and the historic storefronts of the Arts District—I had my pocket notebook open on my lap tray, logging the exact travel times and stop spacing while the interior automated voice announced every single cross street we passed, whether there was a bus stop on that block or not:

*"Robinson Street."*

*"Mulberry Street."*

*"Allison Street."*

*"Meadow Street."*

*"Lombardy Street."*

*"Belvidere Street."*

"Listen to the onboard GPS annunciator, Katie," I murmured with an appreciative grin as the voice called out *"First Street"*, *"Second Street"*, *"Third Street"* in steady sequence down the straight Broad Street corridor. "It announces every single cross street along the route even when it isn't a bus stop—and whenever a JRTC bus completes a turn, it announces both streets on the corner. For a blind rider or someone visiting Richmond for the first time, you always know down to the exact block where you are."

*"Eighth Street. Ninth Street."*

Eleven minutes after boarding outside our apartment, the bus pulled up to the curb at Ninth and Broad Street—directly across from the tall granite tower of the General Assembly Building and the wrought-iron gates of Capitol Square.

*"Caution: bus is kneeling! Caution: lift is deploying!"*

After thanking the driver and rolling down the front ramp onto the brick sidewalk at Ninth and Broad, Katie and I stopped by the downtown transit ticket counter, paid sixty dollars apiece out of our own checking account for two standard thirty-day unlimited JRTC magnetic swipe passes, and spent the next three hours testing the entire downtown pedestrian and transit grid in our powerchairs.

We rolled down the Ninth Street hill to Ninth and Main to time the bus transfer down to Richmond Main Street Station in Shockoe Bottom—listening at the intersection corner as a turning bus announced externally to the crosswalk, *"Caution! Bus is turning right. Pedestrians, look both ways!"* followed inside by both street names as it straightened out onto Main Street. We tested the exterior brick ramps leading into Capitol Square and located the ground-level accessible entrance on the north terrace of Thomas Jefferson's historic white-columned State Capitol. We checked the elevator lobby inside the General Assembly Building at Ninth and Broad, noting exactly how many minutes it took to roll from the Route 6 bus stop curb into the building, clear the security magnetometer, and ride up to the fifth-floor legislative offices.

Then, at one-thirty in the afternoon, we rolled back out to the westbound bus shelter at Ninth and Broad. When the outbound bus pulled up to the curb and the front doors folded open, the automated voice announced once across the sidewalk:

*"Route 6. Oak Lawn. Welcome aboard JRTC!"*

*"Caution: bus is kneeling! Caution: lift is deploying!"*

Rolling aboard, we swiped our new thirty-day JRTC magnetic passes through the farebox reader with a clean electronic *beep* and rode Route 6 all the way past our apartment building out West Broad Street to the Oak Lawn transfer center.

Rolling down the wide sidewalk of the open-air Oak Lawn shopping plaza, we went straight into the Market Square supermarket. With an insulated canvas grocery carrier clipped to the rear frame of each of our SwiftChairs and two hand baskets resting on our lap trays, Katie and I spent an hour picking out two weeks' worth of breakfast cereal, milk, whole-wheat bread, sliced turkey, pasta, fresh apples, and three twelve-packs of ginger ale.

By four o'clock Saturday afternoon, we had ridden JRTC Route 6 ten blocks back east to our apartment stop at Broad and Boulevard, unloaded our groceries into our kitchen cabinets, and spent Sunday afternoon sitting side by side at our front window table writing a two-thousand-word weekend dispatch for Ideas for Coastal Virginia Transit:
