> *What Hampton Roads Can Learn from Richmond's Broad Street Trunk Line: How JRTC Uses a Straight Six-Mile Spine to Deliver Ten-Minute Service*

By Sunday night, we knew every bus stop, every curb cut, and every timetable along Broad Street by heart. We were ready for Monday morning.

### Part 2: Gold License Plates vs. JRTC Route 6, Turning Down the Parking Deck Pass, & The 60-Inch ADA Restroom Showdown

**Date:** 2014-01-06 at 08:15 America/New_York

![At the corner of Ninth and Broad Street outside the General Assembly Building in Richmond on January 6, 2014, 28-year-old Freshman Delegate Katie Prairie and her twin brother Nate roll their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs down the front ramp of a kneeling blue-and-white JRTC Route 6 city bus while veteran lawmakers and corporate lobbyists look on in stunned disbelief.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/jan_2014_ninth_and_broad_jrtc_route_6_ramp_arrival_shocked_lobbyists.jpg)

#### Monday, January 6, 2014, 8:15 AM — The First Time Richmond Politicians See a Delegate Roll Off the City Bus

![At the corner of Ninth and Broad Street outside the General Assembly Building in Richmond on January 6, 2014, 28-year-old Freshman Delegate Katie Prairie and her twin brother Nate roll their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs down the front ramp of a kneeling blue-and-white JRTC Route 6 city bus while veteran lawmakers and corporate lobbyists look on in stunned disbelief.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/jan_2014_ninth_and_broad_jrtc_route_6_ramp_arrival_shocked_lobbyists.jpg)

At eight-fifteen on Monday morning—forty-eight hours before the 2014 General Assembly would formally convene—the intersection of Ninth and Broad Street outside the General Assembly Building looked like a luxury auto dealership convention.

All along the curb leading toward the private legislative parking deck at Seventh and Marshall, gleaming black luxury sedans and massive chrome-trimmed SUVs idled in a bumper-to-bumper line. Nearly every bumper bore a special gold-embossed state license plate reading *VIRGINIA — HOUSE OF DELEGATES* or *VIRGINIA — SENATE*, stamped with the lawmaker's low seniority number. On the wide brick sidewalk flanking the bronze revolving doors of the General Assembly Building, groups of veteran Delegates, State Senators in tailored wool overcoats, and high-priced corporate lobbyists stood clutching leather briefcases and paper coffee cups from the downtown luxury hotels, trading back-slaps and committee gossip in the cold morning sunshine.

None of them paid the slightest attention to the public JRTC bus stop sign planted at the curb thirty feet from the General Assembly Building's accessible side doors—where half a dozen state clerical workers and hospital aides were waiting to step off the morning bus.

With a low rumble of its diesel engine and a crisp hiss of air brakes, our eastbound blue-and-white JRTC Route 6 Broad Street bus pulled up to the Ninth and Broad curb stop after calling out *"Eighth Street"* and *"Ninth Street"* inside the cabin.

As the front doors folded open, the external automated voice rang out across the sidewalk:

*"Route 6. Downtown. Welcome aboard JRTC!"*

*"Caution: bus is kneeling! Caution: lift is deploying!"*

Inside the front vestibule, where Katie and I had just ridden the eleven-minute trip down from Broad and Boulevard after swiping our regular sixty-dollar monthly passes at the farebox, the operator unhooked our floor straps as the stainless-steel wheelchair ramp settled onto the brick sidewalk.

"Have a great first week at the Capitol, Katie and Nate!" the operator called out warmly over his shoulder. "Show 'em how we do things on Route 6!"

"Thank you, Marcus! See you at five-thirty this evening!" Katie called back cheerfully.

Wearing a tailored royal-blue wool blazer over a crisp white blouse—with the small gold seal of the Virginia House of Delegates pinned to her left lapel and her leather legislative portfolio resting on her lap tray—twenty-eight-year-old Freshman Delegate Katie Prairie eased her joystick forward and rolled her compact black SwiftChair briskly down the city bus ramp onto the Ninth and Broad sidewalk.

Three seconds later, wearing my charcoal wool jacket with both of our MagnaBook Pro laptops strapped securely across my lap tray, I rolled my matching SwiftChair down the bus ramp right behind my twin sister.

*"Caution: lift is stowing!"* the automated voice announced behind us as the bus ramp folded back up with a hydraulic *clank* and the blue-and-white JRTC bus pulled away into the Broad Street traffic.

Outside the General Assembly Building doors, the morning chatter stopped dead.

Six veteran Delegates, two senior State Senators who had just stepped out of a town car, and a circle of corporate telecommunications lobbyists standing beside the granite columns all froze in their tracks. Three of the lobbyists literally lowered their coffee cups halfway from their mouths, staring from the retreating tailpipe of the city transit bus to the gold House of Delegates member pin gleaming on the lapel of Katie's blazer as our two power wheelchairs rolled side by side toward the entrance.

One of the veteran lawmakers—a silver-haired, five-term Delegate from Northern Virginia who sat on the House Transportation Committee and still had his gold-plated SUV keys dangling from his gloved fingers—took two steps across the brick sidewalk and blinked down at us in utter bewilderment.

"Excuse me—Delegate-Elect Prairie?" he stammered, glancing back over his shoulder toward the empty bus stop curb as if checking for a hidden camera crew. "From the Eighty-Fifth District in Virginia Beach?"

"Good morning, Delegate!" Katie said brightly, braking her SwiftChair beside mine to shake his hand. "And this is my twin brother, business partner, and volunteer data strategist, Nathaniel Prairie."

"Did—did the two of you just get off the *city bus*?" the veteran Delegate asked, his voice loud enough that a dozen other lawmakers and lobbyists turned their heads to listen. "Don't you have a handicap van or a legislative driver? The Clerk's office reserves oversized accessible spaces on the ground level of the Seventh Street legislative parking deck for members!"

Katie exchanged a quick, amused twin look with me before looking back up at him with complete, unbothered sincerity.

"Why on earth would we drive a car in downtown traffic when JRTC Route 6 picks us up thirty feet outside our apartment on West Broad Street every ten minutes and drops us right here at the front door of the General Assembly Building?" Katie asked smoothly. "A thirty-day unlimited JRTC bus pass costs sixty dollars at the ticket window, the low-floor ramp takes ten seconds to deploy, and my brother and I get to spend our eleven-minute commute talking with the regular working people of Richmond who ride the bus every day. That's how we commute back home on CVTA in Virginia Beach and Norfolk too."

Around the entrance plaza, several lobbyists exchanged stunned glances—realizing at once that the twenty-eight-year-old software developer from Virginia Beach who had just unseated an incumbent by campaigning from her power wheelchair on public buses wasn't doing it as a campaign-season photo op. She actually lived it every single day.

Five minutes later, when we rolled inside the warm marble lobby of the General Assembly Building and checked in at the Clerk's administrative orientation table, the facilities coordinator smiled and slid a thick manila packet across the counter toward Katie's lap tray.

"Welcome to Richmond, Delegate Prairie," the coordinator said, holding up a plastic windshield RFID transponder alongside a DMV application form for special official *HOUSE OF DELEGATES* license plates. "Because both you and your brother use power wheelchairs, we went ahead and blocked off two contiguous van-accessible spaces right next to the basement tunnel elevator in the General Assembly Parking Deck. Here is your garage transponder and your legislative license-plate form."

Katie gently pushed the plastic garage transponder and the *HOUSE OF DELEGATES* license-plate application right back across the counter.

"Thank you so much for thinking of us," Katie said kindly, "but neither Nate nor I can drive due to our medical restrictions, and neither of us owns a car—so there isn't any vehicle to put House of Delegates license plates on. Whenever anyone does drive us in a private vehicle, the only person we want behind the wheel is our dad in his own truck, and as a State Delegate I'm thankfully not the President of the United States being forced to ride around in an armored Secret Service limousine. We bought our thirty-day JRTC bus passes on Saturday and we're riding Route 6 down Broad Street every morning and evening. Please reassign those two ground-floor parking spaces to Capitol custodians or building maintenance staff who have to drive in before dawn—they deserve a close parking spot a whole lot more than we do."

The orientation clerk stared at the returned garage transponder on the table as if nobody in the four-hundred-year history of the Virginia General Assembly had ever voluntarily given back a reserved downtown parking pass.

***

#### Monday Afternoon & Tuesday, January 6–7, 2014 — The Steel Tape Measure & The 60-Inch ADA Restroom Showdown

![Inside the Capitol Facilities Management office in Richmond on January 6, 2014, 28-year-old Freshman Delegate Katie Prairie sits in her black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchair extending a yellow 25-foot steel tape measure across the counter while twin brother Nate displays his 60-inch ADA turning-radius diagram to the flustered Deputy Director reaching for his desk telephone.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/jan_2014_capitol_facilities_steel_tape_measure_60_inch_ada_showdown.jpg)

While Katie didn't care one bit about a VIP parking space or a gold license plate, we discovered at one-thirty that Monday afternoon what she *was* willing to go to war over before her first session even gaveled in.

After spending the morning getting our legislative network credentials, setting up Katie's new fifth-floor office in Room 518 of the General Assembly Building, and eating a quick lunch in the basement cafeteria, Katie and I rode the elevator down to the underground concourse tunnel and rolled up into the first floor of the historic State Capitol to inspect the accessible desk that the Clerk's staff had modified for her at the end of the minority aisle on the House Floor.

The desk itself on the green carpet of the House Chamber was fine—they had removed the standard mahogany swivel chair so Katie's compact SwiftChair could roll straight under the writing surface within easy reach of the gooseneck microphone and the electronic voting buttons.

The problem came ten minutes later, when we rolled out into the first-floor marble corridor near the House cloakroom and Katie went to use the nearest ladies' restroom while I rolled toward the men's room next door.

Less than thirty seconds after Katie pushed her way past the heavy, spring-loaded solid-oak outer door of the women's restroom—which didn't even have a blue ADA automatic push-button opener on the wall—she backed right back out into the corridor with her jaw set and a familiar flash of storm-cloud steel in her blue eyes.

At the exact same moment, I backed my SwiftChair out of the men's restroom entrance twenty feet down the hall.

"How bad is the women's side?" I asked, rolling quickly up beside her.

"Go look inside the doorway while it's empty, Nate," Katie said tightly, reaching into the side pocket of my backpack and pulling out the twenty-five-foot retractable steel tape measure we always carried for site audits. "It's the exact same fake 'retrofitted' stall they have up on the fifth floor near our office."

I checked that the restroom was unoccupied and looked inside the entrance as Katie pulled out the yellow steel tape blade and measured the end stall.

Whoever had signed off on the restroom renovation twenty years earlier had clearly never sat in a wheelchair a day in their life. They had simply bolted two chrome grab bars onto the tile wall of a forty-two-inch-wide stall at the end of a narrow forty-inch aisle and hung an *ACCESSIBLE* plaque on a stall door that swung *inward* toward the porcelain toilet bowl.

When Katie rolled her compact SwiftChair inside the stall frame, her front footrests stopped two inches short of the toilet bowl while the rear battery casing of her wheelchair still stuck eight inches out past the door jamb—making it physically impossible to pull the inward-swinging stall door closed behind her. To use the restroom at all, any wheelchair user would either have to leave the stall door wide open to the entire room or take two separate elevators down through the underground tunnel to a single unisex medical restroom in the far basement corner of the complex—a twenty-minute round trip that would cause a sitting Delegate to miss roll-call floor votes.

"Forty-two inches wide by fifty-four inches deep, with an inward-swinging door and zero sixty-inch turning circle," I said, writing the exact measurements into my notebook while Katie snapped the steel tape measure back into its casing. "That fails federal ADA Accessibility Guidelines Section 4.17.3 on three separate counts."

"And there are plenty of extra square feet at the end of both restroom rows if they simply shift the outer laminate partition twelve inches toward the dead vanity corner and reverse the hinges so the stall door swings outward," Katie said, her voice calm, quiet, and utterly immovable. "Come on, Nate. Let's go pay a visit to the Department of General Services Facilities Director before two-thirty."

Ten minutes later, Katie and I rolled our two SwiftChairs side by side into the Capitol Facilities Management suite on the lower level.

When the Deputy Director for Capitol Facilities came out to the reception counter in his gray suit, he offered Katie the indulgent, patronizing smile of a career bureaucrat who assumed a twenty-eight-year-old freshman in the minority party could be brushed off with paperwork jargon.

"Delegate-Elect Prairie, we appreciate your feedback," the Deputy Director said smoothly, folding his hands across his stomach, "and I assure you that accessibility upgrades are part of our long-term Master Capitol Complex Modernization Plan. However, modifying restroom partitions and installing motorized door actuators in the General Assembly Building and the Capitol requires an architectural engineering review, historical preservation sign-off, and a capital-outlay work order. Realistically, we can put that in the queue for the summer interim after the session adjourns in March."

Katie didn't raise her voice by a single decibel. Instead, she set our steel tape measure down on the counter with a crisp *clack* and looked straight up into his eyes from her SwiftChair.

"Let me explain what is actually going to happen between now and Wednesday at twelve o'clock noon," Katie said evenly. "The partitions on the fifth floor of the General Assembly Building and in the first-floor corridor restrooms outside the House Chamber aren't Thomas Jefferson's historic plaster—they're standard bolt-together powder-coated steel commercial bathroom dividers installed in the nineteen-nineties. Under federal ADA Accessibility Guidelines Section 4.17.3, a standard wheelchair toilet stall is required by federal law to provide a minimum sixty-inch clear width and a stall door that clears the turning envelope. Right now, a sitting member of the Virginia House of Delegates cannot close the bathroom stall door in her own workplace."

The Deputy Director shifted his weight uncomfortably. "Delegate Prairie, our carpenter and electrical shops are completely booked with pre-session podium setups—"

"At twelve o'clock noon on Wednesday, every television network camera in the Commonwealth of Virginia is going to be rolling live in the House Chamber for Opening Day," Katie continued without blinking, her left hand resting on my wrist across our wheelchair armrests. "If the fifth-floor restrooms and the first-floor House corridor restrooms do not have outward-swinging stall doors, a full sixty-inch turning clearance, and working ADA push-button outer door openers by five o'clock tomorrow afternoon, my very first act as a sworn Delegate on Wednesday will be rising on a point of personal privilege on live statewide television—and inviting the Speaker of the House and the entire Capitol press corps to follow me out into the hallway with their cameras so the voters of Virginia can watch a female Delegate in a power wheelchair get wedged halfway out of an illegal forty-two-inch bathroom stall door because Facilities told her to wait until March."

The silence in the Facilities office was absolute.

Behind the reception glass, two maintenance supervisors who had been listening over their clipboards traded a wide-eyed look. The Deputy Director's face went pale as he pictured the six-o'clock Wednesday evening news showing a newly sworn twenty-eight-year-old Delegate in a wheelchair stuck in an open bathroom stall door while trying to cast her first floor votes.

"I—let me call the carpentry foreman and the electrical shop chief right now," the Deputy Director said quickly, reaching for his desk telephone. "We have heavy-duty commercial partition brackets and two power-door actuator kits in the maintenance warehouse off Fourteenth Street."

"Thank you," Katie said politely, picking our steel tape measure back up off the counter. "Nate and I will be working in Room 518 until five o'clock today and all day tomorrow. Feel free to ask us to test the turning radius with our chairs before your crew bolts the brackets down."

By four o'clock on Tuesday afternoon—twenty hours before the Opening Day gavel—the carpentry and electrical crews had shifted the end partitions fourteen inches into the dead alcove space, reversed the heavy chrome hinges so the stall doors swung cleanly outward with interior loop pulls, and mounted blue wireless ADA push-button door openers outside both the women's and men's restrooms on the fifth floor and outside the House Chamber.

When the head carpenter asked Katie and me to test the finished stalls at four-fifteen on Tuesday, Katie rolled her SwiftChair effortlessly inside, spun a full three-hundred-and-sixty-degree circle without her footrests touching a single wall, pulled the outward-swinging door shut with the interior D-ring handle, and rolled back out to shake every carpenter and electrician's hand in person.

"Nobody should ever have to beg for the right to close a bathroom door in privacy," Katie told me quietly as we rolled out the front entrance of the General Assembly Building at five o'clock that Tuesday evening to catch our westbound JRTC Route 6 bus back to Broad and Boulevard.

On Wednesday morning, January 8, 2014, when the blue-and-white JRTC Route 6 bus kneeled at the curb of Ninth and Broad at ten-thirty ahead of the noon Opening Day swearing-in ceremony—with Dad waiting proudly for us on the brick sidewalk outside the Capitol gate in his best navy suit—none of the veteran politicians or lobbyists by the entrance looked surprised anymore when the front wheelchair ramp folded down.

Inside the House of Delegates Chamber at twelve o'clock noon, while Dad stood beside my SwiftChair next to Katie's modified desk on the first-floor chamber carpet, the Clerk of the House called the freshman class forward to take the constitutional oath of office under Article II, Section 7 of the Constitution of Virginia.

Just as she had done when she was sworn onto the Virginia Beach City Council three years earlier, Katie didn't reach for a Bible, and she didn't pretend to believe in a religion or a god that neither of us believed in. Instead, exercising her explicit constitutional right under Article VI, Clause 3 of the United States Constitution, Article II, Section 7 of the Constitution of Virginia, and Section 49-9 of the Code of Virginia to affirm rather than swear—and to omit the optional parenthetical religious phrase at the end—Katie placed her left palm squarely on the gold-stamped cover of the Virginia Constitution resting across my lap tray between our two wheelchairs, raised her right hand toward the Speaker's rostrum, and spoke her constitutional affirmation as the sole elected Delegate for the Eighty-Fifth District in a clear, ringing voice:

"I do solemnly affirm that I will support the Constitution of the United States, and the Constitution of the Commonwealth of Virginia, and that I will faithfully and impartially discharge all the duties incumbent upon me as a member of the House of Delegates, according to the best of my ability."

Across the center aisle, three senior opposition delegates immediately craned their necks, whispering indignantly to a political blogger in the front press row that the new twenty-eight-year-old Democrat from Virginia Beach had placed her hand on a copy of the state Constitution instead of a Bible, said "affirm" instead of "swear," and left out "so help me God." By five o'clock that evening, conservative talk-radio hosts in Richmond and Tidewater—along with the televangelist commentators on *The 777 Circle* broadcasting out of the Covenant Broadcasting Network studios right off Indian River Road back home in Virginia Beach—were already having a field day over it, only for Katie to tell a Capitol corridor reporter with a calm, unbothered smile as we rolled out to catch our evening bus:

"Have the commentators complaining on television actually read the Constitution of the United States or the Constitution of Virginia? Article VI, Clause 3 of the United States Constitution states in plain English that all state legislators shall be bound by Oath or Affirmation to support the Constitution, and that no religious test shall ever be required as a qualification to any office or public trust. And if you open Article II, Section 7 of the Constitution of Virginia—the exact document I placed my left hand on today—the words 'or affirm' and 'so help me God' are printed in parentheses specifically because Virginia law guarantees every non-religious citizen the right to make a solemn secular affirmation. I wasn't elected to be anybody's pastor, and my left hand belongs on the exact Constitution I just affirmed to the people of Virginia Beach that I would defend."

Delegate Katie Prairie of Virginia Beach and her twin brother Nate had arrived in Richmond on the city bus, paid their regular fare, watched Katie affirm her constitutional oath of office on the Constitution of Virginia without bowing to a religious test, and made it crystal clear from Day One that the people's House belonged to everyone.

## House Bill 663 & Live on Meet the Nation

### Part 1: Line 18, Seated by Delegate Ronald Villa on the Floor, & A Question Across the Chamber

**Date:** 2016-02-04 at 11:35 America/New_York

![On the Floor of the Virginia House of Delegates on February 4, 2016, 30-year-old Delegate Katie Prairie sits at her accessible mahogany desk in her black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchair holding up the highlighted pages of House Bill 663 to challenge its 'anatomical sex' restroom inspection mandate while twin brother Nate records the floor feed from his SwiftChair.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/feb_2016_virginia_house_floor_hb663_speech_katie_prairie.jpg)

#### Thursday, February 4, 2016, 11:35 AM — The Capitol Tunnel & Splitting Up at the Chamber Doors

![Rolling side by side through the subterranean marble concourse tunnel connecting the General Assembly Building to the Virginia State Capitol in Richmond on February 4, 2016, 30-year-old Delegate Katie Prairie and her twin brother Nate hold hands across the armrests of their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs moments before Katie's historic floor speech on House Bill 663.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/feb_2016_capitol_tunnel_rolling_to_house_floor_katie_nate.jpg)

"Look at Line 18 on Page 1 again, Nate," my twin sister Katie said, tapping her yellow highlighter against the two-page bill printout resting on her lap tray as our compact SwiftChairs rolled side by side down the long underground concourse tunnel connecting the General Assembly Building to the historic Virginia State Capitol. "'Anatomical sex means the physical condition of being male or female, which is determined by a person's anatomy.' Not a birth certificate, not a driver's license, and not how someone lives their daily life—strictly their physical anatomy. And then look at Line 54 on Page 2: 'Any person who willfully and knowingly violates this section shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than fifty dollars,' enforced by a law enforcement officer's summons."

"I read it three times while I was setting up the daily calendar script this morning—and even Sam, Mandy, and Sarah spotted the flaw in ten seconds flat when they dropped off the morning floor packet in Room 518," I replied, steering my wheelchair smoothly beside hers past the subterranean security desk as the fifteen-minute warning bell for the noon floor session chimed from the bronze wall speakers overhead. "Delegate Cobb and Delegate Marsh put it straight onto today's Second Reading floor calendar out of the General Laws Committee. Because it didn't come through any of your three committees, they think everybody on the Floor is going to treat it like a routine committee bill and wave it through before lunch."

It was thirty-year-old Katie's second two-year term representing the Eighty-Fifth House District back home in Kempsville and Virginia Beach, and she sat as a rank-and-file member of the thirty-four-seat Democratic minority facing a sixty-six-seat Republican supermajority. In the hierarchy of the Virginia House of Delegates, Katie held no leadership office—not Speaker, not Majority or Minority Leader, not Whip, and not a committee gavel. The chamber was presided over from the high marble rostrum by the Republican Speaker of the House, William J. Harwell of Stafford, who referred all legislation to committees and appointed every standing committee roster, while the sixty-six-member Republican majority on the floor was managed from the front row of the center aisle by House Majority Leader Richard Callaway of Danville, flanked by Deputy Majority Leader Todd Gentry, Majority Whip Jackson Milligan, and Republican Caucus Chair Timothy Hughes, across from our Democratic Minority Leader, Tom Toscano, along with Democratic Whip Eileen Fillmore and Democratic Caucus Chair Kenneth Plumley.

As a second-term opposition delegate who used a power wheelchair full-time, medically could not drive, and rode public buses and passenger trains everywhere she went, Katie served on three standing committees where she could do the most practical good for working families: the House Committee on Transportation, the House Committee on Health, Welfare and Institutions, and the House Committee on Education. On the Transportation Committee, whenever a colleague from a suburban district casually remarked in a hearing that "people can always drive," Katie would look calmly across the committee table from her SwiftChair and reply, "No, they can't. I took the bus here."

House Bill 663 had not come through Transportation, Health, Welfare and Institutions, or Education. It had been reported out of someone else's committee—the House Committee on General Laws, chaired by Delegate Gilbert Peace—where the majority had advanced it to the House Floor without anyone asking what the statutory words actually required a human being to do.

Every day the General Assembly was in session during January and February, the two of us operated by the exact same synchronized routine we had followed since her freshman session in 2014: we woke up in our accessible one-bedroom winter-session apartment at the Broad & Boulevard Lofts on West Broad Street, rode the eastbound JRTC Route 6 bus straight down Broad Street to Ninth and Broad, and went over every bill on the daily House calendar line by statutory line the exact same way we audited PHP code or Coastal Virginia Transit Authority bus schedules. Twenty minutes earlier upstairs in Room 518, when our three favorite thirteen-year-old middle-school House Pages—eighth-grade triplets Sam, Mandy, and Sarah Hawkins from Southside Virginia, who followed Katie around the Capitol whenever they had a free courier run—had delivered the printed Second Reading calendar packet to Katie's desk, Katie had handed each of them a copy of House Bill 663.

Thirteen-year-old Sarah had reached the operative language on Line 18 first. She wasn't trying to make a political or constitutional argument; as a literal, rule-following thirteen-year-old autistic girl, she had simply applied the proposed statutory rule to herself—*I am a girl, and this bill says I am allowed into the girls' room because of my anatomy*—read the definition twice, and looked up at Katie with genuine fear in her eyes.

"Delegate Prairie?" Sarah had asked softly, pointing a finger at Line 18 on the page.

"Yeah, Sarah?" Katie had answered.

"Wait," Sarah had said, her voice tight. "Does somebody have to see my parts to prove I'm a girl?"

Katie had stopped reading completely.

Right beside her twin sister, Mandy had immediately looked over Sarah's shoulder at the page. "What?"

"It says which bathroom I can use depends on my anatomy," Sarah had said.

"So how do they know?" their brother Sam had asked, looking up from his copy.

Katie had gently taken the printout back from Sarah's hand. For three seconds, the office had gone dead quiet as my sister read Line 18 and Line 54 again.

"That's a very good question," Katie had said softly.

"Maybe your birth certificate?" Mandy had suggested, squinting at her copy of the bill.

"The bill doesn't say that," Katie had told her.

"A doctor?" Sam had asked.

"Doesn't say that either," Katie had replied.

"But they don't know," Sarah had said literally.

"Right," Katie had agreed.

"Everybody knows Sarah's a girl," Mandy had said reassuringly, taking her sister's hand.

"But how?" Sarah had asked.

"The bill says anatomy," Sam had pointed out. "Not your Page badge, and not how you're dressed."

"Exactly," Katie had said, as the software-developer quality-assurance part of our brains clicked straight into gear. If you stress-tested House Bill 663 the way we stress-tested a software routine before production—input: an accusation that someone used the wrong restroom; required statutory determination: anatomical sex; evidence specified by statute: none; verification procedure: none; authorized investigator: unspecified; standard of proof: unspecified; privacy protections for minors: unspecified—the entire statute collapsed into a terrifying Fourth Amendment hole.

Looking straight into thirteen-year-old Sarah's eyes first so the frightened eighth-grader would know she was safe, Katie had said gently, "Sarah, nobody should ever have to see your private parts for you to use a bathroom."

Sarah had let out a long, relieved breath. "Okay."

Then Katie had looked back down at the yellow-highlighted text of House Bill 663, her blue eyes hardening into flint. "Which means the Gentleman from Spotsylvania has some explaining to do."

We rode the subterranean elevator up into the historic Capitol and rolled out onto the first-floor marble corridor just outside the tall mahogany double doors of the House Chamber. Lobbyists, school groups, and legislative aides were hurrying past the white marble columns as the ten-minute bell sounded.

At the velvet brass rope flanking the Chamber entrance—where the Sergeant-at-Arms staff checked member pins—Katie braked her SwiftChair and turned toward me.

Ever since our very first visit to the State Capitol back in February 2011—when Capitol Police had stopped us outside the third-floor public viewing gallery because the small historic elevator locked out during fire alarms and there was no safe way to evacuate a wheelchair down three flights of eighteenth-century stairs—House Leadership and the Sergeant-at-Arms had maintained a standing ADA floor pass for me (and any visiting constituent in a wheelchair plus one companion) to watch the daily session from a level wheelchair bay inside the first-floor House Chamber itself, right along the outer right aisle beside our fellow Virginia Beach lawmaker, Delegate Ronald Villa of the Twenty-First District.

"Are you set to plug into the floor feed over by Ron's desk?" Katie asked, reaching across our armrests to give my right hand our familiar twin squeeze.

"All set," I said, patting the padded laptop bag strapped across my lap tray where my MagnaBook Pro and my digital stream-capture rig were tucked alongside our daily legislative binder. "I'll have the chamber stream hooked into my laptop before the Speaker bangs the gavel so I can record and caption your remarks for the constituent archive."

"Wait until Delegate Cobb finishes his floor pitch on House Bill 663," Katie said, her blue eyes steady and focused as she tucked the highlighted two-page printout under her left wrist on the lap tray. "I'm going to ask the Speaker to let me put one direct operational question to him on the record."

"Give him hell, Delegate Prairie," I whispered with a small smile.

"See you at the center doors when we recess," Katie said warmly.

Releasing my hand, my twin sister eased her joystick forward, nodded to the doorkeeper holding open the left-hand mahogany door, and rolled her compact black power wheelchair across the green carpet toward her modified accessible desk at the end of the far left minority aisle.

I flashed my gold-stamped ADA floor pass to the Sergeant-at-Arms assistant at the right-hand doorway and rolled quietly inside to the designated wheelchair bay along the outer right aisle, twenty feet from the ground-level emergency exit.

Right beside my bay, seated at his mahogany desk bearing the brass nameplate *MR. VILLA — VIRGINIA BEACH (21ST DISTRICT)*, Delegate Ronald Villa looked up from his leather binder and gave me a warm, familiar nod.

"Morning, Nate," Delegate Villa whispered, reaching over to shake my hand just as he had done the very first day the Sergeant-at-Arms had brought Katie and me onto the Floor back in 2011. "How's the Route 6 bus running down Broad Street this morning?"

"Right on the ten-minute headway, Delegate Villa," I whispered back with a smile as I flipped down my lap tray, opened my laptop, plugged my headphones into the assistive-listening audio jack at the side rail, and launched my digital capture software hooked into the chamber's fixed legislative webcast camera.

Looking across the wide expanse of green carpet under the tall cream-and-gold coffered ceiling and crystal chandeliers of the House Chamber, I had a clear, floor-level view of the Speaker's high marble rostrum at the front of the room, the Clerk's well, the red-and-green electronic voting boards flanking the front wall, and Katie sitting upright in her compact SwiftChair at her accessible desk across the chamber on the minority aisle, her yellow-highlighted copy of House Bill 663 resting squarely in front of her desk microphone.

***

#### Thursday, February 4, 2016, 12:18 PM — Watching Across the House Floor as Katie Challenges the Patron

![On the Floor of the Virginia House of Delegates on February 4, 2016, 30-year-old Delegate Katie Prairie sits at her accessible mahogany desk in her black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchair holding up the highlighted pages of House Bill 663 to challenge its 'anatomical sex' restroom inspection mandate while twin brother Nate records the floor feed from his SwiftChair.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/feb_2016_virginia_house_floor_hb663_speech_katie_prairie.jpg)

At twelve o'clock noon on the dot, the Speaker of the House rapped his wooden gavel against the rostrum block.

Up in the third-floor public gallery overhanging the rear wall—where two dozen college students from Virginia Dominion University and Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute, a handful of off-duty teachers, and several parents sat along the wooden benches—and down across the hundred mahogany desks on the Floor, everyone fell silent for the opening prayer, the Pledge of Allegiance, and the routine morning leaves of absence.

By 12:18 PM, the House had moved into the Second Reading calendar of bills reported out of committee. Half the Delegates on the floor were leaning back in their leather swivel chairs chatting with deskmates or flipping through binders while the Clerk read bill titles in a rapid, monotone cadence.

"House Bill 663, a bill to amend the Code of Virginia relating to single-gender public restrooms and facilities in buildings owned or leased by the Commonwealth, public institutions of higher education, and local school divisions; civil penalty. Patron, Delegate Cobb."

From my wheelchair bay beside the outer right aisle, I clicked the red Record button on my laptop capture window and checked my audio level meters. Right in front of me, I saw Delegate Ronald Villa—a pragmatic coastal Virginia Beach Republican who cared about bus shelters, military families, and Oceanfront tourism, not culture-war stunts—let out a quiet sigh and rub his forehead as the bill was called.

Three rows ahead on the majority side of the House Floor, Delegate Martin Cobb—with his chief co-patron, Delegate Robert Marsh, seated two desks over—stood up behind his mahogany desk, buttoned his navy suit jacket, and leaned into his silver gooseneck microphone.

"Mr. Speaker and members of the House," Delegate Cobb's voice echoed across the chamber and came cleanly through my floor headphones, "House Bill 663 is a simple, common-sense measure to protect personal privacy and public safety across the Commonwealth of Virginia. This legislation directs the Department of General Services, every public institution of higher education, and every local school board to ensure that every single-gender public restroom, locker room, and shower facility in any public building or school is used exclusively by individuals whose anatomical sex matches the designated gender on the door—backed by a fifty-dollar civil penalty enforceable by law enforcement summons. I hope it will be the pleasure of the House to engross the bill and advance it to its third reading."

Across the chamber at the end of the minority aisle, I saw Katie press the white request-to-speak button on her desk console and raise her right hand into the air.

Up on the high marble rostrum, the Speaker glanced down toward the left aisle.

"For what purpose does the gentlewoman from Virginia Beach, Delegate Prairie, rise?" the Speaker asked into his microphone.

Across the green carpet, Katie flipped the toggle switch at the base of her desk microphone so the green indicator ring illuminated, and lifted the two printed pages of House Bill 663 in her right hand.

"Mr. Speaker, to see if the gentleman from Spotsylvania will yield for a question on the bill," Katie's voice rang out crisp and clear across the chamber.

"Does the gentleman from Spotsylvania yield to the gentlewoman from Virginia Beach?" the Speaker asked.

Standing at his desk across the center aisle, Delegate Cobb gave a brief, stiff nod. "I yield for a question, Mr. Speaker."

"The gentleman yields," the Speaker said.

From my wheelchair on the far side of the floor, I watched my twin sister look straight across the House Chamber at the bill's patron.

"Thank you, Mr. Speaker," Katie said. "Look with me for a moment at the exact text printed in House Bill 663, Delegate Cobb. My brother and I write computer software for a living, and when you write code—or when you write a state law—definitions determine how an instruction actually executes in the real world. Unlike bills that reference a birth certificate or a state identification card, your Line 18 on Page 1 explicitly defines anatomical sex as 'the physical condition of being male or female, which is determined by a person's anatomy.' Not their driver's license. Not how they are dressed. Their physical anatomy. And then on Page 2, Line 54, you mandate that a law enforcement officer issue a fifty-dollar civil summons at the restroom door based on that physical anatomy."

Across the floor around me, the background murmur of side conversations suddenly died down. Delegates who had been thumbing through their afternoon calendars looked up from their desks.

"The language of the bill speaks for itself, Mr. Speaker," Delegate Cobb replied stiffly into his desk microphone. "Restrooms in state buildings, public colleges, and public schools will be restricted strictly by anatomical sex, and law enforcement officers are authorized to issue a fifty-dollar civil summons to anyone who enters a restroom that does not match their anatomical sex."

Up at the front row of the center aisle, I saw Deputy Majority Leader Todd Gentry lean sharply across the mahogany divider toward House Majority Leader Richard Callaway's desk. Even from my wheelchair bay along the right rail, I could read the urgent tension in Gentry's posture as he whispered, "Richard, Prairie's gutting the bill. Are you going to do something?"

Majority Leader Callaway didn't even look up from the two-page printout of House Bill 663 resting on his leather blotter. "Like what?"

"Stop her!" Gentry hissed under his breath. "Look what she's doing to Cobb."

"She's asking him how his bill works," the Majority Leader murmured dryly, turning Page 1 over to Page 2 with two fingers. "She's reading the bill. And Cobb seems to be doing an adequate job of gutting it himself."

Over at her accessible desk on the far left aisle, Katie released her joystick brake half an inch, rolling her compact SwiftChair flush against the mahogany desk edge as she held the two printed pages of House Bill 663 high in the air. Across the chamber, I could hear the raw, unmistakable fire rising in my sister's voice.

"Mr. Speaker, when the people of Kempsville and Virginia Beach first elected me to serve in this House of Delegates two years ago," Katie declared, her voice echoing off the marble walls of the Capitol chamber, "I had to fight the facilities bureaucracy in this very Capitol complex just to get an ADA-compliant restroom stall wide enough for my power wheelchair to turn around in and close the door in privacy! Every single day of my life since I was sixteen years old, I have known what it feels like to have strangers stare at my body and treat a basic human necessity like using a public restroom as a public spectacle. And now the gentleman comes onto the Floor of this House with House Bill 663 and tells the women and girls of Virginia that the state government is going to police 'anatomical sex' at the door of every ladies' room from Virginia Beach to Blacksburg for a fifty-dollar fine!"

Up in the third-floor public gallery above us, the college students and parents leaned forward over the brass balcony rail, holding their breath. Down on the House Floor, you could have heard a pin drop.

"Then if the gentleman says there will be no physical inspection, how does the Commonwealth establish that someone's anatomical sex does not match the designation of the facility?" Katie demanded, shaking the printed pages of House Bill 663 across the aisle. "How, exactly, is a police officer or a state building inspector standing outside a restroom door at the Community College of Hampton Roads, or Virginia Dominion University, or right outside in this State Capitol corridor supposed to verify a citizen's 'physical anatomy' before writing your fifty-dollar ticket? If I am accused of being in the wrong women's restroom, what am I supposed to show somebody to prove that I'm female? I return to the exact question a thirteen-year-old girl asked me twenty minutes ago when she read your bill: why on earth should I—or any girl or woman in the Commonwealth of Virginia—have to pull my pants down for a government official or a police officer to prove I have female parts just to use the ladies' room?!"

An audible gasp swept across the chamber, followed half a second later by a sudden burst of applause from the visitors up in the third-floor gallery benches and several sharp "Hear, hear!" calls from the minority desks down on the Floor. Right beside my wheelchair on the Republican side of the floor, Delegate Ronald Villa winced, shook his head at Cobb's bill, and exchanged an unmistakable *she's got him dead to rights* look with his seatmate.

And up at the front row of the center aisle, at the words *a thirteen-year-old girl asked me twenty minutes ago when she read your bill*, I saw House Majority Leader Richard Callaway freeze for half a second and turn his head to look straight back at thirteen-year-old Sarah Hawkins standing at attention in her navy blue House Page blazer behind his desk.

Sarah looked right back at the Majority Leader and gave a single, solemn nod.

Even from across the green carpet, you could practically see the *oh, for heaven's sake—one of my thirteen-year-old Pages found the hole in this bill* realization cross the Majority Leader's face.

*Bam! Bam!*

"The House will come to order! The House will be in order!" Speaker William J. Harwell barked from the marble rostrum, pounding his wooden gavel twice as he looked up toward the third-floor balcony. "The guests in the public gallery are reminded that demonstrations of approval or disapproval are strictly prohibited by the rules of the House!"

Down on the Republican benches two seats over from Delegate Cobb, the bill's chief co-patron, Delegate Robert Marsh, shot to his feet with his face flushed crimson, stabbing a finger toward his microphone button. "Mr. Speaker! Point of order! The gentlewoman from Virginia Beach is using indecorous language on the floor of this House!"

Before the Speaker could rule—and before Democratic Minority Leader Tom Toscano could even rise from the front row of the left aisle—the Republican Majority Leader himself stood up behind his center-aisle desk.

"Mr. Speaker," Majority Leader Callaway called out calmly.

Up on the rostrum, Speaker Harwell paused with his gavel in hand. "The Majority Leader."

Richard Callaway looked once at Delegate Marsh and Delegate Cobb, and then straight up at the rostrum. "Mr. Speaker, the Gentlewoman's phrasing may be uncomfortable, but the Gentlewoman didn't introduce anatomy into this legislation. The bill did. The legislation before us expressly makes anatomical sex determinative. I believe she is entitled to ask the patron how the Commonwealth proposes to determine that fact."

A stunned hush fell over all one hundred desks in the chamber.

Across the green carpet, Katie looked at the Republican Majority Leader in quiet amazement—remembering a sentence she would never forget for the rest of her life—before turning her eyes back to the bill's patron.

Out on the majority aisle of the House Floor, Delegate Martin Cobb stood completely frozen behind his desk microphone for four full seconds, his face turning beet-red under the chamber chandeliers as he looked from Katie's power wheelchair to the uneasy, downward stares of his own party colleagues around him.

"I—Mr. Speaker, the bill does not—nobody is suggesting—" Delegate Cobb stammered into his microphone, shuffling his folder on his desk without answering the question.

"Mr. Speaker, that is literally what the words printed on Page 1 and Page 2 of House Bill 663 require!" Katie replied from her SwiftChair, her voice steady, clear, and unflinching across the silent chamber. "Transgender women are women, transgender men are men, and every citizen in this Commonwealth deserves basic human dignity and privacy without politicians stationing bathroom police at the door to inspect people's anatomy. No woman or girl in Virginia should ever have to pull her pants down to prove she has female parts just to use a public restroom!"

Along the Republican rows from Hampton Roads to the Northern Virginia suburbs, I saw half a dozen moderate delegates—starting with Delegate Ronald Villa right beside my wheelchair and Appropriations Chairman S. Christopher Jennings two rows ahead—emphatically shaking their heads at Majority Whip Jackson Milligan. Milligan hurried up the center carpet and leaned down beside the Majority Leader's ear.

"Leader, we're bleeding votes," the Majority Whip murmured urgently.

"How badly?" Richard asked under his breath.

"Badly."

Majority Leader Richard closed his leather binder with a quiet snap, stood up at his front-row desk, and flipped on his microphone. "Pass it by."

"Mr. Speaker," the Majority Leader announced briskly across the chamber, "I move that House Bill 663 be passed by for the day."

"Without objection, House Bill 663 is passed by for the day," Speaker Harwell announced immediately, rapping his gavel once and hurrying straight ahead. "The Clerk will read the next bill on the calendar."

***

#### Thursday, February 4, 2016, 12:35 PM — Archiving the 95-Second Clip, "Your Bill Killed Your Bill," & Rolling Back Through the Tunnel

In my wheelchair bay beside Delegate Villa's desk, I clicked the Stop button on my capture window and exhaled a quiet breath.

Delegate Villa leaned slightly toward my armrest and whispered out of the corner of his mouth, "Your sister just drove a freight truck straight through the middle of that bill, Nate."

I gave him a quiet grin and looked down at the timeline bar on my laptop screen while the Clerk moved on to a routine highway-naming bill. Checking the timestamp on the video file I had just recorded from the chamber feed, I saw that the entire floor exchange between Katie and Delegate Cobb ran ninety-five seconds.

Just like I did whenever Katie spoke on a bill on the House Floor, I opened Quantum Code right there on my lap tray, typed out a verbatim, frame-accurate WebVTT closed-caption file for the ninety-five-second video, burned high-contrast open captions along the bottom of the frame so constituents watching on mute could read every word, and uploaded the clip to Katie's legislative website archive, StreamTube, and The Grid at 12:35 PM with a standard archival heading:

> Delegate Katie Prairie (D-Virginia Beach) Questions HB 663 Patron on the House Floor Regarding "Anatomical Sex" Restroom Enforcement (Feb. 4, 2016)

Twenty-five minutes later, at one o'clock, the House adjourned its Thursday floor session so members could grab lunch before afternoon committee work.

I unplugged my audio cable from the side rail, packed my laptop and capture rig back into my bag, shook Delegate Villa's hand, and eased my joystick forward to roll toward the right-hand chamber doorway.

Right near the front of the aisle by the Clerk's well—where Speaker William J. Harwell had just stepped down from the marble rostrum to confer with House Majority Leader Richard Callaway while thirteen-year-old House Page triplets Sam, Mandy, and Sarah Hawkins stood dutifully at attention behind the Majority Leader's desk holding stacks of committee folders—a red-faced Delegate Martin Cobb marched up to the Majority Leader with his copy of House Bill 663 crumpled in his fist.

As I slowed my SwiftChair behind a cluster of departing delegates waiting for the doorway to clear, I heard every word.

"Leader, Prairie ambushed me out there!" Delegate Cobb complained bitterly. "Prairie killed my bill!"

Majority Leader Callaway stopped buttoning his suit coat and looked at the Gentleman from Spotsylvania over the top of his reading glasses.

"No," Richard said flatly.

"Leader, you heard what she did on the floor!"

"I certainly did," the Majority Leader replied in his calm, unhurried Danville baritone. "Katie asked how your bill worked."

For two full seconds, nobody around the Clerk's well made a sound.

"Your bill killed your bill, Martin," Richard told him evenly. "And for your information, Sarah found this."

Delegate Cobb blinked past the Majority Leader's shoulder at thirteen-year-old Sarah Hawkins standing in her navy blue House Page blazer. "Leader..."

"Sarah is thirteen," Richard said flatly.

"I understand that."

"Apparently she understood the bill," the Majority Leader replied dryly. "You brought a statute onto the House calendar whose central operative concept collapses under the very first implementation question. Supporters will always tell you why your bill is wonderful; opponents will tell you where it breaks. You should've put this bill in front of Katie before it ever left committee."

Delegate Cobb stared at him as if the Majority Leader had lost his mind. "Prairie would've opposed it!"

"Of course she would've opposed it," Richard replied. "That's why you should've put it in front of her. Give your bill to the smartest person you know who's determined to kill it. If it survives her, you might have something."

Richard glanced half an inch over his shoulder toward the three eighth-grade Pages standing behind his desk.

"Better yet," the Majority Leader added dryly, "you should've given it to Katie and those three Pages who follow her around."

Cobb blinked at the three teenagers in their navy blue Page blazers. "Sam, Mandy, and Sarah?"

"Yes."

"They're thirteen."

"And apparently none of the four of them were going to let you get away with an undefined enforcement mechanism," Richard said.

Beside the Clerk's desk, Speaker Harwell looked from the crumpled printout of House Bill 663 to the three eighth-graders in quiet disbelief. "Three thirteen-year-olds caught this?"

Standing between her brother and her twin sister, thirteen-year-old Sarah nodded solemnly. "We caught it really fast, Mr. Speaker."

Right behind the Majority Leader's back, Sam, Mandy, and Sarah clamped their lips tightly together, their shoulders twitching in unison as all three of them tried desperately not to laugh out loud on the House Floor.

Without even turning his head around, the Majority Leader caught them in the reflection of the brass rail.

"And don't you three start," Richard muttered—though I could see the corner of his mouth twitching as a thoroughly chastened Delegate Cobb turned on his heel and stalked out the side door.

Speaker Harwell let out a long breath, shook his head, and murmured to his floor leader, "Next time somebody brings us a bill about people's anatomy, Richard, have Prairie read it first."

"Actually, Mr. Speaker," Majority Leader Callaway sighed, rubbing the bridge of his nose as he tucked his binder under his arm, "never bring a bill to this floor that failed Prairie—and have those three read it too."

Biting the inside of my cheek to keep from grinning from ear to ear, I rolled out the right-hand chamber doorway into the first-floor marble corridor just as Katie came rolling out the left-hand doorway in her SwiftChair.

"Hey," I said, rolling right up beside her and reaching out to take her left hand. "The ninety-five-second floor clip is captioned and archived on your constituent page—and wait until I tell you what the Majority Leader and the Speaker just told Delegate Cobb by the Clerk's well. First, when you mentioned on the floor that a thirteen-year-old girl asked you that question twenty minutes ago, the Majority Leader turned right around and looked at Sarah standing behind his desk, and Sarah nodded right back at him! Then when Marsh tried to call you out of order, the Majority Leader stood up and told the whole House that you didn't introduce anatomy into the legislation, the bill did. And when Cobb complained after the gavel that you killed his bill, the Majority Leader looked him dead in the eye and told him, 'No, Katie asked how your bill worked—your bill killed your bill, and Sarah found this,' while Sarah told the Speaker, 'We caught it really fast!' The Majority Leader said next time Cobb should have you and Sam, Mandy, and Sarah proofread his legislation before bringing it to the floor!"

Katie's blue eyes lit up with a mixture of surprise, warmth, and quiet respect as she squeezed my fingers and we turned our wheelchairs side by side toward the elevator down to the underground Capitol tunnel. "Looks like Sarah, Mandy, Sam, and I just became the unofficial House Quality Assurance Department. Even if we sit on opposite sides of the aisle on almost everything else, at least the Majority Leader actually reads the bills. Come on—let's go grab a sandwich in the basement cafeteria before our two o'clock Transit Legislative Day meetings."

### Part 2: Transit Legislative Day with Michael & Rachel, Two Meltdowns in Room 518, & The 6:05 AM Train to Meet the Nation

**Date:** 2016-02-04 at 14:15 America/New_York

![Inside the GBS News Washington bureau studio on Sunday morning, February 7, 2016, 30-year-old Delegate Katie Prairie sits in her black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchair in a wide camera frame in front of an illuminated Virginia State Capitol backdrop for a live national interview on Meet the Nation, while twin brother Nate monitors the broadcast from his SwiftChair beside the studio confidence monitor.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/feb_2016_gbs_richmond_studio_meet_the_nation_live_interview_katie_nate.jpg)

#### Thursday, February 4, 2016, 2:15 PM — Virginia Transit Legislative Day in Room 518 & A Visit from Michael and Rachel Ragsdale

Out of all sixty days of the winter session in Richmond, Thursday, February fourth was the day on the legislative calendar that Katie and I looked forward to the most: Virginia Transit Legislative Day.

On almost every other afternoon of the session, the marble corridors of the General Assembly Building were packed wall-to-wall with corporate lobbyists in thousand-dollar tailored suits. On Transit Legislative Day, however, bus and rail riders from every corner of the Commonwealth rode charter coaches, intercity trains, and JRTC buses up to Capitol Square wearing bright blue *RIDE TRANSIT VIRGINIA* lapel stickers to lobby their Delegates and State Senators for state public transportation operating and capital dollars.

At two-fifteen that afternoon inside our fifth-floor office in Room 518, right after Katie and I finished reviewing the Hampton Roads transit allocation table with a group of bus operators from Newport News, two very familiar voices called out from our open doorway.

"Permission to roll into the bus delegate's office?"

Katie and I looked up from our desks and broke into wide grins at the exact same second.

Rolling through the doorway in a folded-frame, blue-upholstered manual wheelchair was our twenty-eight-year-old childhood friend and [former across-the-hall neighbor Michael Ragsdale](https://books.raggiesoft.com/katie/seventeen-senior-year-greenway-court/greenway-court-apartment-a6-the-square-closet-sanctuary/part-1-apartment-a6-on-greenway-court-dad-s-microwave-cart-across-the-hall-neighbors), with his twenty-six-year-old sister Rachel walking right beside him in her glasses and royal-blue Virginia Dominion University jacket, keeping one hand resting lightly on his left rear push-handle and her other hand laced tightly through his fingers. Both of them had blue *RIDE TRANSIT VIRGINIA* stickers pressed over their hearts and carried folders of Coastal Virginia Transit Authority route maps.

"Michael! Rachel!" Katie beamed, nudging her joystick and rolling her SwiftChair out from behind her mahogany desk as I wheeled right up beside her so the four of us could exchange warm hugs across our armrests. "What are you two doing up in Richmond? And Michael, what happened to your ankles?"

"Elective bilateral Achilles heel cord lengthening two weeks ago," Michael smiled, patting the frame of his blue manual wheelchair while never letting go of Rachel's hand. "My heel cords have been too tight to pivot safely between driving pedals my whole life, and Rachel stubbornly refused to get her Learner's Permit until we could walk into the DMV and get our permits together once my surgeon clears me. I can stand and walk short flat distances, but for a full day of marble Capitol hallways, my orthopedic specialist ordered me to use the manual chair and let my Bug guard the push-handles."

"And we came up on the Hampton Roads transit advocacy bus this morning for Transit Legislative Day," Rachel added proudly, adjusting her glasses with a grin. "Technically, our family home on Moosewood Drive is just across the district line in the Eighty-First District, and our campus apartment at VDU is in Norfolk's Eighty-Ninth, so you aren't officially our Delegate on our voter registration cards—but when there's a Virginia Beach Delegate in the General Assembly who actually rides CVTA buses every day and knows the Route 25 and Route 2 timetables by heart, she's our Delegate too! After we finished lobbying our assigned offices for evening bus frequency and Sunday service hours, there was no way we were leaving Richmond without coming up to the fifth floor to see our old Delaney Street and Greenway Court neighbors."

"Wait—were the two of you up in the third-floor House gallery at noon today?" I asked, spotting the green visitor gallery passes tucked into their lanyards.

"Front row center, right behind the brass rail!" Michael laughed, his eyes lighting up. "Katie, watching you hold up the text of House Bill 663 and ask Delegate Cobb why any woman in Virginia should have to pull her pants down for a government official to prove she has female parts just to use the ladies' room was the greatest thing I have ever seen in a government building. Nate, the second you posted the captioned video link at twelve-thirty-five, Rachel and I sent it to every student group chat at VDU and CCHR."

"And tell them what you promised yourself in the hallway afterward, Bear," Rachel said, nudging his shoulder with a laugh.

Michael grinned sheepishly from his blue manual wheelchair. "When we took the elevator downstairs after the floor session let out for lunch, I was still so fired up about that ridiculous bill that I made a solemn promise to myself and Rachel: if I saw Delegate Cobb—or Delegate Robert Marsh, who keeps talking to reporters about bringing his own bathroom bill—heading toward the men's room anywhere in the General Assembly Building while we were making our Transit Legislative Day rounds, I was going to wheel right up to the bathroom door and demand that he pull his pants down right there in the corridor to prove he had male parts!"

Katie clapped both hands over her mouth as she and I burst out laughing together across our armrests.

"Did you see either of them?" I asked through my laughter.

"Sadly, no," Michael sighed, shaking his head with mock disappointment. "Neither of them crossed our path all afternoon, so I never got the chance—Wait until he sees how fast that video is spreading across VDU right now, though. By Monday morning, neither of those guys is going to want to show his face near a microphone."

After spending twenty wonderful minutes catching up on CVTA bus routes, our old first-floor hallway at 801 Greenway Court, and their computer information systems classes at VDU, we rolled alongside Michael and Rachel out to the fifth-floor elevators so they could catch their late-afternoon transit coalition bus back down Interstate 64 to Hampton Roads.

Right as the elevator doors opened for Michael and Rachel at two-forty, an entire New River Valley transit delegation wearing blue *RIDE TRANSIT VIRGINIA* stickers rolled off the elevator and into Room 518—three closely knit families from Christiansburg and Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute in Blacksburg who rode Blue Ridge Transit Route 1 and Route 2 and the Radford Connector around town, and who had been sitting in the third-floor House gallery right beside Michael and Rachel when Katie questioned Delegate Cobb on House Bill 663.

Rolling in first was [Jordan in his power wheelchair alongside Aubrie Jean, Megan, Zoë, and Isabel](https://books.raggiesoft.com/aubrie/spring-semester-2016/off-precautions-megan-s-first-night/part-2-virginia-transit-legislative-day-house-bill-663-delegate-katie-prairie-in-room-518), followed right beside them by [Freddie in his matte-black titanium manual wheelchair, his sixteen-year-old sister Harper in her neon-purple wheelchair, and their sisters Paige, Jessica, Sarah, and Jenna](https://books.raggiesoft.com/paige/system-integration/the-closed-circuit/part-3-virginia-transit-legislative-day-the-bathroom-police-bill-room-518), and right behind them came [Ryan O'Connell propelling his matte-black titanium manual wheelchair with his sister Cassidy holding onto his rear push-handles like a rolling walker alongside their youngest sister Holly and their twin cousins Evan and Tyler Wright](https://books.raggiesoft.com/stardust-engine/book-5-burnout-hiatus-our-own-frequency-neon-on-the-huckleberry-trail-2005-2016/chapter-1-our-own-frequency-the-blue-ridge-regional-aquatic-center-virginia-transit-legislative-day-2008-2016/part-3-virginia-transit-legislative-day-protocol-t-10-vs-house-bill-663-seven-wheelchairs-in-room-518).

"Four powerchairs and three ultralight manual chairs in one legislative office!" I grinned from beside my laptop as Katie and I wheeled our two black SwiftChairs out from behind her mahogany desk to form a wide semi-circle of seven wheelchairs in the center of Room 518. "Now this is what the General Assembly Building is supposed to look like on Transit Legislative Day—and wait a second, Katie, that's Ryan, Cassidy, and Holly O'Connell and Evan and Tyler Wright of The Stardust Engine!"

Even though they lived up in Blacksburg and Christiansburg rather than in the Eighty-Fifth House District—though Aubrie Jean beamed as she told us she had grown up right across the city line from Kempsville in the Emerald Creek neighborhood of Chesapeake before heading to CPI, and Katie's face lit up as she told Ryan and Cassidy that she and I listened to *'Neon on the Huckleberry Trail'* while compiling bus timetables at night and admired how Ryan's rear push-handles were set at the exact height for Cassidy to use as a rolling walker—every single one of them hated House Bill 663 just as fiercely as we did. Speaking through the voice synthesizer on his tablet, Jordan thanked Katie for standing up against a bill that would turn public restrooms into hostile fifty-dollar police checkpoints for wheelchair users and the family members who help them; Freddie, adjusting his glasses with Harper's hand anchored firmly to his right sleeve and Paige's hands resting on his shoulders, told Katie that her ninety-five-second floor cross-examination had exposed a fatal runtime error in Line 18 of Delegate Cobb's statute; and Ryan and Holly thanked Katie on behalf of disabled travelers across the state and Engine Room Records. Before they headed back downstairs to return to Christiansburg and Progress Street NE in Blacksburg, Holly, Zoë, Aubrie Jean, Paige, and Jenna had already pulled out their tablets and phones and shared our captioned ninety-five-second floor video with every student organization, computer science mailing list, Engine Room Records channel, and transit group across Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute.

We spent the rest of the afternoon until five-thirty meeting with special-education parents from Virginia Beach and reviewing coastal flooding amendments with our legislative aide, with both of our laptops closed on our desks.

***

#### Thursday, February 4, 2016, 6:00 PM — The Evening News in Richmond and Norfolk

"Hand me the pepper shaker, Nate," Katie said at six o'clock that Thursday evening, setting two warm plates of baked chicken and rice down on the dining table of Apartment 104 at the Broad & Boulevard Lofts on West Broad Street after we had ridden the 5:35 PM westbound JRTC Route 6 bus home from Ninth and Broad. "And turn on the television so we can see the weather forecast for the weekend."

Picking up the remote control from the corner of the table, I clicked on the wall-mounted television—tuned first to the Richmond local six-o'clock news broadcast, with my laptop open beside my glass of ginger ale streaming our hometown six-o'clock broadcast from Norfolk so we could keep up with Hampton Roads news while we were in Richmond for the winter session.

I barely had time to set the remote down before both my twin sister and I froze with our forks halfway to our mouths.

On the television screen on the wall—and simultaneously on the Norfolk local news stream playing on my laptop—was the exact ninety-five-second video clip I had captured from my wheelchair bay on the House Floor at lunchtime.

*"—and our top story from the State Capitol tonight,"* the Richmond evening anchor announced over the footage of Katie sitting upright in her compact SwiftChair on the House Floor holding up the two printed pages of House Bill 663, *"a fiery floor exchange in the House of Delegates this afternoon over House Bill 663, the controversial bathroom bill restricting public restrooms by 'anatomical sex,' after Virginia Beach Delegate Katie Prairie brought the House Chamber to a standstill with a single question for the bill's patron."*

Before our eyes, both the Richmond station and the Norfolk station aired the floor clip in full—every word of Katie asking Delegate Martin Cobb why she, or any woman or girl in the Commonwealth of Virginia, should have to pull her pants down for a government official or a police officer to prove she had female parts just to use the ladies' room, followed by the four seconds of Delegate Cobb standing frozen and beet-red behind his desk microphone before the Majority Leader hurriedly passed the bill by for the day.

Katie stared at the television screen, her blue eyes wide. "Nate... they're playing the whole floor clip on the six-o'clock news. In Richmond and back home in Norfolk."

I reached over and woke my laptop browser window, refreshing the server dashboard for Katie's legislative archive and The Grid.

My jaw dropped.

"Michael and Rachel weren't kidding when they said they shared your clip with everyone at VDU and CCHR!" I said, turning the laptop screen toward her wheelchair. "Look at the traffic logs! Between the Transit Legislative Day riders sharing your link from the Capitol and the beat reporters from the Richmond and Norfolk papers embedding your captioned video on their blogs at two-thirty while we were in meetings, thousands of office workers and college students at Virginia Dominion University, CCHR, and Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute watched it on their phones all afternoon. That's how the assignment desks at the Richmond and Norfolk TV stations grabbed it for the six-o'clock news!"

***

#### Friday, February 5, 2016, 9:15 AM — The Speakerphone Call on Line One, Two Twin Meltdowns, & The Majority Leader's Triplets

The black multi-line telephone on Katie's desk in our fifth-floor General Assembly Building office rang once on Line One at nine-fifteen on Friday morning, and just as she had done ever since her very first week on the Virginia Beach City Council, Katie reached over from her SwiftChair to press the speakerphone button herself.

In almost every other legislative office in the Capitol complex, a constitutional officer never picked up their own main telephone line; incoming calls were strictly screened by a legislative aide or session receptionist at the front desk so the member wouldn't be interrupted by cold calls. Teaching Katie to let a ringing phone go unanswered when she was sitting right beside it, however, was impossible. In Katie's literal autistic mind, Room 518 was her office, her name was on the brass plate outside the door, and if she was at her desk with a free hand, the polite, honest thing to do was answer the phone herself so the constituent on the other end knew she was actually there working for them. At this point in our time in Richmond—and certainly up in Washington—people outside Virginia Beach were still learning that Katie answered her own phone directly, and as she pressed the button, she fully expected the caller to be a retired shipyard worker from Kempsville reporting a missed CVTA bus connection on Princess Anne Road.

"Delegate Katie Prairie's office, this is Katie speaking," she said, keeping one hand resting on her open municipal transit binder while I sat right beside her left wheel with my silver MagnaBook Pro laptop open on the side table.

There was a brief, startled pause on the other end of the speakerphone. "Oh! Good morning, Delegate Prairie—is this really Delegate Prairie herself? I honestly expected your front-desk scheduler or a legislative assistant to pick up the main switchboard line. My name is Arthur Vance, and I'm a senior producer for Meet the Nation at GBS News up here in Washington. I hope I'm not catching you at a bad time?"

Katie blinked, glancing sideways at me in surprise. To the two of us, Meet the Nation was the quiet Sunday morning news program our dad David used to put on the living room television in Virginia Beach while the three of us ate scrambled eggs and toast together.

"Not at all, Mr. Vance," Katie said politely. "My brother Nate and I were just looking over some bus shelter amendments. How can I help you?"

"Well, Delegate, David Vance and our editorial team here in Washington watched your exchange on the House Floor yesterday afternoon over House Bill 663," Mr. Vance said warmly, his voice remarkably courteous and unhurried. "You raised some serious constitutional questions about how a law like that could ever be enforced in public buildings without violating the Fourth Amendment. David would be honored if you would join him this Sunday morning at nine o'clock for a quiet, one-on-one conversation to walk through the text of the bill—if you'd be willing to make it a Sunday morning exclusive with Meet the Nation."

Katie's shoulders visibly relaxed in her SwiftChair. After answering questions from the local Richmond and Norfolk newspaper reporters the evening before, the word exclusive sounded like a wonderful relief to her: it meant she would only have to put on a stiff blazer, sit under bright lights, state the literal facts of House Bill 663 one time, and then go straight back to our apartment in Richmond without having to repeat the exact same sentences to anyone else.

"Do you mean if I talk to Mr. Vance at nine o'clock on Sunday morning, I only have to tell the story one time and nobody else will ask me to repeat it all afternoon?" Katie asked literally.

On the speakerphone, Arthur Vance let out a soft, warm laugh. "That is the exact agreement, Delegate Prairie. Just you and David Vance one-on-one at nine o'clock sharp, zero cross-talk, and you're completely done by nine-twenty. We would be happy to send a car down to your address in Richmond at five-thirty Sunday morning to drive you up Interstate 95—"

"Oh, you don't need to waste money on a car, Mr. Vance," Katie said right away. "My brother Nate and I always ride public transit and pay our own regular fare, and a car would just get stuck in traffic on the 14th Street Bridge anyway. The suburban Staples Mill station doesn't have Sunday bus service yet, so we'll take the early JRTC bus down Broad Street to Richmond Main Street Station, ride the six-oh-five ARTS Northeast Regional train up to Alexandria, and use our blue CapitalPass cards from our family trips with our dad to take the Capital Transit Yellow Line across the Charles R. Fenwick Bridge into L'Enfant Plaza, and then transfer to the Route P6 bus across the National Mall right to your door at 400 North Capitol Street. We'll be at your studio desk by eight-thirty—and then we can catch the eleven-twelve train out of Alexandria with the connecting ARTS Thruway shuttle back to Main Street Station so I can get back to our apartment and out of my dress blazer by two o'clock."

"You two are taking a Richmond city bus, an intercity train, the Yellow Line subway across the Potomac, and a D.C. bus across the National Mall?" Mr. Vance asked, sounding genuinely charmed. "Well, whatever makes you most comfortable, Delegate. We'll have two security passes waiting for you and your brother at the Washington bureau front desk at eight-thirty Sunday morning. Thank you so much for giving us your word."

"Thank you for being so polite, Mr. Vance," Katie said, and pressed the button to end the call.

Only as the speakerphone clicked off at nine-twenty-two did Katie and I look down at the plastic telephone console on her desk.

While we had been talking cleanly on Line One for the last four minutes, the little red hold lights on Line Two, Line Three, Line Four, and Line Five had all started blinking furiously at the exact same time, though the ringer had been automatically muted while the speakerphone was active.

Before I could even ask Katie why the whole console was lit up like a Christmas tree, our office door flew open. Katie's twenty-four-year-old legislative aide stumbled in carrying a thick stack of pink paper message slips, followed two seconds later by Greg, the Communications Director for the Virginia House Democratic Caucus, who was holding two vibrating cell phones in his hands and breathing like he had just sprinted all the way up the stairs from the third floor.

"Katie! Do not touch that phone until I clear a schedule!" Greg gasped, leaning over the front edge of her desk. "Capitol Sunday is holding on Line Two, This Sunday is on Line Three, Beltway Sunday is on Line Four, and the cable networks are blowing up my cell phone! They all want to book you for Sunday morning! We can set up a full Sunday morning sweep right now—four television shows back-to-back from eight in the morning until noon—"

"Oh, no thank you," Katie said calmly, shaking her head. "I would hate sitting in a stiff blazer repeating the exact same story four times in a row. Besides, I already promised Mr. Vance on Line One that I would only talk to Meet the Nation."

The room went dead silent.

Greg stared down at Katie, then over at my wheelchair, his mouth opening and closing without a sound.

"You... you answered your own phone and promised an exclusive to Meet the Nation without talking to me first?" he whispered, his face flushing red.

I looked up from my laptop keyboard, confused by his sudden anger. "Mr. Vance called while we were looking at CVTA bus stops. He was the first one to ask, he was very polite to Katie, and he told her that if she goes on at nine o'clock, she only has to explain the bill once and then we can catch the eleven-twelve train out of Alexandria and come home."

"Yeah," Katie agreed simply. "Why would I want to go on four television shows on a Sunday morning when I can explain the statute once at nine o'clock and be back in our apartment in sweatpants by two in the afternoon?"

Greg slowly lowered both of his ringing cell phones to his sides, staring at the two of us with his jaw clenched. "I have to go tell the other three networks you're off the board," he muttered tightly, backing out of our office doorway into the outer reception room.

As he pulled the heavy oak door behind him, the latch didn't quite catch, leaving a two-inch gap between the frame and the jamb.

Through that crack, Katie and I heard every single word as Greg snatched up the blinking phones at the legislative aide's desk in the outer room and started barking into the handsets back-to-back.

"Look, Sarah, I'm telling you, I can't put her on Capitol Sunday!" we heard him shout into Line Two, his voice loud and exasperated.
