## Flipping the Seventh Senate District, The Mahogany Senate Ramp, & Madam Chair

### Flipping the Seventh Senate District, Custom-Milling the Mahogany Senate Ramp, & Swearing In as Madam Chair

**Date:** 2019-11-05 at 19:30 America/New_York

![Inside the Senate of Virginia Chamber at the State Capitol in Richmond on Opening Day, January 8, 2020, 34-year-old State Senator Katie Prairie sits in her black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchair beside the newly milled solid-mahogany wheelchair ramp, taking the secular constitutional affirmation of office on the Constitution of Virginia held by her twin brother Nate while their father David watches proudly.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/jan_2020_senate_of_virginia_mahogany_ramp_madam_chair_affirmation.jpg)

#### Tuesday, November 5, 2019, 7:30 PM — Winning the Seventh Senate District & Flipping the Senate of Virginia

"Norfolk precincts around Newtown Road and Glenrock just uploaded to the State Board of Elections server," I called out at seven-thirty on Election Night—Tuesday, November 5, 2019—as my custom PHP precinct-aggregation script refreshed on my laptop screen inside our packed campaign headquarters off Kempsville Road. "And here come the early-vote and seven-o'clock precinct totals from CCHR, Bellamy Manor, Brandon, Pembroke, and the polling place over by Fairlawn Recreation Center on Marlborough Drive!"

Sitting right beside my left armrest in her compact SwiftChair, thirty-four-year-old Katie leaned in while Dad stood behind our two wheelchairs with his hand resting proudly on my shoulder.

Unlike our first House race six years earlier—when we had watched eighteen Kempsville precincts around our kitchen table—the Seventh Senate District spanned fifty-four precincts across western and central Virginia Beach and eastern Norfolk. For seven straight months from April through November, Katie, Dad, and I had ridden every CVTA bus route connecting the two cities—Route 1, Route 12, Route 15, Route 20, Route 25, Route 29, Route 33, and, starting in October 2019, the brand-new Route 24 running along Kempsville Road and Witchduck Road to Pembroke East—canvassing thousands of doors from Kempsville and Larkspur all the way north to Bayside and west across Newtown Road into Norfolk. In fact, the launch of that new Route 24 corridor along Kempsville Road and Witchduck Road in October 2019 (a completely separate north-south route from the historic, long-retired Laskin Road route that had merely shared a recycled route number years earlier) had marked a personal milestone for Katie and me: the exact month Route 24 began rolling down Kempsville Road, we had pooled our software consulting savings to buy our own single-story brick ranch on Lord Nelson Drive strictly fifty-fifty right off the new Route 24 bus line, installing a second custom two-person roll-up hydrotherapy tub and outfitting the master walk-in closet as our enclosed sleeping sanctuary while Dad kept the original brick ranch on Arvin Road off Indian River Road and Military Highway in the family.

And because voters across Virginia Beach and Norfolk remembered Delegate Katie Prairie as the lawmaker who had stood up to the bathroom-bill bullies on Meet the Nation in 2016 and fought every single winter for their buses, schools, and disability waivers, the corporate attack mailers against her hadn't stood a chance.

"Look at the margin in Kempsville and around CCHR, Katie," I said, my voice catching as the green rows populated down my screen at 7:54 PM. "You're carrying your home Eighty-Fifth House precincts by twenty-two points—Andre Askew just won your House seat right on your coattails—and you're winning the Bayside, Pembroke, and eastern Norfolk precincts by eleven points!"

Ten minutes later, at 8:04 PM, the statewide television monitors mounted above the headquarters room chimed in unison.

First came the Seventh Senate District projection:

*PROJECTED WINNER — 7TH SENATE DISTRICT: DEL. KATIE PRAIRIE (D-VIRGINIA BEACH) ELECTED TO THE SENATE OF VIRGINIA (55.8% – 44.2%).*

And eighteen minutes after that, a roar went up across the room that rattled the storefront windows when the statewide banner flashed across the bottom of the screen:

*BREAKING NEWS: DEMOCRATS FLIP CONTROL OF BOTH THE SENATE OF VIRGINIA AND THE VIRGINIA HOUSE OF DELEGATES.*

Katie turned her head toward me, her eyes bright with tears as she threw her arms around my neck across our wheelchair armrests while Dad wrapped both of us in a bear hug from behind.

"No more watching our bills die across the rotunda, Nate," Katie whispered against my shoulder. "Our caucus isn't in the minority anymore. Come January, I hold a committee gavel."

***

#### December 2019 to Wednesday, January 8, 2020 — The Custom-Milled Mahogany Ramp & Swearing In as Madam Chair

![Inside the Senate of Virginia Chamber at the State Capitol in Richmond on Opening Day, January 8, 2020, 34-year-old State Senator Katie Prairie sits in her black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchair beside the newly milled solid-mahogany wheelchair ramp, taking the secular constitutional affirmation of office on the Constitution of Virginia held by her twin brother Nate while their father David watches proudly.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/jan_2020_senate_of_virginia_mahogany_ramp_madam_chair_affirmation.jpg)

In the weeks between Election Night and the January 2020 Opening Day of the General Assembly, the transition from the House of Delegates to the Senate of Virginia looked very different from our first arrival in Richmond six years earlier.

After the Electoral Boards of the City of Virginia Beach and the City of Norfolk completed their official multi-locality canvass and the Virginia State Board of Elections transmitted Katie's gold-sealed Certificate of Election as Senator-Elect for the Seventh Senatorial District under Code of Virginia Section 24.2-675, Katie received a phone call at our home in Kempsville on the first Monday of December.

It wasn't from a mid-level facilities bureaucrat telling her to wait until March. It was from William, the veteran Clerk of the Senate of Virginia, calling personally alongside the newly elected Senate Majority Leader.

"Senator-Elect Prairie," the Clerk said warmly on speakerphone across our desk, "in the two-hundred-and-forty-year history of the Senate of Virginia, you are the very first State Senator ever elected to sit in our chamber in a wheelchair—and the Majority Caucus has just designated you to serve as Chair of the Senate Committee on Rehabilitation and Social Services, as well as a senior member of Senate Transportation and Senate Finance. I want you and Nathaniel to ride up to the Capitol this week so our master architectural woodworkers can measure your SwiftChair in person. When you roll into the Senate of Virginia on January eighth, everything in our chamber is going to look like Thomas Jefferson built it for you himself."

Three days later, when Katie and I rode the morning ARTS train and the JRTC Route 6 bus up to Capitol Square and rolled into the second-floor Senate wing, the Clerk of the Senate was waiting for us with the Capitol's master cabinetmakers and historic preservation carpenters.

Inside the neoclassical Office of the Clerk of the Senate—where tall white marble Ionic columns framed the floor-to-ceiling volumes of the Virginia Acts of Assembly—the carpenters were already constructing a lowered, wheelchair-accessible section of the polished mahogany reception counter so Senator Katie Prairie could sign official Senate parchments and pre-file bills at eye level with me parked right beside her.

And inside the Senate of Virginia Chamber itself, under the tall arched windows and the crimson carpet of the forty-member upper house, the Clerk led us up to the front aisle where the senior committee chairs sat.

Not only had the cabinetmakers modified the front-aisle mahogany desk for the Chair of Rehabilitation and Social Services so Katie's compact SwiftChair rolled smoothly underneath the desktop without a single obstruction, they had also designed a permanent, custom-milled solid-mahogany wheelchair ramp leading directly up to the Clerk's well and the Senate dais—complete with matching turned mahogany balusters and brass handrails stained to the exact eighteenth-century patina of the chamber's historic woodwork.

"Look at the grain on that mahogany, Katie," I murmured as Katie tested the gentle one-in-twelve slope of the new Senate ramp in her SwiftChair and rolled effortlessly up to the Clerk's well. "Anyone looking down from the Senate gallery is going to assume that ramp has been part of this Capitol for two hundred years."

"And it's staying here for the next two hundred years," the Clerk of the Senate smiled.

On Opening Day—Wednesday, January 8, 2020, at twelve o'clock noon—after we had unpacked our familiar winter-session sanctuary at Apartment 104 of the Broad & Boulevard Lofts on West Broad Street the weekend before and ridden the eastbound JRTC Route 6 bus down to Ninth and Broad, thirty-four-year-old Katie rolled down the center aisle of the Senate of Virginia in her compact SwiftChair.

Because the second-floor Senate Chamber had a level ground-accessible entrance off the Capitol elevator lobby and allowed a Senator's immediate family onto the floor specifically for the Opening Day swearing-in ceremony, Dad sat beaming in his best suit in the front row of the Senatorial family section while I rolled my SwiftChair right up beside Katie's desk holding our bound leather copy of the Constitution of the Commonwealth of Virginia.

Up on the high marble rostrum, the Lieutenant Governor of Virginia—serving under the state constitution as President of the Senate—called the forty Senators-Elect forward to take the constitutional oath of office under Article II, Section 7 of the Constitution of Virginia.

Rolling smoothly up the newly installed custom-milled mahogany ramp to the front well with me right beside her left armrest as her ceremonial guest, Katie didn't reach for a Bible while the opposition senators across the carpet held leather Bibles angled toward the press gallery cameras. Neither Katie nor I believed in any religion or any god, and just as she had done on the Virginia Beach City Council and in the House of Delegates, Katie placed her left palm squarely on the gold-stamped cover of the Constitution of the Commonwealth of Virginia resting across my hands, raised her right hand toward the rostrum, and spoke the secular constitutional affirmation under Article II, Section 7 of the Constitution of Virginia and Section 49-9 of the Code of Virginia—omitting the optional parenthetical religious phrase at the end:

"I do solemnly affirm that I will support the Constitution of the United States, and the Constitution of the Commonwealth of Virginia, and that I will faithfully and impartially discharge all the duties incumbent upon me as a member of the Senate of Virginia, according to the best of my ability."

Ten minutes later, after I rolled back out to the accessible viewing bay to watch the formal floor proceedings alongside Dad, the Clerk read the standing committee assignments for the 2020 session and handed Senator Katie Prairie the polished wooden gavel as Madam Chair of the Senate Committee on Rehabilitation and Social Services—sitting right across the chamber from the exact seats where Senator Franklin Ward and his allies had killed her transit and disability bills twenty-two months earlier.

And just as we knew they would, the Republican caucus, right-wing cable networks, and evangelical media had an absolute field day over both what was resting under Katie's left hand and the four words she had deliberately left out of her oath.

Before the Senate had even gaveled out of its Opening Day ceremonial session at two-thirty that afternoon, an opposition party operative up in the press gallery had blasted out a zoomed-in video clip of Katie's left hand resting on the Constitution of the Commonwealth of Virginia instead of a Bible while she said "I do solemnly affirm" and stopped at "according to the best of my ability" without saying "so help me God." Within forty-five minutes, the opposition party's state committee had sent out a breathless statewide fundraising email accusing the newly minted committee chair from Virginia Beach of "refusing to touch a Holy Bible or say 'So help me God' on the floor of Thomas Jefferson's Capitol." Conservative talk-radio switchboards from Richmond to Tidewater were melting down, right-wing cable pundits on Beacon News and LibertyMax were running red "WAR ON FAITH IN VIRGINIA" banners across the bottom of the screen, and back home in Virginia Beach—just five minutes down Indian River Road from our house in Kempsville—the televangelist hosts of *The 777 Circle* on the Covenant Broadcasting Network were interrupting their afternoon broadcast to warn viewers that their own hometown State Senator had "defied the sacred oath precedent set by George Washington in 1789."

When Katie, Dad, and I rolled out of the mahogany doors of the Senate Chamber into the Capitol Rotunda at two-forty-five, camera crews from Beacon News, LibertyMax, and the Covenant Broadcasting Network were waiting in ambush beside Thomas Jefferson's marble statue.

"Senator Prairie! Senator Prairie!" the Beacon News correspondent called out, thrusting a microphone toward Katie's lap tray alongside a reporter holding a Covenant Broadcasting Network mic flag while two opposition state senators lingered behind the marble columns to watch the ambush. "The Republican state chairman and the hosts of *The 777 Circle* back in your own district in Virginia Beach just condemned you for refusing to place your hand on a Holy Bible and refusing to say 'So help me God' during your Senate swearing-in today! Why did you break the precedent that President George Washington set at the founding of our country?"

Katie braked her SwiftChair on the black-and-white marble tiles beneath Thomas Jefferson's statue, looked straight into the cluster of television lenses without a flicker of hesitation, and picked up the leather-bound volume off my lap tray so the gold seal of the Commonwealth gleamed under the camera lights.

"First of all, I would gladly encourage the hosts of *The 777 Circle* down on Indian River Road—and my Republican colleagues hiding behind those marble columns—to actually read the Constitution of the United States, the Constitution of Virginia, and a basic history book," Katie answered, her voice calm, crisp, and loud enough to echo across the entire Capitol Rotunda. "Let's start with the law. Article VI, Clause 3 of the United States Constitution states in black and white that all state legislators shall be bound by Oath or Affirmation to support the Constitution, and that no religious test shall ever be required as a qualification to any office or public trust under the United States. And right here in Article II, Section 7 of the Constitution of the Commonwealth of Virginia—the exact document I placed my left hand on today—the framers put the words 'or affirm' and 'so help me God' inside parentheses, paired with Section 49-9 of the Code of Virginia, specifically so citizens who do not subscribe to a religion can make a solemn, binding secular affirmation without being subjected to an unconstitutional religious test."

The Covenant Broadcasting Network reporter opened his mouth to interrupt—"But George Washington himself added 'So help me God' in 1789—"

"No, he didn't—and historians debunked that myth decades ago," Katie cut in smoothly, her literal, encyclopedic memory firing on all cylinders as the cameras rolled live. "Even the Presidential Oath written by the Founders in Article II, Section 1, Clause 8 of the United States Constitution does not contain the words 'So help me God.' Not a single eyewitness, diary, newspaper, or foreign diplomat standing at Federal Hall in New York on April 30, 1789 recorded George Washington adding 'So help me God' to his oath. That story was invented out of thin air sixty-five years later in an 1854 book written by Rufus Wilmot Griswold, who wasn't even born when Washington was alive, and the first President confirmed by contemporary historical records to have said those words was Chester A. Arthur in 1881. And look at whose marble statue we are gathered under right now: Thomas Jefferson, who wrote the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom right here in Richmond declaring that our civil rights have no dependence on our religious opinions."

Behind the marble columns, the two opposition senators suddenly found something very interesting to look at on their shoes as Katie lowered the Constitution back onto my lap tray and added one final, unbothered smile for the cameras:

"In the Seventh Senate District across Virginia Beach and Norfolk, I represent Christians, Jews, Muslims, Hindus, Buddhists, and non-religious citizens like my brother and me alike. I wasn't elected to be anybody's pastor, and Virginia is a constitutional republic, not a theocracy. My legal obligation as a State Senator is to the Constitution of the United States and the Constitution of Virginia—and if the pundits screaming on Beacon News, LibertyMax, and *The 777 Circle* spent half as much time reading the Constitution as they spend inventing phony history lessons about George Washington, maybe they'd know what Article VI actually says. Now if you'll excuse my brother, my dad, and me, we have a Route 6 bus to catch on Broad Street and a committee docket to gavel in tomorrow morning."

When we rolled into Katie's new Senate of Virginia office at eight-thirty the next morning and the main constituent telephone line rang on her desk before her legislative assistant had even finished hanging up her winter coat in the outer room, Katie didn't wait for staff to screen the call. Just as she had done as a Virginia Beach City Councilwoman and as a Virginia State Delegate—because in her literal autistic mind it was her office and it was only polite to answer the phone when she could so constituents knew she was actually at her desk working for them—she reached over from her SwiftChair, pressed the speakerphone button, and said warmly, "Senator Katie Prairie's office, this is Katie speaking," greeting a stunned retired Navy chaplain calling from Norfolk to thank her for defending Thomas Jefferson's Statute for Religious Freedom.

Down on the Senate floor, just like the House of Delegates across the Rotunda, the Senate of Virginia had its own official Senate Page Program for thirteen- and fourteen-year-old eighth-graders appointed from across the Commonwealth—and within forty-eight hours, Katie and I had become the favorite Senator and brother of the eighth-grade Senate Pages for the exact same reason the House Pages had gravitated to our desks four years earlier. Every floor errand from Senator Prairie's desk came on a neat, color-coded sticky note with the exact room number, committee name, and bill number written in clear block print, and nobody in Katie's orbit ever barked a vague instruction or raised their voice when the brass division bells rang.

As for our three favorite eighth-grade House Pages from February 2016—the autistic triplets Sam Hawkins and his identical-twin sisters Mandy and Sarah Hawkins from rural Southside Virginia near Danville, who had told us over sub sandwiches at the Oak Lawn Diner on West Broad Street after riding JRTC Route 6 that Katie was their absolute favorite constitutional officer in Richmond—they had aged out of the middle-school Page program years earlier, graduated together at the top of their high-school class under the loving roof of their Aunt Marge and their Uncle Richard Callaway (who had since retired as Republican House Majority Leader), and enrolled together that fall at age eighteen as freshmen at Central Virginia University right on the West Broad Street Route 6 bus corridor. True to her word on that winter afternoon four years earlier, the moment Sam, Mandy, and Sarah aged out of high school and arrived in Richmond for college, Katie hired all three triplets to work side by side in her Senate of Virginia office—first as paid legislative session and transit-policy interns throughout their four years at Central Virginia University, and then, the morning after all three graduated with honors in May 2024, as her full-time State Senate Legislative and Transit Policy Assistants.

## The Accessibility Project: Riding Every Bus Across the Commonwealth for the United States Senate

### Part 1: The Living Room Decision in Kempsville, The 10,000-Signature Rule, & The Accessibility Project

**Date:** 2026-01-10 at 19:30 America/New_York

![Inside their warm living room on Lord Nelson Drive in Kempsville, Virginia Beach on January 10, 2026, 40-year-old State Senator Katie Prairie and her fraternal twin brother Nate sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs holding hands across their armrests while their 67-year-old father David sits on the sofa beside them with his yellow legal pad and three tall glasses of ginger ale.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/jan_2026_kempsville_living_room_senate_campaign_decision_katie_nate_david.jpg)

#### Saturday, January 10, 2026, 7:30 PM — The Living Room Decision on Lord Nelson Drive & The 10,000-Signature Rule

![Inside their warm living room on Lord Nelson Drive in Kempsville, Virginia Beach on January 10, 2026, 40-year-old State Senator Katie Prairie and her fraternal twin brother Nate sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs holding hands across their armrests while their 67-year-old father David sits on the sofa beside them with his yellow legal pad and three tall glasses of ginger ale.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/jan_2026_kempsville_living_room_senate_campaign_decision_katie_nate_david.jpg)

"Listen to what Senator Martin Warren's chief of staff just told the political desk at The Potomac Post," I said, reading aloud from my MagnaBook Pro screen inside the warm living room of our brick ranch house on Lord Nelson Drive in Kempsville while the January rain tapped against the front bay window. "Gregory said, and I quote: 'State Senator Katie Prairie and her brother are a cute regional novelty down in Tidewater, but two software developers in wheelchairs riding city buses cannot possibly raise the twenty million dollars required to compete against Preston Holloway in a statewide U.S. Senate primary.'"

Sitting on the sofa right beside my right armrest with his familiar yellow legal pad resting on his knee and a mug of black coffee in his hand, our sixty-seven-year-old dad let out a low, dry chuckle and looked across at my forty-year-old twin sister.

"A cute regional novelty," Dad repeated, shaking his head behind his glasses. "That's the fourth election in sixteen years where the party bosses in Richmond or Washington have called the two of you a long shot before a single voter has cast a ballot."

Parked flush against my left armrest in her compact black-and-silver SwiftChair power wheelchair, Katie didn't look intimidated in the slightest. Her blue eyes were fixed on the muted television screen across the living room, where three-term Democratic U.S. Senator Martin Warren stood at a crystal-chandeliered ballroom podium in McLean raising the arm of his handpicked successor—wealthy Northern Virginia venture capitalist businessman Preston Holloway, whose newly formed super PAC had already banked fourteen million dollars from K Street defense contractors, private-equity hospital chains, and prescription-drug middlemen.

And right below the split-screen video of the McLean donor reception, Global News Network was replaying a clip from the White House South Lawn two hours earlier, where President Garrett Thorne had stopped in front of the Marine One chopper blades to sneer into the press pool microphones about Virginia's newly opened Senate seat.

"Did you hear what Garrett Thorne called you on the South Lawn this afternoon, Katie?" Dad asked quietly, his jaw tightening the way it always did whenever a bully came after his daughter. "He called you 'Broken Katie Prairie rolling around Richmond' and said if Democrats were crazy enough to nominate a spinster on wheels instead of a corporate suit, his Restore the Republic nominee Richard Sterling would bury you in November. And then Vice President Conrad Drayton went straight onto the Liberty First Network at six o'clock to say unmarried, childless, non-religious twins who live together have no stake in the future of the American family."

Katie reached her right hand across our wheelchair armrests, laced her fingers tightly through mine, and turned her head to look at Dad and me.

Six winters had passed since Katie had rolled up the newly milled solid-mahogany ramp in the Senate of Virginia Chamber in January 2020 to take the gavel as Chair of Rehabilitation and Social Services. Across those six years—through the August 2020 pandemic special session inside the Central Virginia University Student Commons Ballroom on West Broad Street, where Katie had legislated behind a three-sided clear polycarbonate shield wearing a NIOSH-approved trifold N95 respirator fitted with an airtight medical drinking valve while I logged classroom and bus ventilation rates on our pocket NDIR carbon-dioxide monitor and wiped our SwiftChair joysticks down with non-alcoholic benzalkonium chloride and hypochlorous acid wipes—she had never missed a single roll-call vote or a single constituent phone call. She had won re-election overwhelmingly in the renumbered Twenty-Second Senate District in November 2023, and just yesterday afternoon at the Capitol in Richmond, she had co-patroned and cast her second-passage YES votes to place three historic Constitutional Amendments directly onto the November 3, 2026 statewide ballot: enshrining the fundamental Right to Reproductive Freedom, locking Marriage Equality into the Constitution of Virginia while repealing the defunct 2006 ban, and establishing automatic Restoration of Voting Rights upon completion of a prison term.

Yet every single morning when we opened the federal register, we watched the Restore the Republic administration in Washington—and their billionaire Apex Efficiency Commission—try to rip away the exact civil rights, Medicaid home-and-community-based disability waivers, rural hospitals, and Federal Transit Administration operating grants that working Virginians depended on to survive. And instead of fighting back with teeth, Senator Martin Warren's handpicked corporate heir Preston Holloway was going on cable television preaching polite, poll-tested incrementalism so he wouldn't offend his K Street donors.

"Martin Warren doesn't own that Senate seat, Dad," Katie said, her voice calm, steady, and ringing with the exact same crystalline resolve she had carried onto the four buses in 2008. "That seat belongs to the eight point seven million people of the Commonwealth of Virginia. Preston Holloway thinks he can buy the June primary from a ballroom in McLean without ever setting foot on a public bus, and Garrett Thorne and Conrad Drayton think calling me 'Broken Katie Prairie' is going to make Nate and me hide in our house. I want to beat Preston Holloway in the June sixteenth primary, I want to beat Richard Sterling on November third, and on January third, 2027, I want to roll down the aisle of the United States Senate and watch Vice President Conrad Drayton—in his constitutional capacity as President of the Senate—be forced to swear me in on the Constitution of the United States without a Bible and without saying 'So help me God.'"

I grinned across our armrests, feeling the familiar electric surge run straight through my ribs. "He is going to turn purple at the rostrum, Katie."

"Let him," Katie smiled, squeezing my hand before turning to Dad. "Are you two with me?"

Dad uncapped his black rollerball pen, tapped it against the top of his yellow legal pad, and wrote *Katie Prairie for United States Senate — 2026* in neat, square block letters across the top margin.

"Every single mile, sweetheart," Dad said warmly. "Alright, Mr. Campaign Manager and Chief Technology Officer—walk your Treasurer through the statutory jump from a forty-district State Senate race to a statewide United States Senate campaign."

I tapped a shortcut on my MagnaBook Pro, pulling up the federal and state election code checklists I had spent the past forty-eight hours compiling in Quantum Code.

"First," I said, "because the United States Senate is a federal office, our campaign finance reporting moves from Virginia's state COMET system to the Federal Election Commission. Tonight we file FEC Form 2—Katie's Statement of Candidacy—and FEC Form 1 registering *Katie Prairie for U.S. Senate* as her principal campaign committee, with you as official Campaign Treasurer and me as Campaign Manager and Chief Technology Officer, plus her mandatory Senate Public Financial Disclosure Report with the Secretary of the United States Senate. And because our campaign donations will process through CivicPulse and Meridian Pay behind Aegis Cloud on the PHP infrastructure we write and maintain ourselves, zero dollars are going to beltway fundraising consultants."

"And what about getting Katie's name onto the June sixteenth Democratic Primary ballot under Virginia law?" Dad asked, poised with his pen.

"That's the biggest hurdle—and the exact reason the Washington insiders think we can't do it without corporate money," I replied, rotating my laptop slightly toward Dad's side of the sofa so both he and Katie could read the statutory table. "When Katie ran for the House of Delegates, Code of Virginia Section 24.2-506 required one hundred and twenty-five voter signatures. When she ran for the Senate of Virginia, it required two hundred and fifty. To qualify for the statewide United States Senate primary ballot in Virginia, Section 24.2-506 requires at least ten thousand qualified voter signatures statewide—and there's a mandatory geographic distribution rule: those ten thousand signatures must include at least four hundred qualified voters from each of Virginia's eleven Congressional Districts."

Dad whistled softly, jotting the numbers onto his legal pad. "Ten thousand verified signatures statewide, with a hard floor of four hundred in all eleven Congressional Districts—from Accomack County on the Eastern Shore and Virginia Beach here in the Second District all the way out to the Ninth District in Blacksburg, Bluewater, Abingdon, and Cumberland Gap."

"Which means if our campaign standard is always collecting more than double the statutory minimum so no party lawyer can challenge us off the ballot," Katie said, her blue eyes lighting up with mathematical focus, "we aren't stopping at ten thousand signatures and four hundred per district. We're collecting at least twenty-four thousand signatures statewide, and at least twelve hundred verified signatures in every single one of the eleven Congressional Districts."

Just then, Katie's smartphone buzzed on the coffee table beside our three tall glasses of ice-cold ginger ale. It was a Washington campaign consultant who had been leaving voicemails all afternoon offering to sign on as a paid strategist. When Katie tapped the speakerphone button and told him she was entering the race, the consultant immediately launched into a slick sales pitch offering to lease our campaign a forty-five-foot custom diesel motorcoach wrapped with a giant photograph of Katie's face for forty-two thousand dollars a month.

Katie looked at me, looked at Dad, and leaned toward the speakerphone.

"Thank you for calling, but our campaign will not be leasing a private tour bus," Katie told him crisply. "For the past sixteen years, my brother Nate, my dad, and I have ridden regular public transit buses and passenger trains everywhere we go, and we pay standard regular fare at the farebox alongside our constituents. If a rural county or a working-class corridor in Virginia has a public bus route, we are riding that bus with the people who live there. And if a rural county doesn't have fixed-route bus service between towns, or if a wheelchair ramp breaks down in the rain, my dad is going to rent a wheelchair-accessible minivan to bridge the gap so I experience that exact transit desert the same way disabled and working-class Virginians do every day. Have a good evening."

She tapped the red disconnect button, and Dad raised his glass of ginger ale with a proud grin.

***

#### Saturday, January 10, 2026, 8:45 PM — Written Permission From The Paper Wall & The Brooks Family for "The Accessibility Project"

Forty-five minutes after we filed Katie's FEC Form 2 electronically, a chime sounded on my laptop as an incoming OmniMeet video call connected from the New River Valley.

When I clicked accept and angled my screen so Katie, Dad, and I could all see it clearly from our chairs, two joyful living rooms filled the split window at once.

On the left side of the screen, gathered inside the sunlit control room of Engine Room Records in Blacksburg alongside Holly O'Connell—the youngest O'Connell sister and longtime Day-to-Day Band Manager and General Counsel—sat the members of The Paper Wall: Julian Croft ("Leo"), Maya Sterling ("Olivia"), sisters Izzy ("Luna"), Bea ("Stella"), and Charlotte ("Charlie") Croft, and cousins Diana Hale, Ellie Cross, and Fiona Croft.

And on the right side of the screen, gathered inside the wide, oak-bumpered communal living room of the Brooks Family Compound along U.S. Route 11 between Christiansburg and Radford, sat the found family whom The Paper Wall's music had chronicled—centered around the original trio from Bennett Hall Room 214: thirty-year-old Jordan Shawn Kelly (clean-shaven, wearing his rectangular prescription glasses and behind-the-ear hearing aids, seated in his custom manual wheelchair with his Pinnacle Vanguard Pro laptop open to his dark-screened NeoEdit terminal on Aura Glade) flanked right beside his armrests by his wife Aubrie Jean Kelly and Madison Elizabeth Scott, along with their Room 216 and Constellation family: Zoë Wren Brooks, Lauren Nicole Barnes, Hannah Parker Anderson, Mark Shawn Anderson, Isabel Claire Dawson, Jessamine "Jess" Mercer, Daniel, Laura, and Megan Brooks, and Australian expats Sarah Kristyn Braithwaite and Jessica Gallagher.

"Senator Prairie! Nate! Mr. Prairie!" Aubrie Jean called out warmly, her long brown side-braid resting over her shoulder as she held up a freshly signed, notarized legal document beside Jordan's wheelchair while Holly O'Connell held up the matching Engine Room Records master licensing execution sheet in Blacksburg. "We just saw your FEC filing go live on the wire five minutes ago, and we wanted to be the very first people in the Commonwealth of Virginia to hand you this!"

On the right half of our screen, Zoë shared a high-resolution PDF onto our workspace: a permanent, royalty-free campaign synchronization and public-performance license for Track 13 of *The Eleventh Child, Book 2: System.Restore*—"The Accessibility Project"—signed in ink by every member of The Paper Wall, by Holly O'Connell on behalf of Engine Room Records, and by Jordan, Aubrie Jean, Madison, Zoë, Lauren, Hannah, Mark, Sarah, Jessica Gallagher, Isabel, Jessamine, and Daniel, Laura, and Megan Brooks.

Katie's hand flew to her collar, her blue eyes shining as she looked at the twenty-plus signatures spanning both pages.

"You all signed this for our campaign?" Katie asked softly.

"Every single one of us," Julian Croft smiled from Blacksburg, his arm around Maya's shoulders while Izzy, Bea, and Charlie cheered behind them. "When we wrote and recorded 'The Accessibility Project,' we wanted it to sound like a triumphant mission briefing—turning accessibility mapping and disability solidarity into an unstoppable anthem. There isn't a candidate in America that song belongs to more than you and Nate."

Beside Aubrie Jean and Madison on the right side of the screen, Jordan's fingers moved swiftly across the tactile keys of his Pinnacle Vanguard Pro laptop, and a moment later he triggered EchoType—filling our Kempsville living room with the warm, clear Australian female cadence of his signature "Sydney" voice profile:

<aac>Listen to the first verse of that song, Senator Prairie. Back in the spring of 2015, when the six of us from Suite 214 and 216 were undergraduate freshmen at Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute mapping the Hillside Pass-Through elevators at Eleanor Bennett Hall for our class project, the lyric in our song was: "We cannot pour the concrete for a ramp, we cannot buy an elevator for the camp—the budget's zero, but the mission's clear." Back then, our budget really was zero. All we could do was draw the map and share the key.</aac>

Jordan smiled warmly behind his glasses as Aubrie Jean and Madison rested their hands on his shoulders and Daniel and Laura Brooks nodded proudly behind him. He typed another line and pressed the speak key:

<aac>Every single eligible Virginian voter in our family—Aubrie Jean, Madison, Zoë, Lauren, Hannah, Mark, Isabel, Jess, Daniel, Laura, Megan, and me—is voting for you in the June sixteenth Democratic Primary and again on November third. And even though Sarah and Jessica are Australian nationals who can't cast a ballot yet, all of us are going to help you gather signatures and campaign across the New River Valley, Bluewater, and Southwest Virginia. Because when you roll onto the floor of the United States Senate and take your seat on the Senate Appropriations Committee, the budget won't be zero anymore. You're going to Washington to pour the concrete for the ramps and fund the elevators for the whole country.</aac>

Across our armrests, Katie squeezed my fingers so tightly I could feel her pulse beating against mine.

"When Nate, Dad, and I ride the bus up to Montgomery County and Carroll County this spring," Katie promised them, her voice clear and steady, "'The Accessibility Project' is going to be playing from every speaker we bring—and we'll meet the Room 214 crew right at the Route 3 bus shelter at the end of your driveway on Lee Highway."

### Part 2: The Jammed Ramp at 3400 Victoria Boulevard, ShoreLine Transit Across the Bay, & Wearing the NFA's 'F' Grade in Fairfax

**Date:** 2026-03-28 at 10:15 America/New_York

#### Saturday, March 28, 2026, 10:15 AM — The Jammed Wheelchair Ramp in the Rain at 3400 Victoria Boulevard in Hampton

![In the pouring March 2026 rain at 3400 Victoria Boulevard in Hampton, Virginia, 40-year-old State Senator Katie Prairie and her twin brother Nate sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs on the wet sidewalk beside a coastal transit bus whose front flip-out wheelchair ramp has jammed halfway out, talking warmly with the bus operator and Peninsula shipyard and hospital commuters while their father David holds an umbrella.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/mar_2026_hampton_3400_victoria_blvd_jammed_ramp_rain_katie_nate_david.jpg)

*<pa>Caution: ramp is deploying!</pa>* the exterior speaker of the twelve-year-old Coastal Virginia Transit Authority Route 103 bus crackled in the pouring March rain at 3400 Victoria Boulevard in Hampton—and then a harsh metallic grind echoed off the wet asphalt as the front flip-out aluminum wheelchair ramp seized halfway out of the threshold, sticking straight up at a forty-five-degree angle twelve inches above the flooded concrete curb.

Inside the open front doorway of the bus, the uniformed operator hit the hydraulic toggle switch twice more, winced as the worn actuator motor whined without budging an inch, and stepped out into the cold rain in his high-visibility vest.

"Oh, Senator Prairie, I am so sorry," the operator said, kneeling on the wet sidewalk beside the jammed hinge plate as water dripped from the bill of his cap. "This coach has three hundred and eighty thousand miles on the chassis, and the shop has been waiting six weeks on replacement hydraulic actuators because the spare-parts budget is tapped out. Let me call dispatch for a road supervisor and a relief bus—it might take thirty-five or forty minutes in this weather."

Parked side by side in our compact SwiftChairs in our rain slickers while Dad stood behind us holding a wide clear umbrella over our laptop bag and petition clipboards, forty-year-old Katie didn't reach for a phone to summon a campaign car, and she didn't get angry at the driver.

Instead, she looked at the seven working commuters waiting under the narrow aluminum shelter overhang at 3400 Victoria Boulevard—two pipefitters from Peninsula Shipbuilding & Drydock in Newport News still wearing their steel-toed boots after an overnight hull shift, three certified nursing assistants in damp scrubs heading to Hampton, and a retired Navy machinist with a cane—each of whom had already signed our Third Congressional District primary petitions five minutes earlier.

"You don't owe us a single apology—you can't drive a bus safely when Washington starves your maintenance shop of spare parts," Katie told the operator warmly, rolling her SwiftChair two feet closer so he could step back under the dry overhang of the shelter. "Nate, Dad, and I aren't going anywhere. If the riders on Victoria Boulevard have to wait forty minutes in the rain for a road supervisor with a pry bar, then the candidate asking to represent them in the United States Senate is waiting right here in the rain with them."

I lifted my mPhone on its armrest mount and tapped the live broadcast button on StreamCast and The Grid.

For the next thirty-eight minutes, while the March downpour drummed against the shelter roof on Victoria Boulevard and Preston Holloway was up in Arlington hosting a two-thousand-dollar-a-plate brunch inside a Sovereign Regency hotel ballroom, forty-two thousand Virginians watched live on their phones as Katie sat in her wheelchair in the Hampton rain listening to shipyard workers and hospital aides explain what happens to an hourly worker's paycheck when a twelve-year-old transit bus breaks down on the way to a shift. When the road supervisor's pickup truck finally splashed up to the curb with a heavy steel pry bar and freed the corroded hinge pin so Katie and I could roll up into the front four-point securement bays, the entire bus broke into applause—and by the time we rolled down the ramp at the Newport News Transit Center, volunteers waiting at the bays had filled nineteen more petition sheets in a single hour.

That same week, Katie, Dad, and I rode every corridor across Eastern and Central Virginia to show voters what a truly connected Commonwealth looked like. In the First Congressional District, we rode the morning ARTS passenger train into the Williamsburg Transportation Center—the exact station where Katie had begun her five-bus escape from Brandon Mercer in November 2005—and rolled thirty yards across the brick plaza from the train platform to pay regular fare on the local CTTA Route 1 bus straight to the front gate of Brewster Gardens, proving to hospitality workers and car-free families that Virginia didn't need to waste millions on duplicative consultant studies when an existing train-to-bus connection was already running and simply needed evening frequency and public promotion.

Two days later, in the Second Congressional District, we experienced firsthand how Virginia's Eastern Shore was stranded on a public-transit island at both ends of U.S. Route 13: at the south end, CVTA Routes 1, 27, and 35 met at the Shore Drive and Pleasure House Road transfer point right at the southern foot of the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel, yet neither CVTA nor ShoreLine Transit ran a single public bus across the seventeen-point-six-mile span to Cape Charles; and at the north end in Accomack County, ShoreLine Transit stopped at Oak Hall and Chincoteague Junction just eleven miles short of the Maryland state line—stopping dead before Pocomoke City, Maryland, where Maryland Shore Transit connected north to Salisbury and Delaware's First State Transit network. So after riding CVTA Route 1 to the Shore Drive and Pleasure House Road transfer point at the foot of the bridge-tunnel, Dad met us with a rented silver side-entry wheelchair-accessible ramp minivan, secured our two SwiftChairs into the four-point floor tie-downs, and drove us across the Bridge-Tunnel to Cape Charles, where we boarded a ShoreLine Transit cutaway bus with a rear hydraulic lift and rode the entire length of Northampton and Accomack Counties up U.S. Route 13 through Eastville, Exmore, Onley, Accomac, and Oak Hall. Outside the processing plant at Eastern Shore Poultry at shift change, women in hairnets and rubber boots crowded around Katie's SwiftChair to sign her petitions as she pledged to fight on the Senate Appropriations Committee for dedicated federal interstate transit funds to close both gaps at once—running a permanent public bus connection from Cape Charles across the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel (where public transit buses were already classified under the Bridge-Tunnel District's Class 8 schedule at a nominal one-dollar toll per crossing) directly into the Pleasure House Road CVTA transfer point on Shore Drive with a mandatory statutory cross-honoring agreement so CVTA and ShoreLine Transit fares and passes would be honored seamlessly on both systems, and extending ShoreLine Transit north across the state line into Pocomoke City and Salisbury with a direct Delmarva corridor link to First State Transit in Delaware.

And when we rode the morning ARTS train from Norfolk up through Petersburg in the Fourth District and Richmond in the Fourth and First Districts—riding JRTC Route 6 down Broad Street with its familiar automated voice announcing *"Route 6. Downtown. Welcome aboard JRTC!"* and calling out every single cross street along the corridor—we continued north to inspect the rail diamond at Doswell Junction in the Seventh District, where the East-West mountain branch tracks crossed the North-South main line less than half a mile from the front gate of Old Dominion Adventure Park.

"Look how close those tracks run to the park entrance, Nate," Katie said, pointing from the window of our ARTS Café Car as we sipped our complimentary ginger ales. "Thousands of teenagers and working families ride up here every summer for seasonal jobs, and there isn't a single platform or bus shuttle off Interstate 95. When we build the East-West Commonwealth Rail Corridor linking Norfolk and Richmond through Doswell Junction to Charlottesville, Fishersville, Roanoke, Christiansburg, and Bristol, we're putting a high-level ADA station right here at Doswell with a dedicated ramp shuttle straight to the gate."

#### Tuesday, April 14, 2026, 1:30 PM — Wearing the National Firearms Association's "F" Grade as a Badge of Honor in Fairfax

When we rolled off the Capital Transit Orange Line elevator in Northern Virginia two weeks later and boarded a local Fairfax Link bus across the Tenth, Eighth, and Eleventh Congressional Districts, our grassroots petition count had already surged past twenty-two thousand verified signatures—and the gun lobby decided it was time to try to scare Katie off the ballot.

At one o'clock that Tuesday afternoon inside their glass corporate headquarters in Fairfax, the National Firearms Association convened a press conference alongside Republican Senate nominee Richard Sterling to announce that they had just issued State Senator Katie Prairie a lifetime "F" rating—pointing to a viral town-hall clip from Alexandria where Katie had called the civilian MR-15 semiautomatic rifle a "weapon of war" and demanded universal background checks, federal extreme-risk red-flag laws, safe storage rules, and a ban on high-capacity magazines and assault weapons.

"Katie Prairie has no business representing Virginia in the United States Senate!" the NFA's chief lobbyist barked into a bank of television microphones while holding up a red cardstock mailer stamped with a giant black letter F over a photograph of Katie in her wheelchair. "She got a lifetime F grade from the National Firearms Association, she calls America's most popular rifle a weapon of war, she wants a government takeover of healthcare, she wants taxpayer-funded abortion on demand, and she led the charge in Richmond to put biological men in women's sports and men in women's restrooms!"

What the NFA lobbyist didn't realize was that Katie, Dad, and I were riding the eastbound Fairfax Link bus right down the boulevard outside their building at that exact moment.

Hearing the live broadcast on my mPhone earpiece, Katie glanced up at the automated destination sign above the windshield, reached up from her SwiftChair, and pulled the yellow stop-request cord for the concrete bus shelter directly across the street from the NFA headquarters lawn.

When the bus knelt and deployed its front ramp at 1:28 PM, six television camera crews who were packing up their tripods on the sidewalk did a collective double-take as forty-one-year-old Katie Prairie and I rolled down the bus ramp side by side with Dad right behind us.

"Senator Prairie!" the GNN and Beacon News correspondents shouted, sprinting across the crosswalk with their cameramen as the NFA lobbyist and Richard Sterling froze on the headquarters steps behind them. "The National Firearms Association just gave you a lifetime F grade for calling the MR-15 a weapon of war, and Richard Sterling just attacked your record on healthcare, abortion, and transgender kids in schools! Do you regret calling the MR-15 a weapon of war?"

Katie braked her SwiftChair right beside the Fairfax Link bus stop sign, took one of the red NFA "F-Grade" mailers from a reporter's hand, and held it straight up beside her lapel so every lens had a crystal-clear shot.

"Regret it?" Katie's voice rang out across the Fairfax boulevard, fearless and unapologetic. "I wear this F grade from the National Firearms Association like a badge of honor! In fact, Nate, let's frame this right on the wall of our campaign headquarters when we get home to Kempsville! Unlike the lobbyists inside that building who cash checks from gun manufacturers, I served on the Virginia Beach City Council in the exact Municipal Center complex where twelve innocent public servants and citizens were murdered in Building 2 in May 2019, and I know the families who lost their loved ones at Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute in Blacksburg. I have zero problem calling an MR-15 what it is: a weapon of war designed to inflict maximum human carnage on a battlefield. Keeping weapons of war out of Virginia classrooms, college campuses, and grocery stores so our children come home alive from school matters a whole lot more to me than pleasing the gun lobby in Fairfax!"

"And what about Richard Sterling's attacks on healthcare, abortion, and his claim that you want men in women's sports and men in women's restrooms?" the Beacon News reporter pressed.

"Let's go down his list one by one, because unlike the politicians hiding on those steps, I don't need a pollster to tell me what I believe," Katie answered without missing a beat. "First: yes, I proudly champion universal healthcare for every single person in the United States of America, because no family should go bankrupt to pay for insulin, cancer treatment, or a power wheelchair! Second: abortion is a deeply personal, private medical decision strictly between a woman and her doctor—probably the hardest decision a woman ever has to make—and no politician, prosecutor, or senator belongs in that exam room, which is why Virginia voters are going to vote YES on Question 1 this November! And third: when Restore the Republic politicians scream their disgusting talking point that I 'want men in women's sports and men in women's restrooms,' they are bullying vulnerable transgender kids—who make up less than one percent of the population and just want to go to school safely—to distract working Virginians while they vote to gut your Medicare, your Medicaid waivers, and your public schools! Transgender women are women, transgender men are men, and as I told the Virginia House of Delegates back in 2016 when they tried to pass a fifty-dollar bathroom-police bill, no woman or girl in Virginia should ever have to pull her pants down for a government official just to use the ladies' room!"

Behind the camera line, a Fairfax County high-school teacher waiting at the bus shelter burst into applause, followed by a dozen office workers on the sidewalk who walked straight over to Dad's clipboard to sign Katie's Eleventh District petition sheets right in front of the stunned NFA officials.

Five days later, when Katie, Dad, and I rolled off the JRTC Route 6 bus at Capitol Square in Richmond to file our primary petitions at the Virginia State Board of Elections, we didn't turn in ten thousand signatures. We turned in twenty-four thousand, eight hundred and twelve verified voter signatures—with more than twelve hundred verified voters in every single one of Virginia's eleven Congressional Districts.

"Watch how fast the unified validator reads the card, Dad," forty-one-year-old Katie smiled at eleven-thirty on Monday morning, May 18, 2026, as the three of us detrained from ARTS *The Patriot* at Roanoke's Third Street Station and rolled across the bus plaza to the waiting forty-five-foot Roanoke Valley Transit coach.

Because the passenger rail extension to Christiansburg Cambria Station at 800 Depot Street NE wouldn't open for regular train service until the following year in 2027, Roanoke Valley Transit operated both the official *ARTS Train Connector* and *The Roanoke Express* out of Third Street Station—linking downtown Roanoke down Interstate 81 to the Christiansburg Transit Center at Falling Branch, New River Valley Mall, and the CPI Transit Center in Blacksburg.

Three Systems. The Entire Valley.*—against the electronic reader, deducting the standard three-dollar RVT Express fare with a crisp green beep.

Forty minutes later, our *Roanoke Express* coach glided off Interstate 81 at Exit 118 into the ground-level eight-bay bus terminal beneath VDOT's eight-level, six-thousand-space garage at the Christiansburg Transit Center at Falling Branch, exited directly onto the grade-separated buses-only flyover ramp onto the US-460 Bypass without touching a single local traffic light, made its intermediate regional stop at the New River Valley Mall Transit Center outside Hudson's and The Spot, and pulled into the multi-bay CPI Transit Center in Blacksburg at 12:30 PM.

Continuing south down Business 460 into downtown Christiansburg to the Pepper Plaza Transit Center right next door to the Montgomery County Courthouse across from 105 Pepper Street and ValueMart, we transferred onto a thirty-five-foot low-floor bus on BT Route 2 (*The Christiansburg Local*, displaying <led>2 NEW RIVER VALLEY MALL</led> / <led>via AQUATIC CTR & CAMBRIA</led>). Rolling past the two Ironwood Collective apartment complexes on Wades Lane and turning down Mill Lane NE past the Blue Ridge Regional Aquatic Center onto Depot Street NE, we inspected the newly paved off-street bus loop at 800 Depot Street NE—Christiansburg Cambria Station—where Katie recorded a campaign video pledging that when ARTS *The Patriot* passenger trains began pulling into Cambria Station in 2027, she would use her seat in the United States Senate to protect federal passenger rail and rural public transit funding all the way to Bristol.

After riding BT Route 4 east out Roanoke Street past the Exit 118C hotels and the Simmons Road NE deviation through the CPI Christiansburg Campus—universally called "the Law School" by every rider on the bus—out to the purpose-built VDOT sixty-foot turnaround loop at Woodland Drive, and taking a loop on 100-percent fare-free Radford Transit aboard *The Radford Connector* down Prices Fork Road and Peppers Ferry Road through Belview, Centerville, and Fairlawn across the New River Bridge into Radford's McConnell Transit Center, we boarded Blue Ridge Transit Route 3 (*The Radford Link*) heading west out of Pepper Plaza along U.S. Route 11.

Halfway between Christiansburg and Radford along Lee Highway, the Route 3 operator tapped his brakes for the privately funded, covered bus shelter sitting on the one-dollar perpetual public transit easement that Daniel Brooks had conveyed at the foot of his family's driveway back in 2014.

When the front ramp folded down onto the concrete pad and Katie, Dad, and I rolled up the heated, zero-grade brushed-concrete walkway onto the front porch, the front double doors swung wide open—and the real-life heroes of "The Accessibility Project" came out to meet us, led by the original trio from Bennett Hall Room 214.

Thirty-year-old Jordan Shawn Kelly rolled his custom manual chair straight up to Katie and me to shake our hands, wearing his rectangular prescription glasses and behind-the-ear hearing aids, flanked on either side by his wife Aubrie Jean Kelly and Madison Elizabeth Scott, along with Zoë Wren Brooks, Lauren Nicole Barnes, Hannah Parker Anderson, Mark Shawn Anderson, Isabel Claire Dawson, Jessamine "Jess" Mercer, Sarah Kristyn Braithwaite, Jessica Gallagher, and Daniel, Laura, and Megan Brooks—every single one of them wearing royal-blue *Katie Prairie for U.S. Senate* lapel buttons.

Rolling side by side down the sweeping forty-eight-inch hallways lined with recessed oak wall bumpers and through the zero-threshold pocket doors into the communal kitchen—where dual-height islands let Jordan, Katie, and me roll right underneath the counter beside Laura, Aubrie Jean, and Madison—Katie looked around the room in quiet awe.

"We've spent twenty-five years designing our own living spaces around our wheelchairs," Katie said warmly, looking from the heated concrete bus-stop walkway outside to the dual-height kitchen islands and the first-floor grandparents' suite. "Rolling off a regular fixed-route Route 3 bus on Lee Highway straight into a house built like this feels like seeing the exact future we're fighting for."

Beside us at the accessible island, Jordan tapped a sentence into NeoEdit on his Pinnacle Vanguard Pro laptop and triggered EchoType's warm "Sydney" voice:

<aac>When Daniel and Laura built this compound on Lee Highway, they proved that universal design isn't a medical burden—it's what makes a home belong to everyone. Now let's go show the rest of Virginia.</aac>

"And we've already registered over fourteen hundred new student voters across CPI and Radford University for the June sixteenth primary," Zoë added, pulling up her tablet angled toward her eyes to read off the campus precinct tallies she, Aubrie Jean, and Mark had organized with the student disability union at Callahan Hall. "Preston Holloway's campaign sent a surrogate to Blacksburg last week who parked in a hundred-and-fifty-dollar VIP lot and left after twenty minutes. Meanwhile, every student on the Route 1 articulated buses and the Radford Connector knows you and Nate actually ride the bus and play our song at every stop."

"And speaking of buses," thirty-year-old Madison Elizabeth Scott smiled, tapping the Blue Ridge Go-Card clipped to her lanyard as Aubrie Jean and Jordan grinned beside her, "the three of us from Room 214 are riding down to Carroll County with you today! Bluewater is my hometown—and the Bluewater Bunker where my parents, my brother Bob, and my cousin Emily live is forty-five minutes down Interstate 81 and Interstate 77 from here. The next southbound *Maroon Express* pulls into the Christiansburg Transit Center at 1:55 PM. Ready to go show Bluewater what a real Senator looks like?"

#### Monday, May 18, 2026, 2:30 PM — Riding Bluewater Transit's Maroon Express Into Bluewater With the Room 214 Crew & Winning the June 16 Primary

Surrounding the bays stood Bluewater Transit's twenty-nine-foot and thirty-five-foot low-floor buses waiting to depart in every direction across the Blue Ridge plateau: the hourly Purple Line heading west on US-58 and US-221 to Galax Community College; the Gold Line heading northeast up US-221 through Dugspur and Willis to the Floyd County Courthouse (where riders connected down State Route 8 to Riner and BT Route 8); the Emerald Line heading east on US-58 across the Blue Ridge Parkway at Meadows of Dan and down scenic Lovers Leap into Stuart and the Martinsville Transit Center (where riders transferred directly onto Piedmont Regional Transit to Danville); the Silver Line heading south down US-52 and Interstate 77 past Fancy Gap to the state-line transfer hub; and a thirty-five-foot low-floor Mountain Empire Transit *Highlands Express* coach waiting to carry riders west toward Wytheville, Marion, Abingdon, and Bristol.

"People in Washington look at a county map of Southwest Virginia and write Carroll County off as deep-red Restore the Republic territory without ever setting foot here," Madison told Katie and me proudly as she, Aubrie Jean, and Jordan greeted Bluewater High School teachers, working parents, and Galax Community College nursing students who gathered around our three wheelchairs on the plaza while "The Accessibility Project" played crisp and bright from our portable speaker. If Bluewater were an independent city like Galax or Radford, it would show up as a solid Democratic blue circle on every election map in America."

Right there in front of the *Maroon Express* coach during the 2:45 PM pulse—with Katie, Jordan, and me parked side by side in our wheelchairs and Aubrie Jean and Madison handing out campaign literature and voter-registration clipboards beside Dad—Katie spent an hour talking eye-to-eye with Carroll County voters before we boarded Bluewater Transit's Emerald Line east across Lovers Leap through Meadows of Dan and Stuart into the Martinsville Transit Center and transferred onto Piedmont Regional Transit eastbound along U.S. Route 58 into Danville.

Waiting for our bus under the Danville transfer shelter—surrounded by television camera crews from Roanoke, Lynchburg, and Danville who had gotten word an hour earlier that a political bombshell was about to drop—were twenty-four-year-old Sam, Mandy, and Sarah Hawkins, our three favorite autistic House Pages from February 2016 whom Katie had hired onto her Senate of Virginia staff as soon as they enrolled at Central Virginia University, standing side by side with their Aunt Marge Callaway and their maternal uncle, retired Republican House Majority Leader Richard Callaway.

For more than two decades in the Virginia House of Delegates—culminating in his years wielding the floor gavel in Richmond as Republican House Majority Leader—Richard Callaway had been a household name in Virginia politics and the undisputed conservative lion of Southside Virginia. Every county sheriff, poultry and tobacco farmer, small-business owner, and civic club from Martinsville and Danville to South Boston knew Richard by his first name. As the Piedmont Regional Transit operator lowered the front hydraulic ramp and Katie, Jordan, and I rolled down onto the Danville sidewalk beside Dad, Aubrie Jean, and Madison, Uncle Richard stepped forward in his navy blazer, shook Dad's hand and mine, leaned down to hug Katie warmly, and peeled the paper backing off a royal-blue *Katie Prairie for U.S. Senate* sticker—pressing it squarely onto his left lapel right in front of the rolling television cameras.

An audible gasp rippled through the cluster of Roanoke and Danville political reporters as Uncle Richard stepped up to the microphone stand with Aunt Marge and the triplets standing directly behind Katie's SwiftChair.

"Everybody along Route 58 knows I served twenty-four years in the House of Delegates as a conservative Republican, and that I had the honor of serving as your Republican House Majority Leader in Richmond," Uncle Richard said, his steady Southside baritone carrying across the entire transit plaza. "Marge and I don't agree with State Senator Katie Prairie on every partisan roll-call vote, and Katie has never once asked us to. Eleven years ago, after Marge and I took legal custody of our thirteen-year-old autistic triplet nephew and nieces—Sam, Mandy, and Sarah—after they survived unspeakable abuse, our kids went up to Richmond to serve as eighth-grade House Pages. When a loud, crowded corridor in the General Assembly Building overwhelmed our kids during their first week on the job, it wasn't the loudmouth politicians preening on cable television about family values who stopped to protect them. It was Katie Prairie and her twin brother Nate, who parked their two wheelchairs around our kids like a shield, sat with them at eye level until their breathing steadied, and rode the Route 6 city bus with our whole family to supper on Broad Street."

Uncle Richard rested a proud hand on Sam's shoulder while Aunt Marge squeezed Mandy's and Sarah's hands.

"Four years later, the day Sam, Mandy, and Sarah graduated high school right here in Southside and started college at Central Virginia University, Senator Katie Prairie kept her promise and hired all three of them to work side by side in her Senate office so they would never be separated," Uncle Richard continued, pointing back toward the Piedmont Regional Transit bus idling at the curb. "And that bus sitting behind us—connecting Martinsville and Danville—is running down Route 58 today because Katie Prairie took a transit bill that three eighth-grade Pages from Southside wrote for their Mock Session ten years ago and fought in the Senate of Virginia until it was funded into law. So when Washington consultants for Preston Holloway or Richard Sterling roll through Southside in chartered luxury buses telling you that Katie Prairie can't win rural voters or doesn't care about families, don't buy a word of it. Marge and I are crossing party lines to endorse Katie Prairie for the United States Senate—because for ten years, Katie Prairie has had our family's back."

In the front row of the press scrum, a Roanoke political correspondent thrust his microphone forward, almost tripping over his own camera cable.

"Leader Callaway, are you leaving the Republican Party?" the reporter shouted.

"No," Uncle Richard answered flatly.

"But you're endorsing the Democratic nominee for the United States Senate!"

"I am."

"How do you reconcile those two things after twenty-four years as a Republican in the House of Delegates?"

Uncle Richard looked straight into the cluster of television lenses, his jaw set with the quiet granite authority of a man who had counted votes and governed a real legislative chamber for nearly a quarter of a century.

"I didn't leave the Republican Party. The Republican Party left me," Uncle Richard said, and you could hear every camera shutter on the sidewalk freeze. "The people of Danville and Southside Virginia didn't send me to Richmond for twenty-four years to serve a President, and they didn't send me there to serve the Republican Party. They sent me there to serve them. They didn't elect me because they wanted to watch Republicans and Democrats scream at each other on cable television—they sent me there to solve problems, pass budgets, maintain our roads and bridges, fund our schools, support our farmers and small businesses, and make sure the Commonwealth of Virginia still functions tomorrow morning. Twenty-four years in Richmond teaches you that ideological speeches don't fill potholes. Sometimes solving problems meant working with Republicans, and sometimes it meant working with Democrats—and one of those Democrats was Katie Prairie."

Uncle Richard glanced down at my sister with a dry, affectionate glint in his eye.

"Katie and I disagreed plenty—if she tells you otherwise, don't believe her," Richard added, making Katie laugh aloud from her SwiftChair along with the entire crowd at the bus shelter. "But I never once doubted that she came to Richmond for the exact same reason I did: to do the work. Ten years ago on the floor of the House of Delegates, when one of my own members brought a badly drafted bathroom bill onto the calendar and tried to call Katie out of order for asking how the Commonwealth was supposed to enforce it, I stood up as Republican Majority Leader and told the Speaker that the Gentlewoman from Virginia Beach didn't introduce anatomy into the legislation—the bill did. Because I learned the hard way in Richmond that when Katie Prairie reads a bill line by line and says there is a problem with how it actually works, you had better hear her out before assuming she's wrong. I've supported Republican Presidents, I've opposed Democratic Presidents, and I've probably been angry at every Governor Virginia has had at least once. That's politics. Nobody elected me to swear personal allegiance to another politician. First the Liberty Tax Movement came along and started screaming that any conservative who compromised to pass a budget was a traitor to be primaried. And then Restore the Republic took over and inverted everything our party ever stood for—replacing principles with a single loyalty test to Garrett Thorne. I'll tell you right here on camera: before 2016, I had never voted for a Democratic candidate in my entire life. Not once. Then Garrett Thorne came down that escalator, mocked disabled Americans on a stage, and demanded personal fealty above the Constitution. In 2016, in 2020, and in 2024, Marge and I voted for the Democrat at the top of the presidential ballot—not because those were votes for the Democrat, but because Garrett Thorne's name was on the ballot and I refused to put that man in the White House. Back then, I still told myself it was just one man at the top of the ticket. And for a man who spent twenty-four years working inside a Capitol alongside clerks, custodians, Capitol Police officers, and thirteen-year-old Pages like my own kids, watching a mob attack the United States Capitol on January sixth while lawmakers and teenaged Pages were locked inside carrying out a constitutional duty was the day I knew that movement had nothing to do with conservatism. Then came our Virginia Governor's race last November, in 2025. Garrett Thorne's name wasn't on the ballot in 2025—that was an election for Governor of the Commonwealth I spent twenty-four years serving. The Governor of Virginia should answer to the People of the Commonwealth of Virginia, not to President Garrett Thorne! Walking into my Danville precinct and voting against the Republican nominee for Governor of Virginia was the hardest ballot I ever cast, and the first one that truly crossed the Rubicon for me—because when our statewide nominee aligned with Thorne and promised to answer to the White House instead of the People of the Commonwealth of Virginia, I realized this sickness wasn't just one man in Washington anymore. Any candidate who aligns themselves with Garrett Thorne has to learn at the ballot box that Virginia does not belong to him. Now Restore the Republic calls me a RINO and an 'Enemy of the Republic' because I refuse to pledge personal fealty to Garrett Thorne—when the whole point of a constitutional republic is that no citizen owes personal loyalty to a President in the first place! And when they call Katie Prairie an enemy of the Republic, I ask them one simple question: *Have you ever actually worked with her? No? I have.* No Super PAC commercial can tell me she hates families when I've watched her take care of my kids for ten years, and no cable pundit can tell me she hates rural Virginia when she listened to three thirteen-year-olds from Danville talk about public transportation. In 2016, 2020, and 2024, I voted against Garrett Thorne himself. In 2025, I voted against a Republican candidate for Governor to send a message that aligning yourself with Garrett Thorne costs you Virginia. And this year is different again—because this year, I am not just voting against Thorne or his movement in the privacy of a voting booth. I am standing here in broad daylight voting wholeheartedly *for* Katie Prairie. I'm still a Republican. Katie's still a Democrat. I haven't changed parties. I've simply reached an age where I don't need anybody's permission to recognize a good public servant."

On the evening bus ride back up U.S. Route 58 toward Bluewater to catch the northbound *Maroon Express*—while video of the former Republican House Majority Leader declaring *"I didn't leave the Republican Party; the Republican Party left me"* at a Danville bus shelter led every six o'clock television newscast from Roanoke to Norfolk and Washington—Sam, Mandy, and Sarah watched our rural Southside traffic and voter-pledge numbers vertical-spike on my laptop screen and grinned in unison, coining a phrase that every political desk in Virginia would be repeating by November: "the Uncle Richard Effect."

Four weeks later—on Primary Night, Tuesday, June 16, 2026—the political establishment in Washington and Richmond learned the hard way what happens when you dismiss the people who ride the bus.

Despite retiring Senator Martin Warren's handpicked corporate candidate Preston Holloway spending fourteen million dollars in Super PAC television ads, voters across all eleven Congressional Districts—powered by historic turnout in Hampton Roads, Richmond, the CPI and Radford corridors, Bluewater, Charlottesville, and working-class neighborhoods across Northern Virginia—delivered a seismic upset.

Inside the quiet bus cabin, every passenger within five rows leaned in to listen. Katie didn't hedge a single word or change a single syllable from what she said in Virginia Beach or Fairfax.

You know the difference between a deer rifle and a battlefield weapon, and keeping weapons of war out of our children's classrooms so grandkids come home alive from school is common sense."

The clinic nurse in the navy scrubs nodded firmly beside the miner.

"Second, let's talk about universal healthcare and abortion," Katie continued. "Right here in Southwest Virginia, Appalachian Mountain Health has closed rural maternity wards and emergency rooms while private health-insurance CEOs cash thirty-million-dollar bonus checks and Appalachian Electric Grid hikes your winter electric bill by forty dollars a month. When a pregnant mother in Wise County or Lee County has to drive ninety minutes over a mountain in winter just to reach an obstetrician, or when a woman faces the most heartbreaking medical complication of her life, that decision belongs strictly between a woman and her doctor—never a politician in Washington or Richmond. And when a retired coal miner with black lung or a diabetic bus rider gets denied a prescription or a wheelchair repair by an insurance bureaucrat, that's why I fight for universal healthcare—so healthcare is a basic human right for every American from Virginia Beach to Big Stone Gap."

Katie leaned forward an inch in her SwiftChair, her voice dropping to an earnest, unmistakable intensity.

"And finally, let's talk about why Richard Sterling and Conrad Drayton spend millions of dollars screaming on television that I 'want men in women's sports and men in women's restrooms,'" Katie said. "My twin brother Nate and I have used these power wheelchairs since the third Friday of September 2001, when we were sixteen-year-old juniors in high school. We know what it feels like to be stared at, mocked by the President of the United States as 'Broken Katie Prairie,' and locked out of buildings just for existing in the bodies we were born with. Transgender kids make up less than one percent of the population, and all they want is to go to school and live their lives without grown politicians bullying them or hiring bathroom police. The Restore the Republic billionaires scream about transgender kids every night on cable news for one reason: they hope that if they keep you angry enough at a sixteen-year-old kid you've never met, you won't notice Richard Sterling and Conrad Drayton voting to cut eight hundred billion dollars out of Medicaid, rural hospitals, and black-lung disability clinics!"

"Look out the right window, Katie—there's Barton Hall and the front gate on Roosevelt Avenue," I murmured on Saturday morning, September 19, 2026, as our Shenandoah Valley Transit Route 250 Connector bus rolled through Fishersville between Waynesboro and Staunton in Augusta County.
