![Inside a Dirksen Senate Office Building transition room overlooking the Capitol dome, forty-one-year-old U.S. Senator-Elect Katie Prairie and her twin brother Nate sit side by side in their compact SwiftChair power wheelchairs auditing raw HTML and WCAG accessibility failures on their MagnaBook Pro laptops over a conference speakerphone while two beltway digital contractor executives sit across the table sweating and shell-shocked]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/dec_2026_prairie_senate_gov_raw_html_wcag_audit_takedown.jpg)

#### Friday, December 11, 2026, 10:00 AM — Static MagnaPad Slides & The Minified ZIP Trick in Dirksen

"You don't need to worry your head about the technical weeds, Senator-Elect—our engineering team in Rosslyn handles all the magic behind the curtain! Just tell us if you like this shade of Senate navy blue on the banner!"

Sitting across the polished mahogany conference table in our temporary transition suite in the Dirksen Senate Office Building, Bradford Vance—the Senior Account Director for Capitol Digital Solutions, one of the beltway IT contractors approved by the Office of the Senate Sergeant at Arms to build official United States Senate constituent websites—beamed with patronizing self-satisfaction as he tapped a static PDF slide deck on his MagnaPad tablet. Beside him sat his junior project manager, Evan, while a black triangular conference speakerphone sat in the center of the table with their lead developers dialed in live from their Rosslyn office across the Potomac.

Four days earlier, on Monday, December 7, the Virginia State Board of Elections had met in Richmond under Code of Virginia Section 24.2-679 to formally certify the November 3 general election results, and the Governor had transmitted Katie's signed Certificate of Election to the Secretary of the United States Senate.

Now, on Friday morning, Katie and I had ridden the morning ARTS train up from Norfolk, detrained on the mobile lift at Alexandria to drop our overnight bags at Dad's two-story brick house on Sunset Drive—where our newly installed interior vertical platform wheelchair lift was already humming smoothly between the first floor and our upstairs three-desk office in Bedroom 4—and taken the Capital Transit Yellow Line across the Charles R. Fenwick Bridge into the District for our ten o'clock website sign-off meeting.

Under United States Senate Internet Services rules, a Senator's official government constituent website had to be strictly separated from our campaign website, which Katie and I had coded ourselves in PHP, and hosted inside the Sergeant at Arms environment using an approved vendor template.

Watching Bradford talk down to my forty-one-year-old twin sister in the exact overly bright, sing-song voice that non-technical consultants often used when they saw two adults sitting in compact SwiftChair power wheelchairs, I didn't say a word. I just kept my hands resting lightly beside my closed MagnaBook Pro and waited for Katie to lower the boom.

"I don't approve websites from static PDF pictures on a MagnaPad, Bradford," Katie said evenly, folding her hands in the lap of her royal-blue blazer without even glancing at his tablet screen. "Before I put my name on a federal domain that sixty thousand disabled veterans, blind commuters, and working families across Virginia are going to use to request constituent casework, my brother Nate and I want to audit the raw HTML, CSS, and JavaScript source code. Please have your build team on the speakerphone drop the staging repository onto our transition VLAN share folder right now."

Bradford blinked twice, his rehearsed sales smile flickering as he exchanged an amused glance with Evan. Clearly, he assumed some twenty-two-year-old campaign intern had fed the incoming Senator a technical buzzword to sound tough.

"Well, Senator-Elect, normally congressional offices just sign the design approval form and let our certified engineers handle the code," Bradford chuckled condescendingly, leaning toward the triangular speakerphone in the center of the table. "Trevor, are you and the build team hearing this in Rosslyn? The Senator-Elect wants to see a copy of the code before she signs off. Go ahead and drop a ZIP file of the build into her transition share drive so we can check that box."

Over the speakerphone, we heard a muffled snicker from the Rosslyn engineering bullpen—the unmistakable sound of developers who thought a United States Senator wouldn't know an HTML tag from a spreadsheet macro—followed by Trevor's voice:

"Sure thing, Brad. Give me ten seconds... alright, I just dropped *prairie-senate-prod-bundle.zip* into the Dirksen transition share folder for her."

***

#### Friday, December 11, 2026, 10:15 AM — "Why Is a U.S. Senator Speaking Our Exact Engineering Language?"

Katie and I opened the unbranded matte-aluminum lids of our two MagnaBook Pro laptops at the exact same second.

Without touching a mouse, I mounted the local Senate transition VLAN share in my MagnaOS terminal, unzipped *prairie-senate-prod-bundle.zip* into our shared workspace, and pushed the extracted directory straight across our local peer link to Katie's machine.

Beside me, Katie hit Command and Space, launched Quantum Code—QCode—and opened the extracted folder across two vertical editor panes.

Bradford's patronizing smile vanished the instant he saw the dark syntax-highlighted IDE panes snap open across both of our screens. "Wait... is that Quantum Code?"

Neither Katie nor I answered him, because both of us were staring at the three files Trevor had packed into the ZIP archive: *index.min.html*, *styles.min.css*, and *app.min.js*.

Every single file had been run through an aggressive production minifier. All line breaks, indentation, and whitespace had been stripped out, crushing thousands of lines of code into a single continuous horizontal wall of characters, with every JavaScript variable and function mangled into single-letter identifiers without a single source map in the directory.

Sitting in her SwiftChair, Katie's blue eyes narrowed to ice. She leaned six inches forward toward the black triangular speakerphone in the center of the mahogany table.

"Trevor," Katie said, her voice cutting through the speakerphone mesh with razor-sharp precision. "Did your build team seriously just send a United States Senator-Elect a webpack-minified production bundle with stripped whitespace, mangled single-letter AST identifiers, concatenated CSS rules, and zero source maps because you thought I wouldn't know the difference between compiled build artifacts and raw source code?"

Across the table, Bradford's jaw literally dropped open.

Over the speakerphone, the muffled background chatter in the Rosslyn engineering bullpen stopped dead. For four full seconds, the only sound coming through the speaker was stunned, ragged breathing.

"Uh... wait—who is this speaking?" Trevor stammered over the line, completely bewildered. "Brad, did the Senator-Elect bring an outside DevOps engineer from the Sergeant at Arms office into the room?"

"No, Trevor, this is Senator-Elect Katie Prairie speaking to you, and my twin brother Nate is sitting right beside me with the exact same minified garbage open in Quantum Code," Katie snapped. "I didn't ask for your minified production output. I asked for your raw, unminified source repository—the actual human-readable HTML templates, uncompiled stylesheets, and unminified JavaScript controllers before your bundler strips the tree. Drop the raw unminified repository into the VLAN folder in the next sixty seconds, or I am calling the Senate Sergeant at Arms contract officer to cancel your task order before lunch."

"Yes, ma'am—right away, Senator-Elect! Exporting the raw source branch right now!" Trevor blurted out over the speakerphone, his voice pitching up an octave as frantic keyboard clacking echoed from Rosslyn.

Across the mahogany table, a bead of sweat rolled down Bradford Vance's temple as he stared in utter disbelief at a forty-one-year-old Senator in a power wheelchair who had just dismantled his lead engineer in fluent full-stack developer shop talk.

***

#### Friday, December 11, 2026, 10:25 AM — Twin Fury Over Barely Commented Code & Every WCAG Failure in the Book

Forty seconds later, a new archive—*prairie-senate-raw-src.zip*—appeared in the network share.

I extracted the raw source tree in terminal, opened *header.html*, *casework-form.html*, *styles.css*, and *nav-controller.js* across my Quantum Code workspace, and glanced over at Katie as she opened the exact same files on her MagnaBook Pro.

The longer the two of us scrolled down those unminified files, the hotter our faces burned. Within two minutes, both Katie and I were flat-out furious.

![Inside a Dirksen Senate Office Building transition room overlooking the Capitol dome, forty-one-year-old U.S. Senator-Elect Katie Prairie and her twin brother Nate sit side by side in their compact SwiftChair power wheelchairs auditing raw HTML and WCAG accessibility failures on their MagnaBook Pro laptops over a conference speakerphone while two beltway digital contractor executives sit across the table sweating and shell-shocked]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/dec_2026_prairie_senate_gov_raw_html_wcag_audit_takedown.jpg)

"Nate, look at *nav-controller.js* and *casework-form.html*," Katie said, her voice vibrating with the cold, surgical fury of a senior software architect who had just uncovered fraud. "There are almost no code comments in this entire repository!"

"Four thousand two hundred lines of unminified HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, and I just ran a grep across the whole source tree," I said angrily, leaning toward the speakerphone so Trevor and his entire Rosslyn team could hear every word. "You have exactly three inline comment lines in the entire project—and one of them on line eighty-four of *nav-controller.js* literally says *TODO: fix keyboard trap later* dated four years ago! There isn't a single architectural block comment at the top of your files, zero function docblocks explaining your state logic, and zero inline comments documenting your DOM event listeners. How is any developer supposed to maintain taxpayer-funded code that isn't even commented?!"

"And the reason you tried to hide it behind a minified ZIP file is even worse," Katie said, pointing her finger straight at her laptop screen while Bradford and Evan shrank back into their leather chairs across the table. "This website as written fails almost every single WCAG accessibility pointer there is!"

Over the speakerphone, Trevor tried to stammer a defense: "S-Senator-Elect, I assure you our template passed our internal visual QA check—"

"Don't you dare talk to me about a visual QA check when I am looking at your raw DOM tree line by line!" Katie fired back. "Let's start at the top of *header.html*. You have no skip-navigation link anywhere in the header, which violates WCAG 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks and forces every keyboard and switch user to tab through forty-two navigation links on every single page load. Your heading hierarchy jumps straight from an H1 banner title to an H4 subheader because your designer used heading tags for font sizing instead of semantic structure, violating WCAG 1.3.1 Info and Relationships. And look at line forty-seven of *header.html*!"

Katie read the offending markup aloud like a prosecutor reading an indictment into the federal record:

"You wrapped the entire *Help With a Federal Agency* constituent dropdown menu inside nested generic div tags with an inline *onclick* attribute—zero semantic button element, zero *aria-expanded* state, zero *aria-controls* binding, and no *tabindex*! Do you know what that means? It means a blind veteran using a screen reader, or a quadriplegic Virginian navigating with a Sip-and-Puff switch or a keyboard Tab key, cannot even open the menu to ask their United States Senator for help with the VA!"

"And look at line one hundred twelve of *styles.css*," I added fiercely, scrolling my right-hand pane down the stylesheet. "Somebody on your team wrote a global wildcard rule setting focus outlines to *none* with an *!important* flag across the entire website! You literally stripped the visible keyboard focus ring off every link and form control on the page—a blatant violation of WCAG 2.4.7 Focus Visible and federal Section 508 law!"

"Wait until you hear what happens on *casework-form.html* at line two hundred four," Katie said grimly.

That page was the Federal Casework Privacy Act Release Form—the most important page on any Senator's website, where disabled constituents, seniors, and military families submit requests for help with delayed Social Security checks, Medicare power-wheelchair prior authorizations, and veterans' benefits.

"Instead of associating explicit HTML label elements with your form inputs using a *for* attribute, your developers just typed instructions into light-gray *placeholder* attributes colored hex 999999 on a white background—a 2.6-to-1 contrast ratio that fails WCAG 1.4.3 Contrast Minimum AND fails WCAG 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions," Katie said. "And because you stripped the labels, listen to what a blind constituent actually hears when they try to fill out your form."

Katie pressed Command and F5 on her MagnaBook Pro keyboard to turn on MagnaVoice—the built-in MagnaOS screen reader—turned her laptop speakers up to maximum volume right beside the conference speakerphone, and hit the Tab key four times.

Across the mahogany table and straight through the open speakerphone line into the Rosslyn engineering bullpen, the synthesized MagnaVoice voice echoed in the dead-silent room:

*"Edit text, blank. Edit text, blank. Image, hero-banner-final-v3.jpg. Unlabeled button."*

Nobody on the other side of the table or on the speakerphone dared to breathe.

Katie pressed Command and F5 to silence MagnaVoice and looked straight across the table at Bradford before addressing the speakerphone.

"S-Senator-Elect..." Trevor whispered over the speakerphone, sounding completely shell-shocked. "How on earth do you and your brother know how to audit raw unminified HTML, CSS specificity, DOM accessibility trees, and WCAG pointers like senior software engineers?"

"Because my brother Nate and I learned how to write raw HTML in seventh grade at Morrison Middle School back in 1997—which is what inspired our dad to go back to school at the Community College of Hampton Roads to earn his computer science degree," Katie said, her voice ringing with every year of our lives. "We learned Quantum Basic 6.0 alongside our dad in 2001, we rolled into the Web Applications Developer lab at Roosevelt Rehabilitation Center in Fishersville in March 2007 after refusing to let their evaluators steer two associate-degree holders into being ValueMart door greeters, we copied the entire PHP and SQL curriculum onto our own laptops when VITA's state computers were too locked down to run modern code, and we have spent the last nineteen years building and maintaining production websites and desktop applications from these two wheelchairs! Did your company actually sign a federal VPAT certifying to the Senate Sergeant at Arms that this uncommented, inaccessible garbage complies with Section 508 of the Rehabilitation Act, or did you just assume a Senator in a wheelchair wouldn't know how to read your source code?"

Bradford swallowed hard, wiping his forehead with a linen handkerchief. "Senator-Elect, I... we will assign a remediation sprint immediately—"

"You don't need to assign a remediation sprint, because Nate and I don't trust your team to write clean code without supervision," Katie said, her fingers already flying across her mechanical laptop keyboard in tandem with mine. "Sit quietly for twenty-five minutes while we show you how professional Web Applications Developers write and document accessible code."

For the next twenty-five minutes, while Bradford and Evan sat frozen in their suits and the entire Rosslyn engineering bullpen watched our live screen-share in humbled silence, Katie and I refactored their core templates in Quantum Code. We replaced every non-semantic div dropdown with proper semantic HTML5 nav and button elements bound to clean ARIA state toggles, restored high-contrast focus-visible rings, bound explicit label elements and 4.5-to-1 contrast tokens to every single input on the constituent casework form, and padded the top of every file and every single logic block with comprehensive architectural block comments and inline WCAG explanations so any future developer could read and maintain it.

At 10:55 AM, I committed our changes to a clean Git patch file—*wcag-508-and-documentation-fixes.diff*—and pushed it straight back into the Rosslyn staging repository.

"Merge our pull request, apply that exact commenting and WCAG 2.2 AA standard to every remaining subpage in the repository, and have the unminified branch ready for our second inspection by Monday at noon," Katie told the speakerphone as she closed the lid of her MagnaBook Pro.

By the time Katie and I unlocked our wheelchair brakes and rolled out into the Dirksen corridor toward the Capital Transit elevator, word was already ripping through every IT vendor and Senate chief of staff on Capitol Hill: *Whatever you do, never send minified code, uncommented spaghetti, or a fake accessibility report to Senator Prairie's office—she and her brother will demand your raw unminified repo, open it in Quantum Code, and debug you live on speakerphone.*

### Part 2: Article IV Section 4, Hand-Delivering Her Resignation in Richmond, & The Writ of Special Election

**Date:** 2026-12-15 at 14:00 America/New_York

![Inside the historic neoclassical Clerk's Office of the Senate of Virginia at the State Capitol in Richmond, forty-one-year-old State Senator and U.S. Senator-Elect Katie Prairie sits in her compact SwiftChair power wheelchair alongside her twin brother Nate in his matching powerchair and formally hands her gold-sealed parchment resignation letter across the mahogany counter to the Clerk of the Senate]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/dec_2026_richmond_state_senate_resignation_hand_delivery.jpg)

#### Tuesday, December 15, 2026, 2:00 PM — The Clerk's Office of the Senate of Virginia & The Dual-Office Holding Ban

"It feels strange holding this envelope in my hand after twelve years in Capitol Square, Nate," Katie said quietly as our two compact SwiftChair power wheelchairs rolled side by side down the polished black-and-white marble corridor of the Virginia State Capitol in Richmond toward the mahogany doors of the Office of the Clerk of the Senate of Virginia.

Resting across my sister's lap on top of her leather portfolio was a heavy cream-parchment letter embossed with the gold seal of the Senate of Virginia and signed in her crisp blue fountain-pen script.

Under Article IV, Section 4 of the Constitution of the Commonwealth of Virginia—as well as Code of Virginia Section 2.2-2800 and the Incompatibility Clause of Article I, Section 6 of the Constitution of the United States—no person holding any office under the United States government is permitted to hold a seat in either house of the Virginia General Assembly. Even more importantly to Katie, the 2027 Session of the Virginia General Assembly was scheduled to gavel in at noon on the second Wednesday in January—Wednesday, January 13, 2027, just ten days after her federal swearing-in in Washington.

If Katie had waited until January 3 to vacate her State Senate seat, the citizens of Virginia Beach and Chesapeake in her district would have been left with an empty chair on the floor of the Senate of Virginia during the opening weeks of the legislative session. By formally submitting her resignation today, on Tuesday, December 15, 2026, she was giving the Lieutenant Governor and the Governor of Virginia the legal window required under the Code of Virginia to immediately issue a Writ of Special Election for early January so her successor could be elected and seated on Opening Day in Richmond.

When we rolled through the tall wooden doorway into the neoclassical Clerk's Office—where white marble Ionic columns framed the floor-to-ceiling bookshelves of Virginia Acts of Assembly dating back to Thomas Jefferson's design—the gray-haired Clerk of the Senate stepped out from behind his high podium and walked straight over to the lowered, wheelchair-accessible mahogany counter that had been built during Katie's very first term in the upper chamber.

![Inside the historic neoclassical Clerk's Office of the Senate of Virginia at the State Capitol in Richmond, forty-one-year-old State Senator and U.S. Senator-Elect Katie Prairie sits in her compact SwiftChair power wheelchair alongside her twin brother Nate in his matching powerchair and formally hands her gold-sealed parchment resignation letter across the mahogany counter to the Clerk of the Senate]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/dec_2026_richmond_state_senate_resignation_hand_delivery.jpg)

"Madam Chair," the Clerk said softly, his voice thick with genuine affection as he looked from Katie to me beside the blue Flag of the Commonwealth of Virginia. "Or I suppose in nineteen days I have to start calling you Senator Prairie of the United States Senate."

"In this building, William, you can just call me Katie," my sister smiled warmly, lifting the gold-sealed cream parchment letter from her lap and extending it across the accessible mahogany counter. "Pursuant to Article IV, Section 4 of the Constitution of Virginia, here is my formal signed letter resigning my seat in the Senate of Virginia, together with the duplicate copy for the Lieutenant Governor so the Writ of Special Election can be issued this afternoon."

With a respectful bow of his head, the Clerk accepted the parchment letter in both hands, stamped the official time and date of receipt onto the ledger copy, and handed the stamped receipt back across the counter to Katie.

"Twelve years between the House of Delegates and the Senate of Virginia, Katie," the Clerk said, resting his hand over the signed parchment. "When you and Nate first rolled through the Bell Tower entrance in January of 2014, half the historic committee rooms in this Capitol complex didn't even have flush thresholds or accessible turning radiuses, and nobody in Richmond thought a first-term Delegate from Virginia Beach could force a subcommittee to table its own bill with a single three-minute speech. This Capitol is a vastly fairer, more accessible house of the people because the two of you were here."

"And we're holding you to keeping every single ramp and every single late-night transit grant intact while we're up in Washington, William," Katie said, her blue eyes shining as she shook his hand across the mahogany counter.

***

#### Tuesday, December 15, 2026, 3:15 PM — One Last Roll Down the Senate Ramp & The Bus to Main Street Station

![Outside the classical white columns of the Virginia State Capitol in Richmond on December 15, 2026, 41-year-old U.S. Senator-Elect Katie Prairie and her twin brother Nate roll their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs toward the deployed front ramp of a kneeling blue-and-white JRTC city bus signed for Main Street Station with their 68-year-old father David walking beside them as Katie looks back one final time at the Capitol.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/dec_2026_richmond_capitol_square_bus_stop_farewell_katie_nate_david.jpg)

After leaving the Clerk's Office, Katie and I took the elevator to the second floor and rolled quietly into the empty gallery aisle of the Senate of Virginia Chamber.

The afternoon December sunlight slanted through the tall arched windows across the crimson carpet and the forty mahogany desks of the upper chamber. Up at the front aisle, right beside the Committee on Rehabilitation and Social Services chair desk that Katie had occupied since January 2020, sat the permanent, custom-milled mahogany wheelchair ramp leading up to the Clerk's well and the dais—installed so seamlessly into the historic woodwork that any visitor looking down from the Capitol gallery would assume it had always been there.

Sitting beside my sister in the quiet chamber, I reached across our armrests and took her left hand.

"Look at that ramp, Katie," I said softly. "First the Virginia Beach City Council chamber at the Municipal Center in 2011. Then the House of Delegates subcommittees in 2014. Then the Senate of Virginia in 2020. And last month in Washington, after Senator Tess Dunmore showed us the chamber ramp she fought for back in 2017, the Senate carpenters finished raising your mahogany desk on riser blocks and widening the dual-chair bays so there are two women in wheelchairs on the floor of the United States Senate."

Katie looked at the mahogany ramp in front of her old desk, then turned her head to smile at me.

"Every time we had to fight for a ramp, Nate, people in suits acted like we were asking for a personal favor," Katie said quietly. "We weren't building those ramps just for me. We were building them so the next kid in a SwiftChair who rides a bus to a field trip at the Virginia State Capitol—or the United States Capitol—never has to sit at the bottom of a staircase wondering if the law belongs to them too."

Twenty minutes later, after carrying the last cardboard banker's box from her constituent office—holding nothing more than our framed copy of the Constitution of the Commonwealth of Virginia and our twin blue hot-chocolate mugs—out the accessible basement entrance onto Bank Street, we didn't call a state pool car or a limousine.

Just as we had done every winter session in Richmond for twelve years, United States Senator-Elect Katie Prairie and I rolled our two compact SwiftChairs half a block down the brick sidewalk to the regular JRTC public transit bus stop at Ninth and Main, waited alongside the four o'clock state office clerks and hospital workers, rolled up the front bus ramp into the dual wheelchair bays, and tapped our fare cards for the seven-minute ride down the hill to Richmond Main Street Station to catch the evening ARTS train home to Norfolk.

## First Train from Norfolk, Swearing In on the Constitution, & Strings Attached for RRC

### Part 1: Three Business Class Tickets for Free Café Car Drinks & The Mobile Lift at Alexandria

**Date:** 2027-01-03 at 05:00 America/New_York

![Forty-one-year-old U.S. Senator-Elect Katie Prairie sits in her compact SwiftChair power wheelchair on the yellow-and-silver ARTS Mobile Lift outside the open ARTS Business Class door at Alexandria Union Station while her twin brother Nate in his matching powerchair holding a Café Car cup and their proud father David wait on the low-level red-brick platform below]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/jan_2027_alx_arts_mobile_lift_senator_elect_katie_prairie.jpg)

#### Sunday, January 3, 2027, 5:00 AM — Norfolk Station & Three Business Class Tickets for Free Café Car Drinks

"Make sure you keep your receipt folded in your wallet, Katie—that Business Class barcode gets the two of you unlimited free ginger ale and gets me hot coffee out of the Café Car all the way up to Alexandria," our sixty-eight-year-old dad said with a grin at five o'clock in the morning, holding his leather garment bag in one hand as the uniformed ARTS station attendant finished cranking our second compact SwiftChair power wheelchair up the yellow mobile lift into the warm stainless-steel vestibule at Norfolk Station.

Outside on the low-level brick platform beside Harbor Park, the January predawn wind off the Elizabeth River was cold enough to turn our breath into white plumes under the station lamps. Inside the front end of the combined ARTS Business Class and Café Car, the air smelled like fresh-brewed dark roast coffee, warm baseboard heat, and polished vinyl headrests.

It was Sunday, January 3, 2027—Opening Day of the One Hundred Twentieth Congress of the United States. In exactly seven hours, at twelve o'clock noon in the Chamber of the United States Senate in Washington, D.C., my forty-one-year-old twin sister was going to raise her right hand and be sworn in as the newest United States Senator from the Commonwealth of Virginia.

Four days earlier, on Wednesday afternoon, a polite young protocol liaison from the Office of the Senate Sergeant at Arms had called our transition office in Virginia Beach to ask which flight Senator-Elect Katie Prairie was taking into Washington National Airport, or whether Capitol Police needed to stage a black SUV motorcade at the VIP circular drive outside Washington Union Station.

Katie had looked across her desk at me, smiled, and given the young man the unvarnished truth.

*"Neither,"* my sister had told him over the speakerphone. *"My brother Nate, my dad, and I are taking the first morning ARTS Northeast Regional train out of Norfolk at five o'clock in the morning."*

Because almost nobody inside the Washington beltway bubble could imagine a newly elected United States Senator navigating rail and subway transfers in a power wheelchair without a dozen handlers, every single person in the Sergeant at Arms office—along with two dozen national television producers who caught wind of her travel plans—had automatically assumed she meant she was riding the train all the way to the end of the line at Washington Union Station.

They didn't know our dad, and they definitely didn't know Katie and me.

Two weeks after Election Night, when Dad had sat down at his kitchen table with his reading glasses on to book our rail tickets for Swearing-In Day on his own credit card, he hadn't booked us to Washington Union Station at all. He had purchased three regular passenger Business Class tickets from Norfolk to Alexandria—station code ALX—on the first train of the morning.

And as Katie and I locked the brakes of our two compact silver-and-black SwiftChair power wheelchairs side by side in the dual accessible bays at the front of the Business Class cabin while Dad hung her pressed royal-blue Senatorial suit bag on the luggage hook, neither one of us was thinking about VIP motorcades.

"First things first before we even cross the river into Suffolk," Katie said, her blue eyes crinkling with the exact same delight she had worn at sixteen on the aft deck of the *Sunward Tropics* with her souvenir soda tumbler as she held up her paper Business Class ticket stub. "Nate, are we getting our free Café Car ginger ales right now, or are we waiting until the conductor scans our tickets?"

"The Café Car attendant just rolled the security grille up on the counter thirty feet behind us," I replied, reaching across the gap between our armrests to squeeze my twin sister's hand as the diesel locomotive gave two low horn blasts and the train glided smoothly away from the Norfolk platform into the dark winter morning. "Let's go get our free ginger ales and Dad's black coffee right now so we get our money's worth before Petersburg."

Besides the promise Katie and I had made to each other behind a locked bedroom door on New Year's Eve when we were seventeen years old, all three of us—Katie, Dad, and I—took a daily prescription maintenance medication where mixing the drug with alcohol or tobacco carried a known, lethal side effect of death. Back in Richmond, and now in Washington, where lobbyists and senior lawmakers loved to clink glasses of expensive cabernet or pass around celebratory cigars in back rooms, that warning label on our pill bottles was our favorite conversational shield: nobody at a Capitol Hill reception ever tried to push a second glass of wine or a cocktail on a Senator after she cheerfully informed them that the known side effect of mixing it with her daily medication was dying on their carpet. For the three of us, cold ginger ale for Katie and me and hot black coffee for Dad from the ARTS Café Car were the only celebratory drinks we would ever need.


***

#### Sunday, January 3, 2027, 9:12 AM — Detraining on the Mobile Lift at Alexandria Union Station

"Next stop, Alexandria—ALX!" the conductor announced over the passenger intercom at ten minutes past nine as our Northeast Regional train slowed past the brick rowhouses and bare winter trees of Northern Virginia. "Passengers detraining at Alexandria, please step toward the vestibule doors. After Alexandria, our final stop will be Washington Union Station in approximately twenty-five minutes."

Up and down the aisle of the Business Class car, several lobbyists and congressional staffers in wool overcoats barely glanced up from their laptops, assuming every person dressed in a suit on a Sunday morning was staying aboard all the way into the cavernous concourse of Washington Union Station.

When Katie and I unlocked our wheelchair brakes, tucked our second round of complimentary Café Car paper cups into our armrest cupholders, and rolled toward the forward vestibule door with Dad walking right behind us carrying his garment bag as the train brakes hissed to a stop beside the low-level red-brick platform of Alexandria Union Station, two passengers in the front row did a sudden double-take over the rims of their coffee cups.

"Wait a second," a woman in a camel wool coat whispered to her husband as the stainless-steel door slid open to the crisp forty-degree Virginia morning sunlight. "Isn't that Senator-Elect Katie Prairie? Why on earth is she getting off here at Alexandria instead of riding into Union Station?"

Katie heard every word, and as she glanced back at me over her shoulder, the two of us shared a quiet, unmistakable twin grin.

There were two reasons we were getting off at Alexandria, and every single person who actually lived on the rails and buses of Virginia understood both of them by heart.

First, for two autistic forty-one-year-olds who had spent our entire lives managing sensory noise so we could stay sharp for the work that mattered, Washington Union Station was an echoing, cavernous sensory ambush—twenty tracks of screeching steel flanges under a vaulted ceiling, booming public-address announcements bouncing off marble columns, and a slow, twenty-five-minute train crawl across the Long Bridge and through the dark First Street Tunnel before you even reached the platform.

Here at Alexandria Union Station, right beneath the grassy slope of Shooter's Hill and the stepped stone tower of the George Washington Masonic National Memorial, the 1905 Federal Revival red-brick depot was small, open-air, quiet, and calm.

Because Alexandria had a low-level red-brick platform rather than a high-level concrete deck, a uniformed ARTS station attendant was already waiting right beside the track, wheeling the yellow-and-silver portable ARTS Mobile Lift flush against the open Business Class doorway.

I rolled onto the steel platform of the mobile lift first. With a smooth hydraulic hum, the attendant lowered me three feet down from the train vestibule onto the herringbone red bricks of the Alexandria platform, where I backed clear and parked beside Dad, who had already walked down the vestibule steps onto the bricks.

Then the attendant raised the lift platform back up to the open doorway for the new junior Senator from Virginia.

![Forty-one-year-old U.S. Senator-Elect Katie Prairie sits in her compact SwiftChair power wheelchair on the yellow-and-silver ARTS Mobile Lift outside the open ARTS Business Class door at Alexandria Union Station while her twin brother Nate in his matching powerchair holding a Café Car cup and their proud father David wait on the low-level red-brick platform below]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/jan_2027_alx_arts_mobile_lift_senator_elect_katie_prairie.jpg)

Standing in the open doorway between our ARTS Business Class coach and the adjacent ARTS Café Car, the attendant held the yellow safety rail steady as Katie steered her compact SwiftChair onto the elevated metal platform, her royal-blue Senatorial blazer gleaming beneath her open navy wool winter coat. Down on the red-brick platform, three morning commuters in winter jackets and knit caps stopped dead in their tracks, their eyes widening in disbelief as they recognized the woman descending on the hand-operated station lift.

"Morning, folks!" Katie called out warmly from the lift platform as the attendant lowered her smoothly down to the bricks beside my chair. "Beautiful morning for a train ride up from Norfolk, isn't it?"

"Senator-Elect Prairie!" a commuter in a puffy down jacket stammered, pulling his smartphone out of his pocket with a huge grin as Katie rolled off the yellow ramp lip onto the red-brick platform right beside me. "Are you taking the train to your own swearing-in?!"

"Every single week the Senate is in session," Katie replied cheerfully, reaching her left hand across the gap between our two wheelchairs to lace her fingers through mine while she held her plastic CapitalPass transit card ready in her right hand. "And my brother Nate and our dad wouldn't miss the first ride for the world."

![Forty-one-year-old Senator-Elect Katie Prairie and her twin brother Nate roll side by side in their compact SwiftChair power wheelchairs holding hands down the open-air red-brick platform of historic Alexandria Union Station with their proud father David walking beside them under the clear winter sky and the George Washington Masonic National Memorial on the hill]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/jan_2027_alx_platform_to_king_st_metro_katie_nate_david.jpg)

As the ARTS train sounded its horn and pulled away northward toward the Potomac River—carrying twenty empty seats toward the television cameras and black government SUVs waiting in vain for us at Washington Union Station—Katie and I rolled side by side down the sunlit red-brick platform of Alexandria Union Station with Dad walking right beside us, leaving the railroad depot behind and following the outdoor brick pedestrian walkway over to the completely separate entrance of King Street–Old Town Capital Transit Station.

### Part 2: The Yellow Line Over the Fenwick Bridge, The Full-Chair Portrait, & Swearing In on the Constitution

**Date:** 2027-01-03 at 09:25 America/New_York

![Official full-seated U.S. Senate portrait of forty-one-year-old U.S. Senator Katie Prairie of Virginia proudly seated in her compact SwiftChair power wheelchair in a royal-blue blazer between the United States and Virginia flags with the Capitol dome visible through the arched window behind her]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/senator_katie_prairie_age_41_us_senate_portrait_og.jpg)

#### Sunday, January 3, 2027, 9:25 AM — King Street–Old Town & The Yellow Line Over the Charles R. Fenwick Bridge

![Emerging from the Capitol South street elevator onto the sunlit brick plaza with the United States Capitol dome gleaming behind them on January 3, 2027, 41-year-old Senator-Elect Katie Prairie and her twin brother Nate roll side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs holding hands while their 68-year-old father David walks proudly beside them.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/jan_2027_capitol_south_elevator_plaza_arrival_katie_nate_david.jpg)

"Excuse me—Senator-Elect Prairie!" a young man in a navy wool overcoat with a congressional staff ID lanyard around his neck called out as Katie and I rolled out of the platform elevator with Dad walking right beside us onto the elevated concrete island platform at King Street–Old Town Station. "If you're heading to the Capitol for noon, don't get on that train—that's a Yellow Line train! The Blue Line on the other track goes straight to Capitol South without having to transfer!"

Katie and I looked at each other across our wheelchair armrests and laughed—the exact laugh of two people who had spent twenty-five years memorizing every route map, transfer pulse, and rail bridge from Coastal Virginia Transit Authority Route 15 on Military Highway to the Washington metropolitan grid.

"Sure, you can take the Blue Line straight through to Capitol South," Katie told the young staffer warmly as the silver Capital Transit Yellow Line train glided up to the platform edge and its pneumatic doors chimed open level with the concrete sill. "If you want to take the long way all the way around through Crystal City, Rosslyn, and Foggy Bottom! We're taking the Yellow Line straight across the Charles R. Fenwick Bridge to L'Enfant Plaza and hopping the Blue Line two stops to Capitol South. Come on—you'll beat your Blue Line train to the Hill by twelve minutes!"

Blinking in surprise as he did the mental map calculation, the staffer grinned and stepped into the Yellow Line car right behind Dad as Katie and I rolled our two SwiftChairs into the center wheelchair bays.

Nine minutes later, right after our train sped past Washington National Airport and the Pentagon, the tunnel walls fell away and our Yellow Line car burst out into the brilliant January morning sunlight high above the Potomac River on the Charles R. Fenwick Bridge.

Through the wide glass window beside our wheelchairs, the entire skyline of the capital opened up across the sparkling water: the white marble colonnade of the Jefferson Memorial in the foreground, the towering obelisk of the Washington Monument to the left, and straight ahead on Jenkins Hill, the cast-iron dome of the United States Capitol gleaming against the clear blue winter sky.

Right inside the middle of that span over the river, Katie's phone buzzed inside her coat pocket.

She glanced at the caller ID—*Office of the Senate Sergeant at Arms*—and tapped the speaker button just loud enough for Dad and me to hear over the rhythmic click of the welded rail joints beneath the bridge.

"Senator-Elect Prairie?" the protocol liaison's voice came through the speaker, breathless and slightly panicked. "Ma'am, I'm standing here with the Capitol Police detail and the press pool at Gate D inside Washington Union Station! The five o'clock ARTS train from Norfolk just pulled onto the track two minutes ago, and the conductor told us you got off the train back in Virginia! Are you alright? Do we need to send a car down the George Washington Parkway to pick you up?"

"Put your SUVs back in the garage, Marcus—we're completely fine," Katie said, her voice calm and ringing with good humor as she glanced forward through the cab window toward the Virginia-to-District shoreline, knowing from years of riding Capital Transit that the cell signal would drop out the second our train left the open-air bridge and plunged into the underground tunnel portal before reaching the station repeaters at L'Enfant Plaza. "Washington Union Station is way too loud and crowded for my brother and me, and the ARTS train takes twenty-five minutes just to crawl from Alexandria into the terminal. We got off on the mobile lift at Alexandria, crossed the plaza over to King Street–Old Town, and rode the Yellow Line across the Charles R. Fenwick Bridge. I have to let you go before we hit the Seventh Street tunnel and lose signal—we're transferring at L'Enfant Plaza to the Blue Line two stops to Capitol South, so we'll see you at the First Street entrance in ten minutes!"

She tapped the screen to end the call right as the concrete retaining walls of the tunnel portal swallowed the morning sunlight outside our window. Beside us, our dad chuckled, shaking his head as he braced one hand on the stainless-steel grab pole.

"You two just outran a Capitol Police motorcade and twenty television vans on a three-dollar CapitalPass card," Dad said proudly.

"And we're going to keep doing it for the next six years, Dad," Katie said, looking from Dad to me as the doors opened at L'Enfant Plaza and we rolled smoothly out onto the lower-level platform toward the elevator up to the Blue Line track. "When we started *Ideas for Coastal Virginia Transit* back in 2008 and realized we couldn't even stay past five-thirty at the Virginia Beach Municipal Center for a six o'clock City Council meeting because the last Route 12 left CCHR at 5:48 PM, I promised myself I would never turn into one of those politicians who only sees Virginia through the tinted window of a town car. Every single time I visit constituents anywhere in the Commonwealth as their United States Senator—whether it's CVTA back home in Hampton Roads, Blue Ridge Transit down at CPI in Blacksburg, or Capital Transit up here in Northern Virginia—we are riding that community's public transit system as part of the visit."

***

#### Sunday, January 3, 2027, 10:45 AM — "Nobody Crops My Powerchair Out of My Senate Portrait"

Fifteen minutes after our Blue Line train let us off at Capitol South and we rode the street elevator up to the sunny sidewalk at First and C Streets Southeast, Katie and I rolled through the bronze doors of the Russell Senate Office Building with Dad walking alongside us and headed up to the third-floor corner suite overlooking the Capitol grounds for Katie's official Senate photograph.

Inside the high-ceilinged room with its dark mahogany wainscot paneling and classical cream pilasters, the official Senate historical photographer had already positioned the United States Flag with its gold fringe to the left of the tall arched window and the deep blue Flag of the Commonwealth of Virginia to the right, framing the white dome of the Capitol in the morning light directly behind the center mark on the marble floor.

As Katie unbuttoned her heavy winter wool coat and handed it to Dad—revealing her tailored royal-blue Senatorial suit blazer with the small gold circular United States Senate pin gleaming on her left lapel—she steered her compact SwiftChair onto the tape mark between the two flags and rested her right hand naturally on her joystick controller.

Behind the studio umbrella lights, the photographer squinted through the viewfinder of his camera and immediately reached for the crank on his heavy aluminum tripod, raising the lens higher and zooming the barrel inward.

"Alright, Senator-Elect, let's bring the frame in nice and tight from the mid-chest up so we match the standard head-and-shoulders portraits down the corridor," the photographer said briskly. "If you could just fold your hands slightly higher near your lapel so the armrests don't—"

"Stop right there, please," Katie said—not unkindly, but with the unmistakable, quiet authority that had once silenced committee rooms in Richmond and bullies in the hallways of Northwood High School.

The photographer's hand froze on the zoom ring.

"Lower the tripod back down and step back six feet so the entire wheelchair is in the frame from my head down to the wheels and the footplate," Katie instructed him, sitting tall and poised between the two flags. "My twin brother Nate and I have rolled in these compact SwiftChairs from the moment we woke up until we went to bed since the third Friday of September in 2001 when we were sixteen years old. I didn't hide my wheelchair when I knocked on doors for Virginia Beach City Council, I didn't hide it in the House of Delegates or the Senate of Virginia, and nobody is cropping my powerchair out of my United States Senate portrait."

![Official full-seated U.S. Senate portrait of forty-one-year-old U.S. Senator Katie Prairie of Virginia proudly seated in her compact SwiftChair power wheelchair in a royal-blue blazer between the United States and Virginia flags with the Capitol dome visible through the arched window behind her]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b005/senator_katie_prairie_age_41_us_senate_portrait.jpg)

From the doorway beside Dad, I watched the photographer blink once, nod with genuine respect, lower his tripod to waist height, and step back across the marble floor until every inch of my sister's silver-and-black SwiftChair was framed proudly between the Stars and Stripes and the Seal of Virginia.

When the studio strobes flashed against the mahogany walls and Katie smiled straight into the lens with her right hand resting on her joystick controller, my throat tightened with a pride so fierce I could barely swallow.

***

#### Sunday, January 3, 2027, 12:00 PM — Swearing In on the Constitution of the United States of America

![Inside the historic Old Senate Chamber of the United States Capitol on January 3, 2027, 41-year-old U.S. Senator Katie Prairie sits in her black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchair affirming her secular constitutional oath of office before Vice President Conrad Drayton with her left hand resting on the family copy of the U.S. Constitution beside her twin brother Nate in his SwiftChair and their proud father David.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/jan_2027_old_senate_chamber_swearing_in_reenactment_katie_nate_david.jpg)

At two minutes before twelve o'clock noon—after riding the subterranean United States Capitol Subway together beneath Constitution Avenue—Dad and I took our places at the front brass railing of the Senate Family Gallery directly above the floor of the United States Senate Chamber.

Looking down from the gallery bay where my wheelchair brakes were locked beside Dad's polished dress shoes, I could see the entire semicircle of one hundred mahogany desks arranged across the blue carpet below us. On the far aisle of the Democratic side—three aisles over from Senator Tess Dunmore of Illinois in her ultralight titanium chair—the Sergeant at Arms carpenters had already modified Senator Katie Prairie's assigned mahogany desk, removing the fixed chair base and setting one-and-a-half-inch mahogany riser blocks beneath the legs so her compact SwiftChair and right-hand joystick controller rolled seamlessly beneath the desktop.

At precisely 12:00 PM, Vice President Conrad Drayton—serving in his constitutional capacity under Article I, Section 3, Clause 4 as President of the Senate—brought the heavy ivory gavel down on the marble rostrum, calling the One Hundred Twentieth Congress of the United States to order.

As the Reading Clerk began calling the Newly Elected Senators forward to the well in alphabetical groups of four—*"Ms. Prairie of Virginia..."*—and Senior Senator Thomas Keane stepped into the aisle to escort his new Virginia partner forward while Senator Tess Dunmore tapped her wheel rim in salute, Dad reached over and gripped my shoulder with a steady, calloused hand.

In the span of three heartbeats, forty-one years of our lives flashed behind my eyes: two nine-year-old twins whispering our *Journey to the Sunlit Valley* cartoon password before unlocking the front door after school; two twelve-year-olds wearing matching maroon shirts on Twins' Day when a sixth-grade boy broke my sister's heart; two sixteen-year-olds learning in Dr. Carter's exam room that the borrowed time in our legs was almost gone; two seventeen-year-olds wedging a fifty-pound power wheelchair against the inside of a locked bedroom door on New Year's Eve while we ate dry toasted oat cereal out of a cardboard box to stay safe from a house full of drunks; and two twenty-three-year-olds holding a camcorder on a CVTA Route 15 bus crossing the Elizabeth River as we exposed why working people couldn't even catch a bus home from a six o'clock City Council meeting.

Down on the blue carpet of the Senate Chamber, Katie didn't need stairs. She nudged her right thumb forward on her joystick, rolled her compact SwiftChair smoothly down the permanent ramp along the chamber aisle into the well of the Senate, looked straight up at Vice President Conrad Drayton on the rostrum, and raised her right hand.

Fifteen minutes later, as the applause from the galleries echoed through the Capitol corridors, the elevator doors brought Dad and me down to the historic Old Senate Chamber for the individual ceremonial swearing-in with Vice President Drayton.

Katie had been looking forward to this exact five-minute appointment for two full months.

All through the autumn campaign—and even after the networks projected her victory on Election Night—President Garrett Thorne had sneered at her from the South Lawn as *"Broken Katie Prairie"* and *"a bitter little cripple on wheels,"* while Vice President Conrad Drayton had gone on the Liberty First Network to mock her wheelchair, her unmarried life, and her bond with me. Ten days before Christmas, hoping to whip up a culture-war pressure campaign that would force her to back down, Drayton's ceremonial protocol office had leaked to Beacon News, LibertyMax, and Virginia Beach's own evangelical flagship broadcast *The 777 Circle* on the Covenant Broadcasting Network that Senator-Elect Prairie had formally notified the Vice President she would be affirming her oath on the Constitution of the United States instead of a Christian Bible and omitting the words "So help me God."

Instead of backing down an inch, Katie had worn their evangelical outrage as a badge of honor. Every time Katie had ever taken an oath of office back home in Virginia—first on the Virginia Beach City Council, then in the Virginia House of Delegates, and then in the Senate of Virginia in Richmond—she had refused to pretend to believe in a religion or a god that neither she nor I believed in. To my sister's clear, literal, fiercely principled mind, Article VI, Clause 3 of the United States Constitution explicitly guaranteed that Senators were bound by Oath or Affirmation and prohibited any religious test for public office—meaning her left hand belonged on the exact secular Constitution she was promising to defend, not a single word of religious theater belonged in her mouth, and Vice President Conrad Drayton had zero constitutional choice but to stand in front of her wheelchair and administer every word of it himself.

Now, as Dad and I positioned ourselves right beside her in the center of the crimson-and-gold Old Senate Chamber while Vice President Drayton stepped up stiffly with the printed oath card in his hand, I held out the thick, gold-stamped navy leather volume Dad had bought for her at the National Archives gift shop that morning: *The Constitution of the United States of America*.

Looking down from his full height at the forty-one-year-old woman he and President Thorne had mocked as "Broken Katie Prairie"—and who had just helped strip him of his tie-breaking vote in a fifty-four-seat Democratic Senate—Conrad Drayton's jaw muscle twitched once as Katie placed her left palm squarely on the gold lettering of *We the People*, raised her right hand high, and locked her unblinking blue eyes on his face.

Reading from the secular affirmation card our transition counsel had required under Article VI, Clause 3 of the Constitution, Title 5, Section 3331, and Title 1, Section 1 of the United States Code—with the optional religious phrase conspicuously absent at the bottom—Vice President Drayton had to speak every syllable aloud:

*"Do you solemnly affirm that you will support and defend the Constitution of the United States against all enemies, foreign and domestic; that you will bear true faith and allegiance to the same; that you take this obligation freely, without any mental reservation or purpose of evasion; and that you will well and faithfully discharge the duties of the office on which you are about to enter?"*

Katie's voice rang out clear, steady, and unshakeable across the historic chamber, never breaking eye contact with the Vice President:

*"I do solemnly affirm."*

As the shutters of the Senate photographers clicked in a rapid burst of white light and Vice President Drayton forced a tight, wooden handshake—"Congratulations, Senator Prairie"—Katie gave him a cool, victorious smile:

"Thank you, Mr. President of the Senate. Keep that gavel warm—Senator Dunmore already showed me the ramp up to your rostrum."

Before Drayton's face could finish turning purple, Katie turned her head toward me first.

Right there on the floor of the Old Senate Chamber, with the Constitution of the United States resting between our two compact power wheelchairs and our father's hands resting proudly on both of our shoulders, United States Senator Katie Prairie slipped her left hand across our armrests and laced her fingers tightly through mine.

Twenty minutes later, when the three of us rolled out onto the East Front plaza of the Capitol toward the Capitol South Capital Transit entrance, a wall of national television cameras from Beacon News, LibertyMax, and Virginia Beach's own evangelical flagship program *The 777 Circle* on the Covenant Broadcasting Network came rushing across the flagstones—breathlessly demanding to know why the new junior Senator from Virginia had affirmed her oath on the Constitution instead of a Christian Bible and omitted "So help me God" on national television.

Katie didn't roll past them. She stopped her SwiftChair right in front of the live satellite microphones, rested her hand on the navy leather cover of the United States Constitution on my lap tray, and smiled brightly into the lenses.

"I'm glad you asked, because it sounds like Beacon News, LibertyMax, and the folks at *The 777 Circle* back home on Indian River Road in Virginia Beach still haven't read the document I'm holding in my hand," Katie said clearly into the live network feeds. "Article VI, Clause 3 of the Constitution of the United States says that all Senators shall be bound by Oath or Affirmation to support this Constitution, and that no religious test shall ever be required as a qualification to any office or public trust under the United States. Even the Presidential Oath written by the Founders in Article II, Section 1, Clause 8 says 'swear or affirm' and does not contain the words 'So help me God.' And before anyone on cable television repeats the myth that President George Washington added 'So help me God' in 1789—historians debunked that fable decades ago. Zero eyewitnesses at Federal Hall in 1789 recorded Washington saying it; a writer named Rufus Wilmot Griswold made it up sixty-five years later in an 1854 book, and no President is recorded saying it until Chester A. Arthur in 1881. I affirmed my oath on the Constitution of the United States because the Constitution is the supreme law of the land—and my brother, my dad, and I are going to spend every single day of this term defending it."

With the cable correspondents left speechless behind us on the Capitol plaza, Katie turned her SwiftChair toward the sidewalk curb cut, gave my hand a warm squeeze between our chairs, and rolled side by side with Dad and me toward the Dirksen Senate Office Building for our swearing-in open house in Room 511—where three newly badged twenty-four-year-old Senate staffers and two very proud guests from Southside Virginia were already waiting for us inside the front reception doors.

Standing beside the three adjacent workstations in the front suite of Dirksen Room 511 were Sam, Mandy, and Sarah Hawkins, wearing their crisp new blue-lanyard United States Senate staff identification badges over their suits: Sam as Legislative Correspondent for Transportation, Infrastructure, and Accessibility Policy; Mandy as Constituent Services Representative; and Sarah as Staff Assistant and Digital Accessibility Correspondent. And standing right behind them in his Sunday suit with his arm around Aunt Marge Callaway's shoulders was their maternal uncle, retired Republican House Majority Leader Richard Callaway, who had ridden the morning train up to Washington with Marge to watch their kids start their congressional careers.

As Katie rolled her SwiftChair across the threshold and handed Sam, Mandy, and Sarah their official gold-embossed Senate onboarding folders, I watched Uncle Richard's eyes move slowly from the bronze *MS. PRAIRIE — VIRGINIA* nameplate outside the door to the three beaming twenty-four-year-old adults standing together behind their desks.

You could see all eleven years written across the old Republican floor leader's face in a single glance: the memory of February 2016, when he had nervously entrusted three recently rescued, terrified thirteen-year-old autistic House Pages to the Virginia General Assembly, and the thirty-year-old Delegate in a wheelchair who had parked her chair around them in a noisy corridor and made Richmond safe enough for them to grow up whole.

Now Katie was a United States Senator, and those three frightened thirteen-year-old Pages were professional congressional staffers on the fifth floor of the Dirksen Building.

Uncle Richard didn't make a grand floor speech. He just looked down at Katie in her SwiftChair, his voice catching slightly in his throat.

"All three?" Richard asked softly.

Katie looked up at him, mildly offended.

"Richard," my sister said. "Of course all three."

For two full seconds, the former Republican Majority Leader of the Virginia House of Delegates couldn't say a word. He just took off his glasses, wiped the corner of his eye with his thumb while Aunt Marge hugged Katie's shoulders, and rested a steady, grateful hand on the back of Sam's chair—proving to everyone in that room what Katie and I had known since the day we were born: nobody in our family ever gets left behind.

### Part 3: The First Invite to Cocktails, A Known Side Effect of Death, & Home to Sunset Drive

**Date:** 2027-01-03 at 16:30 America/New_York

![Inside the gilded Mansfield Room of the United States Capitol on January 3, 2027, 41-year-old U.S. Senator Katie Prairie and her twin brother Nate sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs with their father David standing proudly behind them, clinking three tall glasses of ice-cold ginger ale in a family toast with senior Senators.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/jan_2027_mansfield_room_ginger_ale_toast_katie_nate_david.jpg)

#### Sunday, January 3, 2027, 4:30 PM — The First Invite to Cocktails & "A Known Side Effect of Death"

![Inside the gilded Mansfield Room of the United States Capitol on January 3, 2027, 41-year-old U.S. Senator Katie Prairie and her twin brother Nate sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs with their father David standing proudly behind them, clinking three tall glasses of ice-cold ginger ale in a family toast with senior Senators.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/jan_2027_mansfield_room_ginger_ale_toast_katie_nate_david.jpg)

"There she is—the newest Senator from the Commonwealth of Virginia!" Senator Arthur Harrington, the silver-haired senior chairman of the Appropriations Committee, boomed warmly across the gilded chandeliers and marble fireplace of the Mansfield Room just off the Senate floor. "Katie, bring your brother and your father over here! Waiter—three flutes of the French champagne for Senator Prairie and her family, and then we're heading downstairs to my hideaway office for twenty-year single-malt scotch and celebratory cigars on the West Front terrace!"

A tuxedoed catering steward immediately stepped between our two compact SwiftChairs with a polished silver tray balanced on his palm, lowering three crystal flutes of bubbling gold champagne toward Katie, Dad, and me.

Across the crowded reception room, half a dozen senior Senators and committee chairs raised their wine glasses and crystal tumblers, waiting for the freshman Senator from Virginia to take a flute and join the oldest social ritual on Capitol Hill.

Sitting beside my sister in my powerchair, I didn't even have to glance at her to know what both of us were remembering beneath the polite clink of Capitol crystal: the sour stench of gin on our mother's breath on the boat deck of the *Sunward Tropics* in August 2001; the bass-heavy thump of our cousin Brittany's drunken New Year's Eve party rattling the walls of our brick ranch off Military Highway on December 31, 2002; and two seventeen-year-old twins wedging a fifty-pound wheelchair frame against the inside of a locked bedroom door while we ate dry toasted oat cereal out of a cardboard box, clinked two cold cans of ginger ale together at midnight, and swore we would never touch a drop of alcohol for the rest of our lives.

In a room full of powerful Washington politicians, however, a personal promise made at age seventeen was the kind of thing back-slapping colleagues always tried to talk you into breaking *"just this once."*

Fortunately for the three of us, biology and pharmacology had given Katie, Dad, and me an answer that no Senator in the United States Capitol could ever argue with.

Katie raised her left hand—calm, poised, and completely unbothered—stopping the waiter's silver tray six inches above her armrest.

"Thank you so much, Arthur, and thank you, sir, but please keep the champagne on the tray," Katie said clearly enough for the entire circle of Senators to hear. "My twin brother Nate, my father David, and I can't touch a single drop of alcohol—or go anywhere near cigar smoke or tobacco—for medical reasons."

Senator Harrington's genial smile paused mid-toast as he lowered his crystal tumbler half an inch. "Oh—nothing serious, I hope?"

"All three of us take daily prescription medication where mixing it with alcohol or tobacco has a known side effect of death," Katie replied with matter-of-fact serenity, her blue eyes steady and bright beneath the crystal chandelier.

Across the circle of velvet ropes and gilded mirrors, the silence was instantaneous.

Two committee chairs instinctively took a half-step back with their wine glasses, and Senator Harrington's eyes widened before he immediately gestured for the waiter to pull the champagne tray away.

"Good Lord—say no more, Katie!" Senator Harrington said quickly, waving a second steward over from the refreshment bar across the room. "No alcohol and no cigars anywhere near you three—I'll make sure the whip's office and the cloakroom staff know that permanently! What can we get for you, Nate, and David right now?"

"Three glasses of ice-cold ginger ale would be wonderful, Arthur," Dad said with a warm, easy smile, resting his hand on the back of Katie's powerchair. "That's been the Prairie family toast for twenty-four years."

Thirty seconds later, when the steward returned with three tall highball glasses filled with crushed ice and golden ginger ale, Senator Harrington and the surrounding Senators raised their glasses right alongside ours.

As Katie, Dad, and I clinked our three glasses of ginger ale together in the center of the United States Capitol, Katie caught my eye across our armrests with the smallest, most triumphant glint of amusement. In a single sentence, my twin sister had just permanently exempted all three of us from every late-night Washington cocktail hour, wine-soaked donor reception, and smoke-filled backroom on Capitol Hill for the next six years.

***

#### Sunday, January 3, 2027, 6:15 PM — Across the Potomac & Through the King Street Tunnel to Sunset Drive

At quarter past six that evening, while the winter sky over the National Mall deepened to indigo and the other newly sworn-in Senators climbed into waiting black town cars bound for Georgetown townhouses or Capitol Hill condominiums, Katie and I rolled out of the Capitol South elevator with Dad walking right beside us, our CapitalPass cards in hand.

Riding the Blue Line two stops to L'Enfant Plaza and transferring up to the southbound Yellow Line platform took less than ten minutes. As our silver Yellow Line train glided back out onto the Charles R. Fenwick Bridge high above the dark, glass-smooth waters of the Potomac River, the illuminated white dome of the Capitol receded behind us and the lights of Alexandria rose ahead on the Virginia shore.

"How does it feel, Senator?" I asked quietly over the hum of the traction motors as the train banked south past Washington National Airport toward Old Town. "Leaving the District behind on your very first night?"

"Like I can finally breathe," Katie said, leaning her head back against her wheelchair headrest and letting out a long, contented sigh as the Yellow Line glided onto the elevated platform at King Street–Old Town Station. "Washington is where I work, Nate. Virginia is who we are."

Exiting the station street elevator into the crisp thirty-eight-degree night air, Katie and I rolled past the glowing destination signs of the King Street Station bus loop—where BOLT and Capital Transit buses were idling at the sawtooth curbs—and turned west along the wide, flat concrete sidewalk of King Street with Dad walking alongside us.

Immediately ahead of us stood the heavy dark-green steel girders and white-painted concrete retaining walls of the King Street railroad underpass, carrying the elevated tracks of both Alexandria Union Station and the King Street–Old Town Capital Transit station directly over the street.

As Katie and I guided our two SwiftChairs side by side along the sidewalk beneath the short railroad bridge with Dad walking at our side and emerged into the quiet residential glow on the west side of the tunnel, Dad's two-story Alexandria house rose right on the left where Sunset Drive met the hill.

It was a classic two-story red-brick Virginia house with black louvered shutters framing the multi-pane sash windows, two manicured round boxwood shrubs flanking a white columned front portico topped with a small white Chippendale railing, and a broad green lawn bordered by a shade tree just steps from the railroad overpass. Looking straight back over my shoulder from the front walkway, I could see the illuminated canopy of King Street–Old Town Capital Transit Station and the upper-level rail embankment of Alexandria Union Station right across the bridge.

Back home in Hampton Roads, Katie and I owned our primary residence fifty-fifty in the Kempsville section of Virginia Beach—the house where we claimed legal residency, where we were registered to vote, and where we paid our property taxes to the City of Virginia Beach. Dad, however, had owned this house on Sunset Drive long before Katie ever ran for the Virginia Beach City Council in 2010. The house was one hundred percent paid off and titled one hundred percent in Dad's name, giving Katie and me a permanent family roof in Northern Virginia whenever the Senate was in session so she could take the train into Washington for day trips and truthfully say she slept in the Commonwealth of Virginia every single night. Even better, we never had to publish a street number for reporters or curiosity-seekers—to everyone who knew us, it was simply Dad's house on Sunset Drive, tucked right on the other side of the tunnel with buses and trains at our doorstep.

***

#### Sunday, January 3, 2027, 7:30 PM — The Vertical Platform Lift & Coding in Bedroom 4

![Inside the warm upstairs three-desk family office in Bedroom 4 of the Sunset Drive brick house in Alexandria on the night of January 3, 2027, 41-year-old U.S. Senator Katie Prairie and her twin brother Nate sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs coding in Quantum Studio 2026 and PHP while their father David works at the third desk and an illuminated Capital Transit Yellow Line train and ARTS passenger train glide across the King Street bridge outside the window.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/jan_2027_sunset_drive_bedroom_4_coding_trains_katie_nate_david.jpg)

"Home sweet Virginia," Dad said as he unlocked the white front door beneath the columned portico and held it open for Katie and me to roll inside over the flush threshold ramp.

When the three of us had worked with our Alexandria contractor that autumn to adapt the two-story Sunset Drive house for two full-time powerchair users, we had designed every square foot around both our accessibility needs and our privacy.

Here at the front of the first floor, directly behind the shuttered windows facing the sidewalk and the street, sat a traditional Colonial living room and dining room with a central hallway leading back to an accessible kitchen with roll-under countertops and a curbless roll-in bathroom. Anyone walking past the house on the street at night saw only warm table lamps, bookshelves, and a dining room table through the front windows.

Right alongside the central staircase in the hallway stood the engineering centerpiece that made a two-story historic brick house work for Katie and me: a quiet, enclosed through-floor residential vertical platform wheelchair lift linking the first floor directly to the second-floor landing.

After the three of us heated up bowls of chicken noodle soup and toasted sourdough bread in the kitchen for supper—and took our evening prescription tablets with three tall glasses of cold water—Katie rolled her SwiftChair to the hall lift gate and pressed the illuminated call button.

"Come on, Nate," Katie said, grinning over her shoulder even after sixteen hours awake since our 4:00 AM alarm in Virginia Beach. "Before we turn in, we still have to push the January 3rd schema update to our shared site network—and I want to test the new build in Quantum Studio 2026 while the night ARTS train rolls past the window."

While Dad walked up the central carpeted staircase to meet us on the upper landing, Katie and I rode the vertical platform lift one at a time up through the ceiling opening to the second-floor hallway and rolled past the three upstairs doors that completed our four-bedroom layout.

The first door on the left was Bedroom 2: officially designated as my bedroom whenever congressional staffers, plumbers, or visitors ever saw the upstairs floor plan, completely furnished with a neatly made full-sized bed, a cherrywood dresser, and a nightstand lamp—even though that bed went completely untouched every single night.

Across the hall was Bedroom 3, Dad's upstairs bedroom with his full-sized bed and reading chair.

And at the east end of the upstairs hallway, with two wide sash windows looking directly out over the shade tree and the steel railroad bridge toward the glowing platforms of King Street–Old Town and Alexandria Union Station, was Bedroom 4: our three-desk family office.

Having already changed out of her royal-blue Senate blazer into her favorite soft navy fleece pullover, the newly sworn-in United States Senator from Virginia rolled her powerchair right up to her dual-monitor workstation beside mine, while Dad settled into his ergonomic chair at the third desk in the corner to check his Monday morning remote-work queue.

For the next two hours, the only sounds in that warm upstairs room were the familiar, rhythmic click of three mechanical keyboards, the soft hum of our desktop towers, and the occasional distant rumble of a Capital Transit Yellow Line train or an ARTS locomotive gliding across the King Street bridge outside our window.

Side by side at our desks—just as we had coded together since learning HTML in seventh grade at Morrison Middle School in 1997, studying Dad's *Quantum Basic 6.0* textbooks with him in 2001, and copying the Web Applications Developer PHP and SQL curriculum onto our laptops at Roosevelt Rehabilitation Center in March 2007 to master it alongside Tina, Sheila, and Jim—Katie and I had Quantum Studio 2026, Quantum Code, and our PHP backend templates open across our monitors, maintaining and deploying updates to the network of websites and desktop applications that the two of us shared.

"Look at line two hundred fourteen in the router controller, Nate," Katie said happily, pointing at her screen as a northbound ARTS train whistled softly across the elevated embankment beyond the glass. "Five hours ago I was holding my hand on the Constitution of the United States in the Old Senate Chamber, and right now I'm fixing a trailing array comma in PHP with my twin brother. Tell me any other Senator on Capitol Hill is having a better Sunday night than this."

"Not a single one of them, Katie," I laughed, compiling the build in Quantum Studio 2026 and watching the green deployment checkmarks light up across our shared server dashboard. "Though wait until you see who just requested an appropriations meeting on your Class II Senate calendar for next month: the Virginia Department for Aging and Rehabilitative Services and the leadership of Roosevelt Rehabilitation Center in Fishersville. They're coming to Washington to ask Virginia's new United States Senator for federal discretionary funding."

Katie paused her fingers over her keyboard, and a slow, razor-sharp smile curved across her lips as twenty years of memory flashed in her blue eyes.

"Put them right on the calendar, Nate," Katie said softly. "I can't wait to ask DARS and the director of RRC whether they're still forcing twenty-one-year-old wheelchair users with associate degrees to tour the auto shop, the woodworking shop, and the nursing school before pitching them on a partnership with ValueMart to be a door greeter. And while they're sitting across from our wheelchairs asking for federal tax dollars, we're going to ask them under oath about aides grabbing clients' push-handles, locking twin siblings into separate Level 2 wings, accusing them of sneaking into a closet to have sex and then backing down the second they offer to go home because of the headcount funding formula I suspected back when we were twenty-one, and escorting the guy who attacked Natalie out to a van without calling the police."

***

#### Sunday, January 3, 2027, 10:30 PM — The Private Ground-Floor Back Bedroom Sanctuary

![Inside the ground-floor master bedroom of the Sunset Drive house in Alexandria on the night of January 3, 2027, while the dark mahogany sleigh bed beneath the framed blue butterfly print sits untouched behind their two parked black SwiftChair power wheelchairs, 41-year-old U.S. Senator Katie Prairie and her twin brother Nate cuddle closely in a soothing two-arm embrace inside their navy-blue sleeping bag on the floor of the walk-in closet beneath her hanging navy Senate blazer.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/jan_2027_sunset_drive_senator_night_closet_full_cuddle_sanctuary_katie_nate.jpg)

At ten-thirty, Dad shut down his remote-work laptop at the third desk, stood up with a gentle stretch, and kissed the top of Katie's head before resting a warm hand on my shoulder.

"Goodnight, Senator. Goodnight, Nate," Dad said softly from the doorway of Bedroom 3 across the upstairs hall. "Sleep well, you two."

"Goodnight, Dad—love you," Katie and I said together.

One after the other, my sister and I took the interior vertical platform lift back down to the quiet first floor and rolled past the darkened front living room toward the rear of the house.

Tucked into the private back corner of the ground floor—looking out only onto our high-fenced backyard garden and tall evergreens behind drawn blackout curtains—was the Master Bedroom.

Officially, on paper, this ground-floor suite was Katie's bedroom, while Bedroom 2 upstairs was mine. We had deliberately chosen this room at the very back of the ground floor so that no passerby, reporter, or neighbor walking along the front sidewalk could ever peer through a street-facing window to see two forty-one-year-old opposite-gender twins sharing a bed.

Inside our quiet back-room sanctuary, however, there were no cameras, no Senate galleries, and no outsiders who needed an explanation for why the two halves of the same soul slept safest together.
