"Good," Katie said, steering her SwiftChair out into the marble corridor of Dirksen with me rolling in lockstep beside her left wheel toward the Capitol subway. "Then at eleven-fifteen, President Thorne gets my No vote on his nominee—and as soon as Chief Justice Jonathan Sterling swears in the Senate for their trials, all three of them get my Guilty vote too."

***

#### The 2025 Warning from Richmond & Secretary of Defense Bret Halverson's Norfolk Carrier Leak

As our subway car glided through the subterranean tunnel between the Dirksen building and the Capitol, both Katie and I thought back two years earlier to January of 2025.

Back in that winter of 2025, Katie had still been serving as a State Senator in the Senate of Virginia in Richmond—living with me at Apartment 104 of the Broad & Boulevard Lofts on West Broad Street—when newly inaugurated President Garrett Thorne, backed by a Republican trifecta controlling the White House, the House of Representatives, and a fifty-three-to-forty-seven Senate majority, nominated Bret Halverson to serve as United States Secretary of Defense.

Before Thorne plucked him off television to run the Pentagon, Halverson had spent a decade hosting *Patriot Watch Weekend* on the Liberty First Network—a slick, hair-sprayed weekend cable talk show where he ranted about "woke generals," mocked disabled service members and ADA wheelchair accessibility standards as "weakness," and hawked survivalist supplements and gold coins during commercial breaks. In 2024, Halverson had gone on the Liberty First Network and sneered that military bases shouldn't waste taxpayer money on "wheelchair ramps for bureaucrats."

For anyone representing Hampton Roads—home to Naval Station Norfolk, the largest naval base on earth, alongside Naval Air Station Oceana, Joint Expeditionary Base Little Creek, Newport News Shipbuilding, and tens of thousands of active-duty sailors and military families—putting a cable television talk-show host in charge of three million service members and an eight-hundred-and-fifty-billion-dollar defense budget was an insult to every sailor in uniform.

Because Katie was still a State Senator in Richmond in January 2025 and hadn't yet run for the United States Senate, she didn't have a confirmation vote in Washington. Instead, she and I had stayed up past midnight in our West Broad Street apartment compiling a fourteen-page forensic dossier on Halverson's financial conflicts and erratic record. The next morning, State Senator Katie Prairie had rolled to the well of the Senate of Virginia in Richmond, publicly urged both of Virginia's United States Senators to vote No on Halverson's confirmation, and sent our dossier straight up Interstate 95 to Capitol Hill.

Virginia's retiring senior U.S. Senator had read Katie's letter into the *Congressional Record* and voted No alongside Virginia's other Senator, just as she had urged. Yet because Thorne's party controlled the chamber in January 2025, the majority conference had rammed Halverson's confirmation through on a razor-thin fifty-fifty tie broken by Vice President Conrad Drayton. That weekend, Secretary Halverson had gone back on his old cable network for a victory lap, laughing with his former co-hosts about *"that little wheelchair state senator down in Richmond who thought she could stop the Pentagon."*

It hadn't taken two years for every single warning Katie had issued from Richmond to come true—and when the November 2026 midterm wave swept a two-hundred-and-fifty-three-seat Democratic majority into the House of Representatives, flipped the Senate to a fifty-four-seat majority, and sent United States Senator Katie Prairie of Virginia to Washington in January 2027, the chickens came home to roost.

Within sixty days of the One Hundred Twentieth Congress taking power in January 2027, joint House and Senate subpoenas uncovered a staggering dual crime at the top of the administration:

First, Secretary of Defense Bret Halverson had used an unsecured commercial messaging app on his personal cell phone—on a group chat that included Vice President Conrad Drayton, two of Halverson's old cable-news producers, and a foreign-linked shipping broker—to text classified Fifth Fleet deployment schedules and transit coordinates for an aircraft carrier strike group homeported right at Naval Station Norfolk, putting six thousand Hampton Roads sailors in mortal danger.

Second, when I wrote a custom PHP financial cross-indexing script in Dirksen Room 511 to audit the subpoenaed Pentagon logistics ledgers against Treasury wire records, the data proved beyond a shadow of a doubt that Halverson had fired the Department of Defense Inspector General to cover up four hundred million dollars in no-bid Naval Station Norfolk fleet-supply contracts steered to an offshore shell fund co-owned by Thorne Global Holdings—using Domestic Emoluments and national-security tariff waivers personally signed by both Vice President Conrad Drayton and President Garrett Thorne.

***

#### Thursday Afternoon, March 25, 2027 — Why the Vice President Must Be Convicted Before the President

One week later, on Thursday afternoon, March 25, 2027—minutes after the United States House of Representatives voted two hundred and sixty-eight to one hundred and sixty-seven to impeach Secretary of Defense Bret Halverson, Vice President Conrad Drayton, and President Garrett Thorne for high crimes and misdemeanors—Speaker of the House Clara Morales and the House impeachment managers met with Katie and the Senate leadership inside the Capitol while I sat beside Katie's wheelchair with our constitutional succession timeline open on my laptop.

"Alexander Hamilton wrote in *Federalist Number 65* that impeachment is designed for those offenses which proceed from the misconduct of public men, or, in other words, from the abuse or violation of some public trust," Katie said evenly around the conference table. "And Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. reminded this country that the time is always right to do what is right. All three of these men betrayed the sailors of Naval Station Norfolk and sold out the public trust for four hundred million dollars in offshore kickbacks. None of them—not Thorne, not Drayton, and not Halverson—can be allowed to remain in power."

"Which brings us to the exact sequence of the three Senate trials," Speaker Clara Morales said, looking across the table at Katie and the Senate Majority Leader. "Because under Article II, Section 1, Clause 6 of the Constitution and Section 1 of the Twenty-Fifth Amendment, the order in which the Senate calls the final roll determines who becomes President of the United States."

Katie nodded, tapping the statutory flow chart I had coded on my screen.

"If the Senate convicts and removes President Garrett Thorne first," Katie explained with crystal-clear constitutional precision, "then the exact microsecond Chief Justice Sterling bangs his gavel on the sixty-seventh Guilty vote, Vice President Conrad Drayton—the man who broke the tie to put Bret Halverson in the Pentagon and co-signed the offshore Norfolk contract waivers—automatically ascends to the Presidency. Even if we impeached him the next day, he would already be sitting in the Oval Office with the pardon pen in his hand."

"Whereas if we try and convict them in ascending order of their conspiracy," I added from my chair beside Katie, pointing to the three numbered boxes on my screen, "watch what the Constitution and the United States Code do automatically:

"First, on Wednesday, the Senate votes on Secretary of Defense Bret Halverson—convicting and removing him by a two-thirds supermajority under Article I, Section 3, followed immediately by the simple-majority vote permanently disqualifying him from ever holding federal office again.

"Second, on Thursday, while Garrett Thorne is still President, the Senate votes on Vice President Conrad Drayton. The moment sixty-seven Senators vote Guilty to convict and remove Conrad Drayton, the office of Vice President of the United States becomes completely vacant. Under Section 2 of the Twenty-Fifth Amendment, a replacement Vice President cannot take office unless confirmed by a majority vote of both Houses of Congress—meaning our majorities in the House and the Senate simply decline to consider any nominee, keeping the Vice Presidency empty overnight.

"And third, on Friday afternoon, with the Vice Presidency vacant, the Senate votes to convict, remove, and permanently disqualify President Garrett Thorne. Under the Presidential Succession Act of 1947—Title 3, Section 19 of the United States Code—with both the Presidency and the Vice Presidency vacant at the same time, the line of succession skips straight across the Capitol Rotunda to the Speaker of the House."

Across the mahogany table, Speaker Clara Morales looked at the forty-one-year-old Senator from Virginia Beach and her twin brother in quiet awe.

"Wednesday for Halverson, Thursday for Drayton, and Friday for Thorne," the Senate Majority Leader said, writing the three dates onto the official Senate trial calendar. "And Senator Prairie—because Naval Station Norfolk is your home turf, we want you delivering the final floor speech before the roll is called."

### Part 2: Route 36 to Timberline Shopping Center, Lunch at Don Miller Subs, Retro Games at Neat Stuff, & Suite 756

**Date:** 2027-04-03 at 12:05 America/New_York

![Inside The Tidewater Thorne & RTR Superstore in Suite 756 of Timberline Shopping Center on April 3, 2027, U.S. Senator Katie Prairie and her twin brother Nate sit in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs beside their father David as former Delaney Street neighbor Sharron confronts a stunned Brenda Walsh behind the cash register and drops her Restore the Republic chapter badge onto the glass counter.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/apr_2027_timberline_suite_756_thorne_store_brenda_sharron_confrontation.jpg)

#### Saturday, April 3, 2027, 12:05 PM — Riding CVTA Route 36 to Timberline Shopping Center & Family Lunch at Don Miller Subs

![Inside Don Miller Subs at Timberline Shopping Center on Holland Road in Virginia Beach on April 3, 2027, 41-year-old U.S. Senator Katie Prairie and her twin brother Nate sit in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs clinking tall cups of ice-cold ginger ale in an early 42nd birthday toast with their 68-year-old father David over baskets of grilled steak-and-cheese subs and french fries while counter manager Marcus smiles behind the grill line.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/apr_2027_timberline_don_miller_subs_birthday_lunch_katie_nate_david.jpg)

"Approaching State Route four-ten, Holland Road and Timberlake Road—Timberline Shopping Center," the automated chime announced over the interior speakers of our forty-foot Coastal Virginia Transit Authority Route 36 bus as the driver signaled right and eased into the curb lane just east of where State Route 225 split off toward South Independence Boulevard and the Silverleaf commuter lot.

Up near the front wheel well, my twin brother Nate reached up from his compact SwiftChair and pressed the yellow request-to-stop strip along the wall, while our sixty-eight-year-old dad stood up from the forward-facing bench seat across the aisle and tucked his sunglasses into the breast pocket of his polo shirt.

Unlike the part-time Virginia General Assembly up in Richmond—which met for forty-five or sixty winter days and then sent us home for the rest of the year—the United States Senate stayed in session almost year-round from January 3rd right up to Christmas. Even so, the Senate's weekly floor voting calendar almost always wrapped up around two o'clock on Thursday afternoon, allowing Nate, Dad, and me to catch the afternoon ARTS Northeast Regional train south from Alexandria to Norfolk and spend every Friday, Saturday, and Sunday at home in Kempsville. Better yet, this first full week of April fell during the Senate's scheduled Spring State Work Period, giving the House impeachment managers and the White House defense counsel ten days to file their pre-trial briefs before the Senate impeachment trials of Secretary of Defense Bret Halverson, Vice President Conrad Drayton, and President Garrett Thorne gaveled in on Wednesday, April 14th.

"Have a great Saturday, Senator Prairie, Nate, Mr. Prairie!" the CVTA driver called out warmly as he kneeled the front air suspension, flipped the hydraulic fold-out ramp onto the concrete sidewalk of Holland Road, and waved as all three of us—having tapped our regular fare cards when we boarded—thanked him and rolled out into the bright sixty-eight-degree April sunshine.

Across the six lanes of State Route 410 on the south side of the highway stood Holland Square, anchored by the green signage of the Market Square grocery store. Here on the north side of Holland Road, however, we had just rolled into the parking lot of Timberline Shopping Center—a weathered, familiar 1980s neighborhood strip center anchored at its far end by a General Dollar discount store.

For Nate, Dad, and me, Timberline Shopping Center was one of our favorite Saturday afternoon stops along the Route 36 bus line between Buckner Boulevard and the Silverleaf transfer hub—and today was a special occasion. In five days, on Thursday, April 8th, Nate and I would turn forty-two years old. Every spring on the Saturday before our April 8th birthday, Dad rode the bus with us to Timberline Shopping Center to treat us to our traditional birthday lunch at Don Miller Subs and buy us a pair of vintage video game cartridges next door at Neat Stuff.

Steering our two SwiftChairs side by side along the covered concrete walkway toward the far-left bay of the five-storefront row, we rolled straight through the propped-open glass door of Don Miller Subs, where the warm, savory aroma of grilled ribeye steak, caramelized onions, and freshly baked sub rolls greeted us like an old friend.

"Well, look who's back from Washington—and happy early birthday to the April eighth twins!" Marcus, the counter manager who had been grilling subs for the three of us since my years in the Virginia House of Delegates, beamed from behind the stainless-steel prep line. "The birthday usual for the Prairie crew? Two six-inch grilled steak-and-cheese subs with everything, one turkey-and-provolone, a large basket of hot french fries to share, and three tall cups of ginger ale?"

"You know us by heart, Marcus—and the birthday lunch is on Dad today," Dad laughed, stepping up to the register to tap his debit card before I could reach for my wallet.

For the next thirty-five minutes, sitting at our usual accessible corner table where Nate and I could pull our wheelchairs right up to the laminate top without blocking the aisle, the three of us ate piping-hot subs and crispy french fries out of wax-paper baskets and clinked our three plastic cups of ice-cold ginger ale together in an early forty-second birthday toast. Nobody in the sub shop bothered us for speeches or talking points; a retired Navy chief at the next booth simply nodded with a quiet *"Proud of you up there on Capitol Hill, Senator,"* before letting us enjoy our Saturday lunch in peace.

***

#### Saturday, April 3, 2027, 12:50 PM — Hunting for Forty-Second Birthday Retro Cartridges at Neat Stuff in Suite 732

![Inside Neat Stuff retro video game store in Suite 732 of Timberline Shopping Center on April 3, 2027, U.S. Senator Katie Prairie and her twin brother Nate sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs with their father David standing beside them as store clerk Devon presents vintage PlayBrick and 16-bit Super Kinoka cartridges for their upcoming forty-second birthday.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/apr_2027_timberline_neat_stuff_suite_732_birthday_retro_games.jpg)

At ten minutes to one, after wiping our hands with napkins and tossing our paper baskets into the trash bin by the door, we rolled out of Don Miller Subs and turned one door to the right into Suite 732: Neat Stuff.

While everyone in Hampton Roads knew Pixel Haven as our region's premier retro and modern video game store, Neat Stuff here in Suite 732 of Timberline Shopping Center was Pixel Haven's sister store—a floor-to-ceiling treasure cavern packed with vintage console cartridges, classic handheld games, eight-bit and sixteen-bit hardware, comic books, and retro sci-fi collectibles. Ever since we were kids playing our Super Kinoka and Nova 64 consoles in our bedroom on Delaney Street—and trading PlayBrick cartridges in the back of Dad's car—Nate and I had never outgrown our love for retro video games.

"Katie! Nate! Mr. Prairie—happy early birthday!" Devon, the bearded thirty-something clerk behind the glass cartridge counter, lit up the moment our two SwiftChairs rolled down the wide center aisle between the glass display cases. "You three picked the exact right Saturday to ride the 36 over here. Hold on—I put two cartridges in the lockbox under the register yesterday afternoon because I knew Mr. Prairie would be bringing you two in for your April eighth birthday!"

Devon unlocked the sliding glass door at the back of the counter and set two pristine, gray plastic cartridges on the felt mat in front of our wheelchairs: an original 1994 *Gorilla King '94* cartridge for the PlayBrick with an unblemished holographic label, and a complete-in-box sixteen-bit *Super Kinoka* strategy role-playing game we had been hunting for since 2024.

Nate's blue eyes lit up like he was twelve years old again. Picking up the sixteen-bit cartridge, he tilted the bottom edge toward the overhead fluorescent light to inspect the gold copper contact pins.

"Look at the board pins, Katie—not a single trace of oxidation, and the battery-backed save chip was just soldered fresh," Nate said happily, handing me the cardboard box so I could admire the manual. "We can dump the ROM onto our local emulator in Bedroom 4 to preserve the save states and play the original cartridge on the CRT television in the living room tonight."

"Happy forty-second birthday, you two," Dad smiled, stepping up to the counter to pay for both games while Devon slipped them into a sturdy paper bag and hung the handles over my right armrest.

***

#### Saturday, April 3, 2027, 1:15 PM — The Banners at Suite 756 & Senatorial Curiosity

![Outside along the covered concrete sidewalk of Timberline Shopping Center on Holland Road in Virginia Beach on April 3, 2027, 41-year-old U.S. Senator Katie Prairie (with her Neat Stuff birthday gift bag hanging from her right armrest) and her twin brother Nate sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs with their 68-year-old father David standing beside them in front of Pho 79 Vietnamese Kitchen, staring in astonished curiosity at the newly opened Tidewater Thorne & RTR Superstore in Suite 756 next door.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/apr_2027_timberline_suite_756_exterior_banners_pho_79_katie_nate_david.jpg)

Rolling back out of Suite 732 onto the covered concrete sidewalk of Timberline Shopping Center with our paper bag of retro games tucked beside my armrest, Nate, Dad, and I turned right along the storefront walkway toward the Route 36 bus stop out on Holland Road.

For years, the five-bay strip along this end of Timberline Shopping Center had followed the exact same left-to-right rhythm: Don Miller Subs on the left, Neat Stuff in Suite 732, the quiet pink neon sign of Halo Nails & Spa in the middle, the busy tables of Pho 79 Vietnamese Kitchen in the fourth bay, and then Suite 756 on the far right—a narrow eleven-hundred-square-foot storefront that had sat completely empty behind dusty brown butcher paper since the spring of 2023.

As we rolled past Halo Nails & Spa and reached the front windows of Pho 79 Vietnamese Kitchen—where the rich, mouthwatering scent of simmering star anise, charred ginger, cinnamon bark, and slow-cooked beef pho broth drifted out through the exhaust vent into the April air—all three of us stopped in our tracks.

Suite 756 right next door to the Vietnamese restaurant wasn't empty anymore.

Every square inch of its plate-glass facade had been plastered floor-to-ceiling with glaring crimson, white, and gold vinyl banners that read:

*THE TIDEWATER THORNE & RTR SUPERSTORE — OFFICIAL RESTORE THE REPUBLIC CAMPAIGN HEADQUARTERS!*

Behind the glass stood a six-foot cardboard cutout of President Garrett Thorne giving a grinning double thumbs-up, flanked by neon-red posters reading *THORNE: 3-0 UNDEFEATED — IMPEACH THIS!* and *THORNE 2028: THE REVENGE TOUR!*

"Good grief," Dad muttered, staring at the giant vinyl banner taped right up against the brick pillar separating Suite 756 from Pho 79. "An 'America First' Garrett Thorne shrine sharing a party wall with a Vietnamese pho restaurant. You couldn't make that up if you tried."

Sitting in my SwiftChair on the sidewalk twenty feet from the door of Suite 756, I frowned thoughtfully at the words *OFFICIAL RESTORE THE REPUBLIC CAMPAIGN HEADQUARTERS* printed across the banner.

Over the past six weeks, our constituent caseworkers in Virginia Beach and Norfolk—along with my colleagues on the Senate Commerce Committee's Consumer Protection Subcommittee—had fielded dozens of inquiries about a sudden rash of brick-and-mortar "Thorne Stores" popping up in strip malls across Virginia. Every constituent who called our office believed the exact same rumor: that these storefronts were officially vetted, licensed, and authorized by President Garrett Thorne, Thorne Global Holdings, or his national campaign committee, and that buying forty-dollar hats and sixty-dollar flags inside them went directly to fund the President's impeachment defense.

Neither Nate, nor Dad, nor I had any idea who had leased Suite 756. As far as we knew, it was just another out-of-state novelty vendor looking to make a quick buck off Holland Road traffic before the next Route 36 bus arrived at one-thirty-five.

Curiosity got the better of the Senator in me.

"Wait a second, Nate, Dad," I said, resting my right hand on my joystick. "We still have twenty minutes before the one-thirty-five bus pulls up. People keep asking our Commerce Committee staff whether these 'Thorne Superstores' are actually vetted and licensed by Garrett Thorne, his company, or his campaign—or if they're unlicensed bootleggers tricking voters into thinking retail purchases are campaign contributions. Let's roll inside for sixty seconds and look at the merchandise tags and the business license by the register."

"Sixty seconds of consumer protection fieldwork," Nate agreed, glancing at his watch with a dry smile. "Lead the way, Senator."

***

#### Saturday, April 3, 2027, 1:18 PM — Inside Suite 756: Sharron Connects the Dots & Twenty-Four Years of Truth

![Inside The Tidewater Thorne & RTR Superstore in Suite 756 of Timberline Shopping Center on April 3, 2027, U.S. Senator Katie Prairie and her twin brother Nate sit in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs beside their father David as former Delaney Street neighbor Sharron confronts a stunned Brenda Walsh behind the cash register and drops her Restore the Republic chapter badge onto the glass counter.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/apr_2027_timberline_suite_756_thorne_store_brenda_sharron_confrontation.jpg)

When Dad pulled open the aluminum-framed glass door of Suite 756 and held it for Nate and me to roll our two SwiftChairs across the threshold, a cheap brass bell taped above the door frame jangled loudly.

The first thing that hit us inside the narrow storefront was the sensory clash: the sharp chemical smell of fresh overseas vinyl ink mixing with the unmistakable, delicious aroma of Vietnamese beef pho broth and star anise seeping straight through the thin drywall partition from Pho 79 next door.

Every wall was covered in pegboard hooks and wire racks overflowing with crimson Restore the Republic baseball caps, polyester three-by-five flags showing Garrett Thorne's head superimposed onto a bodybuilder holding an eagle, gold-foil novelty *"One Thousand Dollar Thorne Notes,"* and freshly unpacked shipping cartons stenciled *THORNE: 3-0 UNDEFEATED — ACQUITTED IN THE SENATE!*

Up at the glass checkout counter near the back wall—where a small tabletop television was tuned to a shouting panel on LibertyMax—an older husband and wife in matching red RTR windbreakers were handing a crisp hundred-dollar bill across the counter, while three sixty-something women wearing crimson Restore the Republic lapel pins stood near the back flag rack sipping iced coffees and browsing the shelves.

"We drove over from Kempsville as soon as we saw the sign on Holland Road," the husband was saying earnestly to the woman behind the cash register, whose back was half-turned as she priced a box of white ceramic *THORNE 2028* coffee mugs with a handheld sticker gun. "We bought two flags and two of the '3-0 Undefeated' hats because we want every dollar going straight to President Thorne's Senate trial defense fund!"

"Oh, bless your hearts, patriots—President Thorne appreciates every single bit of your support, and those Senate Democrats don't stand a prayer of getting sixty-seven votes next week!" the woman behind the register replied in a syrupy, familiar voice, never once correcting the couple's false belief that her store was connected to the President's defense fund.

While the couple zipped their new hats into a plastic shopping bag and walked past us out the front door, I reached out from my wheelchair and flipped over the neck tag of a *THORNE: 3-0 UNDEFEATED* t-shirt hanging on the nearest circular rack.

"Look at the collar tag, Nate," I murmured quietly. "Manufactured in Guangdong Province for Wholesale Novelty Imports LLC. Zero union bug, zero Federal Election Commission disclaimer, and zero licensing mark from Thorne Global Holdings."

Nate rolled his SwiftChair three feet closer to the glass checkout counter and pointed past a large plastic jar of five-dollar buttons that had been deliberately positioned at the corner of the register to block the counter mat. Taped flat beneath the jar in tiny eight-point font was a two-sentence notice:

*Privately owned and operated retail establishment. Not authorized by, vetted by, licensed by, or affiliated with Garrett Thorne, Thorne Global Holdings, or any candidate or political committee.*

"Every dime goes straight into the store owner's pocket," Nate said softly, his eyes lifting from the hidden disclaimer to the framed City of Virginia Beach Commissioner of the Revenue Business License hanging on the pegboard wall behind the cash register.

I followed my brother's gaze up to the typed name on the municipal business license.

*PROPRIETOR: BRENDA WALSH.*

Across the narrow aisle beside my right wheel, I heard Dad draw in a sharp, silent breath.

Behind the counter, the sixty-five-year-old woman with dyed blonde hair finished sticking a twenty-four-ninety-nine price tag onto the bottom of a *THORNE 2028* mug, set her pricing gun down on the glass, and turned around with a practiced retail smile on her face.

"Welcome to the Tidewater Thorne Superstore!" she began brightly. "Everything in the store goes to—"

Her voice died in her throat.

The ceramic coffee mug slipped halfway out of her fingers and clattered upright onto the glass countertop.

Standing—and sitting—six feet in front of her cash register were her ex-husband David Prairie, her forty-one-year-old son Nathaniel Prairie, and her forty-one-year-old daughter, United States Senator Katie Prairie.

None of the three of us had laid eyes on our mother since the afternoon of Saturday, July 12, 2003—twenty-four years ago—when eighteen-year-old Nate and I had rolled our wheelchairs out the front door of the brick house on Delaney Street with Dad to move into Greenway Court Apartment A6.

For five full seconds, the only sound inside Suite 756 was the drone of the LibertyMax anchor on the corner television and the muffled clatter of soup spoons coming through the drywall from Pho 79 next door.

Brenda's face drained to chalk white, and then flushed a deep, blotchy crimson from her collar up to her roots. Her eyes darted in sheer panic toward the three women from her Restore the Republic chapter standing ten feet away by the back flag rack.

"What—what are you three doing in here?!" Brenda hissed, her voice dropping from its syrupy customer-service lilt to the sharp, defensive snap Nate and I still remembered from the hallways of our childhood. "Are you following me?! Did David tell you to come in here to harass me?!"

"Nobody knew you worked here, Brenda," Dad said, his voice completely calm, level, and devoid of anger as he stood with one hand resting steadily on the back push-handle of my wheelchair and the other near Nate's shoulder. "Your children turn forty-two on Thursday, April eighth. Just like we've done every spring for the past fifteen years, I rode the Route 36 bus over here with Katie and Nate to buy them their birthday lunch at Don Miller Subs and their birthday video games at Neat Stuff three doors down. We didn't even know Suite 756 had been leased until we rolled out onto the sidewalk two minutes ago."

At the mention of April 8th, Brenda's eyes flickered toward the wall calendar hanging beside her cash register—making it unmistakably clear that until Dad said the date out loud, the woman who had given birth to us forty-two years ago hadn't even remembered that our birthday was five days away.

Before Brenda could utter another word, one of the three women standing by the flag rack stepped forward into the center aisle, lowering her iced coffee cup as she stared in stunned recognition at Dad, then at Nate, and then at me.

It was Sharron—a former neighbor from two streets over in our old Kempsville subdivision who had known our family back in the nineties when Nate and I were growing up on Delaney Street, long before our neuromuscular diagnosis in 2001.

"David?!" Sharron gasped, her eyes widening as she looked from Dad's silver hair down to our two wheelchairs, and then straight across the counter at Brenda. "David Prairie?! Wait a minute... Katie and Nathaniel Prairie! I remember watching you two ride your bikes down Delaney Street when you were kids!"

Sharron spun around toward Brenda, her voice echoing across the narrow storefront as the other two Restore the Republic women—Donna and Carol—froze beside her.

"Brenda, wait a second!" Sharron demanded, pointing from the framed *Brenda Walsh* business license on the wall to my wheelchair. "When you joined our Restore the Republic chapter under the name Brenda Walsh, you told us you didn't even know the Prairie family! For two straight years you've sat at our kitchen tables trashing 'that Prairie woman' on television like she was a total stranger! Wait—your daughter is *our* United States Senator?! *And* their birthdays are coming up on Thursday, and you didn't even remember?! Brenda, it's time for you to come clean!"

Beside Sharron, Donna and Carol stared at Brenda as if the floor had just opened beneath their feet.

"What is she talking about, Brenda?!" Donna asked, her voice rising in disbelief. "United States Senator Katie Prairie is your biological daughter?! You looked us dead in the eye at church coffee hour on Tuesday and swore you weren't related to her!"

Behind the glass counter, Brenda's hands trembled violently as her carefully constructed double life collapsed in front of her own friends.

"I—I went back to my maiden name Walsh because David and the woke universities brainwashed them against their own mother!" Brenda stammered, her face turning a blotchy, furious purple as she tried to fall back on the talking points that usually worked in her chapter meetings. "They turned their backs on me and became godless Washington liberals!"

Sharron didn't buy a single word of it. She took a step closer to the counter, her face tightening with maternal disgust as she did the math out loud in front of Donna and Carol.

"Woke universities?!" Sharron shot back. "Brenda, I lived two streets over from you on Delaney Street in two thousand and one! Katie and Nathaniel weren't at a university when you and David divorced—they were sixteen years old at Northwood High School, right after the doctors diagnosed their muscle condition and put both of them in wheelchairs! Every mother in the neighborhood heard how you threw a fit because you were embarrassed to be seen pushing wheelchairs in public!"

Beside my left wheel, Nate's voice was quiet, steady, and devastatingly clear.

"Dad didn't turn us against you, Brenda," Nate said, looking straight across the counter. "You did that yourself in August of 2001 when we were sixteen years old and our legs were failing—when you maxed out the credit card to drag us onto a cruise ship against our will, screamed at us that we were ruining your vacation because we couldn't walk up the gangway, and tried to force two high school juniors into a toddler character meet-and-greet line so you could take a fake photo for the neighbors. And when the doctors put us in wheelchairs that September, Dad built ramps and carried us up the stairs, while you locked yourself in the kitchen with a bottle of gin."

"And the reason your name is Brenda Walsh on that business license behind you," Dad added calmly, "is because in October of 2001, sixteen-year-old Katie and Nate asked me and my attorney to make restoring your maiden name a condition of paying off your cruise debt in the divorce decree—because neither of your children wanted you carrying the Prairie name ever again."

Sitting in my SwiftChair with Dad's forty-second-birthday gift bag from Neat Stuff hanging beside my armrest, I looked from the six-foot cardboard cutout of Garrett Thorne grinning beside the register to Brenda, and then to Sharron, Donna, and Carol.

"Sixteen days ago, on the morning of March eighteenth," I said evenly, "the man on that cardboard cutout stood on the South Lawn of the White House on live national television and called me a 'nasty, bitter little cripple,' said I was 'slow' and had 'no stamina,' called us 'defective,' and mocked your son Nate as my 'crippled twin brother.' Not only did you build a shrine to the man who hurled derogatory slurs at your own children's wheelchairs on national television, Brenda—you're also deceiving your own friends and customers right here in Suite 756."

I pointed past the plastic jar of five-dollar buttons on the counter to the hidden eight-point disclaimer taped flat against the glass.

"Constituents have been calling my Senate Commerce Committee office all month asking if the rumors are true that these 'Thorne Superstores'—or the local Restore the Republic chapters—are officially vetted, endorsed, and licensed by Garrett Thorne, his company, or his campaign," I said, looking directly at Sharron, Donna, and Carol. "Look behind that button jar on the counter, ladies, and look at the Guangdong wholesale tags inside the collars. Just like the local chapters, this store has zero authorization or endorsement from Garrett Thorne or his campaign. When that couple from Kempsville just handed Brenda a hundred dollars thinking it was going to the President's Senate trial defense fund, every single dime went straight into Brenda's personal bank account."

Donna and Carol stepped up to the glass counter, peered behind the button jar at the tiny eight-point disclaimer, and looked from Brenda's blotchy face to the grinning cardboard cutout of Garrett Thorne.

As mothers and grandmothers themselves, the three women looked at what Brenda had done to make her own two children cut her off—forcing two sixteen-year-old teenagers with failing legs onto a cruise ship, screaming at them when they couldn't walk, retreating to a bottle of gin when they went into wheelchairs, forgetting their forty-second birthday, and then cheering on a man who mocked her own son and daughter on national television while she fleeced her own chapter friends behind a button jar.

In that quiet strip-mall storefront, the entire illusion of the movement they had been pouring their lives into shattered at once.

Sharron stared at the cardboard cutout of Garrett Thorne, and then looked straight across the counter at Brenda in horror.

"Wait—we worshipped a man who has said derogatory things about your own daughter?!" Sharron said, her voice trembling with maternal outrage. "Calling her a cripple, and slow, and saying she has no stamina?! No, Brenda, we can't support this anymore!"

Sharron set the two flags and the coffee mug she had been holding flat down onto the glass counter with a sharp thud—and then reached up to the collar of her cardigan, unpinned her gold-bordered crimson *Restore the Republic — Chapter President* badge, and dropped it onto the glass right in front of Brenda.

"I started our Virginia Beach Restore the Republic chapter three years ago—and just like your phony store, Brenda, President Thorne never endorsed or cared about a single one of us either," Sharron said, her voice shaking with disgust. "I am a mother and a grandmother. Hearing what you did to your own sixteen-year-old twins when they went into wheelchairs—and watching you stand here worshipping a man who calls your own daughter a cripple and slow on national television while you use our members as your personal piggy bank—makes me sick to my stomach."

Beside her, Donna and Carol reached up to their own lapels, unpinned their crimson Restore the Republic pins, and dropped them onto the glass countertop with two sharp metallic clicks.

"We're done with you, Brenda, and we're done with Restore the Republic," Donna said firmly.

"I'm shutting the chapter down tonight," Sharron told Brenda flatly, before turning around in the narrow aisle with Donna and Carol to face Dad, Nate, and me. All three women had tears shining in their eyes.

"David... Katie... Nathaniel," Sharron said softly, her voice thick with genuine remorse as she looked down at our two wheelchairs. "We owe the three of you an apology. We bought into ugly lies on television about a family we should have been proud of all along. What your father did for you two—and what the two of you have built with your lives after what she put you through—is extraordinary."

"We're so sorry, Senator Prairie," Carol said, wiping her cheek with the back of her hand. "Every single one of us—and our husbands—are voting Democrat in the next election, and you have our votes for as long as you run."

"And happy forty-second birthday on Thursday, Katie and Nathaniel," Donna added warmly as the three women stepped to the front door and held it open for us.

"Thank you, Sharron. Thank you, Donna, Carol," I said, genuinely touched as Nate and Dad nodded warmly to all three of them.

Behind the glass counter, Brenda stood frozen in total, trembling silence—abandoned by the family she had mistreated twenty-six years ago and just walked out on by the friends and movement she had traded us for—inside an empty storefront that smelled of cheap vinyl ink and Pho 79's simmering beef broth.

Out on Holland Road beyond the plate-glass window, the amber LED destination sign of the one-thirty-five CVTA Route 36 bus glided into view as it approached the Timberline Shopping Center stop—a bus route that only ran on Saturday afternoons because Nate, Dad, and I had fought to save and expand it sixteen years ago when I first took my seat on the Virginia Beach City Council.

I glanced once more at the stacks of newly delivered cardboard shipping cartons piled behind Brenda's register—every single box stenciled *THORNE: 3-0 UNDEFEATED* and *THORNE 2028*.

"Goodbye, Brenda," I said quietly, turning my SwiftChair smoothly in the narrow aisle alongside Nate's chair as Dad walked beside us toward the open doorway. "And as your United States Senator—I hope you kept the wholesale receipts for those '3-0 Undefeated' and '2028' boxes before the Senate reconvenes on April fourteenth."

The cheap brass bell above the door jangled once more behind us as Nate, Dad, and I rolled out of Suite 756 into the warm, clean Virginia Beach sunshine—waving goodbye to Sharron, Donna, and Carol on the sidewalk while the Route 36 bus kneeled at the curb to take the three of us home to Kempsville.

### Part 3: The Words of Mason, Madison, and Lincoln, Three Guilty Votes, & From Capitol Police Protection Back to Normal Life at Pleasure House Road

**Date:** 2027-07-17 at 13:30 America/New_York

![Inside the United States Senate Chamber on April 16, 2027, 42-year-old U.S. Senator Katie Prairie sits at her custom-height mahogany floor desk in her black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchair casting her historic Guilty vote in the impeachment trial while her twin brother Nate (in his SwiftChair) and their father David watch proudly from the Senate Family Gallery.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/apr_2027_us_senate_impeachment_guilty_vote_katie_nate_david.jpg)

#### Wednesday & Thursday, April 14–15, 2027 — Convicting Secretary Halverson and Vice President Drayton

![Inside the United States Senate Chamber on April 16, 2027, 42-year-old U.S. Senator Katie Prairie sits at her custom-height mahogany floor desk in her black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchair casting her historic Guilty vote in the impeachment trial while her twin brother Nate (in his SwiftChair) and their father David watch proudly from the Senate Family Gallery.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/apr_2027_us_senate_impeachment_guilty_vote_katie_nate_david.jpg)

Two years earlier, in January of 2025, I had been sitting at my desk in the Senate of Virginia in Richmond when President Garrett Thorne nominated Bret Halverson—the slick, hair-sprayed weekend host of *Patriot Watch Weekend* on the Liberty First Network—to serve as United States Secretary of Defense, and when Vice President Conrad Drayton cast the tie-breaking fiftieth vote to put him in charge of the Pentagon over the objections of every military family in Hampton Roads.

That weekend in 2025, Halverson had gone back on his old cable network for a victory lap, laughing with his former co-hosts about *"that little wheelchair state senator down in Richmond who thought she could stop the Pentagon."*

He wasn't laughing anymore.

On Wednesday afternoon, April 14, 2027, Bret Halverson sat pale and sweating at the respondent's table in the well of the United States Senate Chamber while Chief Justice Jonathan Sterling presided from the marble rostrum and the Reading Clerk called the final roll on Article One and Article Two of his impeachment.

Up on the top tier of the Senate Floor beside the accessible upper doorway, I sat alone at my custom-height mahogany Senator's desk in my compact SwiftChair with my electromagnetic drive brakes locked firm and my red-tabbed impeachment evidence binder resting flat across my lap. Because Senate rules strictly limit the chamber floor during an impeachment trial to sworn United States Senators and officers of the court, my twin brother Nate sat in his matching SwiftChair beside our dad at the brass railing of the Senate Family Gallery directly across the chamber, his blue eyes locked steadily on mine.

Down in the well, Halverson's defense attorneys didn't even look up toward my desk. After the House managers had displayed the screenshots of Halverson texting classified Naval Station Norfolk carrier strike group deployment schedules over a commercial phone app alongside the four-hundred-million-dollar Thorne Global Holdings kickback ledger Nate's scripts had uncovered, seventeen institutional Republican Senators from defense and coastal states had announced they were crossing the aisle.

"Mr. Mendoza," the Reading Clerk called out.

"Guilty," Senator Mendoza answered from across the aisle.

The clerk's eyes moved down the alphabetical tally sheet and looked up toward my mahogany desk at the top of the chamber.

"Ms. Prairie."

For half a second, the entire Senate Chamber went dead silent. Down at the respondent's table, Bret Halverson finally raised his head, looking up the tiered steps of the chamber straight at the wheelchair he had mocked on national television two years ago.

I didn't raise my voice, and I didn't take my hands off my armrests. Looking straight down into the well on behalf of every sailor at Naval Station Norfolk whose operational safety he had treated like a cable-news segment, I gave him the vote I had promised from Richmond in 2025.

"Guilty," I said clearly across the quiet chamber.

By a vote of seventy-one to twenty-nine—four votes above the two-thirds constitutional threshold required under Article I, Section 3 of the Constitution—the Senate convicted and removed Bret Halverson from office, followed ten minutes later by a simple-majority vote permanently disqualifying him from ever holding any office of honor, trust, or profit under the United States again.

Twenty-four hours later, on Thursday afternoon, April 15, 2027, the second domino fell.

Confronted with the unredacted Treasury wire tables proving that Vice President Conrad Drayton had personally co-signed the offshore routing waivers for the Naval Station Norfolk logistics kickbacks and sat on the exact same unsecured messaging thread while our Fifth Fleet sailors' movements were compromised, sixty-eight Senators—including me—voted Guilty at four-thirty on Thursday afternoon to convict and remove Conrad Drayton from the Vice Presidency, followed immediately by a second vote permanently disqualifying him from future federal office.

With the Democratic majority in the House of Representatives and our fifty-four-seat majority in the Senate refusing to entertain any Twenty-Fifth Amendment replacement nominee from a disgraced White House, the office of Vice President of the United States stood completely vacant as Thursday night fell over Washington.

***

#### Friday, April 16, 2027, 1:30 PM — The Words of George Mason, James Madison, and Abraham Lincoln

At three o'clock on Friday morning—less than eleven hours before the final Senate deliberation and roll-call vote on the Articles of Impeachment against President Garrett Thorne—the President had gone online from the residence of the White House to unleash one final, desperate tirade against Nate and me.

In all-capital letters, Thorne had called me a *"defective, bitter little cripple on wheels"* and a *"spinster who couldn't keep a man in her twenties and is trying to steal the Presidency from her wheelchair with her shut-in twin brother."*

Even at the very end, Garrett Thorne still didn't understand that every ugly, ableist insult he hurled at my wheelchair and my brother only disgusted more institutional Senators in his own party and cemented the two-thirds coalition against him.

At one-thirty on Friday afternoon, April 16, 2027, inside the closed marble chamber of the United States Senate during the final hour of deliberations before the roll call, I engaged the drive lock on my SwiftChair beside my top-tier mahogany desk, pressed my microphone button, and rested my hands on the edge of my lectern as all ninety-nine of my fellow Senators turned toward my seat.

"Mr. Chief Justice, and my colleagues of the Senate," I said evenly across the silent chamber. "Two hundred and forty years ago, right down the road from where my brother Nate and I grew up in Virginia, George Mason stood at the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia and warned that no man who holds the executive power should ever be placed above the reach of the law when he corrupts his office, asking the delegates: *Shall any man be above justice? Above all, shall that man be above it, who can commit the most extensive injustice?*"

Up in the Family Gallery above the marble columns, Dad rested his hand on Nate's shoulder as Nate looked down at me from his SwiftChair.

"And when another Virginian, James Madison, wrote *Federalist Number 51*," I continued, my voice calm and unhurried, "he didn't tell us to trust the personal goodwill of a President or a Cabinet Secretary. Madison wrote: *If men were angels, no government would be necessary. If angels were to govern men, neither external nor internal controls on government would be necessary. In framing a government which is to be administered by men over men, the great difficulty lies in this: you must first enable the government to control the governed; and in the next place oblige it to control itself.* Madison and the framers gave this Senate the sole power to try all impeachments specifically to guard the republic against men who treat a public trust as a private business."

I looked down into the well toward the respondent's table where President Garrett Thorne's defense lawyers sat staring down at their legal pads.

"Abraham Lincoln once said that nearly all men can stand adversity, but if you want to test a man's character, give him power—and at Gettysburg, he charged every generation of Americans to ensure that government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth," I said. "We gave Garrett Thorne, Conrad Drayton, and Bret Halverson the highest powers under this Constitution. They used that power to trade tariff waivers and Naval Station Norfolk fleet contracts for four hundred million dollars in offshore kickbacks, to leak the movements of six thousand Virginia sailors on commercial phones, and to mock the disabled citizens they swore an oath to serve. Mason, Madison, and Lincoln left us an exact constitutional remedy for men who fail that test—and when the Clerk calls the roll, I will vote Guilty."

***

#### Friday, April 16, 2027, 2:15 PM — Sixty-Eight Guilty Votes, Permanent Disqualification, & President Clara Morales

At two o'clock, the gallery doors were unlocked to the public and the press corps, and Chief Justice Jonathan Sterling rose in his black judicial robe at the marble rostrum.

"The Secretary will call the roll on Article One of the Articles of Impeachment exhibited by the House of Representatives against Garrett Thorne, President of the United States," Chief Justice Sterling announced.

This was the third time in American history that the House of Representatives had impeached Garrett Thorne—and during his first two impeachments back in his first term, he had escaped removal only because the Senate tally had fallen short of the two-thirds constitutional wall.

This third time, the wall broke.

One by one, as the Reading Clerk called the alphabetical roll, fourteen Republican Senators who had voted to acquit Thorne in his earlier impeachment trials rose from their mahogany desks and answered *"Guilty."*

"Mr. Mendoza," the Reading Clerk called out.

"Guilty," Senator Mendoza answered.

"Ms. Prairie."

I kept my hands resting calmly on the armrests of my SwiftChair, my electromagnetic drive brakes locked tight against the blue Senate carpet. Twenty-one years after Brandon Mercer had switched off my powerchair outside the Williamsburg train station in the pouring November rain and told me I was powerless—and thirteen days after rolling into Suite 756 at Timberline Shopping Center on Holland Road and seeing the shrines and unopened crates of *"3-0 UNDEFEATED"* and *"THORNE 2028"* merchandise my own estranged mother had chosen over her children—I looked straight down into the well of the United States Senate.

"Guilty," I said clearly.

Twenty minutes later, when the Reading Clerk handed the certified tally sheet up to the rostrum showing that sixty-eight Senators had voted Guilty on both Articles of Impeachment—exceeding the sixty-seven-vote two-thirds constitutional threshold required under Article I, Section 3—Chief Justice Sterling struck the marble rostrum once with his ivory gavel.

"The Senate having tried Garrett Thorne, President of the United States, upon two Articles of Impeachment exhibited against him by the House of Representatives, and two-thirds of the Senators present having found him guilty of high crimes and misdemeanors," Chief Justice Sterling declared across the hushed chamber, "it is therefore ordered and adjudged that the said Garrett Thorne be, and he is hereby, removed from office."

Before the defense table could even close their briefcases, our Senate Majority Leader rose and moved the second resolution under Article I, Section 3, Clause 7: permanent disqualification from ever holding any federal office again, which under settled Senate precedent required only a simple majority of fifty-one votes. When the clerk called *"Ms. Prairie"* on the permanent disqualification roll call, I delivered my second vote of the hour just as evenly as the first:

"Aye."

The disqualification resolution passed sixty-eight to thirty-two. With that gavel strike, Garrett Thorne, Conrad Drayton, and Bret Halverson were not only stripped of their offices—they were barred for the rest of their natural lives from ever putting their names on a federal ballot or holding any office of honor, trust, or profit under the United States again.

And because we had convicted and removed Vice President Conrad Drayton on Thursday afternoon and left the Vice Presidency vacant, the Presidential Succession Act of 1947—Title 3, Section 19 of the United States Code—took immediate constitutional effect.

Fifteen minutes after the Senate doors swung open, Nate and Dad took the elevator down from the Family Gallery and rolled down the marble corridor beside my wheelchair into the Mansfield Room just off the Senate Floor.

![Inside the Mansfield Room (S-207) of the United States Capitol on April 16, 2027, Chief Justice Jonathan Sterling administers the presidential oath of office to former House Speaker Clara Morales while 42-year-old U.S. Senator Katie Prairie and her twin brother Nate sit side by side in their black motorized SwiftChair power wheelchairs holding hands across their armrests with their father David applauding behind them.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/katie/b006/apr_2027_mansfield_room_swearing_in_president_clara_morales_katie_nate_david.jpg)

Standing beneath the crystal chandelier—having just signed her formal resignation as Speaker and Representative from the House—was Clara Morales, her left hand resting on a bound copy of the Constitution and her family Bible while she raised her right hand before Chief Justice Jonathan Sterling to take the constitutional oath of office as the new President of the United States.

Nate locked his SwiftChair brakes right alongside mine at the front of the room and reached across the two-inch gap between our armrests to squeeze my hand while Dad rested his hands proudly on our shoulders.

"Clean sweep, Senator," Nate whispered against my ear as the room erupted into applause for President Clara Morales. "All three of them gone for good."

"Every single one, Nate," I whispered back, squeezing my twin brother's hand just as tight.

Twenty minutes later, when Nate, Dad, and I rode the subway car back under Constitution Avenue and rolled into Dirksen Room 511, Sam, Mandy, and Sarah Hawkins were standing side by side around the reception television with tears in their eyes and smiles from ear to ear.

On the screen, live from his front porch in Danville with Aunt Marge Callaway standing beside him, former Republican House Majority Leader Richard Callaway was looking straight into a row of Roanoke and Richmond television cameras.

"Every conservative in the Commonwealth of Virginia who still believes in the United States Constitution owes Senator Katie Prairie and the sixty-seven Senators who stood with her today a debt of gratitude," Uncle Richard declared in his steady Southside baritone as the news chyron beneath him flashed *FORMER VA GOP MAJORITY LEADER RICHARD CALLAWAY ENDORSES SEN. PRAIRIE'S 'GUILTY' & 'AYE' IMPEACHMENT VOTES*. "When Senator Prairie voted Guilty to convict Garrett Thorne, Conrad Drayton, and Bret Halverson for selling out our Naval Station Norfolk sailors, and when she voted Aye to bar all three of those men from ever holding federal office again, she didn't cast a partisan vote. She cast the exact vote that George Mason and James Madison wrote into the Constitution to protect this Republic."

Before the television anchor could ask a follow-up question, the private direct line on Sarah's front desk chimed.

"It's Uncle Richard and Aunt Marge calling from the porch!" Sarah beamed, tapping the speakerphone button as Sam and Mandy leaned in beside our wheelchairs.

"Katie! Nate! David!" Uncle Richard's voice boomed warmly through the speakerphone once the television crew in his front yard had lowered their microphones. "Marge and I just watched President Clara Morales take the oath of office, and we wanted to tell you ourselves how proud we are of the two of you."

"Thank you, Richard—and thank you for going on the air in Danville to back both the Guilty vote and the Aye vote to bar them from office," I said warmly from my SwiftChair.

"Easiest endorsement of my life, Senator," Uncle Richard chuckled, before his voice took on the quiet, determined resolve of the old Majority Leader. "And now that President Morales has been sworn in and Garrett Thorne is barred from ever putting his name on a ballot again, the fever can finally break. Starting tomorrow morning, I'm rolling up my sleeves with every institutional conservative left in Virginia to clean up the Republican Party and bring it back to the honorable, problem-solving party I remembered when I served in the House of Delegates—so that one of these days, Marge and I can finally go back to voting for Republicans again."

Beside my wheelchair, Sam, Mandy, and Sarah exchanged a grin.

"Every Republican, Uncle Richard?" Mandy asked playfully.

Over the speakerphone from Danville, Uncle Richard let out a rich, warm laugh.

"Well, every Republican except one," the old lion of Southside Virginia corrected himself gently. "I already warned the state party committee this afternoon: I'm going back to voting Republican down the line—except when Katie Prairie runs for re-election to the United States Senate. As long as Katie's name is on that ballot, she has Marge's vote and mine."

Seconds after we thanked Uncle Richard and Aunt Marge and hung up the speakerphone, the breaking-news banner across the bottom of the reception television flashed bright red.

Down in Florida—stripped of the Presidency, stripped of his Secret Service successor authority, and barred for the rest of his life from ever putting his name on a ballot again—private citizen Garrett Thorne had just stormed out onto the driveway of his resort club in front of the cable cameras.

Even though sixty-eight United States Senators—including fourteen members of his own party—had just voted to convict and disqualify him, Garrett Thorne's narcissistic, ableist ego could not bear the humiliation that a forty-two-year-old autistic woman in a wheelchair and her twin brother had uncovered his four-hundred-million-dollar Naval Station Norfolk kickback scheme and delivered the closing constitutional case that ended his political life.

On live national television, his face purple with rage, Garrett Thorne launched a full-blown personal vendetta—blaming *"Broken Katie Prairie"* for his removal from office.

*"Broken Katie Prairie did this to me!"* Thorne screamed into the microphones, his voice cracking as he jabbed a finger toward the camera lenses. *"Sixty-eight weak, spineless cowards let Broken Katie Prairie in her little wheelchair and her shut-in brother's rigged computers in Virginia Beach steal my Presidency and ban me from running in 2028! Broken Katie Prairie is the reason I was removed from office—she destroyed our movement, and no real patriot in Restore the Republic should ever give Broken Katie Prairie a single moment of peace!"*

Uncle Richard hadn't even reached his front door in Danville before the impact of Thorne's tirade hit our fifth-floor suite.

Within sixty seconds, all eight external trunk lines on Sarah's front reception console began blinking frantic red at once as furious Restore the Republic extremists—incited by their deposed leader's live meltdown—started flooding our office switchboard.

Sarah's hand hovered over the receiver, her shoulders tensing, when Nate rolled his SwiftChair forward and gently rested his hand over the mute bar.

"Don't pick that up, Sarah," Nate said calmly.

Before the console could ring a third time, the double mahogany doors of Dirksen Room 511 swung open.

Stepping briskly into our reception room was the Senate Sergeant at Arms, flanked by Inspector Marcus Vance of the United States Capitol Police Threat Assessment Section and four plainclothes special agents wearing the gold lapel pins of the Capitol Police Dignitary Protection Division.

"Leave the phones on mute, Ms. Sarah—our telecom unit in the Capitol Police Command Center is cutting in on your external trunk lines right now," Inspector Vance said with calm, professional authority as two Senate telecommunications technicians stepped behind Sarah's desk and plugged a hardware trap-and-trace filter into the switchboard wall jack. "Every incoming call, voicemail, and IP packet threatening Senator Prairie, her family, or her staff is being routed directly to the Capitol Police Threat Assessment Section and the FBI Washington Field Office for felony prosecution under Title 18, Section 115 of the United States Code. None of the three of you will have to listen to a single one of those calls."

Sam, Mandy, and Sarah let out a collective breath as the blinking red lights on the console shifted to silent blue law-enforcement recording indicators.

Inspector Vance turned toward Dad, Nate, and me, his expression grave.

"Senator Prairie, we monitored former President Thorne's broadcast from Florida in real time," the Capitol Police Inspector said. "Because he singled you out by name and blamed you personally for his conviction and disqualification, our Threat Assessment Section has elevated your protective posture to Tier One. Uniformed Capitol Police officers are now posted outside Room 511 around the clock, and we've already coordinated twenty-four-hour residential patrols with the Alexandria Police Department on Sunset Drive and the Virginia Beach Police Department on Lord Nelson Drive. In addition, the Capitol Police Board has assigned a full-time plainclothes Dignitary Protection detail to accompany you and your brother everywhere you travel—and we have an armored black Capitol Police SUV waiting downstairs in the Dirksen courtyard to drive you, Nate, and Mr. Prairie home to Alexandria right now."

Inside Dirksen Room 511, the room went quiet.

Dad looked down at Nate and me, a knowing smile tugging at the corner of his mouth, while Sam, Mandy, and Sarah watched my wheelchair.

I kept my hands resting evenly on the armrests of my SwiftChair and looked up at Inspector Vance.

I wasn't the slightest bit afraid of Garrett Thorne—not after surviving Brandon Mercer switching off my wheelchair in the rain twenty-one years ago, and not after staring Thorne's lawyers down from the top tier of the Senate floor—but I took the protection of the United States Capitol Police very seriously, especially when it came to keeping Dad, Nate, and my staff safe.

"Inspector Vance, thank you—first and foremost for stepping in immediately to protect Sam, Mandy, and Sarah at the front desk, and for coordinating with Alexandria and Virginia Beach police," I said clearly. "We take your Threat Assessment team's protocols very seriously, and our office will follow every security procedure you set for Room 511 and our travel schedules. We will gladly accept your plainclothes Capitol Police Dignitary Protection detail, subject to two non-negotiable rules."

"Name them, Senator," Inspector Vance said.

"Rule one: nobody on the detail ever touches the push-handles of my wheelchair or my brother's wheelchair without asking our permission first," I said.

"Understood and already briefed to every agent on the team," Vance nodded. "And rule two?"

I glanced toward the framed purple-and-blue crayon drawing from Natalie Brooks hanging on our office wall, then over at Sam's desk—where Sam, Nate, and I had spent every spare hour between impeachment trial sessions drafting the federal transit appropriations rider to fund a public bus link across the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel—and finally at my twin brother Nate sitting in his SwiftChair beside me.

"Rule two, Inspector, is that you can send the armored SUV back to the garage," I said calmly. "Garrett Thorne is a disgraced private citizen who just got fired from the Presidency and permanently barred from ever holding public office again. I respect your officers' mission, and we will give your detail our exact train and bus times in advance so your agents can position themselves safely around us—but if I let Garrett Thorne's temper tantrum scare my brother and me off public transportation and lock us inside an armored truck, then Garrett Thorne wins. Plus, Sam, Nate, and I still have an hour of work left on our federal transit grant connecting Cape Charles on the Eastern Shore across the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel to the CVTA transfer point at Shore Drive and Pleasure House Road. At five-fifteen, Nate, Dad, and I—along with Sam, Mandy, and Sarah—are rolling down the elevator and out the accessible door to Capitol South Station to ride the Blue Line home to Alexandria, and tomorrow morning we are catching the ARTS train and the CVTA Route 24 bus home to Virginia Beach."

Nate grinned from his SwiftChair and held up his blue plastic transit card between two fingers.

"Your Dignitary Protection agents are more than welcome to ride with us, Inspector," my twin brother added cheerfully. "Just make sure every agent brings a loaded CapitalPass card—because on Senator Prairie's detail, everybody pays their fare and everybody rides the bus."

***

#### Saturday, July 17, 2027, 10:15 AM — How Thorne's Vendetta Heat Died Down & Rolling Off the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel Bus at Shore Drive and Pleasure House Road

For the next ten weeks, we followed every protocol the United States Capitol Police put in place—and while the cable pundits wondered how long Garrett Thorne's post-conviction vendetta against *"Broken Katie Prairie"* would last, we kept our heads down and did the legislative work the people of Virginia had sent us to Washington to do.

When reporters outside the Capitol South elevator asked me to respond to Thorne's latest rant from his Florida driveway, I didn't give his ego a single drop of the oxygen he was starving for.

"I'm grateful to the United States Capitol Police officers riding the Blue Line with us today, and I have complete confidence in federal law enforcement," I told the cameras without looking up from my committee folder. "Mr. Thorne is an unemployed private citizen in Florida with a federal court date. Right now my brother Nate, my Legislative Correspondent Sam, and I are marking up the federal funding to connect ShoreLine Transit in Cape Charles across the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel to the CVTA transfer point at Shore Drive and Pleasure House Road—because working families on the Eastern Shore and in Hampton Roads still have to get to work and the hospital tomorrow morning."

Watched closely by Inspector Vance's Threat Assessment team, the heat of Garrett Thorne's vendetta collapsed faster than anyone in Washington had predicted—extinguished by five cold, unmistakable realities.

First, within seventy-two hours of Thorne's April sixteenth outburst, the United States Capitol Police Threat Assessment Section and the FBI used the hardware trap-and-trace logs from Dirksen Room 511 to arrest the first fourteen Restore the Republic extremists who had called our switchboard with threats. When those callers were led into federal courthouses in handcuffs on the six o'clock news facing ten-year felony sentences under Title 18, Section 115 of the United States Code—and suddenly realized that Garrett Thorne was no longer President of the United States, possessed zero constitutional pardon power to save them, and wasn't paying a single dime toward their defense lawyers—the nerve of the online mob shattered overnight. Within two weeks, the threatening calls to our office dropped to zero.

Second, under Article I, Section 3, Clause 7 of the United States Constitution, removal by the Senate stripped Garrett Thorne of every shred of presidential immunity and left him, as a private citizen, *"liable and subject to Indictment, Trial, Judgment and Punishment, according to Law."* On May 12, 2027, a federal grand jury returned a thirty-four-count felony indictment against Garrett Thorne, Conrad Drayton, and Bret Halverson for federal bribery, wire fraud, money laundering, and Espionage Act violations over the four-hundred-million-dollar Naval Station Norfolk kickback scheme, while the Department of Justice froze Thorne Global Holdings' offshore accounts. At Thorne's federal arraignment that afternoon, as a strict condition of pre-trial release under Title 18, Section 3142 so he wouldn't await trial behind bars, the United States District Judge imposed an ironclad gag and no-harassment order: if Garrett Thorne uttered or posted the name of Senator Katie Prairie, her family, her staff, or any congressional witness on television or online, his bail would be revoked immediately and United States Marshals would remand him straight into a federal detention cell. Terrified of spending a single night in a jail cell, Thorne shut his mouth on the spot.

Third, our sixty-eight-vote *Aye* tally permanently barring Thorne from ever holding federal office again drained every ounce of his political leverage. A movement built on personal fealty to one man cannot survive once that man is legally barred from ever appearing on a ballot again. Within a month, the cable cameras at LibertyMax and the Liberty First Network stopped cutting to his driveway in Florida, ambitious politicians started fighting over the wide-open 2028 nomination as if Thorne were already ancient history, and back home in Virginia, Uncle Richard and a coalition of institutional conservatives began methodically cleaning out the state Republican party apparatus.

By Monday, July 12, 2027—after sixty consecutive days without a single credible threat logged against our office or our homes—Inspector Marcus Vance walked into Dirksen Room 511 with a warm smile, unplugged the trap-and-trace unit from Sarah's reception console, and informed Dad, Nate, Sam, Mandy, Sarah, and me that the Capitol Police Threat Assessment Section had officially downgraded our posture back to routine baseline and stood down our round-the-clock protective detail.

Five days later—on Saturday morning, July 17, 2027—all six of us celebrated getting our normal, quiet everyday lives back in the only way that felt right.

Having seen President Clara Morales sign our bipartisan Federal Rural & Bridge-Tunnel Transit Connectivity appropriation into law the month before—establishing dedicated Federal Transit Administration Section 5311(f) intercity operating funds to cover the seventeen-point-six-mile cross-bay span and the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel District's nominal Class 8 public-transit toll of one dollar per crossing via the agency fleet transponder, together with a mandatory statutory stipulation requiring a reciprocal cross-honoring agreement for all fares and passes between CVTA and ShoreLine Transit—Nate, Dad, Sam, Mandy, Sarah, and I rode the inaugural southbound revenue run of the ShoreLine Transit / CVTA Bay Bridge-Tunnel Express south from Cape Charles.

Without a single armored SUV or protective detail trailing us, our low-floor bus glided through the electronic Class 8 toll lane at the North Toll Plaza for a single dollar, rolled out across the high trestles, and plunged through the two mile-long underwater tunnels of the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel—where the silver-green waves of the Chesapeake Bay met the open Atlantic Ocean—before climbing onto the south toll plaza at Wise Point and turning onto Shore Drive in Virginia Beach.

"Approaching Shore Drive and Pleasure House Road—Coastal Virginia Transit Authority Transfer Point," the automated interior chime announced at ten-fifteen in the morning as our driver pulled smoothly into the concrete transfer bay just west of the bridge-tunnel approach, right beside a waiting low-floor CVTA bus with its amber LED destination sign glowing in the July sunshine.

As the driver kneeled the air suspension and deployed the front hydraulic ramp onto the Virginia Beach sidewalk at Pleasure House Road, Sam, Mandy, and Sarah stepped down onto the concrete with Dad, turning back to smile as Nate and I rolled our two SwiftChairs side by side down the ramp into the warm coastal breeze.

Up at the CVTA bus shelter, commuters in navy shipyard shirts, Eastern Shore hospital nurses, and summer beachgoers with backpacks were already stepping off our coach and walking ten feet across the sidewalk—where, thanks to the cross-honoring stipulation in our bill, the CVTA farebox accepted their ShoreLine Transit passes and transfers without charging them a single extra dime to continue into Norfolk and Virginia Beach.

Dad rested one hand on my shoulder and the other on Nate's, looking back toward the shimmering span of the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel stretching out to the northern horizon.

"No cameras, no guards, and a bus running right across the Bay to Pleasure House Road," Dad said softly. "How does it feel to have your normal Saturday back, Senator?"

I looked over at Sam, Mandy, and Sarah chatting happily with the CVTA operator by the open front door, then up at Dad, and finally across the two inches between our armrests at my twin brother Nate.

"It feels like home, Dad," I smiled, unlocking my joystick as Nate and I rolled side by side toward the open ramp of the waiting CVTA bus with our cross-honored passes in hand. "Come on—let's tap our passes before we miss the transfer."
